Testing Mastery

What a test is worth, rather than how to write one. The five kinds of test double and the two distinctions that decide anything; state versus behaviour verification; boundary analysis and case selection; design for testability. Then the levels — a real PostgreSQL started by the suite, HTTP APIs, contract tests, the DOM and a real browser — and property-based testing, coverage and mutation testing, flaky tests, test smells and the pipeline.

How to use this course

  • This course is about how you prove the code is right. It assumes the Python and JavaScript courses, or equivalent experience in both. It does not assume you have written tests beyond the obvious ones; §1 starts with what a test is for.
  • It is genuinely dual. Every idea is taught in pytest and in a JavaScript runner — Vitest, and Node's built-in node:test where the difference between runners is the point — with end-to-end tests driven through Playwright's Python API, because a working team meets testing in whichever language the code is in, and because an idea that only makes sense in one runner is usually a runner feature rather than an idea.
  • Every test report is the one the tool printed. Pass and fail counts, the failing line, the summary line and pytest's rewritten assertion explanation are copied from real runs. When your own report differs, §2 teaches you how to find out why.
  • The authority is the vocabulary practitioners share. The syllabus was derived from the martinfowler.com testing index and its core articles, fetched on 2026-09-03, and from the pattern and smell catalogue of xUnit Test Patterns, which supplies the terms used throughout — SUT, depended-on component, the five double kinds, and the named smells.
  • The course moves from a single test to a whole suite. §1–§5 are the unit of work: what a test claims, running tests, assertions, choosing test cases, and fixtures. §6–§9 are isolation and design: test doubles, state versus behaviour verification, design for testability, and test-driven development. §10–§15 are the levels: the shape of a suite, integration testing against a real database, HTTP APIs, contract tests, testing in a DOM, and end-to-end in a real browser. §16–§20 are the techniques that keep a suite honest: property-based testing, coverage and mutation testing, flaky tests, test smells, and tests in the pipeline. §21 builds a suite for code you did not write.
  • Each section has numbered subsections, runnable projects with their real reports, and exercises with worked solutions. When a report differs from yours, the difference is usually a plugin or a configuration file, and §2 teaches you how to find out which.

You need a Python environment with pytest and Playwright, and Node with Vitest. The end-to-end sections also need Playwright's Chromium, and the integration sections a PostgreSQL server. Check the toolchain before starting:

python3 --version             # 3.12 or newer
python3 -m pytest --version   # pytest 9.x
node --version                # v24 or newer
npx vitest --version          # vitest 5.x
python3 -m playwright --version   # Version 1.62 or newer

Versions every report in this course was produced against: Python 3.12.7 · pytest 9.1.1 · hypothesis 6.167.1 · coverage 7.16.0 · mutmut 3.7.0 · Playwright 1.62.0 · Node 24 · Vitest 5.0.0 · fast-check 4.9.0.

What you are actually learning

Not a runner's API. Five ideas that decide whether a suite makes change safe or makes it expensive — two outcomes that look identical from the outside:

  1. A test is a claim, and its value is what it would catch. One assertion, a name a colleague can read, and an expected value a human computed rather than one the code produced. A test that cannot fail is not a test (§1, §3).
  2. Testing is sampling. Exhaustive testing is unavailable, so inputs are chosen: partition into equivalence classes, take each side of every boundary, and stop. Off-by-one defects live at the boundaries and nowhere else (§4).
  3. A double is a tool with a direction. Stub versus spy is which way the data flows; mock versus spy is where the assertion lives. Verify state where you can see it, behaviour only where you cannot, and treat a test that needs seven doubles as the code reporting a design problem (§6–§8).
  4. Each behaviour belongs at one level. Verify it in detail where it is cheapest, connect it at the levels above, and run the real thing — a real database, a real browser — only where the real thing is the point (§10–§15).
  5. The coverage number is not the question. Uncovered code is definitely untested, but covered code may be tested by nothing: against 100% statement and branch coverage, ten of eighteen mutants survived, and every survivor was a missing boundary value (§17).

By the end you should be able to choose the inputs, the doubles and the level for any behaviour; diagnose a flaky test instead of retrying it; read a coverage report without believing the number; and review a colleague's tests by asking the one question that matters — what would this catch?

SECTION 1

What a Test Is For

A test is a claim about your code, written so a machine can settle it. That is the whole idea, and everything in this course is a consequence of taking it seriously.

Most of what makes testing hard is not the syntax. Two runners are covered here — pytest for Python and node:test and Vitest for JavaScript — and you will have the syntax of all three within an hour. What takes longer is knowing which claims are worth making, how to write a claim that survives the code changing, what to do when a collaborator makes the claim impossible to check, and how to tell a test that failed from a test that is merely unreliable. Those are the subjects of the next twenty sections.

This section establishes the vocabulary the rest of the course leans on. It is a vocabulary with a source: Gerard Meszaros's xUnit Test Patterns named these things once and carefully, and using his words precisely is the difference between a conversation about testing and an argument about what "mock" means.

Every output in this course was produced by running the code. Not adapted from documentation, not recalled — run, twice, and compared. The tooling that enforces that is described in §17.

1.1 The Claim a Test Makes

Here is a function and a claim about it.

# money.py
def split(total_cents, ways):
    """Split a sum of money as evenly as possible, largest shares first."""
    base, extra = divmod(total_cents, ways)
    return [base + 1] * extra + [base] * (ways - extra)

The claim: splitting 100 cents three ways gives 34, 33, 33. Written as a test:

# tests/test_money.py
from money import split


def test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares():
    assert split(100, 3) == [34, 33, 33]

Two things about that test are worth noticing before running it.

It names the claim, not the function. test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares says what must be true. A test called test_split says only that somebody tested split, and when it fails you learn nothing from the name — you have to read the body to find out what broke. The name is the failure message you get for free, and it is the one part of a test that is read far more often than it is written.

It is a claim someone could disagree with. "Splitting 100 three ways gives 34, 33, 33" is a decision: the extra cent could have gone to the last share instead, or the function could have refused to split unevenly. Writing it down turns an accident of implementation into a documented rule. That is why tests are so often the most accurate documentation a project has — not because anyone set out to write documentation, but because a comment can go stale silently and this cannot.

To run it, one more file. pytest needs to be able to import money, and by default it cannot:

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

That line matters more than it looks, and §2.9 explains it properly. In short: the pytest command does not put the current directory on sys.path, so from money import split fails with a collection error unless you tell it to. python -m pytest does put it there, which is why the same project can work under one invocation and fail under the other.

1.2 The Four-Phase Test

Meszaros's name for the shape almost every test has is the four-phase test, and it is worth learning as a shape because a test that does not have it is usually a test doing too much.

fixture setup
Put the world into the state the claim is about. Create the objects, seed the rows, set the clock.
exercise SUT
Do the one thing under test. Usually a single call — if it is three calls, ask which of them the claim is really about.
verify outcome
Compare what happened against the claim. This is where the assertion lives.
fixture teardown
Put the world back. Often nothing at all — and §5.14 explains why "often nothing" is a design goal rather than luck.

You will also meet two other spellings of the same shape. Arrange-act-assert collapses teardown into the framework's hands and is the phrasing most JavaScript projects use. Given-when-then comes from behaviour-driven development (§9.11) and is the same three phases written as a sentence: given a cart with two items, when I total it, then I get 650.

They are not rival ideas. Arrange-act-assert is the four-phase test with the fourth phase automated, and given-when-then is arrange-act-assert written for someone who does not read code. Use whichever vocabulary your team already uses; what matters is that the phases are visible, because a test where setup, exercise and verification are interleaved is a test nobody can skim.

The test in §1.1 has all four, three of them implicit:

def test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares():
    # fixture setup:  nothing — the inputs are literals
    assert split(100, 3) == [34, 33, 33]
    # exercise SUT:   split(100, 3)
    # verify outcome: == [34, 33, 33]
    # teardown:       nothing — split has no side effects

A function with no state to set up and nothing to clean up is the easiest thing in the world to test. Keep that observation; it is the whole argument of §8.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: fixture teardown.

1.3 Your First Run

pytest -q

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 0.94s

The dot is the test passing. [100%] is the progress column. 1 passed is the summary, and it is the line CI reads.

Now make the claim false — change the function to give the extra cent to the last share instead of the first:

# money.py
def split(total_cents, ways):
    """Split a sum of money as evenly as possible, largest shares first."""
    base, extra = divmod(total_cents, ways)
    return [base] * (ways - extra) + [base + 1] * extra

pytest -q

F                                                                        [100%]
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
_________________ test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares _________________

    def test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares():
>       assert split(100, 3) == [34, 33, 33]
E       assert [33, 33, 34] == [34, 33, 33]
E
E         At index 0 diff: 33 != 34
E         Use -v to get more diff

tests/test_money.py:6: AssertionError
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_money.py::test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares - as...
1 failed in 0.95s

Read what pytest printed there, because it is doing something that is not obvious.

It did not just say "assertion failed". It re-printed the source line, then explained the comparison: which list it got, which it expected, at which index they first differ, and a full diff. pytest gets this by rewriting the assert statement at import time — it recompiles assert a == b into code that captures both sides and formats them on failure. This is why in Python you write a plain assert rather than self.assertEqual(a, b): the framework recovers the information the method call was there to provide, and you keep the language you already know.

That rewriting is examined in detail in §3.2, including the case where it silently does not happen.

Restore the function before continuing:

# money.py
def split(total_cents, ways):
    """Split a sum of money as evenly as possible, largest shares first."""
    base, extra = divmod(total_cents, ways)
    return [base + 1] * extra + [base] * (ways - extra)

1.4 The Same Claim in JavaScript

Node ships a test runner. No install, no config, no dependency to keep current:

// src/money.js
export function split(totalCents, ways) {
  const base = Math.floor(totalCents / ways);
  const extra = totalCents % ways;
  return [...Array(extra).fill(base + 1), ...Array(ways - extra).fill(base)];
}

// test/money.test.js
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { split } from '../src/money.js';

test('a remainder goes to the earliest shares', () => {
  assert.deepStrictEqual(split(100, 3), [34, 33, 33]);
});

cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{ "type": "module" }
EOF
node --test

✔ a remainder goes to the earliest shares (1.1ms)
ℹ tests 1
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 1
ℹ fail 0
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 63.4

Three details in that file are load-bearing.

node:assert/strict, not node:assert. The non-strict module's assert.equal uses ==, so it will happily accept '34' for 34 and null for undefined. The strict module makes every function its strict variant. There is no reason to use the loose one, ever; import node:assert/strict and stop thinking about it.

deepStrictEqual, not equal. assert.equal([34, 33, 33], [34, 33, 33]) fails, because two arrays with the same contents are different objects. Every runner has this pair — the identity comparison and the structural one — and choosing wrong is the single most common beginner error in JavaScript testing. §3.6 lays out the whole family.

Bare node --test, with no argument. Node's runner discovers test files itself, matching names like *.test.js and anything under a test/ directory. Passing node --test test/ does not mean "the test directory" — it is read as a single file path and fails with Cannot find module. To narrow the run, pass a glob in quotes: node --test 'test/**/*.test.js'.

Vitest, the third runner this course uses, is covered in §2.14. It is the choice most JavaScript projects actually make, and the reason is not the assertions — it is that it shares a project's existing Vite transform pipeline, so test files and source files resolve identically and one class of configuration drift disappears.

The term this subsection introduced: test runner.

1.5 What a Failure Is Supposed to Tell You

A failing test has one job beyond failing: it should tell you where to look. Meszaros calls the property defect localization, and it is the reason "one behaviour per test" is advice worth following rather than a style preference.

Compare two tests of the same function.

# tests/test_money.py
from money import split


def test_everything_about_split():
    assert split(100, 3) == [34, 33, 33]
    assert split(100, 4) == [25, 25, 25, 25]
    assert split(1, 3) == [1, 0, 0]
    assert sum(split(9999, 7)) == 9999

pytest -q

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 0.94s

That passes, so it looks fine. But now suppose a change breaks the third claim. The first assertion that fails ends the test: the fourth claim is never checked, so you learn that something broke, not how much. Worse, the test's name tells you nothing, and its report names one failure where there might be three.

Meszaros's name for the smell is assertion roulette — a failure and no way to tell which of several assertions produced it. It is worst when the assertions carry no messages, which is exactly the case above.

The same claims, separated:

# tests/test_money.py
from money import split


def test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares():
    assert split(100, 3) == [34, 33, 33]


def test_an_exact_division_gives_equal_shares():
    assert split(100, 4) == [25, 25, 25, 25]


def test_more_ways_than_cents_gives_empty_shares():
    assert split(1, 3) == [1, 0, 0]


def test_the_shares_always_sum_to_the_total():
    assert sum(split(9999, 7)) == 9999

pytest -q

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 0.95s

Four tests instead of one. They cost four names to write, and in exchange a failure report tells you which rule broke and the other three keep reporting. That trade is almost always worth taking, and §3.14 gives the cases where it is not.

To have in hand before moving on: defect localization.

1.6 The System Under Test, and Everything Around It

Two terms, used precisely for the rest of the course.

The system under test — universally abbreviated SUT — is whatever the test is making a claim about. It is not necessarily a class or a function: for an end-to-end test the SUT is the whole deployed application, and for a unit test it might be one method. The word is deliberately vague about size, because the ideas do not change with size. What changes is cost, and that is §10.

A depended-on component — DOC — is anything the SUT talks to in order to do its job: a database, a clock, an HTTP service, another object. The interesting problems in testing are nearly all problems about DOCs. A SUT with no DOCs is split(), and it is trivial to test. A SUT with five is a checkout flow, and it is where §6, §7 and §8 earn their length.

system under test
What the claim is about. May be a function, an object, a service or a whole system.
depended-on component
Anything the SUT needs in order to run. Every hard testing problem is a problem about one of these.
test double
A stand-in for a DOC, installed by the test. Five distinct kinds, told apart in §6.

1.7 Direct and Indirect Inputs and Outputs

This is the distinction that makes the rest of the course possible to state clearly, and it is skipped by nearly every introduction to testing.

A direct input is something the test hands the SUT — an argument, a constructor parameter, a request body. A direct output is something the SUT hands back — a return value, a rendered string, a response. split(100, 3) == [34, 33, 33] is a claim purely about direct input and direct output, which is why it needed no machinery.

An indirect input is something the SUT gets from a DOC rather than from the test: the row a database returned, the current time, the body of an HTTP response. An indirect output is something the SUT sends to a DOC: the row it wrote, the email it sent, the log line it emitted.

The point of naming them is that the two pairs need completely different techniques.

# billing.py
from datetime import date


def invoice_number(sequence):
    """PREFIX-YYYY-NNNN, where the year comes from the system clock."""
    return f"INV-{date.today().year}-{sequence:04d}"

sequence is a direct input. The year is an indirect input — the function reached out to the clock and got it. A test cannot pass the year in, so a claim about the output is a claim about what day it is:

# tests/test_billing.py
from datetime import date

from billing import invoice_number


def test_the_number_carries_the_current_year():
    assert invoice_number(7) == f"INV-{date.today().year}-0007"

pytest -q tests/test_billing.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 0.94s

That passes, and it is a bad test, in a way worth being precise about: it re-implements the thing it is checking. If invoice_number used the wrong year the test would use the wrong year too and still pass. The only defect it can catch is one in the formatting.

The fix is not a cleverer assertion. It is to turn the indirect input into a direct one, which is the entire subject of §8:

# billing.py
from datetime import date


def invoice_number(sequence, today=None):
    """PREFIX-YYYY-NNNN. Pass `today` to make the year an argument rather than a fact."""
    today = date.today() if today is None else today
    return f"INV-{today.year}-{sequence:04d}"

# tests/test_billing.py
from datetime import date

from billing import invoice_number


def test_the_number_carries_the_year_it_is_given():
    assert invoice_number(7, today=date(2021, 3, 4)) == "INV-2021-0007"


def test_the_sequence_is_padded_to_four_digits():
    assert invoice_number(7, today=date(2021, 3, 4)).endswith("-0007")
    assert invoice_number(12345, today=date(2021, 3, 4)).endswith("-12345")

pytest -q tests/test_billing.py

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 0.95s

The claim is now checkable, it is checkable in March and in December, and it says what it means. One default argument bought all of that. §8.6 gives the version of this you would use when you cannot change the signature.

1.8 Control Points and Observation Points

Two more terms from the glossary, and they are the practical form of §1.7.

A control point is a place where the test can influence the SUT: an argument, a setter, a constructor, a seeded database row, a substituted collaborator. An observation point is a place where the test can see what happened: a return value, a stored row, a recorded call.

A piece of code is hard to test exactly when it lacks one of these. invoice_number before the change had no control point for the year; you could not influence it, so you could not make a firm claim about it. Code that writes a file and returns None has no observation point for what it wrote — the test has to go and look at the filesystem, which is why such code needs §11's techniques.

Meszaros calls the two ways in front door and back door. A test that drives the SUT through its real public interface uses the front door; one that reaches around it — seeding the database directly, reading a private attribute, inspecting a log file — uses the back door. Both are legitimate. Back door manipulation is often the only affordable way to set up state, and §11.6 uses it constantly. The rule is to prefer the front door for the exercise phase, because a test that drives the SUT the way nothing else ever will is a test that can pass while the real path is broken.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: back door manipulation.

1.9 Assertion Methods and Messages

The assertion method is the thing that turns a comparison into a pass or a fail. Python's is the assert statement, and pytest makes it good enough that you rarely need another. JavaScript has three families in common use:

// test/styles.test.js
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('the three assertion styles', () => {
  // 1. node:assert — function-call style, the xUnit tradition
  assert.strictEqual(2 + 2, 4);
  assert.deepStrictEqual({ a: 1 }, { a: 1 });

  // 2. an assertion message, for when the values will not explain themselves
  const shares = [34, 33, 33];
  assert.equal(shares.length, 3, `expected three shares, got ${shares.length}`);

  // 3. assert.throws — the claim that something fails
  assert.throws(() => JSON.parse('{oops'), SyntaxError);
});

node --test 'test/styles.test.js'

✔ the three assertion styles (1.4ms)
ℹ tests 1
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 1
ℹ fail 0
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 62.1

The third family, expect(x).toBe(y), comes from Vitest and Jest and is covered in §3.9. It reads left to right and produces better failure messages for free, at the cost of a dependency.

The assertion message is the second argument above, and the guidance about it is more specific than "write good messages". A message that repeats the comparison is worse than none, because the runner already prints the values:

assert.equal(total, 640, 'total should be 640')     // useless — the runner prints both
assert.equal(total, 640, `cart was ${JSON.stringify(items)}`)   // useful — adds context

The rule: a message should add what the runner cannot see. The values are printed for you. The state that produced them is not.

The vocabulary here: assert.throws.

1.10 Self-Testing Code

Martin Fowler's term for the goal is self-testing code: a codebase that ships with a suite you can run with one command, that passes, and that you believe. His definition is deliberately behavioural rather than numerical — you have self-testing code when you are confident that if the tests pass, the code is free of significant defects.

Notice what that definition does not mention. It does not mention coverage, or the number of tests, or a ratio of test code to production code. It mentions a state of mind, and it is the right thing to measure because it is the thing that changes your behaviour. A suite you believe lets you refactor aggressively, upgrade a dependency on a Friday, and accept a contribution from a stranger. A suite you do not believe is a tax you pay for nothing — you run it, it goes red for reasons unrelated to your change, and you learn to ignore it. That is the beginning of test cancer (§9.16), where the suite steadily rots because nobody trusts it enough to fix it.

The economic argument is worth stating in one line, because it is frequently made badly. Tests are not free and they do not pay for themselves in defects prevented alone. They pay for themselves in change made cheap. A codebase's cost is dominated by the changes made to it after it is first written, and the thing that makes change expensive is not typing — it is the fear of breaking something invisible. That is what a suite you trust removes.

The corollary is uncomfortable and worth accepting early: a test that does not change your willingness to modify the code is not earning anything. §4.11 is about deciding which those are.

1.11 What a Test Suite Cannot Do

Being clear about this now saves believing something false later.

A passing suite does not mean the code is correct. It means every claim you thought to write is true. Dijkstra's line — testing shows the presence of bugs, not their absence — is not pessimism, it is arithmetic: split has more possible inputs than there are atoms in the observable universe, and the suite above checks four of them. §16 is about buying back some of that gap with generated inputs, and §17 is about measuring how much of it you have.

Coverage does not measure quality. A test that runs a line without asserting anything about it produces coverage and no confidence. §17.9 demonstrates a suite with 100% line coverage and no assertions at all, passing against code that is definitely wrong.

A green suite says nothing about the things you did not build. Tests check the code you wrote against the claims you made. If the requirement was misunderstood, both are wrong together and every light is green. That is what exploratory testing (§20.13) and talking to users are for, and no amount of automation replaces them.

Tests are code, and rot like code. They can be duplicated, over-coupled, slow, and wrong. A buggy test is worse than no test, because it produces confidence you have not earned. §19 is a catalogue of the specific ways this happens, and every entry in it is a mistake that has shipped in real projects, repeatedly.

1.12 The Words Everyone Uses

A short glossary before the rest of the course, because most of these words are xUnit's rather than pytest's, and the next twenty sections use them precisely.

Test automation is the practice this whole course is about: turning a check a person would otherwise perform into one a machine performs on every commit. Meszaros states the goals of test automation explicitly, and they are worth knowing because they pull against each other — tests should improve quality, help you understand the system, reduce risk, be easy to run, be easy to write and maintain, and require minimal maintenance as the system evolves. Nearly every judgement in this course is a trade between the last two and the first three.

A test method is one test — a function, in pytest, and a method in the frameworks the name comes from. A testcase class groups several of them. A testcase object is one instance of that class, and every xUnit framework creates a fresh one per test method, which is where "each test gets a fresh fixture" (§5.5) originally comes from. A test suite object is the runner's internal collection of the tests it is about to run; pytest builds one during collection and you can see its contents with --collect-only (§2.3).

Getting from files to that suite is three steps, and each has a name. Test discovery finds the files. Test enumeration finds the tests inside them. Test selection narrows that set to the ones this run should execute — a marker expression, a name filter, a list of node ids. Knowing which of the three is failing is most of the diagnosis when a test mysteriously does not run, and §2 is those steps in detail.

Tests are also sorted by who they are for. A developer test — Beck's programmer test — is written by the person writing the code, in the code's vocabulary, to answer "did I build it right". A customer test is written with the person who wanted the feature, in the domain's vocabulary, to answer "did we build the right thing"; §9.13's acceptance tests are these. The distinction is not about tooling. It is about audience, and therefore about what a failure means: a failing programmer test says the code is wrong, and a failing customer test may mean the code is right and the requirement was misunderstood.

A regression suite is the accumulated set of tests that exist to stop something which once broke from breaking again. Most of a mature suite is this, and §9.9 argues that it is the cheapest kind of test to justify — a defect happened, in production, and this test proves it cannot happen again unnoticed.

Test debt is the gap between the suite you have and the one the system needs: untested modules, tests that cannot fail (§17.7), a shape that does not match where your defects actually come from (§10.12). Like any debt it is not automatically bad. It is bad when it is unrecorded, because then nobody is choosing to carry it.

And one pair of words from the original xUnit interfaces that survives because it is shorter than the alternatives: a red bar is a failing run and a green bar is a passing one. "Keep the bar green" is still the shortest statement of what continuous integration asks of you (§20.1).

What to carry forward from this subsection: testcase object, test suite object, test discovery, test enumeration, test selection, red bar, green bar, developer test, a regression suite, test debt, goals of test automation and fresh fixture.

1.13 What This Section Established

A test is a claim, made so a machine can settle it. Its name is the failure message you get for free; write the name as the rule, not as the function.

The four-phase test — fixture setup, exercise SUT, verify outcome, fixture teardown — is the shape. Arrange-act-assert and given-when-then are the same shape in other words.

pytest rewrites your assert so a plain comparison produces a full explanation on failure. In JavaScript, import node:assert/strict and use deepStrictEqual for structures — the loose module and the identity comparison are the two standard beginner traps.

The SUT is what the claim is about; a depended-on component is anything it needs. Direct inputs and outputs pass through the test; indirect ones pass through a DOC — and the indirect ones are where all the difficulty is. A control point is where the test can influence the SUT and an observation point is where it can see the result; code is hard to test exactly when one is missing.

Assertion roulette is a failure you cannot attribute. Separate claims into separate tests and get defect localization in return.

Self-testing code is defined by confidence, not by coverage. Tests pay for themselves by making change cheap, not by catching bugs — and a test that does not change your willingness to modify the code is not earning anything.

Exercises

1. Name the claims. Take split and write down, in English, every rule you think it should obey. Aim for at least six. Then mark which of them your four tests actually check, and which you assumed.

2. Break it four ways. Introduce one defect at a time into split — swap the two list halves, use // where divmod was used, drop the + 1, return the shares reversed. For each, record which of the four tests failed. Then say which defect was caught by the fewest tests and what that tells you about the suite.

3. Read a failure properly. Change one test to expect [34, 33, 34] and run pytest with -q, then without it, then with --tb=line. Write down what each level of detail gives you and when you would want each.

4. Find the indirect input. Write a function greeting(name) that returns "Good morning, X", "Good afternoon, X" or "Good evening, X" depending on the hour. Test it. Then explain in two sentences why your test is either unreliable or re-implementing the function, and fix it by adding a control point.

5. Both runners, one claim. Implement split in JavaScript so that split(1, 3) gives [1, 0, 0] and write the four claims from §1.5 as node:test tests. Then state one thing the JavaScript version made harder than the Python version and one thing it made easier.

6. Assertion messages that earn their place. Take the four-assertions-in-one-test version from §1.5 and add a message to each. Then argue in three sentences for or against keeping it as one test with good messages rather than four tests.

Solution

1. Name the claims.

A reasonable list, and the point of the exercise is that it is longer than the suite:

  1. The shares sum to the total.
  2. There are exactly ways shares.
  3. No two shares differ by more than one cent.
  4. The larger shares come first.
  5. An exact division gives all-equal shares.
  6. No share is negative when the total is non-negative.
  7. ways of zero is an error rather than a wrong answer.
  8. A total smaller than ways gives some zero shares rather than fractions.

The four tests in §1.5 check 1 (for one input), 4 (implicitly, for one input), 5 (for one input) and 8 (for one input). Nothing checks 2, 3, 6 or 7 at all, and every check that exists is a check at one point. That gap is precisely what §16 exists to close: claims 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 are properties — they hold for every input, not just the ones you thought of — and property-based testing checks them against hundreds of generated cases instead of one.

Claim 7 is the interesting one, because the function does not currently obey it: split(100, 0) raises ZeroDivisionError from inside divmod, which is an error but not a documented one. Deciding what should happen is a design question the test forced you to ask, which is §9's argument in miniature.

2. Break it four ways.

Swapping the halves (the §1.3 defect) is caught by test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares and by nothing else — the sum is unchanged, the exact-division case has no remainder to misplace, and split(1, 3) gives [0, 0, 1] which the third test does catch. So two of four.

Replacing divmod with // and dropping extra entirely gives [33, 33, 33]: caught by the remainder test and by the sum test, not by the exact-division test.

Dropping the + 1 gives [33, 33, 33] again — same result, same two tests.

Reversing the output is caught only by the remainder test, and only because that input has a remainder.

The lesson: test_the_shares_always_sum_to_the_total is the most valuable test in the file, because it is the only one making a claim that does not depend on a specific input. It is a property wearing a unit test's clothes. And test_an_exact_division_gives_equal_shares caught nothing at all in four attempts, because a case with no remainder cannot detect a remainder bug — a real example of a test that exists without earning anything (§1.10).

3. Read a failure properly.

-q gives the progress line, the failure with its rewritten explanation, and the short summary. Without -q you additionally get the session header — platform, Python version, pytest version, rootdir, active plugins — which is what you want when the question is "why does this behave differently on CI than on my machine". --tb=line collapses each failure to a single line naming the file, line number and exception, which is what you want when forty tests failed for the same reason and you need to see the shape rather than the detail.

The general rule: default verbosity while writing a test, --tb=line or --tb=no -q while fixing a mass failure, and full output with the header when reproducing someone else's report.

4. Find the indirect input.

The bad version:

def greeting(name):
    hour = datetime.now().hour
    part = "morning" if hour < 12 else "afternoon" if hour < 18 else "evening"
    return f"Good {part}, {name}"

Any test of it is either unreliable — asserting "Good morning, Ada" passes before noon and fails after it, which is a flaky test and the subject of §18 — or it computes the expected part with the same conditional, which re-implements the function and can only catch a typo in the word "afternoon".

The fix adds a control point:

def greeting(name, hour=None):
    hour = datetime.now().hour if hour is None else hour
    part = "morning" if hour < 12 else "afternoon" if hour < 18 else "evening"
    return f"Good {part}, {name}"

Now the boundaries are directly testable — hour=11, 12, 17, 18 — and §4.4 will argue those four are the only interesting values. Note if hour is None rather than or: with or, an hour of 0 is falsy and silently becomes the current time, which is a defect the boundary tests would find.

5. Both runners, one claim.

The JavaScript implementation is given in §1.4. split(1, 3) gives [1, 0, 0] there because Math.floor(1/3) is 0 and 1 % 3 is 1.

Harder in JavaScript: the assertion. assert.equal(split(100,3), [34,33,33]) fails, because arrays are compared by identity; you must know to reach for deepStrictEqual. Python's == on lists is structural, so the obvious thing is the correct thing.

Easier in JavaScript: no import path configuration. node --test needs no equivalent of the pythonpath line, because ES module specifiers are relative paths and resolve without a search path at all.

6. Assertion messages that earn their place.

Against keeping it as one test, on three grounds. The first failing assertion still ends the test, so the three claims after it go unchecked regardless of how good the messages are — messages fix attribution, not truncation. The name still describes nothing, so a CI report lists one opaque failure where four names would have located the defect. And the messages have to be maintained in step with the assertions, which is duplication of exactly the kind §19.6 catalogues.

The honest case for one test with messages: when the four assertions are genuinely one claim — four fields of a single returned object, say — splitting them into four tests means running the same expensive setup four times, and §5.7's shared fixtures are the better answer. The distinction is whether the assertions are four claims or four facets of one.

SECTION 2

Running Tests

A test runner does four things: it finds test files, collects the tests inside them, runs them, and reports what happened. Every option in this section belongs to one of those four steps, and knowing which is most of what makes a runner's documentation readable.

It matters more than it sounds. The most common first day with a test suite is spent not on assertions but on ModuleNotFoundError, on a test that will not run because the file is named wrongly, and on a report that scrolls past too fast to read. Those are not incidental — they are the runner doing exactly what it was configured to do, and five minutes of understanding replaces an afternoon of guessing.

This section covers pytest in depth, then node:test and Vitest, which share the concepts and disagree about almost every spelling.

2.1 The Four Steps

1
discovery
Which files are test files. Decided by a naming convention and a set of directories to look in.
2
collection
Which tests are inside them. Each file is imported, which is why an import error here stops everything before a single test runs.
3
selection
Which of the collected tests to actually run. Names, markers, node ids, last-failed.
4
reporting
Verbosity, tracebacks, summaries, machine-readable formats, and the process exit code.

The step that surprises people is the second. Test collection imports your test files. A syntax error, a missing dependency, a module-level assert, or a print that raises will all fail at collection — before any test runs, and reported as an error rather than a failure. That distinction is worth keeping: a failure is a test making a claim that turned out false; an error is the runner never getting far enough to ask.

Here is the project this section works on:

# tests/test_collection.py
import pytest


def test_addition_is_commutative():
    assert 2 + 3 == 3 + 2


def test_subtraction_is_not():
    assert 5 - 3 != 3 - 5


class TestStrings:
    def test_upper(self):
        assert "widget".upper() == "WIDGET"

    def test_strip(self):
        assert "  widget  ".strip() == "widget"


@pytest.mark.parametrize("n", [1, 2, 3])
def test_squares_grow(n):
    assert n * n >= n

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]

pytest

============================= test session starts ==============================
platform linux -- Python 3.12.7, pytest-9.1.1, pluggy-1.6.0
rootdir: /project
configfile: pyproject.toml
testpaths: tests
plugins: cov-7.1.0, asyncio-1.4.0, xdist-3.8.0, anyio-4.15.0, timeout-2.4.0, hypothesis-6.167.1
asyncio: mode=Mode.STRICT, debug=False, asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope=None, asyncio_default_test_loop_scope=function
collected 7 items

tests/test_collection.py .......                                         [100%]

============================== 7 passed in 0.95s ===============================

That is the default report in full, and every part of it is useful once. The header names the platform, the Python version, the pytest version, the rootdir, the config file it found and the plugins that are active — which is the first thing to compare when a suite behaves differently on CI than on your machine. Then one character per test, then the summary line.

The term above, for reference: test collection.

2.2 Discovery: Which Files Are Test Files

pytest's defaults are conventions, all of them changeable:

python_files
test_*.py and *_test.py
python_classes
Test* — and a class with an __init__ is skipped, silently, which is a classic hour lost
python_functions
test*
testpaths
Where to look when no path is given on the command line. Without it, pytest walks the whole rootdir — including node_modules, .venv and every build artefact.

testpaths is the one worth setting on day one. A suite that takes four seconds to collect is almost always one that is walking a directory tree full of things that are not tests.

node:test has the same concept with different defaults: any file named *.test.js, *-test.js, *_test.js, anything directly inside a test/ directory, and test.js itself. Vitest defaults to **/*.{test,spec}.?(c|m)[jt]s?(x) and takes an include array to change it.

One to keep in hand: python_files.

2.3 --collect-only

The single most useful diagnostic in the runner, and the one people discover last. It performs discovery and collection and then stops.

pytest --collect-only -q

tests/test_collection.py::test_addition_is_commutative
tests/test_collection.py::test_subtraction_is_not
tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_upper
tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_strip
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[1]
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[2]
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[3]

7 tests collected in 1.13s

Use it whenever the question is "why is my test not running", which it answers immediately: if the test is not in this list, the problem is discovery or collection, and no amount of fiddling with the test body will help. It is also the fastest way to see how many tests a parametrized decorator really produced (§4.12), and to check that a marker expression selects what you meant.

Without -q it prints the collection tree — directory, module, class, function — which is the view that makes an unexpectedly skipped class obvious.

2.4 Selecting Tests: node ids and -k

A node id is the full address of a test: path::class::function[params]. Anything pytest prints in a failure summary can be pasted back as an argument, and that round trip is the workflow — read the failing id out of CI, paste it, run one test.

pytest -q "tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_upper"
pytest -q "tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[2]"

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 1.91s
.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 1.33s

-k selects by a substring expression over the id, with and, or, not and parentheses:

pytest -q -k "strings or squares" --collect-only
pytest -q -k "not commutative and not squares" --collect-only

tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_upper
tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_strip
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[1]
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[2]
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[3]

5/7 tests collected (2 deselected) in 1.17s
tests/test_collection.py::test_subtraction_is_not
tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_upper
tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_strip

3/7 tests collected (4 deselected) in 0.95s

Two things to know about -k.

It matches against the whole node id, not only the function name, so -k "test_collection" selects the entire file and -k "2" selects the parametrized case whose id contains a 2 — including, unhelpfully, any test whose name happens to contain that character. Long, specific test names (§4.17) make -k far more useful, which is a small argument for them nobody mentions.

Nothing matching is not an error, it is exit code 5 (§2.11). A CI job that silently ran zero tests because a -k expression stopped matching after a rename is a real and quiet failure; §20's advice to assert on the test count exists for this.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: -k expression.

2.5 Markers and -m

A marker is a label on a test. The -m marker expression selects by a boolean expression over those labels, which differs from -k in exactly one way that matters: markers are declared, so an -m marker expression is checked against a list rather than matched as a substring — a typo in a -k expression silently selects nothing, and a typo in a marker is caught at collection.

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "--strict-markers"
markers = [
    "slow: takes more than a second; excluded from the fast suite",
    "external: needs the network",
]

# tests/test_marked.py
import pytest


def test_fast_one():
    assert True


@pytest.mark.slow
def test_slow_one():
    assert True


@pytest.mark.slow
@pytest.mark.external
def test_slow_and_external():
    assert True

pytest -q -m "not slow" tests/test_marked.py
pytest -q -m "slow and not external" tests/test_marked.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed, 2 deselected in 1.08s
.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed, 2 deselected in 1.42s

--strict-markers in addopts is the setting that makes markers trustworthy. Without it, a typo produces a warning and a test that is silently in no group at all — so -m "not slow" runs a test you meant to exclude, and nothing tells you. With it, the typo is a collection error:

# tests/test_typo.py
import pytest


@pytest.mark.sloq          # a typo: the declared marker is "slow"
def test_with_a_mistyped_marker():
    assert True

pytest -q tests/test_typo.py

==================================== ERRORS ====================================
_____________________ ERROR collecting tests/test_typo.py ______________________
'sloq' not found in `markers` configuration option
=========================== short test summary info ============================
ERROR tests/test_typo.py - Failed: 'sloq' not found in `markers` configuratio...
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! Interrupted: 1 error during collection !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
1 error in 2.06s

That is the whole argument for --strict-markers: the failure arrives at the moment of the mistake rather than as a silently missing test six months later. addopts is where it belongs, so nobody has to remember to type it.

addopts is worth understanding generally: it is a string of options prepended to every invocation. Anything the whole team should always get — --strict-markers, --strict-config, a default --tb style, -ra — goes there. Anything a person might want to vary does not, because an option in addopts is difficult to turn off from the command line.

2.6 rootdir, config files and conftest.py

The pytest rootdir is pytest's anchor. It is computed from the arguments and the config file it finds, it never changes during a run, and it is what relative paths in the report are relative to. The pytest rootdir is printed in the header, and reading it is the first step in diagnosing "it works here and not there".

Configuration can live in pyproject.toml (under [tool.pytest.ini_options]), pytest.ini, tox.ini or setup.cfg. Prefer pyproject.toml in a new project and pytest.ini if you want a file whose only job is pytest. Do not have two: pytest picks one by a precedence order, and the file you edited may not be the file it read. --strict-config turns a typo in a config key into an error instead of a silent default.

conftest.py is different in kind. It is not configuration; it is code that pytest imports automatically, for the directory it sits in and everything below. It holds fixtures (§5), hooks, and plugin registration. Its two important properties:

  • It is hierarchical. A fixture in tests/conftest.py is available to every test under tests/; one in tests/integration/conftest.py only to those. A more specific conftest.py can override a name from a less specific one, which is the intended way to specialise a fixture for a subtree. That arrangement is the conftest hierarchy, and §5.10 uses it to give an integration subtree its own settings without duplicating the base ones.
  • It is imported without being requested, so it is the one place where a sys.path change, an import-time side effect or a plugin registration can happen before anything else. That is powerful and is exactly why an error in a conftest.py produces a confusing failure with no test in the traceback.
# tests/conftest.py
import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def widget():
    """Available to every test under tests/, with no import anywhere."""
    return {"sku": "widget", "price_cents": 300}

# tests/test_uses_conftest.py
def test_the_fixture_arrives_without_an_import(widget):
    assert widget["price_cents"] == 300

pytest -q tests/test_uses_conftest.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 1.21s

No import statement anywhere connects those two files. That is convenient and it is also the most common complaint about pytest, because a name appearing from nowhere is hard to trace. pytest --fixtures lists every available fixture with the file it came from, and it is the answer to "where on earth is widget defined".

The term this subsection introduced: conftest hierarchy.

2.7 Import Modes and the src Layout

Collection imports test files, and how it imports them has consequences.

The default mode is prepend: pytest inserts the test file's rootdir-relative base directory at the front of sys.path and imports the module by its dotted name. That has one sharp edge. Two test files with the same basename in different directories, with no __init__.py to distinguish them, are the same module name — and pytest reports a collision:

import file mismatch: tests/unit/test_api.py and tests/integration/test_api.py

The three ways out, in increasing order of how much they fix:

add __init__.py
Makes the test directories packages, so the module names differ. Works, and makes the test tree importable, which some people dislike.
rename the files
test_api_unit.py. Free, and arguably clearer in a failure report anyway.
--import-mode=importlib
Imports each file directly without touching sys.path at all. No collisions, no path manipulation, and the recommended mode for new projects.

The related question is where your application code lives. The src layout puts it in src/yourpackage/ rather than at the repository root:

pyproject.toml
src/
  shop/
    __init__.py
    billing.py
tests/
  test_billing.py

Its virtue is precisely that import shop cannot accidentally work from the repository root. You must install the package — pip install -e . — so the tests import it the way a user would, through the installed distribution. That catches a whole class of packaging defect on the first test run rather than after release: a module missing from the package data, a subpackage without an __init__.py, a dependency you had installed for other reasons and never declared.

The flat layout is simpler and fine for an application that is never packaged. For anything published, use src.

To have in hand before moving on: --import-mode=importlib.

2.8 pytest and python -m pytest

Which brings us to the single most common first-run failure in Python testing, and it is not a testing problem at all.

# money.py
def split(total, ways):
    """Split `total` cents into `ways` shares, remainder to the earliest."""
    base, extra = divmod(total, ways)
    return [base + 1] * extra + [base] * (ways - extra)

# tests/test_money.py
from money import split


def test_a_remainder_goes_to_the_earliest_shares():
    assert split(100, 3) == [34, 33, 33]

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]

pytest -q tests/test_money.py 2>&1 | tail -7

tests/test_money.py:2: in <module>
    from money import split
E   ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'money'
=========================== short test summary info ============================
ERROR tests/test_money.py
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! Interrupted: 1 error during collection !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
1 error in 1.80s

A collection error, on a two-line test, against a four-line module sitting in the same directory. Now change nothing except how the runner is started:

python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_money.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 1.42s

python -m pytest prepends the current directory to sys.path. The pytest command does not. That is the entire difference, it is a documented property of python -m, and it explains an enormous amount of confusion: the same project works for a colleague who types one and fails for you who types the other, and neither of you has done anything wrong.

Three ways to make it work under both, in order of preference:

install the package
pip install -e . with a real pyproject.toml. The correct answer for anything packaged, and the one the src layout forces.
pythonpath = ["."]
One line in [tool.pytest.ini_options]. Explicit, visible in the config, and works under both invocations. This is what this course's examples use.
sys.path.insert in conftest
Works, is invisible, and is how a project ends up importing a different copy of itself than the one it installs. Avoid.
# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
pythonpath = ["."]

pytest -q tests/test_money.py
python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_money.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 1.01s
.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 1.28s

One line, and both invocations now agree. Note that this is a genuine difference between the tools rather than a bug in either: python -m is documented to add the working directory, and a console script deliberately does not, because doing so would make any directory's contents shadow installed packages.

2.9 Reading the Report

The default report is tuned for a developer watching one failure. Four groups of options retune it.

Verbosity. -q gives one line per file and a summary; the default gives the header and a progress line; -v gives one line per test with its outcome; -vv stops truncating long values in assertion diffs, which is what you want when a comparison says ... at the interesting moment.

Tracebacks. --tb=long (the default) prints the full frame stack with source. --tb=short prints one frame per level. --tb=line collapses each failure to a single line, which is the right choice when forty tests failed for one reason and you want to see the shape. --tb=no prints none, and pairs with -ra.

Summaries. The -ra summary prints everything that was not a plain pass — failures, errors, skips with their reasons, xfails, xpasses. Skips are the reason to use it: a suite that quietly skips 300 tests looks identical to one that runs them, and -ra is what makes the difference visible.

Capture. pytest captures stdout and stderr and only prints them for failing tests. --capture=no (or -s) turns that off, which is what you need when debugging with a print or when the code under test is interactive. --log-cli-level=INFO streams log records live, which is usually more useful than -s because it keeps the formatting and the level filtering.

pytest -q --tb=no -ra tests/test_collection.py
pytest --no-header -v tests/test_collection.py

.......                                                                  [100%]
7 passed in 2.53s
============================= test session starts ==============================
collecting ... collected 7 items

tests/test_collection.py::test_addition_is_commutative PASSED            [ 14%]
tests/test_collection.py::test_subtraction_is_not PASSED                 [ 28%]
tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_upper PASSED                 [ 42%]
tests/test_collection.py::TestStrings::test_strip PASSED                 [ 57%]
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[1] PASSED                    [ 71%]
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[2] PASSED                    [ 85%]
tests/test_collection.py::test_squares_grow[3] PASSED                    [100%]

============================== 7 passed in 2.20s ===============================

--durations=N prints the N slowest tests, and --durations-min sets the threshold below which they are hidden. Run it once a month; the answer is almost always that three tests are responsible for half the suite's runtime, and one of them is doing something it should not (§20's ten-minute build). Its numbers are measurements rather than facts, which is why §18.3 uses it as the example of output you must never assert on.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: --no-header, the -ra summary, --capture=no and --log-cli-level.

2.10 Exit Codes

The runner's exit code is what CI actually reads. pytest's are documented — and available as the ExitCode enum, which is what a plugin or a wrapper script should compare against rather than a bare integer. It is worth knowing all seven, because the difference between "tests failed" and "the run never happened" is the difference between a red build you understand and one you do not.

# tests/test_two_outcomes.py
def test_that_passes():
    assert True


def test_that_fails():
    assert 1 == 2

# exit_codes.py
import subprocess
import sys

CASES = [
    (["tests/test_collection.py"], "everything passed"),
    (["tests/test_two_outcomes.py"], "a test failed"),
    (["--not-a-real-option"], "a bad command line"),
    (["-k", "no-test-has-this-name"], "the selection matched nothing"),
    (["--max-warnings=0", "tests/test_noisy.py"], "passed, but too many warnings"),
]

for args, why in CASES:
    done = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", "-q", *args],
                          capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(f"exit {done.returncode}   {why}")

# tests/test_noisy.py
import warnings


def test_that_warns():
    warnings.warn("this API is going away", DeprecationWarning)
    assert True

python3 exit_codes.py

exit 0   everything passed
exit 1   a test failed
exit 4   a bad command line
exit 5   the selection matched nothing
exit 6   passed, but too many warnings
0
OK
Everything that ran, passed.
1
TESTS_FAILED
The ordinary red build.
2
INTERRUPTED
Ctrl-C, --maxfail reached, or a collection error — including the --strict-markers failure above.
3
INTERNAL_ERROR
pytest itself broke. Usually a plugin.
4
USAGE_ERROR
A bad command line or config.
5
NO_TESTS_COLLECTED
The dangerous one. Nothing ran, and a pipeline treating "not 1" as success is now green on zero tests.
6
MAX_WARNINGS_ERROR
New in pytest 9: everything passed, but --max-warnings was exceeded. A warning budget that a build can enforce.

The operational lesson is about 5. A pipeline step must check for exit code 0, never for "not 1". A renamed directory, a -k that stopped matching, a testpaths pointing at a path that no longer exists — all of them produce 5, and all of them look like a passing build to a script that only knows about 1.

node:test and Vitest are simpler: 0 for success, 1 for anything else. That simplicity is a real disadvantage, and both benefit from a separate assertion on the test count in CI.

The vocabulary here: ExitCode.

2.11 The Cache: Re-running What Matters

pytest records the outcome of every test in a .pytest_cache directory, which powers four options that change the debugging loop more than anything else in this section.

--last-failed
Run only the tests that failed last time. The single most useful flag in pytest: fix, re-run four tests instead of four thousand, repeat until it says all passed.
--failed-first
Run everything, but the previous failures first. The full safety net with a fast answer at the top.
--new-first
Tests in new or recently modified files first — the ones most likely to fail.
--stepwise
Stop at the first failure, and on the next run start there. For working through a large breakage one test at a time.

Note the long spellings. pytest accepts --lf, --ff, --nf and --sw, and the short forms are what you will type — but --ff also means fast-forward in git, and in written material the long form is unambiguous.

The cache lives in cachedir, which is .pytest_cache under the rootdir; add it to .gitignore. -p no:cacheprovider disables the plugin entirely, which is what you want in CI and in any environment where the working directory is read-only or shared between parallel jobs. A stale cache is also a real source of confusion — --cache-clear resets it.

What to carry forward from this subsection: --last-failed, --failed-first, --new-first, --stepwise, cachedir and parallel jobs.

2.12 node --test

Node has a test runner built in. There is nothing to install, which is its main argument.

// src/money.js
export function split(total, ways) {
  const base = Math.floor(total / ways);
  const extra = total % ways;
  return Array.from({ length: ways }, (_, i) => (i < extra ? base + 1 : base));
}

// test/money.test.js
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { split } from '../src/money.js';

test('a remainder goes to the earliest shares', () => {
  assert.deepStrictEqual(split(100, 3), [34, 33, 33]);
});

test('an exact division gives equal shares', () => {
  assert.deepStrictEqual(split(99, 3), [33, 33, 33]);
});

test('a name pattern can select this one', () => {
  assert.equal(split(1, 3).length, 3);
});

cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{ "type": "module" }
EOF
node --test
node --test --test-name-pattern="name pattern"

✔ a remainder goes to the earliest shares (10.152713ms)
✔ an exact division gives equal shares (1.250407ms)
✔ a name pattern can select this one (3.681102ms)
ℹ tests 3
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 3
ℹ fail 0
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 979.978504
✔ a name pattern can select this one (8.817659ms)
ℹ tests 1
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 1
ℹ fail 0
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 539.348899

The flags, and how they map onto pytest:

--test-name-pattern
A regular expression over test names — pytest's -k, but a real regex.
--test-skip-pattern
The inverse. Together they cover most of what markers do.
--test-only
Run only tests marked { only: true }, which is how node spells "focus on this one".
--test-concurrency=N
How many test files run at once. Files are separate processes, so isolation is genuine.
--test-shard=2/4
Run one quarter of the files. For splitting a suite across CI machines (§20).
--test-randomize
Shuffle the order, with --test-random-seed to reproduce. §18's order-dependence detector.
--test-rerun-failures
Re-run from a saved state file — pytest's --last-failed, with the state file named explicitly.
--test-global-setup
A module run once before everything — a session-scoped fixture, spelled as a file.

And the trap from §1: bare node --test discovers, while node --test test/ treats the argument as a file path and fails with Cannot find module. To narrow the run, quote a glob: node --test 'test/**/*.test.js'.

The terms above, gathered: --test-only, --test-skip-pattern, --test-concurrency, --test-shard, --test-randomize, --test-random-seed, --test-rerun-failures and --test-global-setup.

2.13 Vitest, and Why

Vitest is the third runner this course uses, and the one most JavaScript projects should choose. The reason is worth stating properly, because it is not about the assertions.

// vitest.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // *.spec.js only: `node --test` claims every *.test.js it can find,
    // anywhere in the tree, so the two runners need separate namespaces.
    include: ['**/*.spec.js'],
    reporters: ['dot'],
    isolate: true,
  },
});

// money.spec.js
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { split } from './src/money.js';

describe('split', () => {
  test('a remainder goes to the earliest shares', () => {
    expect(split(100, 3)).toEqual([34, 33, 33]);
  });

  test('an exact division gives equal shares', () => {
    expect(split(99, 3)).toEqual([33, 33, 33]);
  });
});

npx vitest run --reporter=verbose money.spec.js

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

 ✓ money.spec.js > split > a remainder goes to the earliest shares 26ms
 ✓ money.spec.js > split > an exact division gives equal shares 3ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Start at  23:31:17
   Duration  1.48s (transform 45%, import 30%, tests 14%, worker 11%)

It shares your application's build pipeline. Vitest runs on Vite, so test files are transformed by exactly the same configuration as source files: the same TypeScript settings, the same path aliases, the same JSX transform, the same environment variable handling, the same CSS handling. An entire class of problem — "it imports fine in the app and not in the test" — disappears, and it is a class that costs real days with any runner configured separately.

Everything else follows from that or is a convenience:

  • A DOM without ceremony. environment: 'jsdom' or 'happy-dom' in the config, and DOM tests run (§14). With node:test you assemble that yourself.
  • Watch mode is the default. vitest watches; vitest run runs once and exits. Getting this backwards in CI is a common way to hang a pipeline for its full timeout, so put vitest run in the script.
  • --related runs only the tests affected by changed files, computed from the module graph — a precision the pattern-matching approaches cannot reach (§17's test impact analysis).
  • Test projects run one suite several times under different configurations — jsdom and node, two browsers, two versions of a dependency — from one command.
  • --shard=1/4 for CI splitting, matching node's --test-shard.
  • The isolate option decides whether each test file gets a fresh module registry. isolate: true is the default and is what you want; setting the isolate option to false is meaningfully faster and only safe for a suite with no module-level state — which is to say, it trades §18's first cause of flakiness for speed.

Choose node:test when the project has no build step at all and you want zero dependencies. Choose Vitest when the project already has one, which today is nearly all of them.

One line each, for reference: vitest.config, test projects and --related.

2.14 Reporters

A reporter turns the run into output. Every runner ships several, and the choice is worth making twice — once for a person, once for a machine.

for a person
The spec reporter or a verbose one — one line per test with its name; best while writing. The dot reporter — one character per test; best for a large suite where the names would scroll past. Node spells the spec reporter spec and the dot reporter dot; Vitest calls the first verbose.
for a machine
The junit reporter emits XML understood by every CI system, and it is what makes a failure appear in the run's summary rather than only in the log (§20). The tap reporter emits a line protocol other tools consume. json is for your own scripts. The lcov reporter emits coverage in lcov format, which is what every coverage service reads (§17).
npx vitest run --reporter=dot money.spec.js
node --test --test-reporter=tap

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

··

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Start at  23:31:24
   Duration  1.51s (transform 46%, import 32%, tests 14%, worker 8%)

TAP version 13
# Subtest: a remainder goes to the earliest shares
ok 1 - a remainder goes to the earliest shares
  ---
  duration_ms: 10.530689
  type: 'test'
  ...
# Subtest: an exact division gives equal shares
ok 2 - an exact division gives equal shares
  ---
  duration_ms: 0.843941
  type: 'test'
  ...
# Subtest: a name pattern can select this one
ok 3 - a name pattern can select this one
  ---
  duration_ms: 3.843969
  type: 'test'
  ...
1..3
# tests 3
# suites 0
# pass 3
# fail 0
# cancelled 0
# skipped 0
# todo 0
# duration_ms 706.80265

Two practical notes.

A reporter list is not exclusive. Vitest takes reporters: ['default', ['junit', { outputFile: 'junit.xml' }]], and node takes repeated --test-reporter with a matching --test-reporter-destination. The right CI configuration is almost always a human-readable reporter on stdout and a JUnit file on disk.

Check the names against the version you have. Vitest 5 offers default, agent, minimal, blob, verbose, dot, json, tap, tap-flat, junit, tree, hanging-process and github-actions. basic was removed and now produces a startup error rather than a warning, which is a memorable way to find out that a tutorial is out of date.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: tap reporter, junit reporter, lcov reporter and lcov format.

2.15 Speed, and the Shape of the Run

Three mechanisms, and they are not interchangeable.

Sharding splits the test files across independent machines: --shard=2/4, --test-shard=2/4, pytest --shard-id via a plugin. Each shard is a whole process on its own machine, so isolation is perfect and the only cost is CI capacity. This is the first thing to reach for when the suite is too slow, because it requires no changes to the tests.

Parallelism within one machine runs several workers on one host: pytest -n 4 (via pytest-xdist), --test-concurrency, Vitest's default worker pool. Cheaper than sharding and it is the one that finds bugs: any shared port, temporary path, database or global (§18.12) that survived a serial run will now collide.

Watch mode is not about speed at all, but about the feedback loop. vitest watches by default; pytest needs a plugin. The version worth having reruns only what is affected — Vitest's --related and its watch mode both use the module graph.

The ordering advice: shard first, parallelise second, and only then start making individual tests faster. The last is the most work and the least reliable, and a suite whose slowness is genuinely spread across three thousand tests is usually a suite with an architecture problem (§10) rather than three thousand slow tests.

2.16 What This Section Established

  • A runner discovers, collects, selects and reports. Collection imports your files, which is why an import error stops everything before any test runs, and is reported as an error rather than a failure.
  • Discovery is a naming convention, and testpaths is worth setting on day one so pytest is not walking node_modules.
  • --collect-only answers "why is my test not running" immediately, and nothing else does — it performs discovery and test collection and stops before anything runs.
  • Node ids round-trip: paste the id from a failure report back as an argument. -k matches the whole id as a substring expression; markers are declared, and --strict-markers turns a typo into a collection error instead of a silently missing test.
  • addopts is for what everyone should always get. Prefer one config file; --strict-config catches a typo in a key.
  • conftest.py is code, imported automatically and hierarchically. --fixtures is how you find where a name came from.
  • --import-mode=importlib avoids the same-basename collision; the src layout makes import shop fail unless the package is really installed, which catches packaging defects on the first test run.
  • python -m pytest puts the current directory on sys.path and pytest does not. pythonpath = ["."], or install the package.
  • Exit code 5 means nothing ran. Check for 0, never for "not 1".
  • --max-warnings and exit code 6 are new in pytest 9: a warning budget a build can enforce.
  • --last-failed changes the debugging loop more than any other flag here. Disable the cache in CI.
  • node --test discovers on its own and reads a directory argument as a file path. Its flags map cleanly onto pytest's.
  • Vitest's argument is the shared build pipeline, not its assertions — the same transform for source and tests removes a whole class of configuration drift. vitest run in CI; isolate: false trades isolation for speed.
  • Use two reporters in CI: one for a person, JUnit for the machine. Check reporter names against the version you have.
  • Shard, then parallelise, then optimise. Parallelism is also a flakiness detector.

Exercises

1. Diagnose four failures to run.

For each symptom, name the step (discovery, collection, selection, reporting) and the most likely cause:

(a) a new test file's tests never appear, and the file has no syntax errors; (b) pytest reports 1 error and no tests ran; (c) pytest -m slow runs nothing, but the tests are marked; (d) CI is green and the log shows no tests ran in 0.01s.

2. Read a header.

A colleague's CI log shows a different rootdir from yours, and a plugin list with one extra entry. Give three concrete ways that could change the outcome of a run, and say which one you would check first.

3. Build a marker strategy.

Design the markers for a suite with fast unit tests, tests needing a database, tests needing the network, and tests taking over ten seconds. Write the pyproject.toml section, and the three commands you would put in CI. What does --strict-markers protect you from that a naming convention would not?

4. Reproduce the import problem.

Create a project with money.py at the root and tests/test_money.py importing it, with no pythonpath setting. Run it four ways: pytest, python -m pytest, pytest tests/, and cd tests && pytest test_money.py. Explain each result. Then say which of the three fixes you would use for an application that is deployed as a container and never published to an index.

5. Choose a runner.

For each project, choose between node:test and Vitest and defend it in two sentences: (a) a published npm library with no build step, in plain JavaScript; (b) a React application built with Vite; (c) a TypeScript CLI compiled with tsc; (d) a Node service using path aliases in tsconfig.json.

6. Design the CI invocation.

Write the exact pytest command line for a commit-stage job: it must fail loudly if nothing ran, produce a JUnit file, exclude slow tests, print a summary of skips, not write a cache, and stop after twenty failures. Justify each option, and say which one you would add if the job ran on four parallel machines.

Solutions

1. Diagnose four failures to run.

(a) Discovery. The file does not match python_files, or it is outside testpaths, or its functions do not start with test, or the tests are in a class that does not start with Test — or, the memorable one, in a Test* class that has an __init__, which pytest skips silently. --collect-only settles it in one command.

(b) Collection. The file was imported and the import raised: a missing dependency, a module-level statement that failed, a conftest.py error. The traceback names it; the giveaway is error rather than failed.

(c) Selection, with a cause in collection. Almost always a typo in the marker name, or a marker that was never declared and is silently doing nothing. --strict-markers would have made this a collection error at the moment it was written.

(d) Reporting, and it is the dangerous one. Exit code 5 with a pipeline that checks for a non-1 exit. Something changed the path or the selection so that no test matched. Fix the pipeline to require exit 0, and consider asserting a minimum test count.

2. Read a header.

A different rootdir means a different config file may have been found, so addopts, testpaths, markers and pythonpath may all differ — that is the deepest change of the three.

It also changes what relative paths mean in the report, so -k expressions and node ids that work locally may not match, and any test using a path relative to the rootdir will look in a different place.

The extra plugin can change ordering (pytest-randomly), add or remove fixtures, alter reporting, or change defaults through its own addopts.

Check rootdir first, because it explains the plugin difference as easily as anything else does — a different rootdir can mean a different config file, and a different config file can be what activates the plugin.

3. Build a marker strategy.

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--strict-markers --strict-config -ra"
testpaths = ["tests"]
markers = [
    "db: needs a database",
    "network: needs an external service",
    "slow: takes more than ten seconds",
]

CI:

pytest -m "not db and not network and not slow"     # commit stage, every push
pytest -m "db and not slow"                          # integration stage
pytest -m "slow or network"                          # nightly

--strict-markers protects you from the failure a naming convention cannot detect: a typo. @pytest.mark.sloq under a convention is still a valid mark, so the test is excluded from -m slow and included in -m "not slow" — it runs in the fast suite, slowly, and appears in no group anyone meant. The strict flag turns that into an error at collection, where it is one character to fix.

4. Reproduce the import problem.

pytest — collection error. The current directory is not on sys.path, so money is not importable.

python -m pytest — passes. python -m puts the current directory at the front of sys.path.

pytest tests/ — the same collection error. The argument changes what is collected, not the path.

cd tests && pytest test_money.py — still an error, and for a different reason worth understanding: pytest's prepend import mode inserts the test file's base directory, which is now tests/, and money.py is in the parent. Moving closer to the test does not help; only the search path does.

For a containerised application that is never published, pythonpath = ["."] is the pragmatic choice — one visible line, no install step, works under both invocations.
