The first test is the pattern to internalise: a generated id and a timestamp are not claims, the total is, and expect.any / expect.stringMatching let one structural comparison cover both — instead of five separate assertions, or a toMatchObject that quietly stops checking the fields you left out.

expect.extend earns its place when the same three-line check appears in ten tests. Its real value is the message: a custom matcher can explain the domain rule, and expected 500.5 to be exactly 500 cents teaches a reader something that expected 500.5 to be 500 does not.

One to keep in hand: expect.extend.

3.12 Custom, Delta and Guard Assertions

Three named patterns from the xUnit catalogue, all of them about moving intent out of the test body.

custom assertion
A named function containing the check. assert_is_a_valid_receipt(r) replaces eight lines and says why they are there. Remember register_assert_rewrite (§3.2).
delta assertion
Asserts on the change rather than the absolute value: "the balance dropped by 500", not "the balance is 4500". Independent of the starting state, so it survives a change to the fixture.
guard assertion
Checks a precondition before exercising the SUT, so a broken fixture reports itself instead of failing as though the code were wrong.
# tests/test_patterns.py
import pytest

from accounts import withdraw


def assert_leaves_balance(balance, amount, expected):
    """A custom assertion: named, reusable, and it says why."""
    assert withdraw(balance, amount) == expected, (
        f"withdrawing {amount} from {balance} should leave {expected}")


def test_a_custom_assertion_reads_as_a_sentence():
    assert_leaves_balance(1000, 250, 750)
    assert_leaves_balance(1000, 1000, 0)


def test_a_delta_assertion_survives_a_change_to_the_fixture():
    starting = 1000

    remaining = withdraw(starting, 250)

    # The claim is about the change, not the absolute value. Change `starting`
    # to 5000 and this test still says exactly what it meant to say.
    assert starting - remaining == 250


def test_a_guard_assertion_blames_the_fixture_rather_than_the_code(cart):
    # If this fails, the fixture is wrong, and the message says so — instead of
    # a confusing failure in the assertion below.
    assert len(cart) == 2, "the cart fixture should have two lines"

    assert sum(i["price_cents"] * i["quantity"] for i in cart) == 650


@pytest.fixture
def cart():
    return [{"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2}, {"price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1}]

pytest -q tests/test_patterns.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 0.97s

A guard assertion is the answer to a specific frustration: a test fails, you spend twenty minutes on the production code, and the fixture was wrong all along. One line at the top of the test converts that into an immediate, self-explaining failure. Use them sparingly — every guard is a claim that must stay true — and put them where the setup is complex enough to be doubted.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: delta assertion.

3.13 Skipping, Failing and Bailing Out

Five functions that end a test without an assertion, and the differences matter. pytest.skip, pytest.fail, pytest.xfail, pytest.exit and pytest.importorskip — the last of which is both a skip and an import, and is the reason an optional dependency does not need a try/except in every test that uses it.

# tests/test_outcomes.py
import sys

import pytest


def test_skip_at_runtime_when_the_condition_is_not_known_until_then():
    if sys.platform == "no-such-platform":
        pytest.skip("only meaningful on the imaginary platform")
    assert True


@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.version_info < (3, 10), reason="needs match statements")
def test_skipif_is_decided_at_collection():
    assert True


@pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True, reason="the rounding rule is not agreed yet")
def test_xfail_documents_a_known_gap():
    assert 1 == 2


def test_fail_ends_the_test_with_a_message():
    outcome = "expected"
    if outcome != "expected":
        pytest.fail(f"unreachable in this example; got {outcome}")


def test_importorskip_makes_an_optional_dependency_optional():
    yaml = pytest.importorskip("yaml", reason="PyYAML is an optional extra")
    assert yaml is not None

pytest -q -ra tests/test_outcomes.py

..x..                                                                    [100%]
=========================== short test summary info ============================
XFAIL tests/test_outcomes.py::test_xfail_documents_a_known_gap - the rounding rule is not agreed yet
4 passed, 1 xfailed in 1.22s
pytest.skip
Inside the test, when the reason is only knowable at run time. Every skip needs a reason string, and -ra (§2.9) is what makes skips visible.
skipif
Decided at collection, so the test never starts. Prefer it — the condition is visible without running anything.
xfail
"This should fail, and here is why." Always use xfail strict — strict=True, or xfail_strict = true in the config so xfail strict is the default — so that an unexpected pass fails the build and tells you the gap was closed (§4.13). pytest.xfail is the imperative form, called inside a test to abandon it when the reason is only knowable at run time; unlike the mark, pytest.xfail stops the test immediately.
pytest.fail
An explicit failure with a message, for a branch that should be unreachable.
pytest.exit
Stops the whole session. For "the database is unreachable, nothing after this can mean anything" — and for almost nothing else.

The failure mode to watch for is skip creep. A skip with a good reason is a documented decision; forty skips nobody has read is a suite that is 5% smaller than everyone believes. -ra in addopts and a periodic look at the skip list is the entire remedy.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: pytest.fail, pytest.skip and pytest.exit.

3.14 One Assertion Per Test, and When Not

"One assertion per test" is the most-repeated rule in testing and it is wrong as stated. The defensible version is one claim per test, and a claim can need several assertions.

The rule exists because of assertion roulette (§1.5, §19.4): several assertions in one test, the first failure ends it, and the name does not say which broke. That is a real cost, and splitting is usually right.

Three cases where it is not:

Several facets of one value. A parsed object's four fields are one claim about the parse. Splitting produces four tests that repeat the same setup and report the same defect four times. Compare the whole object in one structural assertion (§3.6) and the failure diff shows every differing field at once — strictly better than four tests and better than four assertions.

A sequence that is the behaviour. "Deposit, withdraw, check balance" is one claim about a sequence. Splitting it into three tests means two of them assert on intermediate states nobody cares about.

Expensive setup. If reaching the state takes four seconds, four tests cost sixteen. Use soft assertions (§3.10) or subtests (§4.16) to keep the reporting while paying the setup once — that combination is the honest resolution of the tension, and it is what the rule was groping toward.

# tests/test_one_claim.py
from cart import total_cents


def parse_order(line):
    order_id, total, currency = line.split(",")
    return {"id": int(order_id), "total_cents": int(total), "currency": currency}


def test_four_assertions_that_are_really_one_claim_split_badly():
    order = parse_order("7,650,GBP")

    # The first failure hides the other three, and the name says nothing.
    assert order["id"] == 7
    assert order["total_cents"] == 650
    assert order["currency"] == "GBP"
    assert set(order) == {"id", "total_cents", "currency"}


def test_the_same_claim_as_one_structural_assertion():
    # One assertion, one claim, and a failure diff that shows every wrong field.
    assert parse_order("7,650,GBP") == {
        "id": 7, "total_cents": 650, "currency": "GBP"}


def test_a_sequence_is_one_claim_even_with_three_assertions():
    cart = []
    assert total_cents(cart) == 0

    cart.append({"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2})
    assert total_cents(cart) == 500

    cart.append({"price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1})
    assert total_cents(cart) == 650

pytest -q tests/test_one_claim.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 0.96s

The test to apply in review is not "how many assertions is this" but: could this test have two different names? If yes, it is two tests. If the only honest name is one sentence, the assertions belong together.

3.15 t.plan and the Unfinished Test Assertion

A test that asserts nothing passes. So does a test whose assertions were never reached — the callback that never fired, the await that was forgotten, the loop over an empty list.

Node's answer is a plan count:

// test/plan.test.js
import test from 'node:test';

test('plan alone does NOT wait for a later callback', (t) => {
  t.plan(2);
  setTimeout(() => {
    t.assert.equal(1 + 1, 2);
    t.assert.equal(2 + 2, 4);
  }, 10);
});

test('await the asynchrony, and plan counts what really happened', async (t) => {
  t.plan(2);
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));
  t.assert.equal(1 + 1, 2);
  t.assert.equal(2 + 2, 4);
});

test('or give plan a wait budget of its own', (t) => {
  t.plan(2, { wait: 1000 });
  setTimeout(() => {
    t.assert.equal(1 + 1, 2);
    t.assert.equal(2 + 2, 4);
  }, 10);
});

test('an empty list would otherwise make this test vacuous', { plan: 2 }, (t) => {
  const results = [{ ok: true }, { ok: true }];

  for (const r of results) t.assert.ok(r.ok);
});

node --test 'test/plan.test.js'

✖ plan alone does NOT wait for a later callback (5.752549ms)
✔ await the asynchrony, and plan counts what really happened (50.610526ms)
✔ or give plan a wait budget of its own (12.033363ms)
✔ an empty list would otherwise make this test vacuous (5.604488ms)
ℹ tests 4
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 3
ℹ fail 1
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 737.757636

✖ failing tests:

test at test/plan.test.js:4:1
✖ plan alone does NOT wait for a later callback (5.752549ms)
  'plan expected 2 assertions but received 0'

Read the first two together, because the difference is the trap. t.plan(n) on its own does not wait: the test function returns, the plan is checked immediately, and the callback that would have made the two assertions has not run yet — so the test fails with plan expected 2 assertions but received 0. That is the correct outcome for a test whose asynchrony is unmanaged, and it is not what most people expect the feature to do.

The three working forms are: await the asynchrony yourself, so the assertions happen before the function returns; pass { wait: ms } to t.plan, which gives it a budget to wait for the count; or declare the count as a test option, { plan: 2 }, which is the tidiest form for a synchronous test.

A plan count converts two otherwise-silent successes into failures: the loop that iterated zero times, and — with wait or an await — the asynchronous callback that never ran.

The unfinished test assertion is the deliberate version of the same idea: a pytest.fail("not written yet") or a test.todo at the top of a test you have sketched but not implemented, so it reports as unfinished rather than passing vacuously.

pytest has no plan count. The equivalent habits are asserting on the collection rather than inside the loop — assert results == [...], which fails on an empty list — and a coverage or mutation check (§17) to find tests that assert nothing at all.

3.16 What This Section Established

  • pytest's assertion API is Python's expression language. No assertEqual vocabulary to learn or mis-choose.
  • Assertion rewriting is what makes that work, and it applies only to collected modules. A custom assertion in a helper module reports a bare AssertionError until pytest.register_assert_rewrite is called in conftest.py. python -O deletes assertions entirely, which is why assert must never be a production security check.
  • Floats need pytest.approx, whose tolerance is max(rel * expected, abs) with rel=1e-6 and abs=1e-12 — so against zero only that one-part-in-a-trillion absolute half survives, and 1e-9 is not approximately zero. Comparisons to zero need an abs= chosen from the domain. Money should not be a float at all.
  • pytest.raises without match= is weak, match is re.search on a regex, and .value is where the exception object lives — assert on structured attributes rather than prose.
  • RaisesGroup is exhaustive by default and RaisesExc is its single-exception building block, with match and an arbitrary check predicate.
  • "Equal" means five different things. A list is not a tuple, True == 1, Decimal("0.1") != 0.1, and comparing a naive datetime to an aware one raises rather than returning False. In JavaScript: toBe is Object.is, toEqual ignores undefined properties, toStrictEqual does not and checks the class, toMatchObject is a subset.
  • pytest.warns and deprecated_call mirror raises, and asserting that something does not warn is how a deprecation stays cleaned up.
  • Import node:assert/strict, never node:assert, and always await assert.rejects and expect(...).resolves — an un-awaited rejection assertion passes unconditionally.
  • Prefer the specific matcher to toBeTruthy, which inherits every coercion surprise in the language.
  • Soft assertions report every failure in one run; pytest's equivalents are subtests or a single structural comparison. Their risk is a cascade from the first failure, and the eager-test smell.
  • Asymmetric matchers assert the claim and ignore the scenery; expect.extend earns its place through its failure message.
  • Custom, delta and guard assertions move intent out of the test body — and a guard assertion blames the fixture instead of the code.
  • xfail is always strict=True. Watch for skip creep; -ra is the remedy.
  • "One claim per test", not one assertion. The review test is whether the test could have two different names.
  • t.plan catches the vacuous pass — a loop over an empty list, and a callback that never fired. But t.plan(n) alone does not wait for a later callback; use await, { wait: ms }, or the { plan: n } test option. In pytest, assert on the collection rather than inside the loop.

Exercises

1. Diagnose a useless failure.

A colleague's CI log says only E AssertionError with a traceback ending in helpers/api.py:42. Give the two most likely causes and the one-line fix for each. Then say what you would change so it cannot happen again in that repository.

2. Pick the equality.

For each, choose toBe, toEqual, toStrictEqual or toMatchObject and defend it: (a) a function returns a Date; (b) a JSON API response with a generated requestId; (c) a serialiser whose output must not contain undefined values; (d) a function that must return the same cached object on the second call; (e) a parser returning a class instance with three fields.

3. Write the exception assertions.

For withdraw in §3.4, write assertions for: the exception type; the message; the shortfall_cents attribute; that withdrawing exactly the balance does not raise; and that a float amount is refused. Which of these is a claim about behaviour and which is a claim about implementation?

4. Repair a float assertion.

def test_vat():
    assert calculate_vat(19.99, 0.2) == 3.998

Give three different repairs — one with approx, one that changes the assertion's claim, one that changes the production code — and say which you would ship.

5. Split or keep.

For each, say whether it is one claim or several, and rewrite if needed:

(a) a test asserting a created user has an id, an email, a hashed password and a created_at; (b) a test asserting a search returns 10 results, sorted by score, with the top result containing the query term; (c) a test asserting a state machine goes new → paid → shipped.

6. Make a vacuous test fail.

def test_all_invoices_are_balanced():
    for invoice in load_invoices():
        assert invoice.debits == invoice.credits

load_invoices() returns an empty list because of an unrelated bug. Give three different ways to make this test fail rather than pass, and rank them.

Solutions

1. Diagnose a useless failure.

Most likely: a custom assertion in a module pytest did not rewrite (§3.2). Fix: pytest.register_assert_rewrite("helpers.api") in the root conftest.py, before anything imports it.

Second: a bare assert with no message in production code that the test happened to trip. Fix: give it a message, or — better — replace it with a real exception, since python -O would delete it.

To prevent recurrence: register the whole test-helper package once in the root conftest.py, and add a review rule that a custom assertion always carries a message. The message is belt and braces — it survives even where rewriting does not.

2. Pick the equality.

(a) toEqual. Two Date objects with the same instant are structurally equal and not identical; toBe would fail. If the exact instant is the claim, toEqual(new Date('2026-03-01T00:00:00Z')).

(b) toEqual with asymmetric matchers, requestId: expect.any(String). toMatchObject is the lazier option and it silently stops checking the fields you omit, which is how an extra unexpected field ships.

(c) toStrictEqual. The presence of undefined is exactly the claim, and it is the one thing toEqual ignores.

(d) toBe. Identity is the claim — that is what caching means. This is the rare correct use.

(e) toStrictEqual. It checks the constructor, so a plain object with the same fields fails — which is what you want from a parser whose return type is part of its contract. toEqual would pass and hide the day the parser started returning plain objects.

3. Write the exception assertions.

with pytest.raises(InsufficientFunds, match=r"short by 500 cents") as caught:
    withdraw(1000, 1500)
assert caught.value.shortfall_cents == 500

assert withdraw(1000, 1000) == 0          # the boundary: exactly the balance

with pytest.raises(TypeError):
    withdraw(1000, 250.5)                  # only if the code refuses floats

The type, the attribute and the boundary are claims about behaviour — a caller can act on all three. The message text is closest to a claim about implementation: it is the field most likely to be reworded for reasons that have nothing to do with correctness, which is why shortfall_cents is the more durable assertion of the two.

The float case is the interesting one, because as written withdraw does not refuse a float — 250.5 > 1000 is False and it returns 749.5. So that test documents a decision that has not been made. Writing it forces the question, which is §4.6's argument.

4. Repair a float assertion.

assert calculate_vat(19.99, 0.2) == pytest.approx(3.998)        # 1
assert calculate_vat(19.99, 0.2) == pytest.approx(4.00, abs=0.005)  # 2
assert calculate_vat_cents(1999, 20) == 400                      # 3

The first makes the existing assertion pass and changes nothing else. The second changes the claim: VAT is a monetary amount rounded to the penny, so the meaningful assertion is about pennies, not about the fifteenth decimal place — and it will fail if the rounding rule changes, which the first will not.

The third changes the production code to hold money in integer cents, and it is what I would ship. The float assertion is not a testing problem; it is the test noticing that money is being held in a type that cannot represent it. pytest.approx on a currency value is a smell, and every repair that keeps the float is deferring the real fix.

5. Split or keep.

(a) One claim — "creating a user produces a complete record". One structural assertion with expect.any for the id and the timestamp, and a separate check that the password field is not the plaintext, which is a genuinely different claim (and a security one, so it deserves its own name).

(b) Three claims, and they should be three tests: the count is about pagination, the order is about ranking, and the relevance of the top result is about matching. Each can break for a completely different reason, and a combined failure tells you nothing about which.

(c) One claim. The sequence is the behaviour, and asserting the intermediate states is what makes it a test of the machine rather than of three unrelated transitions. Keep the three assertions in one test with a name that says so — test_an_order_goes_from_new_through_paid_to_shipped.

6. Make a vacuous test fail.

Assert on the collection first, which is the best answer:

invoices = load_invoices()
assert invoices, "no invoices were loaded"
for invoice in invoices:
    assert invoice.debits == invoice.credits

One line, no dependencies, and it is a guard assertion (§3.12) that blames the loader rather than the invoices.

Assert a count you know, assert len(invoices) == 12, which is stronger but couples the test to the fixture and will need editing whenever the fixture grows.

A plan count, if the runner has one (t.plan in node). Precise and expressive, and pytest does not offer it, so it is unavailable here.

Ranking: the guard first — cheapest, most general, no maintenance. The plan count second where it exists, because it catches the callback-never-fired case too, which the guard does not. The exact count last: it works, and it is the version most likely to be "fixed" by updating the number the next time it fails.

The general lesson is worth more than the three fixes: a loop with an assertion inside it makes a claim only if the loop runs, and nothing in the test says it must. That is one of the few defects mutation testing (§17) reliably finds and coverage does not.

SECTION 4

Choosing Test Cases

Section 1 established what a test claims and section 3 established how to state the claim. Neither answers the question that actually decides whether a suite is worth having: which inputs do you run it on?

That question has a bad default answer — "the ones I thought of while writing the code" — and the failure mode is specific. A developer who has just written a function tests it with the values that were in their head while writing it, which are precisely the values the code already handles. The suite goes green, the coverage report looks healthy, and the defect ships anyway, because it lives at an input nobody imagined.

Test case selection is a discipline with real technique behind it, most of it worked out in the 1970s and 1980s by people testing avionics and telephone switches, and almost none of it is expensive. This section is that technique: how to partition an infinite input space into a finite number of classes, why the interesting values are at the edges of those classes rather than in the middle, what to do when three parameters produce more combinations than you can afford, and — the half most courses skip — how to decide which tests are not worth writing.

The second half is mechanical: once you have a table of cases, pytest.mark.parametrize, subtests, test.each and test.for turn it into a suite where every row reports separately.

4.1 You Cannot Test Everything

Start by making the impossibility concrete, because the number is larger than intuition suggests.

Here is the function this section works on for most of its length. It prices a parcel: a weight band, a destination zone surcharge, and a flat express fee. All money is in cents (§1.1's reasoning about floats applies here too).

# shipping.py
ZONE_SURCHARGE = {"domestic": 0, "eu": 250, "world": 600}
EXPRESS_FEE = 450


def shipping_cost(weight_g, zone, express=False):
    """Price a parcel in cents."""
    if weight_g <= 0:
        raise ValueError("weight must be positive")
    if zone not in ZONE_SURCHARGE:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown zone: {zone!r}")

    if weight_g <= 100:
        band = 300
    elif weight_g <= 500:
        band = 500
    elif weight_g <= 2000:
        band = 900
    else:
        band = 1600

    return band + ZONE_SURCHARGE[zone] + (EXPRESS_FEE if express else 0)

As in §1.1, one line of configuration lets the tests import it:

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

Three parameters. How many inputs are there?

# count_inputs.py
zones = 3
express = 2
# A parcel weight in grams, as an integer, up to the 30 kg postal limit.
weights = 30_000

print(f"weights x zones x express = {weights * zones * express:,}")
print(f"at 10,000 cases per second: {weights * zones * express / 10_000:,.0f} seconds")
print(f"and that is only the *valid* weights; weight_g is an int, so the")
print(f"real domain includes every negative and every large integer too.")

python3 count_inputs.py

weights x zones x express = 180,000
at 10,000 cases per second: 18 seconds
and that is only the *valid* weights; weight_g is an int, so the
real domain includes every negative and every large integer too.

Eighteen seconds. That number is worth sitting with, because it says something more interesting than "exhaustive testing is impossible".

For this function, exhaustive testing over the valid weights is entirely affordable — you could run all 180,000 combinations on every commit and barely notice. What is not affordable is the other half of a test case: knowing the right answer for each one. Producing 180,000 expected values means either writing them by hand, which nobody will do, or computing them, which means re-implementing the function and testing nothing (§4.3). The barrier is almost never the running; it is the oracle.

Widen the domain slightly and the running becomes a barrier too. weight_g is an int, so the real domain includes every negative number and every integer Python can represent. A function of two 32-bit integers has 1.8 × 1019 inputs and, at a billion cases a second, finishes in about 585 years. A function taking a string has an infinite domain. Exhaustive testing is available for a byte, an enum, a small product of enums, and essentially nothing else.

So the whole game is choosing a small sample that behaves like the whole space, and doing it in a way that also gives you an answer to compare against. Everything in the first half of this section is a named technique for that, and they compose: you partition, you take the edges, you check the combinations that interact, and you stop.

4.2 Equivalence Classes

An equivalence class is a set of inputs you have reason to believe the code treats the same way. If that belief is right, one input from the class tests the whole class, and the other several billion members add nothing.

For shipping_cost, the weight parameter partitions cleanly, because the code says so — every if is a partition line drawn by the author:

weight ≤ 0
invalid — raises ValueError. One class, not two: 0 and -5000 take the same branch.
1 – 100 g
band 300
101 – 500 g
band 500
501 – 2000 g
band 900
2001 g and up
band 1600 — unbounded above, which is itself worth noticing

Five classes on weight, four zones (three valid, one "anything else"), two express values. That is 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 combinations, down from 180,000 — and most of those 40 do not interact, which §4.9 exploits to cut it to twelve.

Two rules make partitioning reliable rather than a guess.

Partition the output as well as the input. It is tempting to read the parameter list and stop. But shipping_cost has an output class you cannot see in the inputs: is there a weight at which the price decreases? (There is not, here — but "the price is monotonic in weight" is a claim, and §16 shows how to check it for every weight rather than five.) Partitioning by outcome catches classes that no single parameter defines.

Look for classes the code does not have, but the domain does. The postal service has a 30 kg limit; shipping_cost does not. A 40 kg parcel returns 1600 + surcharge quite happily. That is either a missing validation or a deliberate decision, and the only way it comes up is by partitioning the problem rather than the implementation. A partition derived only from reading the code can never find a missing branch — it can only confirm the branches that exist, which is the same blind spot as writing tests from coverage (§17).

4.3 The Oracle Problem

Choosing an input is half a test case. The other half is knowing what the right answer is, and that half has a name: the test oracle is whatever tells you the observed output is correct.

The oracle problem is that for a great many interesting inputs, no cheap oracle exists. You can run a spell-checker on a million words; you cannot cheaply know which corrections are right. You can render a page at 3,000 widths; you cannot cheaply know which look correct.

There are five oracles worth naming, in rough order of how much they cost and how much they prove.

a literal value
assert shipping_cost(100, "domestic") == 300. Cheapest, strongest, and available only where you can work the answer out by hand.
a property
"the price never decreases as weight increases." Weaker per case, but holds for every input, which is why §16 exists.
a reference implementation
a slow, obviously-correct version to compare against. Powerful and rare; §16.7 uses one.
a previous run
snapshot testing (§14). Detects change and proves nothing about correctness — it will happily pin a bug in place.
a human
exploratory testing (§20). The only oracle for "does this look right", and it does not run in CI.

The failure this framing prevents is the most common bad test in existence: computing the expected value with the same expression the implementation uses.

# tests/test_oracle.py
from shipping import shipping_cost, ZONE_SURCHARGE, EXPRESS_FEE


def test_useless_because_it_reimplements_the_code():
    weight, zone, express = 750, "eu", True
    band = 900  # copied from the implementation's own ladder
    expected = band + ZONE_SURCHARGE[zone] + (EXPRESS_FEE if express else 0)

    assert shipping_cost(weight, zone, express) == expected


def test_useful_because_the_number_was_computed_by_a_human():
    # 750 g is in the 501-2000 band (900), to the EU (+250), express (+450).
    assert shipping_cost(750, "eu", express=True) == 1600

Both pass. The first cannot fail for any change to the ladder, the surcharge table or the fee, because it re-derives its expectation from the same tables; the only defect it can catch is a change to the + in the last line. The second is a genuine claim about the system, arrived at independently, and it will fail the moment any of those three numbers changes without a decision behind it.

The rule of thumb: if the expected value in a test could be produced by running the code, the test is not an oracle. Write the number down. Where you cannot write the number down, that is a signal to reach for a property instead, not a licence to re-implement.

To have in hand before moving on: test oracle.

4.4 Boundary Value Analysis

Equivalence classes tell you which inputs to sample. Boundary value analysis tells you where in the class to sample, and the answer is: at the edges, because that is where the defects are.

The reason is not folklore. Off-by-one errors are the most common arithmetic mistake in programming, and every one of them lives exactly at a class boundary: < written where <= was meant moves the boundary by one and leaves every other input in the class untouched. A test at 250 g cannot detect a boundary that has moved from 100 to 101. A test at 100 g detects it immediately.

0
error
1
300
…interior, tested once…
100
300
101
500
…interior…
500
500
501
900

The technique, stated precisely: for each boundary, test the value on each side of it. For an integer domain that is b and b + 1. Some texts add a third value inside the class; that third value is the one that earns least, and if you are choosing what to drop, drop it.

shipping_cost has four boundaries on weight — 0/1, 100/101, 500/501, 2000/2001 — which is eight values, and they are worth far more than eighty random weights. Here is the difference, made concrete against a planted defect.

# shipping_broken.py
"""Identical to shipping.py apart from one comparison operator."""
ZONE_SURCHARGE = {"domestic": 0, "eu": 250, "world": 600}
EXPRESS_FEE = 450


def shipping_cost(weight_g, zone, express=False):
    if weight_g <= 0:
        raise ValueError("weight must be positive")
    if zone not in ZONE_SURCHARGE:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown zone: {zone!r}")

    if weight_g < 100:          # <-- was <=
        band = 300
    elif weight_g <= 500:
        band = 500
    elif weight_g <= 2000:
        band = 900
    else:
        band = 1600

    return band + ZONE_SURCHARGE[zone] + (EXPRESS_FEE if express else 0)

# tests/test_boundaries.py
import pytest

from shipping_broken import shipping_cost

MIDPOINTS = [(50, 300), (300, 500), (1200, 900), (5000, 1600)]
BOUNDARIES = [(1, 300), (100, 300), (101, 500), (500, 500),
              (501, 900), (2000, 900), (2001, 1600)]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("weight,expected", MIDPOINTS)
def test_a_comfortable_value_from_the_middle_of_each_band(weight, expected):
    assert shipping_cost(weight, "domestic") == expected


@pytest.mark.parametrize("weight,expected", BOUNDARIES)
def test_each_side_of_each_boundary(weight, expected):
    assert shipping_cost(weight, "domestic") == expected

pytest -q --tb=line tests/test_boundaries.py

.....F.....                                                              [100%]
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
E   AssertionError: assert 500 == 300
     +  where 500 = shipping_cost(100, 'domestic')
/project/tests/test_boundaries.py:18: AssertionError: assert 500 == 300
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_boundaries.py::test_each_side_of_each_boundary[100-300] - A...
1 failed, 10 passed in 2.76s

Four midpoint tests, seven boundary tests, one defect. The midpoints — including the one at 50 g, sitting inside the very band whose edge moved — pass without complaint. Exactly one test fails, and its name and parameter say which weight and which number.

Two extensions of the idea are worth having.

Boundaries exist on things that are not numbers. The empty string and the one-character string are boundaries. A list of length 0 and 1 are boundaries (§4.5). The first and last day of a month, the first and last element of a page of results, the maximum length of a database column, the moment a token expires. Any time a domain has an ordering, it has edges.

A boundary you cannot reach from the input is still a boundary. 2**31 - 1 matters if a downstream system stores the value in a 32-bit column; 2**53 matters if it is ever serialised to JSON and read by JavaScript, where it stops being exactly representable. Those boundaries are properties of the pipeline, not of the function, and no amount of reading the function reveals them.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: off-by-one.

4.5 The Cases Everyone Forgets

Beyond the boundaries a specific function defines, there is a standing list of inputs that break code across every language and domain. Run it as a checklist; it costs a minute and it finds things.

Take a second function, deliberately chosen because it takes a collection:

# stats.py
def median(values):
    """The middle value; the mean of the middle two when the count is even."""
    if not values:
        raise ValueError("median of no values")
    ordered = sorted(values)
    mid = len(ordered) // 2
    if len(ordered) % 2:
        return ordered[mid]
    return (ordered[mid - 1] + ordered[mid]) / 2
the empty case
[], "", {}, zero rows. The single most productive test input in existence. Ask what it should do before asking what it does.
the single-element case
Breaks anything that compares neighbours, takes a difference, or assumes a "rest".
the duplicate case
Two equal values. Breaks anything backed by a set, a dict keyed on the value, or an unstable sort.
the even/odd case
Any code with a // 2 in it has two behaviours, and one of them is usually written second and less carefully.
the already-ordered case
And the reverse-ordered one. They are the best and worst cases of most algorithms, and they hide a missing sort entirely.
the aliasing case
The same object passed as two arguments; the input handed back as the output. Catches mutation the caller did not ask for.

Applied to median, that checklist writes itself, and one entry on it finds something the others do not:

# tests/test_median.py
import pytest

from stats import median


def test_the_empty_case_is_an_error_rather_than_a_wrong_answer():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="no values"):
        median([])


def test_the_single_element_case_is_that_element():
    assert median([7]) == 7


def test_an_even_count_takes_the_mean_of_the_middle_two():
    assert median([1, 2, 3, 4]) == 2.5


def test_an_odd_count_takes_the_middle_one():
    assert median([1, 2, 3]) == 2


def test_duplicates_are_not_collapsed():
    # A set-backed implementation gives 2 here; the count is 5, not 3.
    assert median([1, 1, 1, 1, 9]) == 1


def test_the_input_is_not_reordered_in_place():
    values = [3, 1, 2]
    median(values)
    assert values == [3, 1, 2]


def test_a_reverse_ordered_input_gives_the_same_answer():
    assert median([9, 5, 1]) == median([1, 5, 9]) == 5

pytest -q tests/test_median.py

.......                                                                  [100%]
7 passed in 2.64s

All seven pass, which makes two of them look like a waste. They are not, and the reason is worth internalising: test_the_input_is_not_reordered_in_place passes because of a decision in the implementation — sorted(values) builds a new list where values.sort() would have mutated the caller's. That is a genuine claim about the contract, and it is one line away from being false. test_duplicates_are_not_collapsed is the same shape: it passes now, and it is the test that fails the day someone "optimises" the function with set(values).

A test that passes today and pins a decision that could plausibly be reversed tomorrow is earning its keep. A test that could only fail if the language broke is not (§4.11).

In summary, the vocabulary here is the empty case, the single-element case and the duplicate case.

4.6 Negative Tests and the Sad Path

The happy path is the input the feature was built for. The sad path is everything the feature has to survive: bad input, missing input, a collaborator that fails, a permission the caller does not have.

A negative test asserts on the sad path — that the code refuses, and refuses in a specific way. It is not the same as an absence of a positive test, and the distinction matters because the most common defect class in production is not "the feature computes the wrong number" but "the feature accepted something it should have rejected and then computed a number about it".

shipping_cost has two guards, and both deserve a test that pins the manner of failure and not merely its presence:

# tests/test_negative.py
import pytest

from shipping import shipping_cost


@pytest.mark.parametrize("weight", [0, -1, -5000])
def test_a_non_positive_weight_is_refused(weight):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="must be positive"):
        shipping_cost(weight, "domestic")


def test_an_unknown_zone_names_the_zone_it_did_not_recognise():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="moon"):
        shipping_cost(500, "moon")


def test_a_zone_is_matched_exactly_and_not_case_insensitively():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        shipping_cost(500, "Domestic")

pytest -q tests/test_negative.py

.....                                                                    [100%]
5 passed in 0.79s

The third test is the interesting one, because it does not describe a defect — it describes a decision. "Domestic" being rejected may be right or wrong, but it is currently true and nothing else in the suite says so. Writing it down converts an accident of implementation into a documented behaviour, which is the whole of §1.10's argument about tests as documentation. If the team later decides zones should be case-insensitive, exactly one test fails, and its name explains what is being changed rather than what is broken.

Two cautions.

pytest.raises without match= is a weak assertion. with pytest.raises(ValueError) passes for any ValueError raised anywhere in the block, including one raised by a typo in the test's own setup. §3.6 has the full argument; the short version is that the exception type is rarely specific enough on its own.

A negative test asserting on a message string couples you to that string. match="must be positive" will break if the message is reworded. That is a real cost, and the answer is to match on the stable part — a code, an error class, a keyword the user would search for — rather than the whole sentence.

What to carry forward from this subsection: tests as documentation and happy path.

4.7 Right-BICEP and CORRECT

Two mnemonics from Pragmatic Unit Testing condense most of what is above into something you can run through in thirty seconds while looking at a function. They are not theory; they are a checklist against forgetting.

Right-BICEP asks what to test:

Right
Are the results right at all? The happy path, with an oracle you computed rather than copied.
Boundary
Each side of each edge (§4.4), plus the CORRECT list below.
Inverse
Can you check by going backwards? Parse then serialise; encrypt then decrypt. This is §16.5's round-trip property.
Cross-check
Compute it a second, independent way — a slow reference implementation, or a different library.
Error conditions
The sad path (§4.6): full disks, dropped connections, refused input.
Performance
Only as a threshold — "under a second", never "under 340 ms". §18 explains why a tight timing assertion is a flaky test by construction.

The CORRECT acronym asks where the boundaries are, and it is the more useful of the two because the CORRECT acronym names boundary categories that a purely numeric reading misses. Applied to shipping_cost and median:

Conformance
Does the value have the right shape? A zone string that is not one of three; an email with no @.
Ordering
Sorted, reversed, shuffled. median must not care; a paginated query must.
Range
Within the type but outside the sense: a weight of 109 grams, an age of 700.
Reference
What does the code assume exists outside itself? A logged-in user, a populated table, an env var.
Existence
None, empty, zero, missing, absent. The empty case from §4.5, generalised.
Cardinality
The 0-1-many rule: zero, one, many — and "exactly the page size", and "one more than the page size".
Time
Order of events, timeouts, timezones, month ends, leap days, the clock going backwards. §8 makes this testable at all.

Cardinality's 0-1-many rule deserves its own note because it generalises: for any quantity, test none of it, one of it, and several — and then whatever number your own system treats specially. A page size of 20 makes 19, 20 and 21 boundaries, and the bug is almost always at 21.

The term above, for reference: what to test.

4.8 Decision Tables

Once more than one input decides the outcome, the technique changes. A decision table lists the conditions down one side and the resulting action across the top, and its value is that writing it out exposes rules nobody stated.

Take a rule with three conditions: free shipping applies when the order is over £50, unless the parcel is heavy, and always for members.

# freeship.py
def free_shipping(order_cents, weight_g, is_member):
    if is_member:
        return True
    if weight_g > 2000:
        return False
    return order_cents >= 5000

Three booleans give eight rows, which is small enough to write out in full:

# member heavy order ≥ £50 free? note
1 yes yes yes yes membership wins outright
2 yes yes no yes “
3 yes no yes yes “
4 yes no no yes “
5 no yes yes no heavy blocks it even at £50
6 no yes no no
7 no no yes yes the ordinary qualifying case
8 no no no no

Two things fall out of the table that reading the code does not make obvious.

Rows 1–4 are one rule, not four. When is_member is true, the other two conditions are don't-cares, and a decision table normally collapses them into a single row marked —. That collapse is exactly the information a test suite needs: one test for membership, not four. But note the direction of the reasoning — the collapse is justified by the specification, and the test at row 2 is the one that would catch an implementation which checked weight first.

Row 5 is where the disagreement lives. Is a heavy £80 order really not free? The table forces someone to answer, and in practice this is where a decision table earns most of its keep: it is a requirements tool that happens to produce test cases. The eight rows took two minutes and produced one question for the product owner, which is a better return than most testing activities offer.

Once agreed, the table transcribes directly into a parametrized test (§4.12), one row per line, in the same order as the table, so the two can be read side by side.

4.9 Pairwise Testing

Three conditions gave eight rows. shipping_cost's five weight classes, four zone classes and two express values give forty, and a realistic configuration screen with ten checkboxes gives 1,024. This is the combinatorial explosion, and it is the point at which "test every combination" stops being available.

Pairwise testing — also called all-pairs — rests on an empirical observation: most defects that depend on a combination depend on a combination of two factors, not three or more. So instead of covering every combination, cover every pair of values from every pair of factors. The reduction is dramatic and it grows with the number of factors: ten booleans need 1,024 tests exhaustively, and eight for all pairs.

For weight × zone × express, the arithmetic is worth doing rather than asserting. Here is a hand-built table, and a check that it really covers what it claims:

# pairwise.py
import itertools

WEIGHTS = ["tiny", "light", "medium", "heavy"]
ZONES = ["domestic", "eu", "world"]
EXPRESS = [False, True]

# All 12 weight-zone combinations (that many are forced: 4 x 3 pairs must all
# appear), with express chosen so that each weight and each zone sees both
# values.
CASES = [
    ("tiny", "domestic", False), ("tiny", "eu", True), ("tiny", "world", False),
    ("light", "domestic", True), ("light", "eu", False), ("light", "world", True),
    ("medium", "domestic", False), ("medium", "eu", True), ("medium", "world", True),
    ("heavy", "domestic", True), ("heavy", "eu", False), ("heavy", "world", False),
]

FACTORS = [WEIGHTS, ZONES, EXPRESS]


def pairs_of(rows):
    """Every (factor_i, factor_j, value_i, value_j) a set of rows covers."""
    found = set()
    for row in rows:
        for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(FACTORS)), 2):
            found.add((i, j, row[i], row[j]))
    return found


everything = list(itertools.product(*FACTORS))
required = pairs_of(everything)
covered = pairs_of(CASES)

print(f"exhaustive: {len(everything)} cases")
print(f"pairwise:   {len(CASES)} cases")
print(f"pairs that exist: {len(required)}")
print(f"pairs covered:    {len(covered)}")
print(f"missing:          {sorted(required - covered)}")

python3 pairwise.py

exhaustive: 24 cases
pairwise:   12 cases
pairs that exist: 26
pairs covered:    26
missing:          []

Twelve cases instead of twenty-four, with every pair of values still exercised. Twelve is also the floor: the four weight classes and three zones alone force twelve rows, so no smaller covering table exists for these factors.

On this example the saving is unimpressive — halving — because three factors is barely an explosion. The scaling is the point. Adding further two-valued factors, with the same greedy search run over the same code, gives exhaustive counts of 48, 96 and 192 against a pairwise count that stays at twelve every time: the extra factors fit into the columns of a table whose height is already decided by the two largest factors. That is the shape of the technique — exhaustive testing grows multiplicatively, pairwise grows barely at all.

Three limits, stated plainly, because pairwise is oversold:

It finds two-factor interactions only. A defect that needs three specific values together will be missed, and such defects exist. The technique is a cost-benefit trade, not a proof.

The generated table has no idea what matters. A pairwise generator will happily drop the one combination your domain expert knows is dangerous. The fix is to pin the cases you care about first and generate the rest around them — every real tool supports seeding rows.

It composes badly with boundaries. Pairwise operates on classes; boundary analysis operates on values. Feeding all eight boundary weights into a pairwise generator is a category error that produces a large table with no more information in it. Choose one representative per class for the pairwise pass, and test boundaries separately against a single fixed set of other parameters, which is exactly what §4.4's test file does.

One to keep in hand: combinatorial explosion.

4.10 Risk-Based Testing

Every technique so far generates cases. None of them says how many of the generated cases you should actually write, and that question has a real answer: spend effort in proportion to risk, where risk is roughly the probability of a defect multiplied by the cost of one.

The two multiplicands come from different places.

Probability comes from history and from structure. Defects cluster: the modules that had bugs last quarter are where next quarter's bugs are, which is one of the most reproducible findings in software engineering. Structure adds to it — code with many branches, code touched by several people at once, code recently changed under time pressure, code at the seam between two systems, code that does arithmetic on money or dates.

Cost comes from the domain, not from engineering. A wrong shipping price is a support ticket. A wrong charge is a refund and possibly a regulator. A wrong password comparison is a breach. These differ by orders of magnitude and no amount of code reading reveals them.

The practical form is a short conversation, not a spreadsheet. For the shipping module: the ladder is arithmetic on money that a product owner changes quarterly (high probability, high cost — test every boundary), the zone lookup is a dict (low probability, high cost — test the unknown-zone path and stop), and the express flag is a boolean add (low, low — one test).

The useful corollary is that risk-based testing licenses you to test some things badly on purpose. That is not a concession; it is the only way the effort lands where it matters. A suite that tests everything to the same depth has, in effect, decided that a typo in a log message deserves the same attention as a rounding error in a total.

4.11 Which Tests Earn Their Keep

Section 1.10 argued that an unexecuted test is worse than no test. This is the stronger claim: a test that runs and passes can still be a net loss, because every test has a cost that is paid forever — it runs on every commit, it must be read when it fails, and it must be changed when the code around it changes.

A test earns its keep when it can plausibly fail for a reason you would want to know about. Run a candidate test through two questions:

  1. What change would make this fail? If the honest answer is "a change that could not happen" or "any change at all", the test is not earning.
  2. If it failed, would I be glad it existed? If the answer is "I would delete it", delete it now.

Four categories fail those questions consistently.

Testing trivial code, which is the first entry on any honest list of what not to test. A getter that returns a field, a constructor that assigns three arguments, a dataclass's __eq__. The only defect these can have is a typo, which the first real test that uses them will surface anyway. Note the qualifier: a getter that returns self._first + " " + self._last is not trivial, and a getter that lazily initialises is not trivial by a wide margin.

Testing the framework. A test asserting that SQLAlchemy stores what you told it to store, or that Pydantic rejects a string where an int was declared, is testing someone else's library on your CI budget. Your test should start where your code starts. The exception is real: when you have configured the library in a way you are not certain of — a cascade rule, a custom validator, a serialisation format — the test is testing your configuration, and it earns its keep.

A test whose double does all the work. mock.return_value = 5; assert thing.get() == 5 proves that unittest.mock works. §7 has the full treatment, and this is the shape to watch for: if every collaborator is a double and the SUT only forwards, the test asserts that you wired up the mocks correctly and nothing else.

A test with no assertion. It passes unless the code raises. These are not always worthless — a smoke test asserting only "this does not blow up" is a real, cheap test — but they must be deliberate, and §17.9 shows the coverage report treating one as full coverage.

Against that, three shapes almost always earn their keep, and are systematically under-written:

  • The test that pins a decision — test_a_zone_is_matched_exactly from §4.6. It documents a choice that is otherwise invisible.
  • The test written from a defect report (§9). By construction it fails for a reason that has already happened once in production, which is the strongest evidence available that it can happen.
  • The test whose claim does not depend on a particular input — the sum-preservation test in §1's exercises, the properties of §16. One such test typically subsumes a dozen example-based ones.

The failure mode this section is guarding against is not "too few tests". It is a suite of 4,000 tests that takes eleven minutes, breaks on every refactor, and would not have caught the last three production incidents. That suite is expensive and weak, and it got that way one unexamined test at a time.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: what not to test and testing trivial code.

4.12 From Table to Test: pytest.mark.parametrize

Everything above produces a table. pytest.mark.parametrize turns a table into one test per row, which is the difference between a data-driven test and a loop.

The loop version is the thing to avoid, and it is worth seeing why:

# tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py
import pytest

from shipping import shipping_cost

CASES = [
    (1, "domestic", False, 300),
    (100, "domestic", False, 300),
    (101, "eu", False, 750),
    (2000, "world", False, 1500),
    (2001, "world", True, 2650),
]


def test_the_whole_table_in_one_test():
    for weight, zone, express, expected in CASES:
        assert shipping_cost(weight, zone, express) == expected


@pytest.mark.parametrize("weight,zone,express,expected", CASES)
def test_one_test_per_row(weight, zone, express, expected):
    assert shipping_cost(weight, zone, express) == expected

pytest -q tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py
pytest --collect-only -q tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py

......                                                                   [100%]
6 passed in 0.99s
tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py::test_the_whole_table_in_one_test
tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py::test_one_test_per_row[1-domestic-False-300]
tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py::test_one_test_per_row[100-domestic-False-300]
tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py::test_one_test_per_row[101-eu-False-750]
tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py::test_one_test_per_row[2000-world-False-1500]
tests/test_loop_vs_parametrize.py::test_one_test_per_row[2001-world-True-2650]

6 tests collected in 0.67s

Five tests from one decorated function, and the collection listing shows what the loop version costs by comparison: the whole table is one test. Three consequences follow, all of them practical.

The loop stops at the first failure. If row 2 fails, rows 3, 4 and 5 never run, so you learn about one defect where there might be three. This is assertion roulette (§19.4) in its purest form.

The loop cannot be selected. pytest -k "2001" runs the failing row of the parametrized version and nothing else. There is no way to ask the loop for its third iteration.

The loop's failure does not say which row. The traceback points at the assert inside the loop, which is the same line for every row; you must read weight out of the variables display. The parametrized version puts the row in the test's name.

The parameter names go in one string — "weight,zone,express,expected" — or a list of strings; both are accepted and the string form is the convention. The argument values are any iterable of tuples, which means the table can come from a constant (as here), a function, or a file read at collection time.

The term this subsection introduced: data-driven test.

4.13 pytest.param, ids, and Failure Names That Locate

The generated ids in that collection listing were test_one_test_per_row[1-domestic-False-300] and so on: pytest builds an id from the values when it can. That works for numbers, strings and booleans and degrades badly for anything else — a dict, an object, or a long string becomes expected0, expected1, which locates nothing.

pytest.param fixes that, and does two other jobs at the same time.

# tests/test_ids.py
import pytest

from shipping import shipping_cost

@pytest.mark.parametrize("weight,expected", [
    pytest.param(1, 300, id="lightest-possible-parcel"),
    pytest.param(100, 300, id="top-of-the-first-band"),
    pytest.param(101, 500, id="bottom-of-the-second-band"),
    pytest.param(30_001, 3000, id="over-the-30kg-postal-limit",
                 marks=pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True,
                                         reason="an oversize band is agreed, not built")),
    pytest.param(2001, 1600, id=pytest.HIDDEN_PARAM),
])
def test_weight_bands(weight, expected):
    assert shipping_cost(weight, "domestic") == expected

pytest --collect-only -q tests/test_ids.py
pytest -q -ra tests/test_ids.py

tests/test_ids.py::test_weight_bands[lightest-possible-parcel]
tests/test_ids.py::test_weight_bands[top-of-the-first-band]
tests/test_ids.py::test_weight_bands[bottom-of-the-second-band]
tests/test_ids.py::test_weight_bands[over-the-30kg-postal-limit]
tests/test_ids.py::test_weight_bands

5 tests collected in 0.77s
...x.                                                                    [100%]
=========================== short test summary info ============================
XFAIL tests/test_ids.py::test_weight_bands[over-the-30kg-postal-limit] - an oversize band is agreed, not built
4 passed, 1 xfailed in 1.12s

Three features, each of which changes what the report tells you.

Parametrize ids: id= replaces the generated name with a sentence. Good parametrize ids are the difference between a report that locates a defect and one that requires opening the file. test_weight_bands[top-of-the-first-band] in a CI log is a defect report; test_weight_bands[100-300] requires opening the file. Ids must be unique within the test, and pytest will make them unique by appending a number if they are not, which is a signal that two rows are the same case.

marks= attaches a mark to one row. Here xfail documents a known gap — the 30 kg limit from §4.2 — as an executable note rather than a comment. strict=True matters: without it, a row that starts passing stays silently green as XPASS, and with it, an unexpected pass fails the suite, which is what you want from a note that says "this is not implemented yet". The same mechanism attaches skipif for platform-specific rows and slow for rows you deselect locally.

pytest.HIDDEN_PARAM removes the id entirely. The last row collects as bare test_weight_bands, with no brackets at all, sitting in the listing alongside four bracketed siblings — which is precisely why the example puts it there. It is new in pytest 9 and it has exactly one good use: a parametrized test that currently has a single row, where the bracketed id is noise and would churn every id in the file the day someone adds a second. Used on one row of several, as here, it produces a name that looks like the whole test rather than one case of it.

4.14 Stacked and Indirect Parametrization

Two extensions cover most of what remains.

Stacked parametrize produces a cross product. Stacking two parametrize marks runs every combination of their rows. This is the combinatorial explosion of §4.9 available as a one-line mistake, and it is also the clearest way to express a genuine cross product when you want one:

# tests/test_stacked.py
import pytest

from shipping import shipping_cost

@pytest.mark.parametrize("express", [False, True])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("zone", ["domestic", "eu", "world"])
def test_every_zone_and_express_combination_is_priced(zone, express):
    # The claim is only that a price exists and is positive; the exact
    # numbers are pinned by the boundary tests in §4.4.
    assert shipping_cost(500, zone, express) > 0

pytest --collect-only -q tests/test_stacked.py

tests/test_stacked.py::test_every_zone_and_express_combination_is_priced[domestic-False]
tests/test_stacked.py::test_every_zone_and_express_combination_is_priced[domestic-True]
tests/test_stacked.py::test_every_zone_and_express_combination_is_priced[eu-False]
tests/test_stacked.py::test_every_zone_and_express_combination_is_priced[eu-True]
tests/test_stacked.py::test_every_zone_and_express_combination_is_priced[world-False]
tests/test_stacked.py::test_every_zone_and_express_combination_is_priced[world-True]

6 tests collected in 0.80s

Two marks, six tests. Note the ordering in the generated ids: the mark closest to the function varies slowest, which is the opposite of what most people predict, and is worth knowing when you are reading a list of forty ids looking for a pattern.

Indirect parametrization sends the parameter to a fixture instead of the test. The test then receives whatever the fixture built from it. This is the tool for "run this test against three differently-configured versions of the same thing", and it is the bridge between this section and §5:

# tests/test_indirect.py
import pytest

from shipping import shipping_cost


@pytest.fixture
def parcel(request):
    """Builds a parcel from a shorthand name. Receives the parameter itself."""
    weight = {"letter": 50, "book": 800, "crate": 9000}[request.param]
    return {"weight_g": weight, "zone": "eu"}


@pytest.mark.parametrize("parcel", ["letter", "book", "crate"], indirect=True)
def test_every_parcel_shape_is_priced_above_the_zone_surcharge(parcel):
    assert shipping_cost(parcel["weight_g"], parcel["zone"]) > 250

pytest --collect-only -q tests/test_indirect.py
pytest -q tests/test_indirect.py

tests/test_indirect.py::test_every_parcel_shape_is_priced_above_the_zone_surcharge[crate]

The mechanism is request.param, and it is the only way a fixture can see a parametrized value. Three details decide whether this is clearer than the direct form or worse:

  • indirect=True sends every named parameter to a fixture of that name; indirect=["parcel"] sends only that one, which is what you want when a test takes both a fixture-built object and a plain expected value.
  • The ids come from the parameter, not the built object — [letter], [book], [crate] — which is exactly why the shorthand strings are worth using.
  • If no fixture of that name exists, the error is a fixture-lookup failure at setup, not a parametrize error, which is a confusing first encounter.

Use it when the parameter needs work done to it — a database populated differently, a config file written, a client built against three backends. For a plain value, the direct form is shorter and reads better.

To have in hand before moving on: stacked parametrize and request.param.

4.15 test.each and test.for

Vitest has the same idea in two spellings, and the difference between them is not cosmetic.

// shipping.js
export const ZONE_SURCHARGE = { domestic: 0, eu: 250, world: 600 };
export const EXPRESS_FEE = 450;

export function shippingCost(weightG, zone, express = false) {
  if (weightG <= 0) throw new RangeError('weight must be positive');
  if (!(zone in ZONE_SURCHARGE)) throw new RangeError(`unknown zone: ${zone}`);

  let band;
  if (weightG <= 100) band = 300;
  else if (weightG <= 500) band = 500;
  else if (weightG <= 2000) band = 900;
  else band = 1600;

  return band + ZONE_SURCHARGE[zone] + (express ? EXPRESS_FEE : 0);
}

// shipping.test.js
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { shippingCost } from './shipping.js';

const BOUNDARIES = [
  { weight: 1, expected: 300 },
  { weight: 100, expected: 300 },
  { weight: 101, expected: 500 },
  { weight: 500, expected: 500 },
  { weight: 501, expected: 900 },
  { weight: 2000, expected: 900 },
  { weight: 2001, expected: 1600 },
];

test.each(BOUNDARIES)('$weight g costs $expected', ({ weight, expected }) => {
  expect(shippingCost(weight, 'domestic')).toBe(expected);
});

test.each([
  [0, 'domestic'],
  [-1, 'eu'],
])('a weight of %i is refused for %s', (weight, zone) => {
  expect(() => shippingCost(weight, zone)).toThrow(/must be positive/);
});

test.for(BOUNDARIES)('for: $weight g', ({ weight, expected }, { expect }) => {
  expect(shippingCost(weight, 'domestic')).toBe(expected);
});

The title is a template. $weight and $expected interpolate properties of an object case; %i, %s, %d, %f, %j and %# (the index) are printf-style placeholders for positional cases. Between them they do the job pytest.param(id=...) does, and the same argument applies — a title that names the case is the difference between a readable CI log and a line number hunt.

test.each spreads an array case into separate arguments; test.for does not. Given [[1, 3], [2, 4]], an each callback receives (a, b) while a for callback receives the whole array as its first argument. That is the one thing to remember about the pair, because it silently changes what your parameters mean.

test.for passes the test context as a second argument, which is where its scoped expect comes from. That scoped expect is the one you want for toMatchSnapshot inside a table-driven test, because it carries the case's own name into the snapshot key — with the global expect, every row writes to the same snapshot and they overwrite each other.

There is no equivalent in node:test; the idiomatic form there is an ordinary for loop around t.test(...), which is genuinely a subtest (§4.16) rather than the flat separate tests these two produce.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: table-driven test.

4.16 subtests

Parametrization happens at collection time: pytest must know the rows before the run starts. Sometimes you do not — the rows come from a file the fixture just downloaded, or from iterating a data structure the test itself built. The loop comes back, and with it the first-failure-stops-everything problem.

subtests is the answer, and as of pytest 9 it is built in rather than a plugin:

# tests/test_subtests.py
def test_every_word_in_the_list_is_a_palindrome(subtests):
    words = ["level", "rotor", "python", "civic"]

    for word in words:
        with subtests.test(msg="palindrome", word=word):
            assert word == word[::-1]

pytest -q -ra tests/test_subtests.py

subtests = <_pytest.subtests.Subtests object at 0x7d42e82cb290>

        words = ["level", "rotor", "python", "civic"]

        for word in words:

>               assert word == word[::-1]
