E
E                 - nohtyp
E                 + python

tests/test_subtests.py:7: AssertionError
_________________ test_every_word_in_the_list_is_a_palindrome __________________
contains 1 failed subtest
=========================== short test summary info ============================
SUBFAILED[palindrome] (word='python') tests/test_subtests.py::test_every_word_in_the_list_is_a_palindrome
FAILED tests/test_subtests.py::test_every_word_in_the_list_is_a_palindrome - ...
2 failed, 3 subtests passed in 1.76s

Read the report carefully, because it has a shape nothing else in pytest produces.

The failing word is reported with its parameters in the heading — the block's keyword arguments become part of the identification, which is why word=word is worth passing rather than relying on the message alone. The loop continues past the failure, so civic is still checked. And the run ends with two failures for one test function: a SUBFAILED entry for the specific subtest, and a FAILED entry for the enclosing test whose reason is contains 1 failed subtest. The counts in the summary line separate the two populations — passed tests and passed subtests are counted independently.

SubtestReport is the report object behind that; it matters if you are writing a plugin or parsing JUnit XML in CI (§20), where subtests appear as their own entries.

When to use which:

  • Known at collection time → parametrize. The rows appear in --collect-only, can be selected with -k, can be deselected with marks, and can be sharded across workers. None of that is true of subtests, which are invisible until the test runs.
  • Discovered at run time → subtests. Iterating files in a directory the fixture created, or checking every row a query returned.
  • A genuinely single claim with several facets → neither. Use one test with a good assertion, or expect.soft / a soft assertion (§3.10).

In summary, the vocabulary here is SubtestReport and junit xml in ci.

4.17 Naming Tests So the Report Reads Itself

Every technique above ends in a name, and the name is what a colleague will actually read at 2 a.m.

An intent revealing name states the claim, not the mechanics. A test naming convention is worth agreeing once and applying everywhere, because an intent revealing name is what a colleague reads before anything else. The test in §4.5 is called test_the_input_is_not_reordered_in_place, and that sentence is the whole of what it does; test_median_2 would have required reading the body. The reliable structure is subject – condition – expected outcome, and the reliable smoke test for a name is whether it could be pasted into a specification document without editing.

Three spellings of the test naming convention are common; any of them is fine, and consistency matters more than the choice:

  • test_<method>_<condition>_<outcome> — test_shipping_cost_over_2000g_uses_the_heaviest_band
  • should_<outcome>_when_<condition> — should_refuse_a_negative_weight
  • Nested describe/it in JavaScript, where the enclosing block supplies the subject and the title supplies only the rest — describe('shippingCost', ...) with it('refuses a negative weight', ...).

Four failure modes to avoid, all of them common:

A name that describes the input rather than the claim. test_100_grams says which case; it does not say what should happen, so the report cannot tell you what broke. Parametrized ids are the same rule: id="top-of-the-first-band" over id="100".

A name containing "and". test_validates_and_saves is two tests wearing one name, and its failure is ambiguous by construction (§1.5).

A name that will become a lie. test_returns_none_for_missing outlives the day the function starts raising, and nobody renames it. Prefer naming the behaviour — test_a_missing_key_is_reported_rather_than_silently_ignored.

Numbered names. test_case_3 is the giveaway of a suite transcribed from a document nobody has read since. If the number is meaningful — a ticket, an RFC section — put the meaning in the name and the number in a comment.

Long names are fine. A test name is never called by hand, and it is read far more often than it is written; test_a_zone_is_matched_exactly_and_not_case_insensitively is a good name at fifty-eight characters.

4.18 What This Section Established

  • Exhaustive testing is unavailable for almost every function, so testing is sampling and the whole skill is choosing the sample.
  • Equivalence classes cut an infinite input space to a handful, and must be derived from the problem as well as the code, or they can only confirm the branches that already exist.
  • The oracle is the other half of a test case. If the expected value could have been produced by running the code, the test is not an oracle.
  • Boundary value analysis samples each side of every edge, because off-by-one errors live exactly there and nowhere else. Boundaries exist on strings, collections, dates and downstream storage limits, not only on numbers.
  • A standing checklist — empty, single, duplicate, even/odd, ordered, aliased — plus Right-BICEP and CORRECT catch the cases intuition skips.
  • Negative tests pin the manner of refusal, and a test that documents a decision is worth as much as one that catches a defect.
  • Decision tables expose unstated rules and are a requirements tool that happens to emit test cases; pairwise testing covers every two-factor interaction at a fraction of the cost, with the honest limit that three-factor defects escape it.
  • Risk decides how many of those cases you write, and some things should deliberately be tested badly.
  • A test earns its keep when it can fail for a reason you would want to know about. Trivial code, the framework, mock-only tests and assertion-free tests usually cannot.
  • parametrize turns a table into one test per row, which restores independent failure, selection and naming that a loop destroys; pytest.param adds ids, per-row marks and HIDDEN_PARAM; indirect=True routes the parameter through a fixture.
  • test.each spreads array cases, test.for does not, and test.for's scoped expect is what makes snapshots work per row.
  • subtests is for rows discovered at run time, reports the failing case with its parameters, continues past a failure, and counts subtests separately.
  • The name is the deliverable. State the claim, avoid "and", and let it be long.

Exercises

1. Partition and bound a real function.

Here is a password rule from a real system: at least 12 characters, at most 64, at least one digit, at least one letter, and it must not equal the username.

List the equivalence classes, then list every boundary value you would test. How many test cases do you end up with, and which of them would you drop first under time pressure?

2. Find the oracle.

For each of these, name which of §4.3's five oracle kinds you would use, and why the others do not work:

(a) a function that formats a duration in seconds as "2h 5m"; (b) a function that resizes a JPEG to fit a 200 × 200 box; (c) a function that returns the next business day, given a country's holiday calendar; (d) a function that sorts search results by relevance.

3. Build the decision table.

A refund is allowed when the order is under 30 days old, unless the item is marked final-sale; a customer-service override allows it regardless; and digital goods are never refundable, even with an override. Write the decision table, collapse the don't-care rows, and say how many tests you would write and which question you would ask the product owner.

4. Turn a loop into a table.

Take test_the_whole_table_in_one_test from §4.12 and add a sixth row that fails — say (2001, "world", True, 2000). Run both versions. Compare what each report tells you, and say specifically what the parametrized version told you that the loop did not.

5. Choose the mechanism.

For each, say whether you would use parametrize, subtests, test.each or none, and why:

(a) checking that all 14 files in fixtures/invoices/ parse; (b) checking six weight boundaries; (c) checking that a returned user object has the right id, name, email and created_at; (d) checking a function against every locale installed on the machine.

6. Kill a test.

Find a test in a codebase you work on that you believe does not earn its keep. Write down the two questions from §4.11 and answer them honestly. Then, harder: write down what you would lose if it were deleted, and decide.

Solutions

1. Partition and bound.

Classes: length below 12 (invalid), 12–64 (valid), above 64 (invalid); contains a digit / does not; contains a letter / does not; equals the username / does not. That is 3 × 2 × 2 × 2, but the three content rules are independent of length, so the sensible reading is a length partition crossed with a small set of content cases.

Boundaries: length 11, 12, 13, 63, 64, 65. Content boundaries: exactly one digit and nothing else that qualifies, exactly one letter, zero digits, zero letters. Plus the empty string, which is length 0 and hits the length rule — and is worth its own case because it is the input a form submits when the field is untouched.

Around a dozen cases. The first to drop under time pressure are 13 and 63 — the interior-adjacent values — since the boundary pairs 11/12 and 64/65 already pin both edges. The last to drop is "equals the username", because it is the only rule here that is a security rule rather than a formatting one, which is §4.10's cost multiplier doing its work.

2. Find the oracle.

(a) A literal value. format_duration(7500) == "2h 5m" is computable by hand, and the inverse (parsing the string back) is also available as a cross-check. This is the easy case.

(b) A property, and possibly a threshold. You cannot write down the expected bytes of a resized JPEG — the encoder's output depends on its version and settings, so a literal comparison is a snapshot that rots. What you can assert: the output is a valid JPEG, its dimensions fit in the box, its aspect ratio matches the input's within a pixel, and it is smaller than the input. A human oracle covers "does it look right", once, not on every commit.

(c) A literal value, computed from the calendar by hand for a small set of dates — and this is a case where the reference-implementation oracle is a trap, because the obvious reference is the same holiday table the code uses, which makes it §4.3's re-implementation failure. Pick real dates: the Friday before a Monday holiday, 31 December, a leap day.

(d) A human, plus properties. Relevance has no computable oracle; that is the definition of the problem. What is testable: the ordering is a total order, the same query gives the same order (an idempotence property, §16.5), a document containing the exact phrase outranks one that does not. Everything else is exploratory evaluation, offline, against human judgements — not a CI test.

3. Build the decision table.

Conditions: under 30 days, final-sale, override, digital. Sixteen rows, collapsing hard:

digital override final-sale < 30 days refund?
yes — — — no
no yes — — yes
no no yes — no
no no no yes yes
no no no no no

Five rules from sixteen rows, because digital short-circuits everything and override short-circuits the rest. Five tests, one per rule — plus one extra that is not in the table: digital=yes, override=yes, which is the row where the two short-circuits collide. It is covered by the collapsed first rule, but it is precisely the case an implementation gets wrong by checking override first, so write it explicitly rather than trusting the collapse.

The question for the product owner: is the 30-day window inclusive, and measured from order date or delivery date? The table cannot be turned into tests until someone answers, which is the point of §4.8 — the table found a requirements gap, not a code defect.

4. Turn a loop into a table.

The loop reports one failure, on the line assert shipping_cost(...) == expected, with the failing values visible only in the local-variables display; and rows after the failing one never run, so if two rows were wrong you learn about one.

The parametrized version reports test_one_test_per_row[2001-world-True-2000] as the failing test — the row is in the name — the other five rows still run and pass, and pytest -k 2001 re-runs exactly that case while you fix it. That last point is the one people underestimate: the debugging loop is one test rather than six.

5. Choose the mechanism.

(a) subtests, or parametrize with a collection-time glob. Both work; the difference is that a glob evaluated at collection time gives you selectable, individually-named tests, while subtests handles the case where the directory is populated by a fixture. If the files exist in the repository, prefer parametrize.

(b) parametrize (or test.each). Six known rows, known before the run — exactly its case.

(c) None. Four fields of one returned object are four facets of one claim, not four claims. Assert on the object with one structural comparison (§3.6), or use soft assertions if you want all four differences reported at once. Parametrizing here produces four tests that share expensive setup and report a defect four times.

(d) subtests, because the locale list is a property of the machine and is not known when the file is collected. It is also a strong candidate for not testing this way at all — a suite whose test count varies by machine is a suite whose CI report is not comparable between runs, which §18 will say more about.

6. Kill a test.

No fixed answer, but the shape of a good one: the honest reason a test survives an audit like this is usually not "it catches defects" but "it documents a decision" or "it is the only thing exercising this path at all". Both are legitimate — the second especially, since a test that earns nothing on its own may be the only thing standing between a module and zero coverage.

The answer that should worry you is "I do not know what it does, so I am leaving it". That test costs you on every run and every refactor and pays nothing, and the fear of deleting it is exactly the state §19 calls high test maintenance cost.

SECTION 5

Fixtures and Test Data

Section 1 named the four phases of a test: set up, exercise, verify, tear down. Sections 3 and 4 were about the middle two. This one is about the outer two, and they are where most of a suite's maintenance cost lives.

The reason is arithmetic. A codebase has one implementation of place_order and four hundred tests that need an order to exist. Every change to what an order requires — a new mandatory field, a new foreign key, a renamed column — touches the setup of all four hundred unless something stands between them. A fixture is that something, and the quality of your fixtures decides whether a schema change is a one-line edit or a two-day one.

Meszaros calls the state a test runs against its test fixture, and the word is used for two things that are worth keeping apart: the state itself, and the code that builds it. pytest's @pytest.fixture is the second; everything Meszaros says about fresh, shared, minimal and standard fixtures is about the first.

5.1 Setup, Three Ways

Before any framework, there are only three places the setup code can go. Meszaros names them inline setup, delegated setup and implicit setup, and a fourth arrangement — chained tests, where each test leaves behind the state the next one needs — is the one to recognise and refuse, because chained tests make every test order-dependent by construction (§18.6).

# orders.py
class Order:
    def __init__(self, customer, lines, discount_pct=0):
        self.customer = customer
        self.lines = lines
        self.discount_pct = discount_pct

    def subtotal_cents(self):
        return sum(line["price_cents"] * line["quantity"] for line in self.lines)

    def total_cents(self):
        return round(self.subtotal_cents() * (100 - self.discount_pct) / 100)

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

# tests/test_three_setups.py
import pytest

from orders import Order


# --- inline setup: the test builds everything it needs, in the test ----------
def test_inline_setup():
    order = Order(customer={"id": 7, "name": "Ada"},
                  lines=[{"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2},
                         {"price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1}])

    assert order.total_cents() == 650


# --- delegated setup: the test calls a named creation method -----------------
def make_order(discount_pct=0):
    """A creation method. One place to change when Order's shape changes."""
    return Order(customer={"id": 7, "name": "Ada"},
                 lines=[{"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2},
                        {"price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1}],
                 discount_pct=discount_pct)


def test_delegated_setup():
    order = make_order()

    assert order.total_cents() == 650


def test_delegated_setup_says_only_what_differs():
    order = make_order(discount_pct=10)

    assert order.total_cents() == 585


# --- implicit setup: the framework builds it and hands it over ---------------
@pytest.fixture
def order():
    return make_order()


def test_implicit_setup(order):
    assert order.total_cents() == 650

pytest -q tests/test_three_setups.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 1.16s
 
for
against
inline
Everything is visible. No jumping to another file to understand the test.
Duplicated across every test, so a shape change touches all of them.
delegated
One place to change. The call site states only what this test cares about.
One indirection to follow. Tempting to grow parameters until it does everything.
implicit
Teardown is handled, sharing is possible, and the test signature declares what it needs.
The value appears from nowhere — §19's mystery guest if the fixture is far away or unnamed for its content.

The advice that follows is less absolute than the framework documentation implies. Delegated setup is the default worth reaching for, because a creation method is ordinary code with no magic in it. Fixtures earn their extra indirection when there is teardown to do, when the object is expensive enough to share, or when several tests need the same instance rather than an equivalent one.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: implicit teardown.

5.2 @pytest.fixture

A fixture is a function whose name is the parameter name a test asks for. pytest resolves the request by name, at run time, from the nearest definition.

# tests/test_fixture_basics.py
import pytest

from orders import Order


@pytest.fixture
def customer():
    return {"id": 7, "name": "Ada", "country": "GB"}


@pytest.fixture
def order(customer):
    """A fixture may request other fixtures. pytest builds the graph for you."""
    return Order(customer=customer,
                 lines=[{"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2},
                        {"price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1}])


def test_a_fixture_can_depend_on_a_fixture(order):
    assert order.customer["name"] == "Ada"
    assert order.total_cents() == 650


def test_each_test_gets_its_own(order):
    order.lines.append({"price_cents": 100, "quantity": 1})

    assert order.total_cents() == 750


def test_and_the_mutation_above_did_not_leak(order):
    # Function scope is the default: this is a different Order object.
    assert order.total_cents() == 650

pytest -q tests/test_fixture_basics.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 1.22s

Three properties are doing real work there.

Fixtures compose. order asks for customer, and pytest resolves the whole graph before the test runs. That is the mechanism that lets one fixture be specialised without duplicating the rest of the tree.

The default fixture scope is function, so each test gets a fresh object. Fixture scope is the main lever on suite speed and the main source of §18's first cause of flakiness, which is why §5.4 is about nothing else. The third test proves it, and it is the property that makes fixtures safe by default — §18.5's leaking fixture is what happens when you change it.

Resolution is by name, from the nearest conftest.py upward (§2.6). That is convenient and it is the feature people complain about, because a name with no import behind it is hard to trace. pytest --fixtures prints every available fixture with its source file; pytest --fixtures-per-test prints them per test, which is the better command when you are reading someone else's suite.

The term above, for reference: function scope.

5.3 yield, and the Teardown That Always Runs

A fixture that yields hands over its value and resumes afterwards. Everything after the yield is teardown, and it runs whether the test passed, failed or raised.

# tests/test_yield_fixture.py
import pytest

EVENTS = []


@pytest.fixture
def resource():
    EVENTS.append("setup")
    yield {"handle": "open"}
    EVENTS.append("teardown")        # runs even when the test fails


@pytest.fixture
def with_finalizer(request):
    """The older API. addfinalizer registers teardown at the moment of the
    acquisition, which matters when a fixture acquires several things and the
    third one fails — the first two are still released."""
    EVENTS.append("setup-finalizer")
    request.addfinalizer(lambda: EVENTS.append("teardown-finalizer"))
    return {"handle": "open"}


def test_a_failing_test_still_gets_teardown(resource):
    assert resource["handle"] == "open"


def test_addfinalizer_is_the_alternative(with_finalizer):
    assert with_finalizer["handle"] == "open"


def test_the_events_happened_in_the_expected_order():
    assert EVENTS == ["setup", "teardown", "setup-finalizer", "teardown-finalizer"]

pytest -q tests/test_yield_fixture.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 1.05s

The third test is a metatest — a test about the test infrastructure — and writing one occasionally is worth it: fixture ordering is the kind of thing everyone believes they understand and nobody has checked.

yield for one resource, addfinalizer for several. A yield fixture that acquires three things and fails on the third never reaches its teardown, so the first two leak (§18.12). addfinalizer registers each undo at the moment of its acquisition, so partial setup unwinds correctly. In practice, prefer to make three fixtures.

One to keep in hand: yield fixture.

5.4 Scope

Fixture scope decides how often a fixture is built, and it is the main lever on suite speed. pytest offers five: function scope, class scope, module scope, package scope and session scope.

# tests/test_scopes.py
import pytest

ORDER_OF_EVENTS = []


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def expensive_session_thing():
    ORDER_OF_EVENTS.append("session setup")
    yield "a database, a browser, a compiled asset"
    ORDER_OF_EVENTS.append("session teardown")


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def per_module(expensive_session_thing):
    ORDER_OF_EVENTS.append("module setup")
    yield "something built once per file"
    ORDER_OF_EVENTS.append("module teardown")


@pytest.fixture                      # scope="function" is the default
def per_test(per_module):
    ORDER_OF_EVENTS.append("test setup")
    yield "a fresh object"
    ORDER_OF_EVENTS.append("test teardown")


def test_first(per_test):
    assert per_test == "a fresh object"


def test_second(per_test):
    assert per_test == "a fresh object"


def test_the_events_show_which_ran_how_often(per_test):
    assert ORDER_OF_EVENTS == [
        "session setup", "module setup", "test setup",
        "test teardown", "test setup",
        "test teardown", "test setup",
    ]

pytest -q tests/test_scopes.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 1.01s
function
The default, and the right answer unless you have measured a reason otherwise.
class scope
Once per test class. Class scope is rarely the natural unit unless the suite is class-organised.
module scope
Once per file. Module scope is the usual place for a moderately expensive read-only thing — and the usual place a mutable one causes §18.5.
package scope
Once per directory. Package scope is useful when a subtree shares infrastructure — an integration folder with a database.
session
Once per run. For the genuinely expensive: a database server (§11.2), a browser, a compiled bundle.

Two rules keep scope from causing the bugs it is famous for.

A wider-scoped fixture may not depend on a narrower one. A session fixture cannot request a function fixture, because the function one does not exist yet at the time the session one is built. pytest raises a clear ScopeMismatch for this, and it is the error that teaches the rule.

Widen the scope only for things that do not change. A session-scoped connection is fine; a session-scoped object the tests mutate is §18.5. When you need to share something expensive and mutable, the pattern is a session-scoped source and a function-scoped copy.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: session scope.

5.5 Fresh, Shared, Standard and Minimal

Meszaros's adjectives describe the state, not the code, and they cut across pytest's scopes. Four of them matter here; a fifth, the prebuilt fixture — state created once, outside the run, and reused by every run afterwards — is the shared fixture taken to its extreme, and a hand-seeded development database is exactly that.

fresh fixture
Built for this test and discarded. No interference, no order dependence, no teardown surprises. The default and the goal.
shared fixture
Reused by several tests, either within a run or (worse) across runs. Faster; buys the whole of §18.5.
standard fixture
One canonical dataset every test uses. Convenient, and it makes each test's real requirements invisible.
minimal fixture
The smallest state that lets this test make its claim. Harder to write, and the failure it produces is far easier to read.

The standard-versus-minimal choice is the one teams get wrong most often, and it is worth being concrete about why.

A standard fixture is the "reference database": fifty customers, two hundred orders, every status represented, loaded once and used by everything. It feels efficient. What it costs is that no test says what it needs — the test asserting a discount uses customer 17 because customer 17 happens to have the right history, and nobody remembers why. Change the dataset and forty tests fail for reasons unrelated to each other. Meszaros files this under mystery guest (§19.4): the test depends on something not visible in the test.

A minimal fixture builds one customer with one order and the discount under test. It is more code, and every failure names its own cause.

The practical middle ground, and what §5.13's builders exist for: a minimal fixture whose defaults are standard. make_order() gives a valid ordinary order; make_order(discount_pct=10) says exactly what this test is about. The test states the difference and nothing else.

The term this subsection introduced: prebuilt fixture.

5.6 Shared Fixtures, and What They Cost

Sometimes the setup genuinely is expensive, and rebuilding it per test is not affordable. Section 11's PostgreSQL server takes seconds; a browser takes longer; a compiled bundle longer still.

The discipline that makes sharing safe has three parts.

Share the expensive thing, not the state. A session-scoped server with a function-scoped transaction (§11.4) is the archetype: the costly part is built once, and each test still gets a clean slate. The same shape works for a browser (one browser, a fresh context per test — §15) and for a loaded dataset (one parsed file, a copy per test).

If you must share mutable state, make it immutable. A frozen dataclass, a tuple, or a dict the tests are trusted not to touch. The trust is the weak point, which is why the copy is better.

Assert the invariant, do not hope for it. A session-scoped fixture can check on teardown that it is in the state it started in. Ten lines, and it converts "the suite got flaky last month" into "test_x mutates the shared catalogue".

# tests/test_shared_safely.py
import copy

import pytest

CATALOGUE = [
    {"sku": "widget", "price_cents": 250},
    {"sku": "gadget", "price_cents": 150},
]


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def catalogue_source():
    """Built once. Nothing is allowed to mutate this."""
    before = copy.deepcopy(CATALOGUE)
    yield CATALOGUE
    assert CATALOGUE == before, "a test mutated the shared catalogue"


@pytest.fixture
def catalogue(catalogue_source):
    """Function-scoped copy: cheap, and mutation cannot escape this test."""
    return copy.deepcopy(catalogue_source)


def test_one_test_may_change_its_copy(catalogue):
    catalogue[0]["price_cents"] = 999

    assert catalogue[0]["price_cents"] == 999


def test_and_the_next_test_does_not_see_it(catalogue):
    assert catalogue[0]["price_cents"] == 250

pytest -q tests/test_shared_safely.py

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 0.94s

The guard in catalogue_source's teardown is the part worth stealing. It costs one comparison at the end of the run and it makes a whole class of §18 bug report itself, by name, in the right place.

5.7 autouse

An autouse fixture runs for every test in its scope without being asked for. Meszaros's name for a fixture serving many tests rather than being tailored to one is a general fixture, and the warning that goes with a general fixture is §5.5's: the more tests it serves, the less any of them says about what it actually needs. Two more xUnit spellings belong here. Lazy setup builds the state on first use rather than up front — which is what a session-scoped pytest fixture already does, since nothing is created until a test asks for it. And suitefixture setup, declared once for a whole class and implemented with a setup decorator on a method, is the arrangement @pytest.fixture replaced: the decorator form could not be composed or overridden, which is why the fixture graph in §5.2 is the better mechanism.

# tests/test_autouse.py
import pytest

AUDIT = []


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def reset_audit_log():
    """Runs for every test in this module. Nothing requests it."""
    AUDIT.clear()
    yield
    AUDIT.append("torn down")


def test_the_log_starts_empty():
    assert AUDIT == []
    AUDIT.append("something happened")


def test_and_it_starts_empty_again():
    assert AUDIT == []

pytest -q tests/test_autouse.py

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 0.83s

Autouse is right for exactly one kind of thing: a global that must be reset regardless of what the test does. A cache, a registry, a metrics collector, a patched environment variable. The test does not want the fixture's value; it wants the guarantee.

It is wrong for supplying data. An autouse fixture that creates a customer makes every test in the file depend on a customer none of them mention — the mystery guest again, now invisible even from the test's signature. The rule to apply: if a test would want to know it ran, it should ask for it.

Scope autouse as narrowly as you can. In a root conftest.py it applies to the entire suite, which is occasionally right (resetting a global) and usually far more than intended.

To have in hand before moving on: lazy setup, suitefixture setup and setup decorator.

5.8 A Factory as a Fixture

A fixture returning a value gives every test the same thing. A fixture returning a function lets each test say what it needs — and still gets the teardown.

# tests/test_factory_fixture.py
import pytest

from orders import Order


@pytest.fixture
def make_order():
    """A factory fixture: the test decides how many and what shape."""
    created = []

    def _make(discount_pct=0, lines=None, customer_id=7):
        order = Order(
            customer={"id": customer_id, "name": f"customer-{customer_id}"},
            lines=lines or [{"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2},
                            {"price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1}],
            discount_pct=discount_pct)
        created.append(order)
        return order

    yield _make
    created.clear()          # stands in for releasing whatever was created


def test_one_order(make_order):
    assert make_order().total_cents() == 650


def test_a_discounted_order(make_order):
    assert make_order(discount_pct=10).total_cents() == 585


def test_several_orders_for_different_customers(make_order):
    orders = [make_order(customer_id=i) for i in range(3)]

    assert [o.customer["id"] for o in orders] == [0, 1, 2]

pytest -q tests/test_factory_fixture.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 1.17s

This is the shape to reach for whenever a test needs more than one of something, or needs to choose the shape. It is also how a database test creates rows and still gets them cleaned up: the factory records what it made, and the teardown removes them.

The created list is the point of using a fixture at all — a bare creation method (§5.1) cannot clean up after itself.

5.9 Fixture Parametrization and request

params= on a fixture runs every test that uses it once per parameter. That is a different tool from @pytest.mark.parametrize (§4.12), and the difference is worth being precise about: parametrize multiplies one test, params= multiplies every test that touches the fixture.

# tests/test_fixture_params.py
import pytest


@pytest.fixture(params=["memory", "file", "network"], ids=["mem", "file", "net"])
def storage(request):
    """Every test using `storage` runs three times, once per backend."""
    return {"kind": request.param, "durable": request.param != "memory"}


def test_every_backend_reports_its_kind(storage):
    assert storage["kind"] in {"memory", "file", "network"}


def test_only_memory_is_non_durable(storage):
    assert storage["durable"] == (storage["kind"] != "memory")


@pytest.fixture
def described(request):
    """`request` also carries the node itself, which is how a fixture can
    behave differently for a test that asks it to."""
    marker = request.node.get_closest_marker("slow")
    return {"test_name": request.node.name, "is_slow": marker is not None}


@pytest.mark.slow
def test_a_fixture_can_read_its_test(described):
    assert described["is_slow"] is True
    assert "a_fixture_can_read" in described["test_name"]

Seven tests from three functions. This is the mechanism §11.14 uses to run one suite against both a fake and a real database, and it is the cleanest expression of "this behaviour must hold for every implementation".

The request fixture is the one that gives a fixture access to its own context. Every fixture may ask for request, and the request fixture carries: request.param for the current parameter, request.node for the test itself, request.config for command-line options, and request.getfixturevalue("name") to resolve another fixture by name at run time — which is the escape hatch for a fixture whose dependencies are not known statically. Use the last one sparingly; it defeats the dependency graph that makes the rest of this readable.

5.10 Overriding a Fixture

A fixture override is a redefinition of a fixture nearer the test than the original. The conftest.py hierarchy (§2.6) lets a subtree declare one, and — the part people miss — a fixture override can request the original.

# tests/conftest.py
import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def settings():
    return {"env": "test", "feature_flags": [], "timeout_s": 5}

# tests/integration/conftest.py
import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def settings(settings):
    """Same name, and it requests the outer one: pytest resolves the parameter
    to the definition in the *parent* conftest, so this is a specialisation
    rather than a replacement."""
    return {**settings, "timeout_s": 60, "feature_flags": ["slow_path"]}

# tests/test_uses_base_settings.py
def test_the_base_definition_applies_here(settings):
    assert settings["timeout_s"] == 5
    assert settings["feature_flags"] == []

# tests/integration/test_uses_override.py
def test_the_override_applies_in_this_directory(settings):
    assert settings["timeout_s"] == 60
    assert settings["feature_flags"] == ["slow_path"]
    assert settings["env"] == "test"          # inherited from the parent

pytest -q tests/test_uses_base_settings.py tests/integration/test_uses_override.py

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 0.95s

Three levels of override are available and they shadow in this order, nearest first: a fixture in the test module, one in the nearest conftest.py, then each conftest.py upward to the rootdir, then plugins.

The def settings(settings) idiom looks like infinite recursion and is not: the parameter is resolved from the next definition outward. It is the difference between "integration tests have a longer timeout" and "integration tests have a completely separate settings object that will drift from the real one".

pytest.register_fixture (new in pytest 9) registers one imperatively, without the decorator. It exists for plugins that must build fixtures from data at collection time; ordinary suites should keep the declarative form.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: pytest.register_fixture.

5.11 The Built-in Fixtures

pytest ships a set worth knowing by heart, because each replaces code people otherwise write badly.

# tests/test_builtins.py
import logging
import socket
import warnings


def test_tmp_path_is_a_private_directory_per_test(tmp_path):
    report = tmp_path / "report.csv"
    report.write_text("id,total\n7,650\n")

    assert report.read_text().splitlines()[1] == "7,650"
    # The path is unique per test, so parallel runs cannot collide (§18.12).
    assert tmp_path.is_dir()


def test_monkeypatch_undoes_itself(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("APP_REGION", "us-east-2")
    import os
    assert os.environ["APP_REGION"] == "us-east-2"


def test_and_the_environment_is_clean_again():
    import os
    assert "APP_REGION" not in os.environ


def test_capsys_captures_what_the_code_printed(capsys):
    print("processing 3 rows")

    captured = capsys.readouterr()
    assert captured.out == "processing 3 rows\n"
    assert captured.err == ""


def test_caplog_captures_log_records_with_their_levels(caplog):
    with caplog.at_level(logging.WARNING):
        logging.getLogger("billing").warning("retrying in %ds", 5)

    assert caplog.records[0].levelname == "WARNING"
    assert caplog.records[0].getMessage() == "retrying in 5s"


def test_recwarn_collects_warnings(recwarn):
    warnings.warn("deprecated", DeprecationWarning)

    assert len(recwarn) == 1


def test_free_tcp_port_hands_out_one_nobody_is_using(free_tcp_port):
    s = socket.socket()
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", free_tcp_port))
    s.close()


def test_pytestconfig_exposes_the_command_line(pytestconfig):
    assert pytestconfig.getoption("verbose") is not None

pytest -q tests/test_builtins.py

........                                                                 [100%]
8 passed in 0.93s
tmp_path
A unique directory per test, kept for the last few runs so a failure can be inspected. tmp_path_factory is the session-scoped form.
monkeypatch
setattr, setenv, delenv, chdir, syspath_prepend — each with the undo registered (§6.8).
capsys / capfd
capsys captures at the Python level; capfd at the file-descriptor level, which is what you need for output from a C extension or a subprocess. capteesys captures and passes it through, so you can see it while asserting on it.
caplog
Log records as objects, with levels and arguments — far better than asserting on formatted text.
free_tcp_port
New in pytest 9. A port nobody is using, which is the fix for §18.12's collisions.
pytester
Runs pytest inside a test. For writing plugins and for testing your own fixtures.
cache
The cache fixture reads and writes the same store --last-failed uses (§2.11), so a fixture can remember something across runs. Rare, and the right tool for an expensive artefact that only needs rebuilding when one of its inputs changes.
record_property
Attaches a key/value to the JUnit XML, which is how a test tells the CI report something (§20).

caplog deserves the emphasis. Asserting on "retrying in 5s" in caplog.text couples the test to the format string; asserting on caplog.records[0].getMessage() and levelname asserts on the event. The second survives a change to the log format, which is a change nobody thinks of as breaking.

In summary, the vocabulary here is tmp_path_factory, capteesys, the cache fixture, pytester and record_property.

5.12 Object Mothers and Test Data Builders

Two named patterns for the "make me a valid X" problem, and the difference between them decides how well they age.

An object mother is a class or module of named creation methods: OrderMother.standard(), OrderMother.discounted(), OrderMother.with_no_lines(). It reads beautifully and it grows badly — every new case adds a method, and after two years there are sixty with names like standard_with_discount_and_no_address_v2.

A test data builder is a fluent object with defaults: an_order().with_discount(10).build(). Each test states only what it needs, and a new required field is one change to the defaults.

# builders.py
from orders import Order

DEFAULT_LINES = [{"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2},
                 {"price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1}]


class OrderBuilder:
    """A test data builder. Every field has a valid default, so a test states
    only the thing it is about."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._customer = {"id": 7, "name": "Ada", "country": "GB"}
        self._lines = list(DEFAULT_LINES)
        self._discount_pct = 0

    def for_customer(self, **fields):
        self._customer = {**self._customer, **fields}
        return self

    def with_discount(self, pct):
        self._discount_pct = pct
        return self

    def with_lines(self, *lines):
        self._lines = list(lines)
        return self

    def build(self):
        return Order(customer=self._customer, lines=self._lines,
                     discount_pct=self._discount_pct)


def an_order():
    return OrderBuilder()

# tests/test_builders.py
from builders import an_order


def test_the_default_is_a_valid_ordinary_order():
    assert an_order().build().total_cents() == 650


def test_a_test_states_only_what_it_is_about():
    assert an_order().with_discount(10).build().total_cents() == 585


def test_an_empty_order_totals_nothing():
    assert an_order().with_lines().build().total_cents() == 0


def test_a_field_that_matters_is_visible_in_the_test():
    order = an_order().for_customer(country="FR").build()

    assert order.customer["country"] == "FR"
    assert order.customer["name"] == "Ada"        # the rest kept its default

pytest -q tests/test_builders.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 1.15s

Four properties make this worth the twenty lines.

A new required field is one edit. Add currency to Order, give it a default in the builder, and four hundred tests keep working — which is the arithmetic from this section's opening, answered.

The test says what matters. with_discount(10) is the claim; the customer, the lines and the country are scenery, and the reader can tell which is which at a glance.

Invalid objects are possible on purpose. with_lines() builds an order with no lines. An object mother would need a method for that case; the builder already has it.

It composes with fixtures. an_order() inside a factory fixture (§5.8) gives you the fluency and the teardown.

The one real cost: a builder is production-shaped code in your test tree, and it needs to be maintained. That is a smaller cost than four hundred inline constructions, and it is the same trade as any other abstraction.

5.13 The Teardown Ladder, and Why "None" Is the Goal

Meszaros catalogues four ways a test cleans up, and they form a ladder — each rung is better than the one below it.

4
inline teardown
Cleanup written at the end of the test. Does not run when the test fails, which is exactly when the state is dirtiest.
3
implicit teardown
A framework hook — tearDown, an afterEach, the code after a yield. Runs on failure. You still have to write and maintain it.
2
automated teardown
The fixture records what it created and undoes exactly that — §5.8's factory, §11.4's rollback. No list of tables to keep in step with the schema.
1
garbage-collected teardown
Nothing to tear down. The test created objects in memory and the runtime reclaims them. No cleanup code exists, so none can be forgotten.

The top rung is the point, and it reframes the whole section: "this test needs no teardown" is a statement about the design, not about the test. A test needs teardown exactly when it changed something outside itself — a file, a row, a global, a patched module. Every one of those is a dependency the code did not have to have.

That is why §8 is where it is. A function taking its collaborators as arguments (§8.3), reading its clock from a parameter (§8.7), writing to a stream rather than a path (§8.10) — every one of those design moves takes a test up this ladder. The two-hundred-line conftest.py full of cleanup is not a testing problem; it is the shape of the application, written out.

Where the top rung is unreachable — a database, a browser, a filesystem — aim for rung 2 and never rung 4. And note the ordering property that makes rung 4 so bad: inline teardown is skipped on failure, so a failing test leaves the mess, and the next test fails too. One real defect becomes twenty red tests and an afternoon.

What to carry forward from this subsection: garbage-collected teardown and automated teardown.

5.14 beforeEach, afterAll and test.extend

JavaScript's runners take the hook-based route rather than the dependency-injection route, and Vitest adds a fixture mechanism on top that is closer to pytest's.

// orders.js
export function totalCents(lines, discountPct = 0) {
  const subtotal = lines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.priceCents * l.quantity, 0);
  return Math.round((subtotal * (100 - discountPct)) / 100);
}

// hooks.spec.js
import { describe, test, expect, beforeAll, beforeEach, afterEach, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { totalCents } from './orders.js';

const events = [];

describe('the four hooks, in order', () => {
  beforeAll(() => { events.push('beforeAll'); });
  beforeEach(() => { events.push('beforeEach'); });
  afterEach(() => { events.push('afterEach'); });
  afterAll(() => { events.push('afterAll'); });

  test('first', () => { expect(totalCents([{ priceCents: 250, quantity: 2 }])).toBe(500); });
  test('second', () => { expect(totalCents([], 10)).toBe(0); });
  test('the events so far', () => {
    expect(events).toEqual([
      'beforeAll', 'beforeEach', 'afterEach', 'beforeEach', 'afterEach', 'beforeEach',
    ]);
  });
});

// A hook may return its own cleanup, which is the tidiest form: acquisition and
// release sit together, so neither can be moved without the other.
describe('a hook that returns its teardown', () => {
  const opened = [];
  beforeEach(() => {
    opened.push('resource');
    return () => { opened.pop(); };
  });

  test('the resource is there', () => { expect(opened).toEqual(['resource']); });
  test('and it was released before this one', () => { expect(opened).toEqual(['resource']); });
});

// fixtures.spec.js
import { test as base, expect } from 'vitest';
import { totalCents } from './orders.js';

// test.extend is Vitest's fixture mechanism, and it is lazy in the same way
// pytest's is: a fixture is only built if the test destructures it.
const test = base.extend({
  lines: async ({}, use) => {
    await use([{ priceCents: 250, quantity: 2 }, { priceCents: 150, quantity: 1 }]);
  },
  order: async ({ lines }, use) => {
    await use({ lines, total: totalCents(lines) });
  },
});

test('a fixture is requested by destructuring it', ({ order }) => {
  expect(order.total).toBe(650);
});

test('fixtures compose, exactly as pytest fixtures do', ({ lines, order }) => {
  expect(order.lines).toBe(lines);
});

test('a test that asks for nothing builds nothing', () => {
  expect(totalCents([])).toBe(0);
});

The mapping is close enough to be worth writing down:

beforeEach
A function-scoped autouse fixture.
beforeAll
A module-scoped autouse fixture — and it carries all of §5.6's sharing hazards.
afterEach/afterAll
The code after a yield. Returning a cleanup function from beforeEach is the tidier form, and is the same idea as addfinalizer.
test.extend
A real fixture: named, lazy, composable, requested by destructuring, with await use(value) playing yield's role.

A hook is not a fixture, and the difference is the one this section has been circling. beforeEach runs for every test in its block whether or not the test wants it, and it communicates through shared variables in the enclosing scope — which is §18.5's shared mutable state with a nicer syntax. test.extend is lazy and explicit: a test that does not destructure order never builds one, and there is no outer variable to leak.

Playwright's fixtures (§15) work the same way and add aroundEach-style wrapping, which is worth knowing exists: a fixture that runs code before and after while the test runs in between is strictly more expressive than a pair of hooks, because the two halves cannot drift apart.

The term above, for reference: aroundEach.

5.15 What This Section Established

  • A fixture stands between four hundred tests and one constructor. How good it is decides whether a schema change is a one-line edit or a two-day one.
  • Three places setup can live: inline (visible, duplicated), delegated (one place to change — the default worth reaching for), implicit (teardown and sharing, at the cost of a value appearing from nowhere).
  • pytest fixtures compose and resolve by name from the nearest conftest.py outward. --fixtures-per-test is how you read someone else's suite.
  • yield handles one resource; addfinalizer handles several, because a yield fixture that fails partway never reaches its teardown.
  • Function scope is the default and the right answer unless you have measured otherwise. A wider fixture may not depend on a narrower one, and widening the scope of anything mutable buys §18's first cause of flakiness.
  • Share the expensive thing, not the state: a session-scoped server with a per-test transaction, a session-scoped dataset with a per-test copy. Assert the shared thing is unchanged at teardown.
  • Standard fixtures make each test's real requirements invisible — the mystery guest. Minimal fixtures with sensible defaults are the resolution.
  • autouse is for guarantees, not data. If a test would want to know it ran, it should ask for it.
  • A factory fixture is the shape to reach for when a test needs several of something or needs to choose the shape — and it is the only form that can clean up after itself.
  • params= on a fixture multiplies every test that uses it, which is how one suite runs against two implementations (§11.14).
  • def settings(settings) is a specialisation, not recursion: the parameter resolves to the next definition outward.
  • Know the built-ins: tmp_path, monkeypatch, capsys/capfd/capteesys, caplog, recwarn, free_tcp_port, pytester, record_property. Assert on log records, not on formatted text.
  • A test data builder ages better than an object mother: defaults for everything, the test states only the difference, and a new required field is one edit.
  • The teardown ladder ends at "none". Inline teardown does not run on failure; automated teardown undoes what it recorded; needing no teardown is a statement about the design, which is why §8 is where it is.
  • A hook is not a fixture. beforeEach communicates through shared variables; test.extend is lazy, explicit and composable.

Exercises

1. Climb the ladder.

For each, say which rung of §5.13's teardown ladder it is on and what design change would move it up one: (a) a test that writes /tmp/report.csv and deletes it at the end; (b) a test that inserts a row and rolls back in a fixture; (c) a test that sets os.environ["TZ"] in a try/finally; (d) a test that builds an Order and asserts on its total.

2. Standard or minimal.

A team has one seed_database() fixture loading 50 customers and 200 orders, used by every one of its 300 integration tests. Give three concrete problems this causes, and describe the migration you would run to fix it without rewriting all 300 tests at once.

3. Choose the scope.

For each, choose a scope and justify it: (a) a compiled WebAssembly module; (b) an HTTP client pointed at a test server; (c) a Decimal context; (d) a logged-in browser session; (e) a temporary directory holding fixture files the tests read but never write.

4. Write the builder.

Order gains two required fields: currency and placed_at. Show what changes in a suite using inline setup, one using a creation method, and one using a builder. Then say what the builder should do about placed_at specifically, given §8.7.

5. Autouse or not.

For each, decide and defend: (a) resetting a module-level cache; (b) creating a logged-in user; (c) failing any test that leaves an open database connection; (d) setting the timezone to UTC; (e) seeding the random number generator.

6. Diagnose the fixture.

A module-scoped fixture returns a dict. One test in the file mutates it. Three months later a new test is added at the top of the file and four unrelated tests start failing. Explain the mechanism precisely, name the two rules from this section that were broken, and give the two-line fix.

Solutions

1. Climb the ladder.

(a) Rung 4, inline teardown — and it does not run when the test fails, so a failing test leaves the file for the next run to find. Move to rung 2 with tmp_path, which needs no cleanup code at all and is unique per test; that is arguably a jump straight to rung 1, since nothing you wrote is responsible for the cleanup.

(b) Rung 2, automated teardown. The database undoes exactly what was done, with no list of tables to maintain. Rung 1 would mean not touching a database at all, which is right for the tests that are really about business rules (§11.1) and wrong for the ones about SQL.

(c) Rung 3 at best, and rung 4 in practice — try/finally runs on failure, so it is implicit rather than inline, but it is still hand-written and easy to get wrong. monkeypatch moves it to rung 2. Rung 1 means injecting the timezone (§8.7) so no global is touched.

(d) Rung 1. Nothing outside the test changed. This is the target, and the reason so much of §8 is about making more tests look like this one.

2. Standard or minimal.

Three problems. Every failure is ambiguous: a test using customer 17 fails and nobody knows which of the seed's properties mattered. The seed cannot change: adding a customer to support a new test risks breaking any of the 300, so the file only ever grows. Setup is slow and shared, so it is either rebuilt 300 times or shared and mutable, which is §18.5.

The migration, without a rewrite: add builders (§5.12) alongside the seed and require new tests to use them; then, whenever a test fails or is touched for any other reason, convert it — the boy-scout rule, which distributes the cost over the work you were doing anyway. Add a guard that asserts the seed is unmodified at session teardown (§5.6), which stops the problem getting worse today. The seed shrinks as tests leave it, and the last few can be converted deliberately.

3. Choose the scope.

(a) Session. Compilation is expensive and the module is immutable. The classic case for the widest scope.

(b) Function, unless the client is genuinely stateless — cookies, auth headers and connection pools are all state, and sharing them across tests is a leak waiting to happen. If construction is expensive, share the transport at session scope and build the client per test (§5.6).

(c) Function, and via monkeypatch or a context manager: a Decimal context is global state, so a test that widens the precision must not widen it for the next test.

(d) Session for the browser, function for the context. This is §5.6's rule exactly, and it is what Playwright's default fixtures do (§15) — one browser process, a fresh isolated context per test.

(e) Session. Read-only files, built once. But note the "never write" in the premise is a hope: put them somewhere read-only, or verify at teardown, because the day a test writes into the shared directory is the day the suite becomes order-dependent.

4. Write the builder.

Inline setup: every test that constructs an Order is edited — potentially hundreds, mechanically, in a single large diff nobody can review.

Creation method: one edit to make_order, plus a decision about the default. Tests that care about currency start passing it.

Builder: one edit to OrderBuilder.__init__ for the defaults, plus a with_currency method for the tests that care. Identical in cost to the creation method here — builders win as the number of optional variations grows, not on the first field.

placed_at should not default to datetime.now(). That makes every test's data depend on when it runs, which is §8.1's time bomb reintroduced through the fixture. Default it to a fixed date — datetime(2026, 3, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc) — so tests are deterministic, and add placed_on(when) for the tests that care about dates. If the production code needs the current time, that comes from an injected clock, not from the builder.

5. Autouse or not.

(a) Autouse. A guarantee, not data; every test needs it and none wants to mention it.

(b) Not autouse. That is data, and an autouse version makes every test in the file depend on a user none of them name — the mystery guest, invisible even from the signature. Make it an ordinary fixture that tests request.

(c) Autouse, and it is an excellent use: a session- or function-scoped autouse fixture whose teardown asserts an invariant turns a diffuse flakiness problem into a named failure (§5.6, §11.10).

(d) Autouse, with a caveat. Forcing UTC makes the suite deterministic and hides every timezone bug your users will hit. Do it, and separately write explicit tests for the non-UTC cases (§18.11) — otherwise you have bought determinism with coverage.

(e) Not autouse, and preferably not at all. Seeding a global generator is global state that leaks (§8.9). Inject the generator instead. If you must seed globally, an autouse fixture that seeds and restores is the least-bad version.

6. Diagnose the fixture.

The mechanism: scope="module" builds the dict once for the whole file and hands the same object to every test in it. The test that mutates it changes what every later test sees. The four failures were latent the whole time — they only appeared because the new test at the top of the file changed the execution order, moving the mutating test earlier relative to them. Nothing about the four tests changed; they were always order-dependent, and the file order was hiding it.

Two rules broken: do not widen the scope of anything mutable (§5.4), and share the expensive thing, not the state (§5.6).

The two-line fix: keep the module-scoped fixture as a private source and add a function-scoped copy.

@pytest.fixture
def config(config_source):
    return copy.deepcopy(config_source)

And the line worth adding alongside it: an assertion in the source fixture's teardown that it is unchanged, so the next attempt to mutate it is reported against the test that did it rather than against four innocent ones.

SECTION 6

Test Doubles

A test double is anything you put in place of a real depended-on component (§1.6) so that a test can run. The name is Meszaros's and it is a deliberate borrowing from film: a stunt double stands in for the actor, looks enough like them from the camera's angle, and does the one dangerous thing the production needs.

There are five kinds. They are not five words for the same idea, and the difference between them is not stylistic — it decides what your test can catch, what it will break on, and whether it is still true after a refactor. The industry uses "mock" for all five, which is why this section spends its first half on distinctions before writing a line of framework code.

The five, then the tools: unittest.mock and monkeypatch in Python, mock.fn and mock.module in node:test, and vi.fn, vi.spyOn and vi.mock in Vitest.

6.1 The Five Kinds

Meszaros's taxonomy sorts doubles by what the test uses them for, not by what library made them.

dummy object
Passed in to satisfy a signature and never used. If it is ever called, that is a bug. Often literally None.
test stub
Feeds the SUT indirect input: canned answers that drive it down the path you want to test. Answers questions; asks none.
test spy
Records the SUT's indirect output so the test can assert on it afterwards. Observes; does not judge.
mock object
A double carrying an expectation — a statement, made before the SUT runs, about the calls it must receive — which fails the test itself the moment a call does not match.
fake object
A real working implementation, simplified past production use. An in-memory store standing in for a database. Has behaviour, not answers.

Two of those distinctions do real work and the rest are bookkeeping.

Stub versus spy is the direction of the data. A stub exists so the SUT can receive something; a spy exists so the test can see what the SUT sent. That maps exactly onto §1.7: a stub supplies indirect input, a spy captures indirect output. Many library objects are both at once, which is fine — the words describe the role in this test, not the object's type. unittest.mock.Mock can play all five roles; what makes it a stub in one test and a spy in the next is which of its features that test uses.

Mock versus spy is where the assertion lives. A spy records, and the test asserts at the end. A mock carries the expectation, and fails at the moment of the wrong call. That sounds like a small difference and it is the single most consequential choice in this section, which is why §7 is devoted to its consequences.

A fake is the odd one out, and the one people under-use. The other four are configured with answers; a fake is written, once, and then behaves. An in-memory repository with a dict in it is a fake. sqlite::memory: standing in for PostgreSQL is a fake — and a dangerous one, for reasons §11.13 makes concrete.

One line each, for reference: dummy object, test stub, test spy, mock object, fake object and an expectation.

6.2 All Five, By Hand

Before any library, here is one SUT exercised with each kind, written from scratch. Doing it by hand once is worth an hour of documentation, because every framework feature after this is a shorthand for one of these.

# notifier.py
class Notifier:
    """Sends a receipt, unless the customer has opted out."""

    def __init__(self, prefs, mailer, audit_log):
        self.prefs = prefs
        self.mailer = mailer
        self.audit_log = audit_log

    def send_receipt(self, customer_id, amount_cents):
        if not self.prefs.wants_email(customer_id):
            return "skipped"
        self.mailer.send(customer_id, f"You paid {amount_cents / 100:.2f}")
        return "sent"

Three DOCs: prefs supplies an answer, mailer receives an action, audit_log is never touched by this method at all. As in §1.1, one line of configuration lets the tests import it:

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

# tests/test_notifier.py
from notifier import Notifier


# --- a dummy: required by the signature, never used by this code path ---------
def test_the_audit_log_is_never_touched_on_this_path():
    class AlwaysYes:
        def wants_email(self, customer_id):
            return True

    class RecordingMailer:
        def __init__(self):
            self.sent = []

        def send(self, customer_id, body):
            self.sent.append((customer_id, body))

    notifier = Notifier(AlwaysYes(), RecordingMailer(), audit_log=None)
    assert notifier.send_receipt(7, 1250) == "sent"


# --- a stub: supplies indirect input to drive the other branch ----------------
class OptedOutPrefs:
    """A test stub. Answers one question, one way, always."""

    def wants_email(self, customer_id):
        return False


def test_an_opted_out_customer_is_skipped():
    notifier = Notifier(OptedOutPrefs(), mailer=None, audit_log=None)
    assert notifier.send_receipt(7, 1250) == "skipped"


# --- a spy: records indirect output so the test can assert afterwards ---------
class MailerSpy:
    """A test spy. Records what it was asked to do and answers nothing."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = []

    def send(self, customer_id, body):
        self.calls.append((customer_id, body))


class AlwaysYesPrefs:
    def wants_email(self, customer_id):
        return True


def test_the_receipt_carries_the_amount_in_units():
    spy = MailerSpy()
    Notifier(AlwaysYesPrefs(), spy, audit_log=None).send_receipt(7, 1250)

    assert spy.calls == [(7, "You paid 12.50")]


# --- a mock: carries the expectation and fails at the wrong call --------------
class MailerMock:
    """A mock object. It knows what it should receive and enforces it itself."""

    def __init__(self, expected):
        self.expected = expected
        self.satisfied = False

    def send(self, customer_id, body):
        assert (customer_id, body) == self.expected, (
            f"unexpected call: got {(customer_id, body)!r}, "
            f"expected {self.expected!r}"
        )
        self.satisfied = True

    def verify(self):
        assert self.satisfied, f"expected a call to send{self.expected!r}, got none"


def test_the_mailer_is_called_exactly_as_specified():
    mock = MailerMock(expected=(7, "You paid 12.50"))
    Notifier(AlwaysYesPrefs(), mock, audit_log=None).send_receipt(7, 1250)
    mock.verify()


# --- a fake: a real implementation, simplified past production use ------------
class InMemoryPrefs:
    """A fake object. Genuine behaviour, backed by a dict instead of a database."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._opted_out = set()

    def opt_out(self, customer_id):
        self._opted_out.add(customer_id)

    def wants_email(self, customer_id):
        return customer_id not in self._opted_out


def test_opting_out_stops_the_next_receipt():
    prefs = InMemoryPrefs()
    spy = MailerSpy()
    notifier = Notifier(prefs, spy, audit_log=None)

    assert notifier.send_receipt(7, 1250) == "sent"
    prefs.opt_out(7)
    assert notifier.send_receipt(7, 900) == "skipped"
    assert len(spy.calls) == 1

pytest -q tests/test_notifier.py

.....                                                                    [100%]
5 passed in 0.50s

Five tests, five kinds of double, no library. Look at what each one bought.

The dummy — audit_log=None — documents a fact about the code: this path does not audit. If someone adds an audit call, that test fails with AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ..., which is an ugly message carrying real information. A Mock() there would have silently absorbed the new call and told you nothing.

The stub made an unreachable branch reachable. Without it there is no way to test the opt-out path except by having a real preferences service and a real opted-out customer.

The spy let the test assert on something the SUT returned nothing about. send_receipt returns "sent"; the fact that the body says 12.50 and not 1250 is invisible from the return value. That assertion is only possible because the spy recorded the indirect output.

The mock checked the same thing and read worse. Note where its failure comes from: inside send, during the exercise phase, not during verification. That is the definition, and it is the source of both its advantage (the failure points at the moment of the wrong call) and its cost (§7.6).

The fake tested something none of the others could: a sequence. Opt out, then send again. A stub returning a fixed answer cannot express "the answer changes because of what happened", and that is the class of behaviour fakes exist for.

6.3 The Same Five in JavaScript

// src/notifier.js
export class Notifier {
  constructor(prefs, mailer, auditLog) {
    this.prefs = prefs;
    this.mailer = mailer;
    this.auditLog = auditLog;
  }

  sendReceipt(customerId, amountCents) {
    if (!this.prefs.wantsEmail(customerId)) return 'skipped';
    this.mailer.send(customerId, `You paid ${(amountCents / 100).toFixed(2)}`);
    return 'sent';
  }
}

// test/notifier.test.js
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { Notifier } from '../src/notifier.js';

const alwaysYes = { wantsEmail: () => true };

test('a stub drives the opted-out branch', () => {
  const optedOut = { wantsEmail: () => false };          // test stub
  const notifier = new Notifier(optedOut, null, null);   // null mailer: a dummy
  assert.equal(notifier.sendReceipt(7, 1250), 'skipped');
});

test('a spy records the indirect output', (t) => {
  const send = t.mock.fn();                              // test spy
  new Notifier(alwaysYes, { send }, null).sendReceipt(7, 1250);

  assert.equal(send.mock.callCount(), 1);
  assert.deepStrictEqual(send.mock.calls[0].arguments, [7, 'You paid 12.50']);
});

test('a fake has behaviour rather than answers', (t) => {
  const optedOut = new Set();                            // fake object
  const prefs = {
    optOut: (id) => optedOut.add(id),
    wantsEmail: (id) => !optedOut.has(id),
  };
  const send = t.mock.fn();
  const notifier = new Notifier(prefs, { send }, null);

  assert.equal(notifier.sendReceipt(7, 1250), 'sent');
  prefs.optOut(7);
  assert.equal(notifier.sendReceipt(7, 900), 'skipped');
  assert.equal(send.mock.callCount(), 1);
});

cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{ "type": "module" }
EOF
node --test 'test/notifier.test.js'

✔ a stub drives the opted-out branch (4.72339ms)
✔ a spy records the indirect output (4.775071ms)
✔ a fake has behaviour rather than answers (0.971049ms)
ℹ tests 3
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 3
ℹ fail 0
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 322.760249

Notice how little JavaScript needs. A stub is an object literal with one arrow function in it; a fake is a Set and two closures. JavaScript's structural typing means you never need the real interface, which makes hand-rolled doubles cheap enough that reaching for a library is often the worse choice — a point §6.15 returns to.

t.mock.fn() is node's spy. t.mock is scoped to the test: everything it creates is restored automatically when the test ends, which is the whole reason to take the mock tracker off the test context rather than importing the global mock.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: mock.fn( and hand-rolled double.

6.4 unittest.mock: One Object, All Five Roles

Python's standard library ships a configurable test double — one you set up per test — as against the hard-coded test double of §6.2, whose answers are written into the class itself. It is powerful, it is the default in most codebases, and its defaults are more permissive than most people realise.

Mock and MagicMock are the two you will meet. MagicMock is a Mock that also configures Python's dunder methods, so it supports len(), in, iteration, comparison and arithmetic without complaint, where a plain Mock raises TypeError for all of them. MagicMock is what patch gives you by default, and the difference matters exactly when you want the TypeError — a plain Mock is the stricter choice for a collaborator that should never be iterated.

Two more pieces of the API earn their place. mock.sentinel.anything produces a unique, named, otherwise-featureless object, which is the honest way to pass a value the SUT must carry through without inspecting — and a failure prints sentinel.anything rather than <Mock id=...>. And PropertyMock doubles an attribute rather than a method: an ordinary Mock attribute simply holds a value, while a PropertyMock is called on access, so it can raise, count reads, or answer differently each time.

# tests/test_mock_basics.py
from unittest.mock import Mock

from notifier import Notifier


def test_a_mock_answers_anything_you_ask_it():
    m = Mock()
    # Every attribute access creates a new child Mock, on demand, forever.
    assert m.anything.at.all() is not None
    assert m.wants_email(7) is not None       # truthy by default
    assert m.wants_email.called is True
    assert m.wants_email.call_args.args == (7,)


def test_return_value_makes_it_a_stub():
    prefs = Mock()
    prefs.wants_email.return_value = False    # now it is a test stub
    assert Notifier(prefs, None, None).send_receipt(7, 1250) == "skipped"


def test_the_same_object_is_also_the_spy():
    prefs = Mock()
    prefs.wants_email.return_value = True
    mailer = Mock()

    Notifier(prefs, mailer, None).send_receipt(7, 1250)

    mailer.send.assert_called_once_with(7, "You paid 12.50")

pytest -q tests/test_mock_basics.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 0.50s

That first test is the thing to internalise. A bare Mock says yes to everything. m.anything.at.all() is not an error; it silently invents an attribute, then a call, and returns another Mock — which is truthy. That is what makes it convenient and it is exactly what makes it dangerous:

# tests/test_mock_lies.py
from unittest.mock import Mock


def test_a_typo_in_an_assert_name_is_refused():
    mailer = Mock()
    mailer.send(7, "hello")

    # The real method is assert_called_once_with. What does a bare Mock do with a typo?
    mailer.assert_called_onec_with(999, "completely wrong")

pytest -q --tb=line tests/test_mock_lies.py 2>&1 | grep -v '^/'

F                                                                        [100%]
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
E   AttributeError: 'assert_called_onec_with' is not a valid assertion. Use a spec for the mock if 'assert_called_onec_with' is meant to be an attribute.. Did you mean: 'assert_called_once_with'?
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_mock_lies.py::test_a_typo_in_an_assert_name_is_refused - At...
1 failed in 0.81s

pytest reported that as a failure, and the message is worth reading closely:

E  AttributeError: 'assert_called_onec_with' is not a valid assertion. Use a spec for
   the mock if 'assert_called_onec_with' is meant to be an attribute..
   Did you mean: 'assert_called_once_with'?

Mock.__getattr__ refuses any attribute whose name starts with assert, assret, asert, aseert or assrt — the word plus four common misspellings of it — and additionally refuses seven exact names that look like an assertion with the prefix dropped: called, called_once, called_with, called_once_with, any_call, has_calls and not_called. So m.assert_calledd(), m.assrt_called_with() and m.called_once_with() all raise, and the message suggests the name you meant.

That is a real guard, and it covers the typo people actually make. What it cannot cover is a name that does not look like an assertion at all:

# tests/test_mock_lies.py
from unittest.mock import Mock


def test_a_homemade_assertion_name_checks_nothing():
    mailer = Mock()
    mailer.send(7, "hello")

    # None of these starts with a guarded prefix or matches the deny list, so each is
    # silently invented, called, and discarded. Every line "passes".
    mailer.was_called_with(999, "completely wrong")
    mailer.verify(999, "completely wrong")
    mailer.expect_send_to(999)

    # Proof that nothing was checked: the invented attributes exist and were called,
    # and the arguments they were handed were never compared with anything.
    assert mailer.was_called_with.called
    assert mailer.verify.called
    assert mailer.expect_send_to.call_args.args == (999,)

pytest -q tests/test_mock_lies.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 0.48s

Three lines that look like assertions, assert nothing, and the run is green. This is not hypothetical: every codebase that wraps unittest.mock in house-style helpers — verify_called, expect_call, should_have_been_called — has built a way to write a test that cannot fail, and the guard cannot help, because the name carries no signal for it to read.

Two rules follow. Use only the documented assert_* methods, so the guard is working for you. And give the double a spec, so it refuses unknown names of every shape — which is §6.5.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: configurable test double, hard-coded test double and mock.sentinel.

6.5 autospec: Making the Double Have the Real Shape

A Mock will accept any call with any signature. create_autospec builds a double from the real object, so calling it wrongly fails the way the real thing would.

# tests/test_autospec.py
import pytest
from unittest.mock import Mock, create_autospec

from notifier import Notifier


class Prefs:
    """The real collaborator, for shape only."""

    def wants_email(self, customer_id):
        raise NotImplementedError


def test_a_bare_mock_accepts_a_call_the_real_object_would_reject():
    prefs = Mock()
    prefs.wants_email()                      # the real one requires customer_id
    prefs.wants_email(1, 2, 3, unexpected=True)
    assert prefs.wants_email.call_count == 2


def test_autospec_enforces_the_real_signature():
    prefs = create_autospec(Prefs, instance=True)
    prefs.wants_email.return_value = False

    with pytest.raises(TypeError) as exc:
        prefs.wants_email()
    assert "missing a required argument" in str(exc.value)

    # It still works as a stub for correct calls.
    assert Notifier(prefs, None, None).send_receipt(7, 1250) == "skipped"


def test_autospec_rejects_a_method_that_does_not_exist():
    prefs = create_autospec(Prefs, instance=True)
    with pytest.raises(AttributeError):
        prefs.wants_emial(7)

pytest -q tests/test_autospec.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 0.53s

The second and third tests are the argument for autospec in one place. A double that does not match the real interface is a double that can go stale silently. Rename wants_email to wants_notification in production and every bare-Mock test keeps passing, cheerfully calling a method that no longer exists on anything. That is not a small failure mode — it is the mechanism by which a suite drifts into asserting the behaviour of a version of the code that no longer exists.

spec=Prefs is the lighter version: it restricts attribute names but not signatures. spec_set=Prefs additionally refuses setting an attribute that the real class does not have. The hierarchy, weakest to strongest: Mock() → Mock(spec=X) → Mock(spec_set=X) → create_autospec(X).

Use create_autospec unless you have a reason not to. The usual reason is speed — autospec introspects the whole object graph — and it matters only in suites with thousands of doubles.

6.6 patch: Replacing Something You Were Not Given

Everything so far worked because the SUT accepted its collaborators. When it constructs or imports them instead, you have to reach in.

# weather.py
import urllib.request


def fetch_temperature(city):
    with urllib.request.urlopen(f"https://example.invalid/temp/{city}") as r:
        return int(r.read())


def describe(city):
    t = fetch_temperature(city)
    return "freezing" if t <= 0 else "mild" if t < 25 else "hot"

describe gives you no control point (§1.8) at all. patch installs one:

# tests/test_weather.py
from unittest.mock import patch

import weather


def test_describe_reads_the_bands():
    with patch("weather.fetch_temperature") as fetch:
        fetch.return_value = -3
