The situation is familiar. A function reads the clock, so its result changes overnight. A method builds its own database connection, so there is nowhere to put a fake. A class reads an environment variable at import time, so the test has to set it before the import statement runs. None of these are testing problems that a better assertion or a cleverer mock will solve. They are design problems, and the test is simply the first consumer honest enough to complain.

Design for testability is the name for taking that seriously, and it begins with a reframing: testability is not a property a test has, it is a property the code has — the property of having somewhere you can substitute a value and somewhere you can observe a result. Section 1.8 named those the control point and the observation point. This section is about putting them there.

Design for testability is therefore not an extra activity bolted onto writing code. It is also the section where testing pays for itself in something other than defect detection. Almost every change below makes the production code better on its own terms — fewer hidden dependencies, narrower interfaces, logic separated from plumbing — which is why "the tests made me do it" is a weak justification and rarely the real one.

8.1 What Untestable Looks Like

Design for testability begins by looking at code that has none. Start with a small function that has all the usual problems and none of the usual excuses.

# billing.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone

GRACE_DAYS = 3


def renewal_status(subscription):
    """'active' before expiry, 'grace' for a few days after, then 'lapsed'."""
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    days_over = (now - subscription["expires_at"]).days
    if days_over < 0:
        return "active"
    if days_over < GRACE_DAYS:
        return "grace"
    return "lapsed"

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

Eight lines, one hidden dependency, and two ways to test it — both bad.

Write the expected value relative to now. expires_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=1), expect "grace". This is §4.3's re-implementation failure: the test computes the boundary with the same arithmetic the function uses, so it cannot detect a wrong GRACE_DAYS, a wrong comparison, or a timezone mistake. It also passes for a function that always returns "grace" if you only wrote the one case.

Write a literal date. expires_at = datetime(2026, 9, 1, ...), expect "grace". Now the test is a genuine claim — and a bomb with a timer on it.

That second failure is usually described rather than demonstrated, because demonstrating it means waiting a month. It does not: freezegun can move the clock, which makes the bomb go off on demand.

# tests/test_time_bomb.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from freezegun import freeze_time

from billing import renewal_status

SUB = {"expires_at": datetime(2026, 9, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)}


@freeze_time("2026-09-02")
def test_the_day_after_it_was_written():
    assert renewal_status(SUB) == "grace"


@freeze_time("2026-10-02")
def test_the_identical_test_one_month_later():
    assert renewal_status(SUB) == "grace"

pytest -q --tb=short tests/test_time_bomb.py

.F                                                                       [100%]
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
___________________ test_the_identical_test_one_month_later ____________________
tests/test_time_bomb.py:18: in test_the_identical_test_one_month_later
    assert renewal_status(SUB) == "grace"
E   AssertionError: assert 'lapsed' == 'grace'
E
E     - grace
E     + lapsed
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_time_bomb.py::test_the_identical_test_one_month_later - Ass...
1 failed, 1 passed in 1.90s

The same assertion, the same fixture, the same code — and the only difference is what day it is. Nothing in the test file mentions time, which is what makes this class of failure so unpleasant in practice: the suite goes red on a Monday morning with no commit to blame.

Note also what had to happen to demonstrate the problem: an external library reached into the interpreter and replaced datetime.now. That is a large hammer, and the rest of this section is about the smaller ones.

The term above, for reference: design for testability.

8.2 Seams

Michael Feathers' term for the thing you are looking for is a seam: a place where you can change the behaviour of a program without editing the code at that place. Every seam has an enabling point — the place where you choose which behaviour you get.

Three kinds, in descending order of how much you should like them:

an object seam
The code calls a method on something it was given. The enabling point is wherever that thing is passed in — a constructor, an argument, a factory. Ordinary code, no magic, works in every language.
a link seam
The name is resolved at load time and you can arrange for a different thing to be found. In Python that is module patching; in JavaScript, module mocking; in C, the linker. Powerful, invisible in the source, and easy to get wrong (§6.7).
a preprocessor seam
Text substituted before compilation. Mostly a C and C++ concern, mentioned so the taxonomy is complete, and a last resort where it exists at all.

renewal_status has no object seam at all. datetime.now is called by name inside the function, so the only enabling point is the link seam — patching billing.datetime — which is why every naive attempt to test it reaches for mock.patch. Reaching for the link seam because there is no object seam is the diagnostic: it means the design has no control point, and patching is compensating for that rather than fixing it.

The practical value of the seam idea is that it turns "this is hard to test" into a specific question with a specific answer: where is the enabling point, and if there is not one, what is the smallest change that adds one?

One line each, for reference: mock.patch and a seam.

8.3 Dependency Injection

The smallest change that adds an object seam is to stop looking things up and start being handed them. That is the whole of dependency injection, and it needs no framework — the word describes a parameter.

Three forms, and they are not equal.

# injection_styles.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone


class ConstructorInjection:
    """The dependency is required, and the object is never in an invalid state."""

    def __init__(self, clock):
        self._clock = clock

    def stamp(self):
        return self._clock.now()


class SetterInjection:
    """The dependency is optional, and the object has a period of being wrong."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._clock = None

    def set_clock(self, clock):
        self._clock = clock

    def stamp(self):
        return self._clock.now()          # AttributeError if nobody called the setter


class ParameterInjection:
    """The dependency is per-call, which is right when it genuinely varies per call."""

    def stamp(self, clock):
        return clock.now()


class SystemClock:
    def now(self):
        return datetime.now(timezone.utc)

Constructor injection is the default and it is not close. The object cannot exist without its collaborators, so there is no order-of-calls rule to remember and no half-built state for a test to stumble into. It also makes the dependency list visible in one place: a constructor taking seven arguments is a design review that happens automatically, which is a diagnostic §19 will use.

Setter injection buys mutability you almost never want. Its legitimate uses are circular dependencies you cannot otherwise break, and frameworks that must construct an object before they know what to give it. Its cost is that every method must tolerate the dependency being absent, or crash confusingly when it is.

Parameter injection is right when the dependency really is per-call — a request context, a transaction, a user. Passing the same clock as an argument to fourteen methods is constructor injection written out longhand, badly.

None of this needs a container. A DI framework solves the problem of wiring a large object graph, which is a real problem at scale and an entirely different one from the problem of having a seam. A test can always call the constructor directly.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: setter injection.

8.4 Dependency Lookup and the Service Locator

The alternative to being given a dependency is going to find one, which is dependency lookup. Its most common form is the service locator: a global registry the code asks for what it needs.

# locator.py
_REGISTRY = {}


def register(name, thing):
    _REGISTRY[name] = thing


def get(name):
    return _REGISTRY[name]

# invoices.py
import locator


def send_invoice(customer_id):
    mailer = locator.get("mailer")           # goes and finds it
    mailer.send(customer_id, "Your invoice")
    return "sent"

This is testable — the registry is an enabling point, and a test can register a double. So it is not in the same category as a hardcoded datetime.now(). But it is a meaningfully worse seam than injection, for three reasons that matter in a real suite:

The dependencies are invisible. send_invoice(customer_id) claims to need a customer id. It actually needs a registered mailer, and the only way to discover that is to run it and read the KeyError. Multiply by a hundred functions and the setup for any test becomes trial and error.

The registry is shared mutable state between tests. Whatever the last test registered is still there. That is test pollution, it makes results depend on order, and §18 is largely about the class of bug it creates. Every service-locator test suite grows a global teardown that resets the registry, and every one of them eventually forgets a key.

It couples every consumer to the locator. invoices.py now imports the registry module, so the dependency graph runs through a global. Injection leaves consumers depending only on the thing they use.

The honest exception: a locator is a reasonable pattern at the edge of an application — a composition root, a plugin registry, a framework's app context — where something must map names to implementations. The rule is that it belongs in the wiring layer and should not be reached for from inside domain logic.

The term this subsection introduced: test pollution.

8.5 Global State and Singletons

A service locator is one instance of the general problem, which is global state: anything a function can read or write without it appearing in the signature.

The catalogue is longer than people expect. Module-level variables. Class attributes used as caches. Singletons. os.environ. The current working directory. The default locale and the default timezone. A logging configuration. A connection pool held in a module. random's global generator. Even the import system itself, which caches modules and runs their top level exactly once.

Each one produces the same three symptoms:

order dependence
A test passes alone and fails in the suite, or the reverse. §18's most common cause, and the reason pytest-randomly exists.
no parallelism
Two tests mutating one global cannot run at once, so the suite stays serial exactly when it has grown too slow to be (§20).
teardown you must not forget
Every mutation needs an undo, and the one that is forgotten fails a different test, in a different file, days later.

The singleton deserves a specific note because it is usually defended on the grounds that "there should only ever be one". That is a statement about production, and it is enforced in the wrong place: making the class refuse to be instantiated twice means the test cannot have its own. The alternative gives you both — write an ordinary class, and create exactly one at the composition root. Production gets its single instance; each test gets a fresh one.

Where a global is genuinely unavoidable, monkeypatch (§6.8) is the tool, precisely because it registers the undo at the moment it makes the change:

# tests/test_environment.py
import os


def read_region():
    """A function with a hidden dependency on the environment."""
    return os.environ.get("APP_REGION", "eu-west-1")


def test_the_default_region_when_nothing_is_set(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.delenv("APP_REGION", raising=False)
    assert read_region() == "eu-west-1"


def test_the_environment_overrides_the_default(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("APP_REGION", "us-east-2")
    assert read_region() == "us-east-2"


def test_the_previous_test_did_not_leak(monkeypatch):
    # monkeypatch undid the setenv when that test's fixture torn down.
    assert os.environ.get("APP_REGION") is None

pytest -q tests/test_environment.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 0.92s

The third test is the one that matters, and it is worth writing once in a codebase as a demonstration: it passes only because monkeypatch's teardown ran. Replace monkeypatch.setenv with a bare os.environ[...] = ... in the middle test and the third fails — with a message about a variable it never mentions, in a file it does not own, which is exactly the debugging experience §18 is about.

Reading the environment at import time is worse still, because by the time a fixture runs, the value has already been captured. Read it inside a function, or better, pass it in.

8.6 Adding a Control Point Without Changing the Signature

Back to renewal_status. The design problem is real, and so is the constraint that usually accompanies it: there are already forty callers, and you are not going to change all of them today.

There are exactly three ways to get a control point in, and they differ in what they cost the production code.

One: an optional parameter with a default.

# billing.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone

GRACE_DAYS = 3


def renewal_status(subscription, now=None):
    """'active' before expiry, 'grace' for a few days after, then 'lapsed'.

    `now` exists so callers — tests included — can ask about a moment other
    than this one. It is a genuine parameter, not a testing hook.
    """
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc) if now is None else now
    days_over = (now - subscription["expires_at"]).days
    if days_over < 0:
        return "active"
    if days_over < GRACE_DAYS:
        return "grace"
    return "lapsed"

Every existing caller keeps working, because the parameter is optional. The test now states its own boundary, and the boundaries become directly reachable (§4.4):

# tests/test_renewal.py
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import pytest

from billing import renewal_status

EXPIRY = datetime(2026, 9, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
SUB = {"expires_at": EXPIRY}


@pytest.mark.parametrize("offset_days,expected", [
    (-1, "active"),
    (0, "grace"),
    (1, "grace"),
    (2, "grace"),
    (3, "lapsed"),
    (400, "lapsed"),
])
def test_each_side_of_each_boundary(offset_days, expected):
    assert renewal_status(SUB, now=EXPIRY + timedelta(days=offset_days)) == expected


def test_the_default_is_still_the_real_clock():
    long_expired = {"expires_at": datetime(2000, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)}
    assert renewal_status(long_expired) == "lapsed"

pytest -q tests/test_renewal.py

.......                                                                  [100%]
7 passed in 0.87s

Note the is None rather than or: with or, a caller passing a falsy value would silently get the real clock — the same defect §1's exercises found in a greeting(name, hour=None).

Note also the last test, which pins that the default still works. A control point that nobody exercises in its default configuration is a control point that can rot: change the default to datetime.now() without a timezone and every parametrized test still passes while production breaks.

Two: a module-level indirection.

# billing_indirect.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone

_now = lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc)     # the enabling point


def renewal_status(subscription):
    days_over = (_now() - subscription["expires_at"]).days
    return "active" if days_over < 0 else ("grace" if days_over < 3 else "lapsed")

A test does monkeypatch.setattr(billing_indirect, "_now", lambda: fixed). The signature is untouched — genuinely untouched, not just compatibly extended — which is why this is the form to reach for when the function is called from code you cannot recompile, or when it is a __init__ you would rather not widen.

Its cost is that the seam is a link seam (§8.2): invisible at the call site, only discoverable by reading the module, and dependent on the test patching the right module (§6.7). It is also a test hook in a way the first form is not — _now exists for no reason a reader of production code can see.

Three: patch the library. freeze_time and vi.setSystemTime change nothing in production at all. That is their appeal and their whole problem, and §8.7 takes it up directly.

The judgement, stated as a rule: prefer the optional parameter when the value is something a caller could legitimately want to choose. A moment in time, a random seed, a base URL, a page size — these are genuine parameters, and adding one improves the API for reasons unrelated to testing. Prefer the module-level indirection when the value is genuinely never a caller's business and you cannot restructure. Reach for library-level patching when neither is available, and know that you have bought speed with fidelity.

To have in hand before moving on: test hook.

8.7 The Clock

Time is the dependency that produces the most untestable code, so it is worth solving properly rather than case by case.

The principle: time is an input. Code that reads the clock has an undeclared parameter, exactly like code that reads a global. The fix is the same — declare it — and the standard shape is a clock wrapper: a tiny interface with one method, a real implementation that calls the system clock, and a fixed one for tests. The pattern has two other names you will meet. An injectable clock is the clock wrapper described by how it reaches the code; a virtual clock is the fake implementation described by what it does — it advances when the test says so and not otherwise. A virtual clock is strictly more useful than a frozen one, for the reason given at the end of this subsection.

# clock.py
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Protocol


class Clock(Protocol):
    """The role interface (§7.11). One method, named for what the caller needs."""

    def now(self) -> datetime: ...


class SystemClock:
    def now(self) -> datetime:
        return datetime.now(timezone.utc)


class FixedClock:
    """A fake (§6.1), not a stub: it has behaviour, and the test can advance it."""

    def __init__(self, at: datetime):
        self._at = at

    def now(self) -> datetime:
        return self._at

    def advance(self, **kwargs) -> None:
        self._at += timedelta(**kwargs)

# trials.py
class TrialService:
    """Everything time-dependent here goes through the injected clock."""

    def __init__(self, clock, trial_days=14):
        self._clock = clock
        self._trial_days = trial_days

    def start(self, account_id):
        return {"account_id": account_id, "started_at": self._clock.now()}

    def days_remaining(self, trial):
        elapsed = (self._clock.now() - trial["started_at"]).days
        return max(0, self._trial_days - elapsed)

    def is_expired(self, trial):
        return self.days_remaining(trial) == 0

# tests/test_trials.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from clock import FixedClock
from trials import TrialService


def test_a_trial_runs_for_fourteen_days_and_then_expires():
    clock = FixedClock(datetime(2026, 3, 1, 9, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc))
    service = TrialService(clock)

    trial = service.start(account_id=7)
    assert service.days_remaining(trial) == 14

    clock.advance(days=13, hours=23)
    assert service.days_remaining(trial) == 1
    assert not service.is_expired(trial)

    clock.advance(hours=1)
    assert service.days_remaining(trial) == 0
    assert service.is_expired(trial)


def test_the_clock_is_read_afresh_on_every_call():
    clock = FixedClock(datetime(2026, 3, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc))
    service = TrialService(clock)
    trial = service.start(account_id=7)

    clock.advance(days=30)

    # If start() had cached "now", this would still say 14.
    assert service.days_remaining(trial) == 0

pytest -q tests/test_trials.py

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 0.99s

Four things this buys that patching does not:

The test runs in microseconds and reads like a story. advance(days=13, hours=23) then advance(hours=1) states the boundary in the vocabulary of the domain. A fourteen-day trial is tested in the time it takes to add two timedeltas.

The dependency is visible. TrialService(clock) says what it needs. Nothing has to know which module to patch.

It works for code you do not own the import graph of. Patching requires knowing where the name was looked up; injection does not.

The same seam serves production. A back-dated migration, a "what will this look like on the 1st" preview, a simulation — all of them want to pass a different clock, and none of them are tests.

The second test is the one people forget to write. days_remaining calling self._clock.now() rather than caching it is a real decision, and a version that cached would pass every other test in the file.

Two cautions.

Freezing time is not the same as controlling it. A frozen clock that never moves hides bugs in code that measures a duration — every elapsed time is zero, so a timeout can never fire and a rate limiter never resets. FixedClock.advance exists so the test can move it deliberately.

Timezones are a separate dependency, and one the clock wrapper does not solve. SystemClock above returns UTC always, which is a decision worth making explicitly; code that formats for a user's local time needs the timezone injected too, and "the report boundary is midnight" is a claim that is false for most of your users most of the time.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: injectable clock.

8.8 Fake Timers

JavaScript's version of the problem is bigger, because time is not only Date.now() — it is setTimeout, setInterval, queueMicrotask, requestAnimationFrame, and everything built on them: debounce, throttle, retry with backoff, polling, animation. Testing those by waiting is the sleep antipattern (§18), and it is how a suite grows a twelve-second test that is still flaky.

Both runners can replace the whole timer machinery.

// debounce.js
export function debounce(fn, waitMs) {
  let timer = null;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), waitMs);
  };
}

export function tokenAge(issuedAt) {
  return Date.now() - issuedAt;
}

// debounce.test.js
import { test, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { debounce, tokenAge } from './debounce.js';

afterEach(() => { vi.useRealTimers(); });

test('a debounced call fires once, after the quiet period', () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  const calls = [];
  const save = debounce((v) => calls.push(v), 300);

  save('a'); save('b'); save('c');
  expect(calls).toEqual([]);          // nothing yet: the timer has not run

  vi.advanceTimersByTime(299);
  expect(calls).toEqual([]);          // still nothing, one millisecond short

  vi.advanceTimersByTime(1);
  expect(calls).toEqual(['c']);       // exactly one call, with the last value
});

test('setSystemTime makes Date.now a value the test chose', () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-03-01T12:00:00Z'));

  expect(new Date().toISOString()).toBe('2026-03-01T12:00:00.000Z');
  expect(tokenAge(Date.parse('2026-03-01T11:59:30Z'))).toBe(30_000);
});

cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{ "type": "module" }
EOF
npx vitest run --reporter=verbose debounce.test.js

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

 ✓ debounce.test.js > a debounced call fires once, after the quiet period 33ms
 ✓ debounce.test.js > setSystemTime makes Date.now a value the test chose 5ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Start at  22:46:48
   Duration  684ms (transform 43%, import 25%, tests 24%, worker 8%)

The 299-then-1 pair is the whole technique: fake timers turn a duration into a boundary value (§4.4), so the assertion "not before 300 ms, yes at 300 ms" becomes directly testable instead of approximately observable.

node:test has the same facility, enabled per test rather than globally:

// node-timers.test.js
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { debounce } from './debounce.js';

test('node:test drives the same timers', (t) => {
  t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'Date'],
                         now: new Date('2026-03-01T12:00:00Z') });

  const calls = [];
  debounce((v) => calls.push(v), 300)('only');

  assert.equal(new Date().toISOString(), '2026-03-01T12:00:00.000Z');
  assert.deepStrictEqual(calls, []);

  t.mock.timers.tick(300);
  assert.deepStrictEqual(calls, ['only']);

  t.mock.timers.setTime(Date.parse('2027-01-01T00:00:00Z'));
  assert.equal(new Date().getUTCFullYear(), 2027);
});

node --test node-timers.test.js

✔ node:test drives the same timers (15.533165ms)
ℹ tests 1
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 1
ℹ fail 0
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 262.076722

timers.tick(ms) runs due callbacks and timers.setTime(ms) moves the clock without running them — timers.tick( for "what happens after 300 ms", timers.setTime( for "what does this look like next year". enable({ apis: [...] }) is opt-in per API, which is the detail that saves you: faking Date but not setTimeout — or the reverse — is often exactly what you want, and faking everything can hang a test that awaits something the fake timers never advance.

The same caution applies as in Python, with more force: fake timers do not fake await. A promise that resolves from a real I/O event still resolves in real time, and mixing faked timers with real asynchrony produces tests that hang. §18 has the deterministic-waiting patterns for that case.

8.9 Randomness, and the Rest of the Environment

Everything true of the clock is true of every other ambient input, and the list is short enough to memorise:

the clock
Inject it (§8.7).
randomness
Inject a generator, or a seed — a seeded random is reproducible where a global one is not. Never call a global random.seed() in a test: that is global state, and it leaks (§8.5).
identifiers
uuid4() is randomness wearing a hat. Inject the factory, or assert on the shape rather than the value.
the filesystem
tmp_path and a base directory parameter. Never the current working directory.
the environment
Treat the environment as a dependency: read it once at the composition root and pass the values down as configuration. monkeypatch.chdir is the same idea for the working directory, which is an ambient input people forget is one.
the network
A client object, injected. §12 and §13 are about what to put in its place.

Randomness is worth a worked example, because the injectable form is less obvious than the clock's and the payoff is larger — it turns an untestable function into one with exact expected values.

# tokens.py
import random
import string

ALPHABET = string.ascii_uppercase + string.digits


def coupon_code(rng=None, length=8):
    """A human-readable coupon code.

    `rng` takes any random.Random. Passing a seeded one makes the output
    reproducible, which is what the tests — and the fixture loader — need.
    """
    rng = random.Random() if rng is None else rng
    return "".join(rng.choice(ALPHABET) for _ in range(length))

# tests/test_tokens.py
import random
import string

from tokens import ALPHABET, coupon_code


def test_a_seeded_generator_gives_the_same_code_every_run():
    assert coupon_code(random.Random(20260301)) == coupon_code(random.Random(20260301))


def test_two_seeds_give_different_codes():
    assert coupon_code(random.Random(1)) != coupon_code(random.Random(2))


def test_the_code_has_the_requested_length_and_alphabet():
    code = coupon_code(random.Random(7), length=12)
    assert len(code) == 12
    assert set(code) <= set(ALPHABET)


def test_no_lowercase_or_punctuation_survives():
    # The claim people actually care about: this can be read down a phone line.
    codes = [coupon_code(random.Random(seed)) for seed in range(200)]
    assert not any(set(c) & set(string.ascii_lowercase + string.punctuation)
                   for c in codes)

pytest -q tests/test_tokens.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 0.52s

Three things about that file are deliberate.

No test asserts a literal code. coupon_code(random.Random(20260301)) == "K3M7..." would be true, and it would break on any Python version that changed the generator's internals — which has happened. Asserting reproducibility rather than a specific value keeps the useful property without the brittleness.

The last test is a property in disguise (§16): it holds for every seed, and running 200 of them is a poor version of what hypothesis would do properly.

The parameter is a genuine one. A fixture loader that wants a reproducible dataset passes a seeded generator; so does a demo environment. That is §8.6's rule — the control point earns its place independently of the test.

For cryptographic material the same shape applies with one difference: the production default must be secrets, not random, and the injected generator must be impossible to configure from outside the process. A "seed" parameter reachable from a request is a vulnerability, not a control point.

In summary, the vocabulary here is monkeypatch.chdir, seeded random and environment as a dependency.

8.10 The Humble Object

Some code cannot be made testable, because the untestable part is the point: the code that talks to the framework, paints the screen, or hands bytes to a socket. The humble object pattern accepts that and shrinks it.

The move: extract testable component — split the thing in two. One part holds all the logic and no environment; the other is so trivial that not testing it is a defensible decision. The second part is the humble object — humble because it has nothing to say.

# report.py
from datetime import date


def overdue_rows(invoices, today):
    """All the logic. No I/O, no clock, no formatting decisions hidden inside."""
    rows = []
    for invoice in invoices:
        days = (today - invoice["due"]).days
        if days > 0:
            rows.append({
                "reference": invoice["reference"],
                "days_overdue": days,
                "amount_cents": invoice["amount_cents"],
                "severity": "critical" if days > 30 else "warning",
            })
    return sorted(rows, key=lambda r: -r["days_overdue"])


def print_overdue_report(invoices, today, out):
    """The humble object. One loop, one format string, no decisions."""
    for row in overdue_rows(invoices, today):
        out.write(f"{row['reference']:<10} {row['days_overdue']:>4}d  "
                  f"{row['amount_cents'] / 100:>9.2f}  {row['severity']}\n")

# tests/test_report.py
import io
from datetime import date

from report import overdue_rows, print_overdue_report

INVOICES = [
    {"reference": "INV-001", "due": date(2026, 1, 15), "amount_cents": 125_00},
    {"reference": "INV-002", "due": date(2026, 3, 1), "amount_cents": 40_50},
    {"reference": "INV-003", "due": date(2026, 4, 30), "amount_cents": 9_99},
]
TODAY = date(2026, 3, 20)


def test_only_overdue_invoices_appear():
    assert [r["reference"] for r in overdue_rows(INVOICES, TODAY)] == ["INV-001", "INV-002"]


def test_the_most_overdue_comes_first():
    rows = overdue_rows(INVOICES, TODAY)
    assert [r["days_overdue"] for r in rows] == [64, 19]


def test_thirty_days_is_the_boundary_between_warning_and_critical():
    on_the_edge = [
        {"reference": "A", "due": date(2026, 2, 18), "amount_cents": 1},   # 30 days
        {"reference": "B", "due": date(2026, 2, 17), "amount_cents": 1},   # 31 days
    ]
    severity = {r["reference"]: r["severity"] for r in overdue_rows(on_the_edge, TODAY)}
    assert severity == {"A": "warning", "B": "critical"}


def test_the_humble_part_writes_one_line_per_row():
    out = io.StringIO()
    print_overdue_report(INVOICES, TODAY, out)
    assert len(out.getvalue().splitlines()) == 2

pytest -q tests/test_report.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 0.48s

Three of the four tests never touch output at all — they are ordinary value-in, value-out tests, which is why they can afford to check boundaries exhaustively. The fourth checks the humble part, and note how little it claims: one line per row. It does not assert the column widths, because that would be pinning a format nobody has agreed is a requirement (§7.8).

The pattern generalises everywhere the environment is in the way:

  • A GUI or a web page: the presenter computes what should be shown, the view puts it on the screen. This is Model-View-Presenter's whole argument.
  • A message consumer: the handler takes a parsed message and returns commands; the consumer does the acking and the retrying.
  • A CLI: parse arguments into a request object, run a pure function, print the result. Testing main() end-to-end is then one smoke test rather than the whole suite.

The measure of success is whether the humble half can be described in one sentence with no "and" in it. print_overdue_report writes one formatted line per row. If your humble object needs a paragraph, the split is in the wrong place.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: extract testable component.

8.11 Functional Core, Imperative Shell

Push the humble-object idea up to the level of an application and you get functional core imperative shell, usually written "functional core, imperative shell": all the decisions live in pure functions that take values and return values; all the effects live in a thin outer layer that does no deciding.

The shell reads, the core decides, the shell writes.

# core.py
def decide_refund(order, today):
    """Pure. Takes facts, returns a decision. No I/O, no clock, no exceptions."""
    age_days = (today - order["placed_on"]).days
    if order["kind"] == "digital":
        return {"refund": False, "reason": "digital goods are not refundable"}
    if order["override"]:
        return {"refund": True, "reason": "customer service override"}
    if order["final_sale"]:
        return {"refund": False, "reason": "final sale"}
    if age_days > 30:
        return {"refund": False, "reason": f"{age_days} days is outside the window"}
    return {"refund": True, "amount_cents": order["amount_cents"], "reason": "within 30 days"}

# shell.py
from core import decide_refund


def handle_refund_request(order_id, orders, payments, clock, audit):
    """Impure. Gathers facts, calls the core, carries out the decision."""
    order = orders.get(order_id)
    decision = decide_refund(order, clock.now().date())

    if decision["refund"]:
        payments.refund(order["payment_id"], decision["amount_cents"])
    audit.write(order_id, decision["reason"])
    return decision

# tests/test_core.py
from datetime import date

from core import decide_refund

BASE = {"placed_on": date(2026, 3, 1), "kind": "physical", "override": False,
        "final_sale": False, "amount_cents": 4999, "payment_id": "pay_1"}
TODAY = date(2026, 3, 20)


def order(**overrides):
    return {**BASE, **overrides}


def test_a_recent_physical_order_is_refundable():
    assert decide_refund(order(), TODAY) == {
        "refund": True, "amount_cents": 4999, "reason": "within 30 days"}


def test_digital_goods_beat_an_override():
    decision = decide_refund(order(kind="digital", override=True), TODAY)
    assert decision == {"refund": False, "reason": "digital goods are not refundable"}


def test_an_override_beats_a_final_sale():
    assert decide_refund(order(final_sale=True, override=True), TODAY)["refund"] is True


def test_thirty_one_days_is_outside_the_window():
    decision = decide_refund(order(placed_on=date(2026, 2, 17)), TODAY)
    assert decision == {"refund": False, "reason": "31 days is outside the window"}

pytest -q tests/test_core.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 0.65s

Every rule from §4.8's decision table is now tested with no doubles, no fixtures and no setup — four lines each. The shell needs tests too, but far fewer of them, and they are about plumbing: was the refund carried out when the decision said so, was the audit line written either way. Those are §7's interaction tests, and they are the right place for them because carrying out a decision is exactly the fire-and-forget case.

The trade is real and worth naming. The core cannot short-circuit — it must be handed everything it might need before it starts deciding — so a decision that depends on a lookup only in one rare branch forces you either to fetch eagerly or to split the decision in two. That is the cost of the pattern, and it is why it fits domain rules better than it fits code whose control flow is genuinely interleaved with I/O.

The term above, for reference: functional core imperative shell.

8.12 Ports and Adapters

The architectural statement of the same idea is hexagonal architecture, or ports and adapters. The application defines ports — interfaces named for what it needs — and each external technology gets an adapter implementing one. The dependency arrow points inwards: the application knows nothing about PostgreSQL, and the PostgreSQL adapter knows about the port.

driving adapters — HTTP handler, CLI, message consumer, test
↓ call inwards ↓
the application — use cases and domain rules. Knows only ports.
↓ call outwards through a port ↓
driven adapters — PostgreSQL repository, SMTP mailer, Stripe client, system clock
 
in tests
The test is a driving adapter, and in-memory fakes are driven adapters. The application under test is the real thing — no doubles inside it at all.

That last row is the payoff, and it is worth stating precisely: with ports and adapters, a test can exercise the entire application — every use case, every domain rule, every branch — with fast in-memory fakes at the edges and zero mocking inside. The OrderService of §7 was already a small instance of this: InMemoryStock and InMemoryOrders are driven adapters.

Two obligations come with it.

Every fake is a claim about a real adapter, and something must check the claim. Running the same test suite against both the in-memory repository and the PostgreSQL one is the classic technique, and §11 does exactly that. Without it, §7.12's warning applies at architectural scale.

A port must be named for the need, not the technology. OrderRepository is a port; PostgresGateway is an adapter that has leaked its name inwards. The test is whether you could plausibly write a second adapter for a different technology without renaming anything.

The cost, stated honestly: the indirection is real, and for a small application it is overhead that buys nothing. It earns its keep when there is domain logic worth protecting from the technology around it, and it does not when the application is the technology — a thin CRUD service over one database is not improved by a port per table.

One to keep in hand: hexagonal architecture.

8.13 Legacy Code: Sprout and Wrap

All of the above assumes you can change the design. Feathers' definition of legacy code is code without tests, and its characteristic problem is circular: you cannot safely change it because there are no tests, and you cannot write tests because of how it is written.

Two techniques break the circle without requiring you to fix the design first. Both take the same starting point: a long method with an entanglement in the middle.

# legacy.py
def process_batch(rows, connection, logger):
    """Pretend this is 300 lines with a database handle threaded through it."""
    total = 0
    for row in rows:
        logger.write(f"processing {row['id']}")
        total += row["amount_cents"]
        connection.execute("UPDATE rows SET seen = true WHERE id = %s", row["id"])
    logger.write(f"batch total {total}")
    return total

The sprout method — sprout a function, or sprout a class: write the new behaviour as a new, tested unit, and call it from the old code. Suppose a surcharge must now be applied to rows over £100.

# surcharge.py
SURCHARGE_THRESHOLD_CENTS = 10_000
SURCHARGE_RATE = 0.02


def with_surcharge(amount_cents):
    """New behaviour, born tested. Nothing in here knows about the batch."""
    if amount_cents <= SURCHARGE_THRESHOLD_CENTS:
        return amount_cents
    return amount_cents + round(amount_cents * SURCHARGE_RATE)

# tests/test_surcharge.py
import pytest

from surcharge import with_surcharge


@pytest.mark.parametrize("amount,expected", [
    (1, 1),
    (10_000, 10_000),        # on the threshold: no surcharge
    (10_001, 10_201),        # one cent over: 2% applied, rounded
    (50_000, 51_000),
])
def test_the_surcharge_boundary(amount, expected):
    assert with_surcharge(amount) == expected

pytest -q tests/test_surcharge.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 0.70s

The change to process_batch is then one line — total += with_surcharge(row["amount_cents"]) — and while the old method remains untested, the new behaviour never was. Over months this is how a legacy module acquires a tested core: not by a rewrite, but because every change sprouts.

The wrap method: rename the old method and put a new one with the old name in front of it, so you can add behaviour before or after without touching the original body.

def process_batch(rows, connection, logger):
    total = _process_batch_original(rows, connection, logger)
    notify_finance(total)          # new, tested, and the old body is untouched
    return total

The rule for choosing: sprout when the new behaviour goes in the middle, wrap when it goes at the edges. Both are deliberately conservative — neither requires you to understand the 300 lines, which is the property that makes them usable on the day you actually need them.

Two things worth knowing alongside them. A characterisation test — pinning what the code currently does, right or wrong — is often the first move before any change; it is a snapshot (§14) with all of a snapshot's weaknesses and it is still better than nothing. And where the entanglement is a hardcoded constructor, the smallest legal change is usually to extract it into a method you can override in a test-specific subclass (§6.1), which is ugly, temporary, and vastly better than not testing.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: test-specific subclass, sprout method and wrap method.

8.14 Test Logic in Production, and Back Doors

Every technique in this section adds something to production code for the benefit of tests. There is a line, and it is worth being precise about where.

On the acceptable side are control points that are genuine parameters: an optional now, an injected clock, a constructor argument, a seeded generator. A reader who knows nothing about the tests sees an ordinary, slightly more configurable API, and the configurability has non-test uses.

On the unacceptable side is code that behaves differently because it is being tested:

# never_do_this.py
import os


def charge(card, amount_cents):
    if os.environ.get("TESTING"):        # <-- a branch that only runs in tests
        return {"ok": True, "id": "fake"}
    return real_gateway.charge(card, amount_cents)

This is test logic in production, and it fails on three counts at once. The path that runs in tests is not the path that runs in production, so the tests verify code the users never execute. The branch is a production defect waiting for an environment variable to be set by accident. And it removes the pressure that would otherwise have produced an injected gateway — the design stays bad and is now harder to fix.

Back door manipulation is the related question on the setup side: putting a row directly into the database, or reading one out, rather than going through the application. Unlike the branch above, this is sometimes right:

front door
Set up through the application's own API. Slower, and exercises the setup path — so a defect there fails many tests at once, which is useful information stated badly.
back door
Insert the state directly. Fast, precise, and able to create states the API cannot — a corrupted row, an interrupted migration, an account in an impossible state.

The rule most teams settle on: front door for the behaviour under test, back door for the scenery. A test of the checkout flow should check out through the API; the customer, the catalogue and last month's orders can go in the back. And a back-door assertion deserves more suspicion than back-door setup, since asserting on a database row rather than on the API's answer pins a schema the API was free to change.

8.15 Subcutaneous and Layer Tests

The last question this section answers is where to attach the test, once the design gives you a choice.

A subcutaneous test goes in just below the skin: it drives the application through its outermost programmatic interface — the service layer, the use-case objects — rather than through the UI. A layer test deliberately exercises one horizontal slice with the layers beneath it doubled.

 
gets you
costs you
subcutaneous
Nearly all the behaviour, at a fraction of an end-to-end test's cost and flakiness. Survives a UI rewrite.
Says nothing about the UI — which is where a large share of user-visible defects live (§14, §15).
layer
Precise localisation: a failure names the layer.
One behaviour is now asserted at three levels, so a change breaks three suites (§10's duplication argument).

Ports and adapters makes the subcutaneous test the natural default, since the outermost application object is a programmatic interface by construction. That is the connection between this section and §10: the shape of your test suite is largely decided by the shape of your code, and a design with clean seams is one where the cheap tests can be the numerous ones.

8.16 What This Section Established

  • Testability is a property of the design. "Hard to test" is a fact about the code, and almost every fix improves it for reasons unrelated to testing.
  • A seam is a place to change behaviour without editing there. Object seams are ordinary code and preferable; link seams (patching) are invisible and are what you reach for when the design has no seam at all.
  • Constructor injection is the default. Setter injection buys unwanted mutability; parameter injection is right when the dependency really varies per call. No framework is required.
  • A service locator is a testable but worse seam: invisible dependencies, shared mutable state between tests, and coupling to a global. It belongs in the wiring layer, not in domain logic.
  • Global state produces order dependence, prevents parallelism, and requires teardown you will forget. A singleton enforces uniqueness in the wrong place; write an ordinary class and create one at the composition root.
  • Three ways to add a control point: an optional parameter (prefer it when a caller could legitimately choose the value), a module-level indirection (when the signature truly cannot move), and library-level patching (fastest to write, least faithful).
  • Time is an input. A clock wrapper makes a fourteen-day trial testable in microseconds, keeps the dependency visible, and serves production features too. Freezing time is not the same as controlling it.
  • Fake timers turn a duration into a boundary value — 299 ms then 1 ms — and neither runner's fake timers fake await.
  • Randomness, ids, the filesystem, the environment and the network are the same problem, and asserting reproducibility beats asserting a generated literal.
  • The humble object shrinks the untestable part until not testing it is defensible; functional core, imperative shell is the same move at application scale, and its cost is that the core cannot short-circuit.
  • Ports and adapters lets a test exercise the whole application with fakes at the edges and no mocking inside — provided something verifies that each fake matches its real adapter.
  • Sprout and wrap add tested behaviour to untested code without understanding all of it. Sprout for the middle, wrap for the edges.
  • A branch that only runs under test is a defect. A back door is legitimate for scenery and suspicious for assertions.

The term this subsection introduced: a singleton.

Exercises

1. Find the seam.

def send_welcome(user_id):
    user = Database.instance().fetch_user(user_id)
    if datetime.now().hour < 18:
        greeting = "Good day"
    else:
        greeting = "Good evening"
    smtplib.SMTP("mail.example.com").sendmail(
        "noreply@example.com", user.email, f"{greeting}, {user.name}")

List every ambient dependency. For each, say which seam is available today and which one you would add. Then say which single change would buy the most testability for the least disruption.

2. Three control points, one function.

Take renewal_status and implement all three of §8.6's approaches. Write a test for each. Then answer: which one would you keep if the function were called from 200 places across four services you do not own?

3. Fake timers, precisely.

Write a retryWithBackoff(fn, { attempts, baseMs }) that waits baseMs, then 2 × baseMs, then 4 × baseMs between attempts. Test with fake timers that a function failing twice and then succeeding is called exactly three times, and that the total simulated elapsed time is exactly baseMs + 2 × baseMs. What goes wrong if you write the same test with real timers?

4. Split a humble object.

Here is a method that resists testing:

def export_daily_report(self):
    rows = self.db.query("SELECT ...")
    path = f"/var/reports/{date.today():%Y-%m-%d}.csv"
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        for r in rows:
            if r.status == "active" and r.balance_cents > 0:
                f.write(f"{r.id},{r.balance_cents / 100:.2f}\n")
    self.s3.upload(path)
    return path

Split it into a functional core and an imperative shell. Say exactly which assertions become possible that were not, and which one test you would still write against the shell.

5. The line.

For each, decide whether it is an acceptable control point or test logic in production, and say why:

(a) a dry_run=False parameter on a deletion function; (b) if settings.ENV == "test": bcrypt_rounds = 4; (c) an injected IdGenerator whose production implementation is uuid4; (d) a /__test__/reset HTTP endpoint enabled by a config flag; (e) a clock argument defaulting to SystemClock().

6. Sprout into legacy.

process_batch in §8.13 must now skip rows whose id appears in a suppression list, and log one summary line saying how many were skipped. Do it by sprouting rather than by editing the loop's body, and say what you have and have not made testable.

Solutions

1. Find the seam.

Four ambient dependencies: the database singleton, the clock, the SMTP server, and the hardcoded sender address (a configuration value hiding as a literal).

Available today, all of them are link seams only: mock.patch on Database.instance, on datetime, on smtplib.SMTP. That is three patches for a five-line function, which is the diagnostic §8.2 describes.

What to add: a constructor or parameters taking a user_repository, a clock and a mailer, with the sender address as configuration. Then no patching at all.

The single highest-value change is the mailer, and the reason is not testability alone — it is the only dependency that reaches the outside world, so it is the one that makes the function unrunnable in a test at all rather than merely unpredictable. The clock is second, because it is the one that makes the test flaky rather than impossible: half the day it passes.

2. Three control points.

The optional parameter and the module indirection both go as §8.6 shows; the third is @freeze_time with no production change at all.

With 200 external callers, keep the optional parameter. It is the only one of the three that is additive and permanent: existing callers are untouched, new callers gain a genuine capability, and the seam is visible in the signature so nobody has to know a convention. The module indirection would work equally well mechanically, but it leaves a _now in the module whose purpose is invisible, and a colleague will eventually "clean it up".

freeze_time is the wrong answer here specifically because of the scale: it patches globally, so it affects every module the test touches, and in a suite that spans four services that is a large blast radius for a small need.

3. Fake timers, precisely.

export async function retryWithBackoff(fn, { attempts, baseMs }) {
  for (let i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
    try { return await fn(); }
    catch (err) {
      if (i === attempts - 1) throw err;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, baseMs * 2 ** i));
    }
  }
}

The test needs vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync rather than the synchronous version, because the waits are awaited promises: advancing the timers synchronously runs the callbacks but does not give the microtask queue a chance to resume the await. That is the practical form of §8.8's warning that fake timers do not fake await, and it is the single most common reason a fake-timer test hangs.

With real timers the test takes baseMs + 2 × baseMs of wall-clock time — trivial at 10 ms, unacceptable at the production value, and you cannot test the production value at all. Worse, the assertion "the total elapsed time is exactly 300 ms" becomes untestable in principle: real elapsed time is 300-and-a-bit, so the test must assert a range, and the range has to be wide enough to survive a loaded CI machine, at which point it no longer distinguishes 300 from 400. That is §18's argument in miniature.

4. Split a humble object.

Core: def exportable_rows(rows) returning the filtered, formatted rows — the status == "active" and balance_cents > 0 rule and the .2f formatting. Possibly a second pure function report_path(day) for the filename.

Shell: query, open, write the lines the core produced, upload.

Newly possible: every combination of status and balance, including the boundary at zero (balance_cents > 0 versus >= 0 is exactly the off-by-one §4.4 predicts) and negative balances, which the current code silently drops; the formatting of a half-cent; the filename for a date; the behaviour on an empty result. None of these need a filesystem, a database or S3.

The one shell test worth keeping: that it writes the file at the path the core computed and uploads that path — the wiring. Assert it with a tmp_path and a fake uploader. Everything else is now covered more cheaply elsewhere.

5. The line.

(a) Acceptable, and a good idea. dry_run is a genuine feature — operators want it — and its test-time use is incidental.

(b) Test logic in production. It is the exact shape of §8.14's example: production behaviour keyed on the environment. The legitimate version passes the cost factor in as configuration, so the test sets it explicitly and no branch exists.

(c) Acceptable. An injected IdGenerator is an ordinary dependency, and there are non-test reasons to want a different one — deterministic ids in a demo environment, a sequential generator in a migration.

(d) The hard one, and it is a qualified yes. A reset endpoint is a common and pragmatic need for end-to-end tests (§15), and it is genuinely dangerous: it must be off by default, impossible to enable in the production configuration rather than merely disabled, and ideally absent from the production build entirely. Treat the flag as a security control, not a convenience, and note that it is a back door — §8.14's rule says that is acceptable for scenery.

(e) Acceptable, and it is §8.7's recommendation. The default keeps every existing caller working, and the parameter has real non-test uses.

6. Sprout into legacy.

# suppression.py
def partition(rows, suppressed_ids):
    """New behaviour, born tested. Knows nothing about batches or databases."""
    keep = [r for r in rows if r["id"] not in suppressed_ids]
    return keep, len(rows) - len(keep)

process_batch gains two lines at the top — rows, skipped = partition(rows, suppressed_ids) and a logger.write(f"skipped {skipped}").

Made testable: the suppression rule itself, including the cases the loop would have made awkward — an empty suppression list, an id appearing twice in rows, a suppression id that matches nothing, and the count when everything is suppressed. All of it with no connection, no logger and no rows-shaped fixture.

Not made testable: everything that was untestable before. process_batch still takes a connection and a logger, still executes SQL inline, and is still 300 lines. That is the deal sprouting offers — it does not improve the old code, it just stops adding to the problem. What it does buy is that the next change has a tested module to sprout into, and after enough of them the old method is a thin caller of tested parts, at which point wrapping or extracting it is finally safe.

SECTION 9

Test-Driven Development

Everything so far has assumed the code exists and the test comes after it — test-last development, which is how most code in the world is written. Test-driven development inverts it: the test is written first, it fails, and the code is written to make it pass. The neutral name for the ordering alone is test-first development; TDD is test-first development plus the refactor step and the discipline of small cycles, and the difference between the two is §9.6.

Stated that way it sounds like a scheduling preference. It is not. Writing the test first changes what gets built, because the first consumer of every function is a test — so a function that is awkward to call is awkward immediately, while it is still three lines long and free to change. That feedback is the point, and it arrives at the only moment when acting on it is cheap.

TDD also attracts more heat than any other practice in this course, and some of the criticism is correct. This section runs a real kata start to finish so the rhythm is concrete, names the techniques that make the middle of a cycle tractable, and then takes the arguments against it seriously — including the failure mode where a TDD suite becomes the thing that stops the code from changing.

9.1 Red, Green, Refactor

The cycle — red-green-refactor, and it is always written with the hyphens — is three steps, and each has a rule. Test-first development is the first step taken seriously: the test exists before the code it describes, which is what separates test-first development from test-last development, where the test is written afterwards and can only describe what was already built.

1
red
Write a test for behaviour that does not exist. Run it and watch it fail. A test you never saw fail is a test you have no evidence about.
2
green
Make it pass by the quickest route, including one you know is wrong. Speed here is not laziness; it is what keeps the cycle short enough to stay in.
3
refactor
Improve the design without changing behaviour, with the tests proving you did not. This step is where the value is, and it is the one people skip.

Watching the test fail is the step that looks ceremonial and is not. It is the only evidence you will ever have that the test can fail — that it is wired up, that it is selected by the runner, that its assertion is reachable. A test written after the code and never seen red might be asserting nothing at all, and §3.15's vacuous pass is exactly that failure.

The other property, less often stated: the failure message is a design review of your test. If watching it fail tells you nothing about what is missing, the test's name or its assertion needs work — and fixing that now costs nothing.

To have in hand before moving on: red-green-refactor.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: test-first development and test-last development.

9.2 The Three Laws

Robert Martin's three laws of TDD are a tightening of the cycle, best read as a description of what the rhythm feels like at its shortest. The three laws of TDD are:

  1. Write no production code until you have a failing test.
  2. Write no more of a test than is sufficient to fail — a compilation failure counts.
  3. Write no more production code than is sufficient to pass the current failing test.

Taken literally these produce cycles measured in seconds. That is a deliberate exaggeration, and it is a useful one to try for an afternoon: it makes the rhythm physical, and it demonstrates how small a step can be.

It is not how experienced practitioners work all the time. The realistic version is that step size is a variable you control, and you shrink it when you are unsure. Familiar code gets large steps; a tricky algorithm gets tiny ones. Beck's own advice is to take the smallest step that still teaches you something — and to notice that when you are getting steps wrong, the fix is almost always to make them smaller.

9.3 A Kata, Run for Real

Here is the string-calculator kata, every cycle shown, nothing skipped. The rule for reading it: the code at each step is the least that passes the tests written so far, even where you can already see the general solution.

Cycle 1 — the empty string

# tests/test_calculator.py
from calculator import add


def test_an_empty_string_sums_to_zero():
    assert add("") == 0

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

# red — there is not even a module yet
pytest -q tests/test_calculator.py 2>&1 | tail -5

# calculator.py
def add(numbers):
    return 0

# green — the first cycle closes
pytest -q tests/test_calculator.py

return 0 is obviously wrong and it is exactly right. This is fake it (§9.4): the constant is a placeholder that the next test will force out. Nothing has been guessed about the general solution yet.

Now the refactor the last three cycles have been asking for, done with the new behaviour rather than before it — the parsing has become a thing of its own, and it wants a name.

# calculator.py
def _parse(numbers):
    """Turn the input into a list of integers. Knows about the delimiters."""
    if numbers == "":
        return []

    delimiter = ","
    if numbers.startswith("//"):
        header, _, numbers = numbers.partition("\n")
        delimiter = header[2:]

    return [int(part) for part in numbers.replace("\n", delimiter).split(delimiter)]


def add(numbers):
    """Sum a delimited string of numbers. Refuses negatives."""
    values = _parse(numbers)

    negatives = [v for v in values if v < 0]
    if negatives:
        raise ValueError("negatives not allowed: "
                         + ", ".join(str(v) for v in negatives))

    return sum(values)

# green after a refactor — the whole file, which is what makes the refactor safe
pytest -q tests/test_calculator.py -ra --tb=short

......                                                                   [100%]
6 passed in 1.23s

Six cycles, six tests, and a function whose shape was discovered rather than designed up front. Three observations about what actually happened:

No cycle needed more than five lines of production code. The design never had to be held in your head, because the tests held it.

The refactor happened once, late, when the shape was obvious. Extracting _parse on cycle 3 would have been guessing. By cycle 6 the split was not a judgement call — the function had two jobs and one of them had grown.

The last test drove a design decision, not just a behaviour. "The message names every one" is a requirement that only becomes visible when you write the test. A code-first implementation raises on the first negative, and nobody notices until a user reports it.

9.4 Fake It, Triangulate, Obvious Implementation

Beck's three ways to get from red to green, and the skill is choosing between them.

fake it
Return a constant. Cycle 1's return 0. Proves the test is wired up, and defers every decision. Use it when you do not yet know how to do it.
triangulate
Add a second, different example that the fake cannot satisfy. Two points determine the line. Cycles 2 and 3.
obvious implementation
Just write it. When the code is genuinely obvious, faking it is theatre. Most cycles for an experienced developer are this one.

The rule that connects them: use the obvious implementation, and drop to triangulation the moment you get a surprise. Two failed attempts at "obvious" is the signal to slow down — not because small steps are virtuous, but because you have evidence that your model of the problem is wrong, and small steps are how you find out where.

Faking it has a second use worth knowing. When a test is hard to write, a fake makes it green immediately, which tells you whether the difficulty was in the test or in the implementation. If the test is still awkward against a constant, the problem is the interface (§8), and no amount of implementation will fix it.

The vocabulary here: triangulation.

9.5 The Transformation Priority Premise

Uncle Bob's observation that the code changes in a TDD cycle come in a rough order of increasing complexity, and that preferring the simpler ones produces better algorithms:

({} → nil)
no code at all → a null return
(nil → constant)
cycle 1's return 0
(constant → variable)
cycle 2's int(numbers)
(unconditional → if)
cycle 2's empty-string special case
(scalar → array)
cycle 3's split
(array → container)
a richer structure
(statement → recursion)
the expensive one, last
(if → while)
looping, later still
(expression → function)
extraction — usually a refactor rather than a transformation

Two honest caveats. The premise is a heuristic, not a theorem — the claim that following it avoids getting stuck in a local minimum is plausible and unproven. And the exact ordering is disputed even among its advocates.

What survives the caveats is the useful half: when a cycle makes you jump several rows at once, the test was too big. That is a diagnosis available in the moment, and it is worth more than the ordering itself. The kata above never jumps more than one row per cycle, which is why no cycle needed more than five lines.

9.6 The Refactor Step Is Not Optional

Skipping the third step is the most common way TDD fails in practice, and the result has a predictable shape: a green suite, and code that is a pile of special cases nobody dares touch.

The step has rules of its own.

Refactor only when green. Refactoring under a red bar means two things can be wrong at once, and you cannot tell which. Get to green — even by reverting — and then improve.

Do not change behaviour. If a refactor requires a test change, it was not a refactor. That is the definition, and it is what makes the tests a safety net rather than a formality.

Refactor the tests too. Duplicated setup, a fixture that has drifted, a name that no longer describes the claim. §19 is the catalogue, and the refactor step is where it gets applied. Test code that is never cleaned up is what turns a suite into a liability.

Look for the duplication. Beck's formulation of what the refactor step is for is removing duplication — and duplication between the test and the code counts. When cycle 3's implementation stopped restating the test's examples and started expressing a rule, that was the duplication going away.

The economic case is simple: the value of a test suite is that it makes change safe, and if you never change anything, you have paid for a safety net you do not use. The refactor step is where the investment is redeemed. A team that writes tests first and never refactors has all of TDD's costs and none of its benefit.

9.7 Tests as a Design Tool

The claim that TDD improves design is easy to state vaguely and worth making precise. Four specific pressures:

Writing the call before the implementation. You choose the signature while looking at the call site, which is where a bad signature is visible. split(total, ways) reads well; Splitter(config).execute(request) does not, and you find that out in the first thirty seconds rather than after forty call sites exist.

A test needs a seam. Anything the code reaches for globally — a clock, a connection, a config module — has to be injectable before a test can control it, so TDD applies §8's design pressure continuously rather than as a later refactor.

A test needs an observation point. Code whose effect is invisible cannot be tested, so TDD pushes toward returning values rather than mutating hidden state — which is §8.11's functional core arriving by a different road.

Pain is a signal. Awkward setup means too many collaborators. A test needing six mocks means the SUT is doing six things (§7.13). A test that must be written in a particular order means shared state. Each of these is a design problem announcing itself, and the discipline is to hear it as one rather than reaching for a bigger fixture.

The honest limit: TDD produces good small-scale design and has little to say about large-scale design. It will not tell you your service boundaries are wrong, that you need a queue, or that the data model does not fit the domain. Those decisions are made before the first test and are not discovered by cycling. Treating TDD as a substitute for architecture is a real failure mode, and it is the strongest version of the criticism in §9.15.

9.8 Emergent Design, and Where It Stops

Emergent design is the claim that a good structure appears from the cycle rather than being planned. The kata is a small demonstration: _parse was not designed, it emerged when the function got two jobs.

Where it works: within a module, for structure that is reversible. Extracting a function, splitting a class, introducing a value type — all cheap to do later, so deferring them costs nothing and deciding early risks guessing wrong.

Where it does not: for decisions that are expensive to reverse. A database schema with a million rows in it. A public API other teams have integrated with. A choice between a queue and a synchronous call. A distributed transaction boundary. These do not emerge; they are chosen, and choosing them badly is not fixed by a refactor step.

The workable position is plan the expensive things, evolve the cheap ones — and know which is which, because the answer is different in every codebase. A useful test: if getting it wrong means a migration, a deprecation window or a coordinated release, it is not a candidate for emergence.

9.9 Test-Driven Bug Fixing

The single highest-value application of TDD, and the one to adopt first even if you adopt nothing else. It works whether or not the codebase was built this way.

The sequence:

  1. Reproduce the defect as a failing test. Not a script, not a manual click-through — a test in the suite, with a name that describes the defect.
  2. Watch it fail, and check the failure message says what the bug report says. If it does not, you have reproduced a different bug.
  3. Fix the code.
  4. Watch it pass.
  5. Keep the test. It is now a regression test, and it is the only thing standing between you and the same defect returning.
# tests/test_regression.py
import pytest

from calculator import add


def test_issue_412_a_delimiter_that_is_a_regex_metacharacter():
    """Reported 2026-03-01: add("//|\\n1|2") raised instead of returning 3.

    The parser used str.split, which is literal, so this was never a regex
    problem — the reporter's diagnosis was wrong and the test is what settled it.
    """
    assert add("//|\n1|2") == 3


def test_issue_419_every_negative_is_named_not_just_the_first():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match=r"-1, -4"):
        add("1,-1,3,-4")

# the regression suite: two defects that will not come back silently
pytest -q tests/test_regression.py

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 0.85s

Two things make this worth insisting on.

It is the cheapest possible test to justify. No argument about coverage or about whether the code is testable — a defect happened, in production, and this test proves it cannot happen again unnoticed. §4.11 called this the strongest evidence available that a test earns its keep.

It forces you to understand the defect before fixing it. A fix applied without a reproducing test is a guess, and the way you find out it was the wrong guess is the same bug being reported again in a month. The first test above is a real instance: writing it revealed that the reported cause was not the actual cause.

The one discipline that makes it work: write the test before the fix. A test written afterwards passes immediately, and you have no evidence it would have caught anything.

9.10 A Spike

Sometimes you cannot write the test because you do not understand the problem well enough to know what to assert. The answer is not to abandon the practice; it is to stop pretending you are doing it.

A spike is a deliberately throwaway experiment: write whatever code answers the question — no tests, no structure, no review — and then delete it and start again test-first with what you learned.

Two rules make it work rather than become an excuse.

Timebox it. "Two hours to find out whether this library can do X." Without a limit a spike becomes the implementation.

Actually delete it. Spike code is optimised for answering a question, not for living in a codebase. Keeping it is how untested, unstructured code enters the system with the story that it was "already working". The knowledge is what you keep.

Spikes are the honest answer to "TDD does not work when you do not know what you are building". That is true, and it describes a research activity rather than a construction one. Do the research, then build.

9.11 Specification by Example, and Given-When-Then

Section 1.2 introduced given-when-then as a phrasing of the four-phase test. Here is what it is actually for.

Specification by example — also called example-driven development when it drives the code rather than only the requirements — is the practice of writing requirements as concrete examples rather than as prose. Instead of "customers with a gold membership receive a discount on orders over £50", you write:

Given a gold member and an order of £60 When the order is priced Then the total is £54

The value is not the format. It is that a concrete example cannot hide an ambiguity. The prose version leaves at least four questions open — is £50 inclusive, is the threshold before or after the discount, does it apply to the shipping, what about a gold member who joined yesterday — and every one of them surfaces the moment somebody has to write a number down.

That is the same argument §4.8's decision table made, and it is why both practices belong to requirements as much as to testing. A conversation with a product owner that produces six examples has produced six test cases and settled six ambiguities, and the second is worth more.

# pricing.py
GOLD_DISCOUNT_PCT = 10
DISCOUNT_THRESHOLD_CENTS = 5_000


def price(order_cents, membership):
    """Given/when/then, as executable examples, in tests/test_pricing.py."""
    if membership == "gold" and order_cents >= DISCOUNT_THRESHOLD_CENTS:
        return round(order_cents * (100 - GOLD_DISCOUNT_PCT) / 100)
    return order_cents

# tests/test_pricing.py
import pytest

from pricing import price


@pytest.mark.parametrize("membership,order_cents,expected,why", [
    ("gold", 6_000, 5_400, "a gold member over the threshold gets 10% off"),
    ("gold", 5_000, 4_500, "the threshold is inclusive — this was the ambiguity"),
    ("gold", 4_999, 4_999, "one penny under, and there is no discount"),
    ("standard", 6_000, 6_000, "a standard member gets nothing, however large"),
    ("gold", 0, 0, "an empty order is not a special case"),
])
def test_the_agreed_examples(membership, order_cents, expected, why):
    assert price(order_cents, membership) == expected, why

# the specification, executable
pytest -q tests/test_pricing.py

.....                                                                    [100%]
5 passed in 0.84s

The second row is the point of the whole exercise. "Over £50" does not say whether £50 itself qualifies; the example does, the product owner had to answer, and the answer is now enforced. That is a boundary value (§4.4) discovered by a requirements conversation rather than by a testing technique — and it is the same value.

The why column is doing real work too: it makes the table readable as a specification, and it becomes the assertion message when a row fails.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: example-driven development.

9.12 BDD and Gherkin

Behaviour-driven development — behavior-driven development in its original spelling — started as a renaming exercise. Dan North's observation was that people struggled with TDD for linguistic reasons — "test" made them think of QA, and "what should I test" is a harder question than "what should it do". Renaming test to should, and the class to a behaviour, removed a surprising amount of friction.

It then grew a second half: Gherkin, a structured natural-language format with tooling that maps each line to a step definition.

Feature: Membership discounts

  Scenario: A gold member spending over the threshold
    Given a gold member
    And an order of 6000 cents
    When the order is priced
    Then the total is 5400 cents

  Scenario: Exactly on the threshold
    Given a gold member
    And an order of 5000 cents
    When the order is priced
    Then the total is 4500 cents

Each Given/When/Then line is matched by a regular expression to a function that does the work. The promise is that non-programmers can read and even write the scenarios.

Be clear-eyed about the trade, because this is where BDD most often disappoints:

What it genuinely buys. A shared vocabulary between developers and the people who know the domain, and a specification that cannot silently drift from the system, because it executes. When a product owner really does read the scenarios, this is valuable and there is no substitute.

What it costs. A second language, a step-definition layer, and a regular-expression matching system between the words and the code. Refactoring is harder — renaming a concept means updating scenarios, step definitions and code. And the parametrized table in §9.11 expresses the same five examples in a fifth of the space, with the full power of the language available.

The failure mode. A team adopts Gherkin, no non-programmer ever reads a .feature file, and the layer is pure overhead: developers writing English to match a regex to call a function they could have called directly. This is common, and it is worth checking honestly before adopting the format.

The decision rule: adopt Gherkin when non-programmers will genuinely read or write the scenarios; use plain parametrized tests otherwise. The valuable half of BDD — thinking in behaviours, writing examples with the people who know the domain, naming tests as sentences — needs none of the tooling, and this course uses it throughout without a single .feature file.

9.13 Acceptance Tests and Executable Specifications

A story test or acceptance test answers "is this feature done?" rather than "does this function work?". It is written from the user's perspective, in the user's vocabulary, and it is the executable form of the definition of done (§20).

who writes it
