Ideally the team together, before the work starts. An acceptance test written after the feature describes what was built rather than what was wanted.
what it asserts
A business outcome. "The customer is charged £54" — not "the pricing service returns 5400".
where it runs
Subcutaneously (§8.15) if you can — through the application's API rather than its UI. End-to-end only when the UI is genuinely part of the claim.
how many
Few. One or two per story. They are the slowest and most brittle tests you own, and §10 explains why their number must stay small.

An executable specification is the same artefact seen from the other side: a document that is also a test, so it cannot describe a system that no longer exists. That property is the whole appeal — every specification document ever written has drifted from its system, and one that runs in CI cannot.

The term above, for reference: story test.

9.14 Double-Loop TDD

Putting §9.13 and §9.1 together gives the shape most teams actually work in: two nested cycles.

outer loop — the acceptance test
Write a failing test for the feature as a user would describe it. It stays red for hours or days.
↓ while the outer test is red ↓
inner loop — unit cycles
Red, green, refactor, in minutes, over and over, building the pieces the outer test needs.
↓ when the last piece lands ↓
the outer test goes green — and that, not the developer's judgement, is what "done" means.

Two practical consequences.

The outer test is red for a long time, and that is fine — but it must not be red in the shared build. Keep it excluded by a marker (§2.5) until it passes, or on a branch. A permanently red pipeline is worse than no pipeline (§18.1).

The outer test tells you when to stop. Without it, "done" is a judgement made by the person least able to make it objectively — the one who just wrote the code. This is the strongest argument for the outer loop, and it is not really about testing at all.

This is also §7.12's outside-in development, seen from the process side rather than the design side: the outer test discovers the collaborators, and each collaborator becomes an inner loop.

9.15 Is TDD Dead?

David Heinemeier Hansson's 2014 essay and the conversations that followed with Kent Beck and Martin Fowler produced the most useful public argument about this practice, and it is worth engaging with rather than summarising as a slogan.

The strongest criticisms, stated fairly:

Test-induced design damage. Contorting a design to make it unit-testable — layers of indirection, interfaces with one implementation, a service object per verb — produces code that is harder to read in exchange for tests that are easier to write. This happens, it is a real cost, and "the tests made me do it" is not a defence.

Mock-heavy suites verify nothing. A design driven by "every collaborator must be doubled" produces exactly §7.2's failure: every unit passes against doubles and the system does not work. That is a genuine and common outcome of dogmatic outside-in TDD without contract tests (§13).

It is not free. Written honestly, TDD costs more up front. The claim is that it pays back through defect reduction and change safety, and that claim is empirically mixed — the studies do not show a large, consistent effect.

Some code is not amenable. Exploratory work, UI layout, performance tuning, anything where you do not know what "correct" looks like until you see it. Insisting on a test first is theatre.

What survives the criticism, and it is most of the value:

  • Write the test before the fix, always (§9.9). Nobody argues against this, and it is where most of the benefit is.
  • Testability pressure is real and usually good (§9.7) — up to the point where it starts distorting the design, which is a judgement rather than a rule.
  • The refactor step (§9.6) is what makes a codebase changeable, and it needs a suite you trust regardless of when the tests were written.
  • Fast feedback in small steps is the underlying mechanic, and it is valuable whether or not the test comes first.

The position this course takes: test-first is a tool, applied where it earns its place — non-obvious logic, bug fixes, anything with awkward edge cases — and not a rule to be applied uniformly. What is not optional is that the tests exist, that they are good, and that the refactor step happens.

One line each, for reference: edge case and outside-in tdd.

9.16 Test Cancer

The failure mode that deserves its own name, because it is what a bad TDD suite turns into, and because it is the mechanism behind most of the criticism above.

Test cancer is a suite that has grown so coupled to the implementation that it prevents the code from changing. The tests are green, numerous and useless: every refactor breaks dozens of them, so refactors stop happening, so the design decays, so the code gets harder to change, so more tests are needed to feel safe.

The mechanism, step by step:

1
Tests are written against interactions rather than outcomes (§7.7), because that is what mocking makes easy.
2
A refactor changes the interactions without changing the behaviour. Thirty tests go red, none of them describing a defect.
3
Fixing them is an afternoon. The refactor is abandoned, or done without the improvement.
4
Repeat. The design ossifies, and the suite — the thing bought to make change safe — is now the main obstacle to it.

The symptoms are recognisable and worth checking for:

  • A refactor with no behaviour change breaks tests. The single clearest diagnostic. It should be impossible.
  • Tests are updated to match the code, routinely, without anyone asking whether the behaviour changed.
  • The suite's assertions restate the method bodies (§7.13's review heuristic).
  • Nobody deletes tests, because deleting a green test feels like removing safety.

The treatment is the same set of moves this course has been building toward. Assert on outcomes, not interactions (§7.13). Test at a coarser grain — a suite of behaviour tests over a module is far more refactor-resistant than a test per class (§10). Delete tests that earn nothing (§4.11), which requires the cultural permission to do so. And make the refactor step routine, because a suite that survives refactoring is one that has been refactored against regularly.

The connection to §9.15 is direct: most of what is criticised as "TDD damage" is test cancer, and it comes from how the tests were written rather than when. A test-first suite of state-verifying behaviour tests has none of these symptoms. A test-last suite of mock-heavy interaction tests has all of them.

9.17 What This Section Established

  • Red, green, refactor — and watching the test fail is the only evidence you will ever have that it can fail.
  • The three laws describe the shortest version of the rhythm. Step size is a variable: shrink it when you are surprised.
  • The kata is the argument. Six cycles produced a function whose shape was discovered rather than designed, and no cycle needed more than five lines of production code.
  • Fake it, triangulate, obvious implementation. Use the obvious one, and drop to triangulation after two surprises.
  • The transformation priority premise is a heuristic, and its useful half is a diagnosis: jumping several rows in one cycle means the test was too big.
  • The refactor step is where the value is, and skipping it gives you all of TDD's costs and none of its benefit. Refactor only when green, never change behaviour, and refactor the tests too.
  • TDD applies design pressure — a seam, an observation point, a signature chosen at the call site — and it has little to say about large-scale design. Plan the expensive things; evolve the cheap ones.
  • Test-driven bug fixing is the highest-value application, works in any codebase, and forces you to understand the defect before fixing it.
  • A spike is a timeboxed, deliberately deleted experiment — the honest answer to "I do not know what I am building yet".
  • Specification by example works because a concrete example cannot hide an ambiguity, and the boundary it exposes is worth more than the test it produces.
  • Gherkin is worth its cost only when non-programmers really read the scenarios. The valuable half of BDD needs no tooling.
  • The outer loop tells you when to stop, which is a judgement the author of the code should not be making alone.
  • The criticisms of TDD are partly right: design damage, mock-heavy suites that verify nothing, real up-front cost, and code that is not amenable. Test-first is a tool applied where it earns its place; good tests and the refactor step are not optional.
  • Test cancer is a suite so coupled to the implementation that it prevents change. Its clearest diagnostic is a behaviour-preserving refactor breaking tests, and its cause is how the tests were written, not when.

Exercises

1. Run the kata yourself.

Do the string-calculator kata from scratch without looking at §9.3, and record how many cycles you take and where you were tempted to skip ahead. Then do it a second time with a rule: no cycle may add more than three lines of production code. What was different?

2. Identify the transformation.

For each cycle in §9.3, name the transformation from §9.5's list that the production change corresponds to. Which cycle jumped more than one row, and could a smaller test have avoided it?

3. Write the failing test first.

A bug report says: "Exporting a report for a customer with no orders produces a CSV with a header and one blank line, instead of just a header." Write the test you would add, in full, before touching the code. Then say what you would check about its failure before writing the fix.

4. Fake it or write it.

For each, choose fake-it, triangulate, or obvious implementation, and defend it: (a) is_leap_year(year); (b) a function computing a customer's loyalty tier from six rules; (c) slugify(title); (d) a rate limiter using a sliding window.

5. Diagnose the suite.

A team reports: 3,400 tests, 94% coverage, an eleven-minute suite, and "we can't refactor anything without breaking fifty tests". Three of the last four production incidents were not caught by the suite. Diagnose it using this section and §7, and give the first three things you would do, in order.

6. Gherkin or not.

Your product owner asks for Gherkin scenarios because they read about it. Write the two questions you would ask before agreeing, say what you would propose if the answers are unfavourable, and describe what you would keep from BDD either way.

Solutions

1. Run the kata yourself.

No fixed answer, but the two reliable observations: almost everyone is tempted to skip to the general split solution at cycle 2, and almost everyone who does then writes cycle 4's newline handling as a special case bolted onto a structure that was guessed rather than derived.

The three-line rule changes the experience because it makes the test the thing you design. When only three lines of production code are available, a test that demands ten is obviously too big, and you split it — which is exactly §9.5's diagnosis arriving from the other direction.

2. Identify the transformation.

Cycle 1: (nil → constant) — return 0. Cycle 2: (constant → variable) plus (unconditional → if): two rows in one step, and it is the only cycle that jumps.

Cycle 3: (scalar → array) — split and a sum. Cycle 4: no new transformation at all; replace is a variable change within the existing shape, which is why it was the easiest cycle. Cycle 5: (unconditional → if) again, for the header. Cycle 6: (unconditional → if) plus a new expression, and it triggered the extraction — which is a refactor, not a transformation, and the premise is right to keep the two apart.

Cycle 2's double jump could have been avoided by splitting it: a test asserting add("7") == 7 with the empty-string test temporarily deleted would need only (constant → variable), and re-adding the empty-string test would then need only (unconditional → if). Whether that is worth it is a judgement — but the fact that it is possible is the premise's point.

3. Write the failing test first.

def test_a_customer_with_no_orders_exports_a_header_and_nothing_else():
    csv = export_report(customer_id=7, orders=[])

    assert csv == "order_id,placed_at,total_cents\n"
    assert csv.count("\n") == 1

Two assertions because they fail differently: the first says what is wrong, and the second is the one that stays meaningful if the header changes.

Before writing the fix, check that the failure message matches the report. If it says assert 'order_id,...\n\n' == 'order_id,...\n' then you have reproduced the reported defect. If it says something else — a TypeError on the empty list, say — you have found a different bug, and the reported one is still unreproduced. That check is the whole reason for step 2 in §9.9, and skipping it is how a fix ships for the wrong problem.

4. Fake it or write it.

(a) Obvious implementation. The leap-year rule is four lines and everyone knows it. Faking it is theatre — though the tests should still triangulate: 2024, 1900, 2000 and 2023 are four genuinely different branches (§4.4).

(b) Triangulate, one rule at a time. Six interacting rules is exactly where the obvious implementation goes wrong, and where a decision table (§4.8) should be built first so the cycles have somewhere to go.

(c) Fake it, then triangulate. slugify looks obvious and is not: accents, punctuation, double spaces, leading and trailing hyphens, empty results, non-Latin scripts, and length limits. Starting with return "hello-world" and letting each new example force out one rule keeps you from writing a regular expression you cannot explain.

(d) Neither, initially — spike it (§9.10). A sliding-window rate limiter has a design question at its centre (what data structure, what precision, what happens at the boundary) that you cannot answer from the outside. Spike for two hours, throw it away, and then TDD it with the design question already settled — at which point most of it becomes obvious implementation, and the clock is injected (§8.7) because you already know you will need to control it.

5. Diagnose the suite.

The diagnosis is test cancer (§9.16), and the evidence is all three symptoms at once: high coverage with low defect detection means the tests execute code without making meaningful claims about it (§17.9); "can't refactor without breaking fifty tests" is the clearest possible sign of coupling to implementation (§7.7); and eleven minutes for 3,400 tests suggests they are not the fast unit tests their number implies.

The missed incidents are the most informative number, and the first move should be about them rather than about the suite's shape.

First: read the four incidents and ask, for each, what test would have caught it. That will almost certainly point at integration boundaries (§11) and at behaviour the unit tests mock away — which tells you what to build rather than leaving you to guess.

Second: stop the bleeding on new tests. Agree that new tests assert on outcomes, not interactions (§7.13), and that a test needing more than two doubles gets a design conversation instead.

Third: make one refactor cheap. Pick the module that most needs changing, replace its interaction tests with a smaller number of behaviour tests over the module's public surface, and do the refactor. That demonstrates the fix on real work instead of proposing a suite-wide rewrite nobody will fund.

What not to do first: raise the coverage target, which would make every one of these problems worse.

6. Gherkin or not.

The two questions: "Who will read these, and when?" and "Will anyone outside the development team write or change one?" Both are questions about behaviour rather than intention, so ask for a concrete commitment — a person and an occasion.

If the answers are unfavourable — the honest common case is that the product owner will read them once and never again — propose the parametrized example table from §9.11 instead, and offer to review it together in the same conversation Gherkin would have prompted. That gets the entire benefit: the examples are written jointly, the ambiguities surface, and the table is readable by anyone who can read a table.

What to keep from BDD either way: thinking in behaviours rather than methods, which changes what you test; writing the examples with the people who know the domain, before the code; naming tests as sentences (§4.17); and the given-when-then structure as a way to organise a test (§1.2). None of that needs a .feature file, and it is where the practice's value actually lives.

SECTION 10

The Shape of a Suite

Every section so far has been about individual tests. This one is about the population: how many of each kind you should have, and why the answer is a shape rather than a number.

The question matters because the kinds are not interchangeable. A unit test runs in a millisecond and tells you nothing about whether the pieces fit together. An end-to-end test tells you the system works and takes forty seconds, fails for six reasons that are not defects, and points at nothing in particular when it does fail. A suite made entirely of either one is a bad suite, and the interesting engineering is in the mix.

There is also genuine terminology confusion here, and it is not pedantry. "Unit test" means at least three different things to working developers, "integration test" means at least four, and a team can argue for an hour about the pyramid while meaning different things by every word in it. This section fixes the vocabulary first, then uses it.

10.1 What Is a Unit?

The word has two established meanings and the disagreement between them explains most of the arguments about test suites.

a unit of code
A class, or a function. One test class per production class; a collaborator is a collaborator and gets doubled. The London reading (§7.5).
a unit of behaviour
One piece of behaviour, however many classes it takes. A test may exercise six objects and still be a unit test, because it makes one claim and uses no infrastructure. The classical reading.

This course uses the second, and the reason is §9.16. A test-per-class suite is coupled to the class structure, so changing that structure — which is what refactoring is — breaks tests that describe no behaviour change. A behaviour-per-test suite over a module survives the same refactor untouched, because the module's observable behaviour did not move.

The practical definition that follows, and the one worth adopting: a unit test is one that runs in memory, in milliseconds, with no infrastructure and no shared state. That says nothing about how many objects it touches, which is exactly the point — the size of the SUT (§1.6) is not what makes a test fast or reliable. Its dependencies are.

10.2 Solitary and Sociable

Jay Fields's pair of adjectives is the useful refinement, because it separates the question from the pyramid argument entirely.

a solitary unit test
Every collaborator is a double. The SUT is exercised alone. Failures are precisely localised — and the doubles are unverified assumptions (§7.12).
a sociable unit test
Real collaborators, where they are fast and deterministic. Exercises the real wiring — and a defect anywhere in the graph fails many tests at once.

Both are unit tests by the definition above. Choosing between a solitary unit test and a sociable unit test is a trade between localisation and fidelity, and it is a per-test decision rather than a policy:

  • Solitary where the collaborator is slow, non-deterministic or not yours. A clock, a payment gateway, an email service.
  • Sociable where the collaborator is a fast, deterministic value or domain object. Doubling a Money class, a validator or a pure calculator buys nothing and costs fidelity.

The failure mode of an all-solitary suite is §7.2's: green everywhere and broken as a system. The failure mode of an all-sociable suite is that one defect fails four hundred tests, and the report tells you nothing about where it is. Neither is fatal; the first is worse, because it fails silently.

10.3 The Pyramid

Mike Cohn's shape, and the reason it has survived twenty years of argument:

end-to-end
tens · minutes
integration / service
hundreds · seconds
unit
thousands · milliseconds

The claim is not that unit tests are better. It is an argument from cost per test held constant against value per test: a test one level up costs an order of magnitude more to run, more to write, and much more to maintain, while catching a defect the level below could usually have caught. So the cheap ones should be numerous and the expensive ones should be few and chosen carefully.

Two things the pyramid is usually misread as saying:

It is not about a ratio. "70/20/10" is a slogan, not a finding. The shape says more at the bottom, and the actual numbers depend entirely on what the system is.

It is not about the levels being named those three things. Cohn's original names were Unit, Service and UI, and the middle layer has been renamed in every retelling since — which is a symptom of the real problem, that "integration test" does not name one thing.

10.4 The Practical Test Pyramid

Ham Vocke's version, which is the one to actually use, because it replaces the argument about layer names with a rule about what each test is allowed to touch.

unit
In memory, no infrastructure. Sociable by default; solitary at the boundaries.
integration
Exactly one piece of real infrastructure — a database, a queue, an HTTP client against a stub (§11, §12).
component
One deployable service, running for real, with its own database and every other service stubbed.
contract
The agreement between a consumer and a provider, verified separately on each side (§13). Replaces most of what people use end-to-end tests for.
end-to-end
The whole system, through the user's interface (§15). A handful, covering the journeys that would be catastrophic to break.

The contract layer is the addition that makes the pyramid work for systems with more than one service, and it is the answer to the obvious objection — that a suite of unit and component tests verifies each service against its assumptions about the others. §13 is that layer.

Vocke's rules of thumb are worth having verbatim: write tests at different granularities, the more high-level you get, the fewer tests you should have, and — the one people resist — if a higher-level test catches a defect that a lower-level test could have caught, add the lower-level test and consider deleting the higher one.

10.5 The Ice-Cream Cone

The anti-pattern, and it is the most common real shape in the industry:

manual testing
a person, before every release
automated end-to-end
hundreds · hours · flaky
integration
unit

Nobody plans this. It arrives one reasonable decision at a time: the code is hard to unit-test, so the test goes at the UI level; a defect escapes, so an end-to-end test is added; the suite gets slow, so it moves to nightly; it gets flaky, so a manual pass is added before releases.

The symptoms are recognisable: a suite measured in hours, a flake rate high enough that failures are re-run rather than read (§18.1), a release process with a person in it, and — the diagnostic one — defects that a five-line unit test would have caught, found by a forty-second browser test.

Inverting it is slow work and there is a shortcut worth knowing: for each escaped defect, write the lowest-level test that would have caught it. That directs the effort at real gaps instead of at a coverage number, and it inverts the cone from the bottom over months, which is the only rate at which it actually happens.

10.6 The Testing Trophy and the Honeycomb

Two alternative shapes, each a reasonable response to a real weakness in the pyramid.

Kent C. Dodds's testing trophy, from front-end work: a base of static analysis and types, a thin unit layer, a fat integration layer, and a few end-to-end tests.

e2e
integration — the bulk of it
unit
static — types, linting

The argument behind it — "the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you" — is a real observation about user interfaces specifically. A React component tested through the DOM, with its children rendered, catches the defects users hit; the same component tested with every child mocked catches almost none of them (§14). And the static base is genuine: a type checker is a test that runs on every keystroke and covers a whole defect class for free.

Spotify's test honeycomb makes the same move for backend services: a small core of unit tests, a large middle of integrated tests covering one service with its dependencies stubbed, and a thin outer ring of integration tests across services.

Both are the same claim in different domains: the pyramid's middle layer is where the value is, and the classic shape under-weights it. Both are also easy to misread as a licence to skip unit tests, which neither author says.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: test honeycomb.

10.7 Why the Argument Never Ends

Because there is no single right shape, and Fowler's "diverse shapes of testing" is the honest conclusion: the right shape follows from the system's failure modes, not from a diagram.

algorithm-heavy
A pricing engine, a scheduler, a compiler. Defects are in the logic — a tall pyramid, plus property-based tests (§16).
integration-heavy
A service that mostly moves data between systems. Almost all defects are at the boundaries — a honeycomb, and unit tests of the glue would prove nothing.
user-interface-heavy
Defects are in rendering, state and interaction — a trophy, with a real DOM in the middle layer.
data-pipeline
Defects are in data shape and volume — schema checks, property tests, and assertions on the data itself rather than a shape from any of these diagrams.

The question to ask is not "what shape should we have" but "where do our defects actually come from?" — and the answer is in your incident history, which is a document you already have. A suite shaped by the last twenty incidents will beat a suite shaped by any diagram.

The term this subsection introduced: diverse shapes of testing.

10.8 The Rest of the Vocabulary

The terms you will meet, sorted so they can be used precisely.

narrow integration test
Exercises the code that talks to one external service, against a double or a real instance of just that service. Fowler's term, and the one most people mean by "integration test".
broad integration test
Requires live versions of several services. Expensive, slow, and what most teams end up with when they say "integration environment".
broad stack test
Through the whole stack including the UI. Effectively end-to-end.
component test
One deployable unit, in isolation, with its dependencies stubbed. The most under-used level in most backend suites.
contract test
Verifies an agreement, not a system. Runs on both sides independently (§13).
smoke test
A tiny, fast check that the thing is alive at all — after a deploy, before a longer suite. "Is it on fire?" (§20).
threshold test
Asserts a bound rather than a value: under a second, under 50 queries, under 2 MB. The only honest form of a performance assertion (§4.7).
business-facing test
Written in the domain's vocabulary, readable by someone who does not code (§9.13). The opposite of a technology-facing test.
exploratory testing
A person, deliberately, looking for what the automated tests cannot express (§20.13). Not a shape layer — a different activity entirely.

The practical remedy for terminology confusion is smaller than the list suggests: agree what your team means by three or four words and write it down. The words matter far less than the agreement, and an hour spent on definitions saves the recurring argument.

To have in hand before moving on: narrow integration test, broad integration test, broad stack test, business-facing test, threshold test and terminology confusion.

10.9 The Cost of a Test

The pyramid's argument is economic, so it is worth doing the arithmetic rather than asserting it.

# suite_cost.py
"""Cost of a suite, per commit, for three shapes of the same coverage."""

# Seconds per test, measured orders of magnitude rather than exact figures.
COST_S = {"unit": 0.002, "integration": 0.25, "component": 2.0, "e2e": 30.0}

# Probability that a run fails for a reason that is not a defect (§18).
FLAKE = {"unit": 0.0000, "integration": 0.0005, "component": 0.002, "e2e": 0.02}

SHAPES = {
    "pyramid":        {"unit": 3000, "integration": 300, "component": 40, "e2e": 8},
    "ice-cream cone": {"unit": 200, "integration": 150, "component": 100, "e2e": 400},
    "trophy":         {"unit": 800, "integration": 1500, "component": 60, "e2e": 10},
}

print(f"{'shape':16} {'tests':>7} {'serial':>10} {'8-way':>9} "
      f"{'runs that go red for nothing':>30}")
for name, counts in SHAPES.items():
    total = sum(counts.values())
    seconds = sum(n * COST_S[k] for k, n in counts.items())
    # P(at least one spurious failure) = 1 - P(none of them flake)
    clean = 1.0
    for kind, n in counts.items():
        clean *= (1 - FLAKE[kind]) ** n
    print(f"{name:16} {total:>7} {seconds:>9.0f}s {seconds / 8:>8.0f}s "
          f"{1 - clean:>29.1%}")

python3 suite_cost.py

shape              tests     serial     8-way   runs that go red for nothing
pyramid             3348       401s       50s                         32.4%
ice-cream cone       850     12238s     1530s                        100.0%
trophy              2370       797s      100s                         65.8%

The numbers are illustrative and the orders of magnitude are not: an end-to-end test really is four orders of magnitude more expensive to run than a unit test, and really is one to two orders of magnitude more likely to fail spuriously.

Read the last column first. The cone's suite is red on a clean commit essentially always, which means the build has stopped carrying information (§18.1) — and it gets there at a per-test flake rate of 2%, a rate most teams would call acceptable for a browser test.

The pyramid's 32% is the more uncomfortable number, and it is worth sitting with rather than tuning away. Almost all of it comes from eight end-to-end tests: at 2% each, the chance that none of them flakes is 0.988, or about 85%. The bottom two layers contribute under half of the remainder despite being three hundred times more numerous.

Two conclusions follow, and neither is the one the diagram alone suggests. The tip of the pyramid dominates the flake rate, so keeping it small is not only about runtime — it is the main lever on whether the build is believed. And the top layer is the one place a recorded retry policy is defensible (§18.13), because it is the only layer where the flakiness is genuinely environmental rather than a bug in the test.

Three costs the table does not show, and they are larger than the runtime:

Writing. An end-to-end test needs a running system, test data, authentication, and a way to wait for asynchrony. That is hours, against minutes for a unit test.

Diagnosing. A failing unit test names a function. A failing end-to-end test names a journey and could implicate anything in the system, so the first hour goes on finding out where.

Maintaining. A change to a page's markup breaks every end-to-end test that touched it. A change to a domain rule breaks the handful of unit tests that assert it, which is the correct number.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: retry policy.

10.10 Duplication Between Levels

Avoid test duplication is the rule, and the failure that follows naturally from having several levels is exactly that: the same behaviour asserted at three of them. The discount rule is tested in a unit test, again in a component test, and again in an end-to-end journey. Changing the rule now means three edits, and the two upper tests were never adding information.

Here is the same rule at two levels, so the duplication is visible rather than described:

# discount.py
def discounted_cents(order_cents, membership):
    if membership == "gold" and order_cents >= 5_000:
        return round(order_cents * 0.9)
    return order_cents


class Checkout:
    """The layer above: gathers facts, applies the rule, records the result."""

    def __init__(self, orders, mailer):
        self._orders = orders
        self._mailer = mailer

    def place(self, customer_id, order_cents, membership):
        total = discounted_cents(order_cents, membership)
        order_id = self._orders.save(customer_id, total)
        self._mailer.send(customer_id, f"total {total}")
        return order_id

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

# tests/test_levels.py
from unittest.mock import Mock

import pytest

from discount import Checkout, discounted_cents


# --- the rule, at the level where it is cheap ---------------------------------
@pytest.mark.parametrize("order_cents,membership,expected", [
    (6_000, "gold", 5_400),
    (5_000, "gold", 4_500),
    (4_999, "gold", 4_999),
    (6_000, "standard", 6_000),
    (0, "gold", 0),
])
def test_the_discount_rule(order_cents, membership, expected):
    assert discounted_cents(order_cents, membership) == expected


# --- the wiring, at the level above, asserted ONCE ----------------------------
def test_checkout_saves_the_discounted_total_and_tells_the_customer():
    orders, mailer = Mock(), Mock()
    orders.save.return_value = 41

    Checkout(orders, mailer).place(customer_id=7, order_cents=6_000,
                                   membership="gold")

    # One case, chosen because it proves the rule was applied at all. The five
    # rows above are what say the rule is *right*.
    orders.save.assert_called_once_with(7, 5_400)
    mailer.send.assert_called_once_with(7, "total 5400")

# five cases where they are cheap, one case where the wiring lives
pytest -q tests/test_levels.py

......                                                                   [100%]
6 passed in 0.87s

The discipline in that file is the whole subsection. The rule has five cases at the cheap level. The level above has one, chosen to prove the rule is reached — not to re-verify it. Adding the four boundary cases to Checkout would triple the setup cost and detect nothing new.

The rule, stated for review: each behaviour is verified in detail at exactly one level, and connected at the levels above. Vocke's version — if a higher test catches something a lower one could have, add the lower one and consider deleting the higher — is the same rule applied after the fact.

Two qualifications keep this from being over-applied. Some duplication is deliberate: a smoke test re-covering the login journey is not redundant, because it is checking that the deployed system works rather than that login is correct. And the levels are not always cleanly separable — a rule that only manifests through a database query genuinely has to be tested there.

The vocabulary here: avoid test duplication.

10.11 Speed of Feedback

The suite's shape is really a statement about how quickly you learn you were wrong, and the intervals are what the shape has to serve.

 
what runs
what you keep in your head
< 1 second
The tests for the file you are editing, on save.
Everything. This is the TDD loop (§9).
< 10 seconds
The module's whole suite, before a commit.
The change you just made.
< 10 minutes
The commit stage: units, integration, component (§20).
The branch. You are still waiting for it.
< 1 hour
End-to-end, contract verification, the slow suite.
You have moved on. A failure is now an interruption.

The thresholds are not arbitrary — they are about attention. Under a second, you are still in the loop. Under ten minutes, you are still waiting rather than context-switching, which is where the ten-minute build rule comes from (§20). Past that, a failure costs a re-entry into a problem you had put down, and the cost of a defect roughly doubles at each row.

That is the real argument for the pyramid, and it is stronger than the cost-per-run one: the shape decides which failures you learn about while you can still act on them cheaply.

10.12 Choosing a Shape

A procedure, rather than a diagram.

Start from the failure history. List the last twenty defects that reached production. For each, ask what the cheapest test would have been that caught it. Tally the answers. That distribution is your shape, derived from evidence rather than from a picture.

Then check the two failure modes. If most answers are "a unit test would have caught it", you have too few unit tests and probably an ice-cream cone. If most are "nothing below end-to-end would have caught it", your components are too coupled — the fix is architectural (§8.12), not a bigger e2e suite.

Set a budget, not a ratio. "The commit stage stays under ten minutes" is a constraint that forces the right decisions continuously; "70% unit tests" is a number nobody can act on.

Push each test down as far as it will go. For any test, ask what would have to change for it to run one level lower. Sometimes the answer is a seam (§8.2), and adding it is worth more than the test.

Keep a few at the top on purpose. The pyramid's tip is not zero. A handful of end-to-end tests covering the journeys whose breakage would be catastrophic — sign-up, checkout, payment — earn their cost, because they are the only tests that check the deployed system rather than a model of it.

10.13 What This Section Established

  • "Unit" means either a unit of code or a unit of behaviour, and choosing the first couples the suite to the class structure — which is §9.16's mechanism. The practical definition is: in memory, milliseconds, no infrastructure, no shared state.
  • Solitary and sociable is a per-test choice, trading localisation against fidelity. All-solitary fails silently as a system; all-sociable fails loudly and imprecisely.
  • The pyramid's argument is economic, not aesthetic: a test one level up costs an order of magnitude more and usually catches what the level below could have.
  • The practical pyramid replaces layer names with a rule about what each test may touch, and adds a contract layer — which is what keeps a suite of isolated tests honest.
  • The ice-cream cone arrives one reasonable decision at a time. Its diagnostic is a defect that a five-line unit test would have caught, found by a forty-second browser test. Invert it by writing the lowest-level test for each escaped defect.
  • The trophy and the honeycomb are responses to a real weakness — the classic pyramid under-weights the middle — in the UI and service domains respectively. Neither says to skip unit tests.
  • There is no single right shape. The right one follows from where your defects actually come from, and that is in your incident history.
  • Cost is dominated by writing, diagnosing and maintaining, not by runtime — and a 2% per-test flake rate at the top of a cone makes the build red on clean commits most of the time.
  • Verify each behaviour in detail at exactly one level and connect it at the levels above. A smoke test re-covering a journey is a deliberate exception.
  • The shape decides which failures you learn about while you can still act cheaply. Budget the pipeline's time; do not legislate a ratio.

Exercises

1. Classify ten tests.

Take ten tests from a codebase you work on. For each, record: solitary or sociable, what infrastructure it touches, its runtime, and which pyramid layer it belongs to. Then draw the shape. Is it the shape you expected?

2. Derive a shape from history.

Take the last ten defects that reached production in a system you know. For each, name the cheapest test that would have caught it. What shape does the tally imply, and how does it differ from your current suite?

3. Find the duplication.

A checkout feature has: 12 unit tests of the pricing rules, 4 component tests of the checkout endpoint (each asserting a different price), and 2 end-to-end tests (one asserting a discounted total). Which assertions are duplicated, which should be removed, and what should each remaining test at the upper levels assert instead?

4. Push a test down.

An end-to-end test logs in, adds three items to a basket, applies a
promotion code, and asserts the displayed total is £54.

What would have to be true for this to run one level lower? Two levels? Give the design changes required, and say which of them you would want anyway.

5. Defend the cone.

Argue the strongest possible case for a suite that is mostly end-to-end tests. Under what circumstances is it the right choice? Then say what you would insist on if you accepted it.

6. Budget a pipeline.

You have a ten-minute budget for the commit stage and these measured costs: 4,000 unit tests at 1.5 ms, 400 integration tests at 180 ms, 60 component tests at 2.2 s, 30 end-to-end tests at 45 s. Design the stages, say what runs where, and what you would do first if the numbers do not fit.

Solutions

1. Classify ten tests.

No fixed answer. The two findings that recur: more tests touch infrastructure than people expect — an "in-memory" test that imports a module which opens a connection at import time is an integration test wearing a unit test's name — and runtime is heavily skewed, so a handful of tests account for most of the suite's time (§2.9's --durations is how to find them).

The useful follow-up is to compare the shape you drew against the shape you would have guessed. That gap is the thing worth acting on, because it means the team's model of its own suite is wrong.

2. Derive a shape from history.

The characteristic result: a third to a half of the answers are "a unit test would have caught this" — usually a boundary or a null (§4.5) — a smaller group are "only an integration test would have", almost always at a database or serialisation boundary, and a small tail are "nothing but end-to-end", which are usually configuration or deployment problems rather than code defects at all.

That tail is the informative one. Configuration defects are not fixed by more end-to-end tests; they are fixed by validating configuration at start-up and by a post-deploy smoke test (§20), which is a different intervention entirely and much cheaper.

3. Find the duplication.

The four component tests each asserting a different price are re-verifying the pricing rules through an expensive path — that is the duplication, and three of the four should go. The one that remains should assert that the endpoint returns the price the rule produced, not a specific number: it is testing the wiring.

The end-to-end test asserting a discounted total is the same problem one level higher. It should assert that a checkout journey completes and produces an order, with the total present but not the subject of the claim.

What each upper test should assert instead: the component test, that the request reaches the pricing rule and the response carries its result; the end-to-end test, that the journey works at all in the deployed system. Both become claims about connection rather than about calculation, which is §10.10's rule.

4. Push a test down.

One level lower — a component test against the running service's API: log in via an API call, add items via the API, apply the promotion, and assert the returned total. Needs an API that can do everything the UI does, which is worth having anyway; a UI that can do things the API cannot is a design problem.

Two levels lower — an integration or unit test of the promotion engine, given a basket and a code, asserting the total. Needs the pricing logic to be callable without a session, a basket loaded from a database, or an HTTP request: that is §8.11's functional core, and it is also worth having anyway.

The pattern generalises: the design changes that let a test move down the pyramid are almost always changes you wanted for other reasons. That is the strongest argument for testability pressure (§9.7), and it is why "we cannot test that at a lower level" is usually a statement about the design rather than about testing.

What remains at the top is one journey test asserting that the page shows the total the API returned — a claim about rendering, which is genuinely the UI's job.

5. Defend the cone.

The strongest case: when you do not control the code. Testing a legacy system with no seams (§8.13), a third-party platform configured rather than programmed, or a system whose internals are about to be replaced — in all three, the only stable interface is the outside, and tests written against the internals would be thrown away. Michael Feathers's characterisation tests are exactly this argument, and it is a good one.

The second case: a very small system. Twenty end-to-end tests over a service with four endpoints run in a minute and give excellent confidence. The pyramid is a claim about what happens as scale grows, and below some size it does not apply.

What to insist on if you accept it: a hard time budget, so the suite cannot silently grow to an hour; a measured flake rate (§18.14), because at this shape flakiness is the thing that will kill it; retries with recorded counts rather than silent ones; and an agreement that every escaped defect gets its lowest-level test, which is what stops the shape from becoming permanent by default rather than by choice.

6. Budget a pipeline.

Serial: 6 s + 72 s + 132 s + 1,350 s. The first three total 210 seconds, which fits comfortably; the end-to-end tests alone are 22 minutes and do not.

So: commit stage = units + integration + component, 3.5 minutes serially and well under a minute with modest parallelism. A later stage = the 30 end-to-end tests, sharded across 6 machines at about 4 minutes each, running after the commit stage passes rather than blocking it.

If the numbers did not fit, the order of moves is §2.15's: shard first (no test changes, buys a linear factor), parallelise within a machine second (cheap, and it will find real isolation bugs — §18.12), and only then make individual tests faster, starting with --durations to find the handful responsible for most of the time.

What not to do first: delete tests to fit the budget. That trades a measurable cost for an unmeasurable one, and the tests deleted will be the ones that were annoying rather than the ones that were useless.

SECTION 11

Integration Testing

Every test so far has run entirely inside one process. Section 6's doubles and section 8's fakes exist so that they can: an in-memory repository is fast, deterministic and completely under the test's control.

It is also a claim about something you have not checked. InMemoryOrders behaves the way you decided a database behaves. The real one has a schema, a type system, constraints, transactions, isolation levels, a connection pool, and a dialect — and every one of those is a chance for the fake and the real thing to disagree.

An integration test exercises the code together with something real: a database, a message broker, a filesystem, an HTTP service. It is slower and more awkward, and that is exactly why the interesting question is not "should we write them" but how few can we get away with, and how do we keep them from being flaky.

This section is about databases, because that is where nearly all of it lives. Everything here runs against a real PostgreSQL server — started by the test suite, on a port of its own, torn down afterwards. Not a mock, not sqlite pretending; §11.13 shows exactly what that pretence costs.

11.1 What an Integration Test Is For

A useful definition, because the word is used for three different things (§10 sorts out the taxonomy properly): an integration test checks the boundary between your code and something you did not write.

That framing tells you what to test and — more valuably — what not to.

worth an integration test
Does the SQL this repository builds actually run? Does the constraint fire? Does the transaction roll back what you think? Does the type round-trip — a Decimal, a timezone, a JSON column, an array?
not worth one
Business rules. A discount ladder does not become more correct for having been computed next to a database, and testing it there costs a hundred times more per case (§8.11).

The rule that follows is the one §10 will formalise: push logic down to where it can be tested cheaply, and use integration tests for the seam. A repository whose methods are thin — one query each, no branching — needs a handful of integration tests. A repository with business rules inside it needs dozens, and each of them is slow.

11.2 A Real Database, Started by the Suite

The first practical problem is where the database comes from — what Meszaros calls a database sandbox, an instance whose contents belong to one test run and nobody else. Four answers, and only two of them are good:

a shared server
One database everyone's tests point at. Fails as soon as two people run tests at once, and every failure is somebody else's leftovers (§18).
one you install by hand
Works, until a new joiner has a different version, or CI does. "Works on my machine" with a version number attached.
a container
Testcontainers or a compose file. The mainstream answer, pinned by image tag, identical everywhere (§11.12).
a private cluster
The suite runs initdb into a temporary directory and starts a server on a free port. No daemon, no image pull, no root. This is what the examples here do.
# pgcluster.py
"""Start a private PostgreSQL cluster for the test session, and stop it after."""
import os
import pathlib
import shutil
import socket
import subprocess

def find_pgbin():
    """Where initdb and pg_ctl live: $PGBIN if set, then PATH, then Debian's layout."""
    if os.environ.get("PGBIN"):
        return pathlib.Path(os.environ["PGBIN"])
    if shutil.which("pg_ctl"):
        return pathlib.Path(shutil.which("pg_ctl")).parent
    return next(p for p in sorted(pathlib.Path("/usr/lib/postgresql").glob("*/bin"))
                if (p / "initdb").exists())


PGBIN = find_pgbin()


def free_port():
    """Ask the OS for a port nobody is using (§18.12)."""
    with socket.socket() as s:
        s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
        return s.getsockname()[1]


class Cluster:
    def __init__(self, datadir):
        self.datadir = pathlib.Path(datadir).resolve()
        self.port = free_port()

    def start(self):
        if not (self.datadir / "PG_VERSION").exists():
            # -E UTF8 --locale=C: a test cluster must not inherit the machine's locale.
            # Without them initdb follows the environment, and under LC_ALL=C that means an
            # SQL_ASCII database — where psycopg hands back `bytes` for every text column and
            # `version.startswith("PostgreSQL")` raises TypeError.
            subprocess.run([str(PGBIN / "initdb"), "-D", str(self.datadir),
                            "-U", "postgres", "-A", "trust", "--no-sync",
                            "-E", "UTF8", "--locale=C"],
                           check=True, capture_output=True)
        # TCP only: a deep temporary directory can exceed the 107-byte limit on a
        # Unix socket path, which fails in a way that names neither the test nor
        # the directory.  fsync=off is safe here and only here — this cluster is
        # thrown away, and durability is the single largest cost in a write test.
        opts = (f"-p {self.port} -c listen_addresses=127.0.0.1 "
                f"-c unix_socket_directories= -c fsync=off")
        subprocess.run([str(PGBIN / "pg_ctl"), "-D", str(self.datadir),
                        "-o", opts, "-l", str(self.datadir / "log"), "-w", "start"],
                       check=True, capture_output=True)
        return self

    def stop(self):
        subprocess.run([str(PGBIN / "pg_ctl"), "-D", str(self.datadir),
                        "-m", "immediate", "-w", "stop"], capture_output=True)

    def dsn(self, dbname="postgres"):
        return f"host=127.0.0.1 port={self.port} user=postgres dbname={dbname}"

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

# tests/conftest.py
import psycopg
import pytest

from pgcluster import Cluster

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accounts (
    id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
    email         text   NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    balance_cents integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance_cents >= 0),
    created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
"""


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def cluster():
    """One server for the whole session. Started lazily, stopped afterwards."""
    server = Cluster("pgdata").start()
    with psycopg.connect(server.dsn(), autocommit=True) as setup:
        setup.execute(SCHEMA)
    yield server
    server.stop()

# tests/test_real_server.py
import psycopg


def test_this_is_a_real_postgresql_server(cluster):
    with psycopg.connect(cluster.dsn()) as conn:
        version = conn.execute("SELECT version()").fetchone()[0]
    assert version.startswith("PostgreSQL")


def test_the_things_a_fake_would_not_have(cluster):
    with psycopg.connect(cluster.dsn()) as conn:
        # generate_series, jsonb and window functions all exist, because this
        # is the actual server and not an approximation of one.
        rows = conn.execute("""
            SELECT n, sum(n) OVER (ORDER BY n) AS running
            FROM generate_series(1, 4) AS n
            ORDER BY n
        """).fetchall()
    assert rows == [(1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 6), (4, 10)]

pytest -q tests/test_real_server.py

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 4.80s

Four properties make this arrangement work, and they are the properties to look for in whatever mechanism you choose:

Its own port. free_port() asks the OS rather than hardcoding 5432, so two suites — or two CI jobs on one machine — never collide.

Its own data directory. Nothing is shared with a development database, so a test cannot destroy real data and a developer's data cannot make a test pass.

Started lazily, once. A session-scoped fixture pays the startup cost only if some test asks for a database, and only once for the whole run.

Stopped afterwards, unconditionally. The yield fixture's teardown runs whether the tests passed, failed or raised. A leaked server is §18.12's resource leak with a process attached.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: database sandbox.

11.3 The Isolation Problem

One server, many tests, one set of tables. Every test can see every other test's rows, which is §18's first cause of flakiness in its purest form.

There are four strategies, and choosing between them is the main design decision in this section.

 
speed
the catch
rollback
Fastest by far. Nothing is ever written.
The code must use your connection, and cannot commit.
truncation
Fast. One statement per test.
You must remember every table, and sequences keep counting unless you say otherwise.
schema per test
Moderate. Create and drop.
The schema must be rebuilt each time, which means migrations run repeatedly.
database per worker
Slowest to create, then free.
Isolates workers, not tests — combine it with one of the others.

Most working suites use rollback for most tests, truncation for the few that cannot roll back, and a database per parallel worker on top. The next three subsections build exactly that.

11.4 Transaction Rollback Teardown

The trick is simple enough to state in one line: open a transaction, run the test in it, and roll it back. The database does the cleanup, atomically, in microseconds.

# tests/conftest.py
import psycopg
import pytest

from pgcluster import Cluster

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accounts (
    id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
    email         text   NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    balance_cents integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance_cents >= 0),
    created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
"""


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def cluster():
    server = Cluster("pgdata").start()
    with psycopg.connect(server.dsn(), autocommit=True) as setup:
        setup.execute(SCHEMA)
    yield server
    server.stop()


@pytest.fixture
def connection(cluster):
    """A connection whose work is always thrown away.

    Everything the test does happens inside one transaction that is never
    committed, so teardown is a rollback and costs nothing.
    """
    conn = psycopg.connect(cluster.dsn(), autocommit=False)
    try:
        yield conn
    finally:
        conn.rollback()
        conn.close()

# accounts.py
class AccountRepository:
    """A thin repository: one query per method, no rules of its own (§11.1)."""

    def __init__(self, connection):
        self._conn = connection

    def create(self, email, balance_cents=0):
        row = self._conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO accounts (email, balance_cents) VALUES (%s, %s) "
            "RETURNING id", (email, balance_cents)).fetchone()
        return row[0]

    def get(self, account_id):
        row = self._conn.execute(
            "SELECT id, email, balance_cents FROM accounts WHERE id = %s",
            (account_id,)).fetchone()
        return None if row is None else {
            "id": row[0], "email": row[1], "balance_cents": row[2]}

    def count(self):
        return self._conn.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM accounts").fetchone()[0]

    def debit(self, account_id, cents):
        self._conn.execute(
            "UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - %s WHERE id = %s",
            (cents, account_id))

# tests/test_rollback.py
import psycopg
import pytest

from accounts import AccountRepository


def test_a_created_account_can_be_read_back(connection):
    repo = AccountRepository(connection)

    account_id = repo.create("ada@example.com", 5_000)

    assert repo.get(account_id) == {
        "id": account_id, "email": "ada@example.com", "balance_cents": 5_000}


def test_the_previous_test_left_nothing_behind(connection):
    # Same table, same server, and it is empty: the other test's transaction
    # was rolled back. No DELETE, no TRUNCATE, no ordering requirement.
    assert AccountRepository(connection).count() == 0


def test_the_unique_constraint_is_real(connection):
    repo = AccountRepository(connection)
    repo.create("ada@example.com")

    with pytest.raises(psycopg.errors.UniqueViolation):
        repo.create("ada@example.com")


def test_the_check_constraint_refuses_an_overdraft(connection):
    repo = AccountRepository(connection)
    account_id = repo.create("ada@example.com", 100)

    with pytest.raises(psycopg.errors.CheckViolation):
        repo.debit(account_id, 500)

pytest -q tests/test_rollback.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 1.34s

The second test is the demonstration: it runs after a test that inserted a row, against the same table on the same server, and the table is empty. Teardown was one ROLLBACK.

The last two are the reason integration tests earn their place at all. UNIQUE and CHECK are behaviour, they live in the database, and no in-memory fake has them unless you reimplemented them — at which point you are testing your reimplementation. Every constraint your schema declares is a claim the application depends on, and this is the only place it can be checked.

Three limits, and they are why §11.5 exists:

The code under test must use your connection. Anything that opens its own gets a different transaction and sees an empty table. That is a design requirement on the application — the connection or session must be injectable (§8.3) — and it is usually the single biggest change a codebase needs before this technique works.

The code under test must not commit. A COMMIT inside the SUT ends your transaction and the rollback has nothing left to undo. §11.8's savepoints handle the common cases.

Nothing outside the transaction sees the data. A second connection, a background worker, or a subprocess will not see uncommitted rows. Any test that needs two connections cannot use this strategy.

11.5 Truncation, and When You Need It

When rollback is unavailable, delete the data instead. Table truncation teardown is the name, TRUNCATE is much faster than DELETE for it, and its two options matter.

# tests/test_truncation.py
import psycopg
import pytest

from accounts import AccountRepository


@pytest.fixture
def committed_connection(cluster):
    """Autocommit, so rollback teardown is not available. Truncate instead."""
    conn = psycopg.connect(cluster.dsn(), autocommit=True)
    conn.execute("TRUNCATE accounts RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE")
    yield conn
    conn.execute("TRUNCATE accounts RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE")
    conn.close()


def test_ids_start_from_one_again(committed_connection):
    repo = AccountRepository(committed_connection)
    first = repo.create("ada@example.com")
    assert first == 1


def test_and_they_start_from_one_in_the_next_test_too(committed_connection):
    # Without RESTART IDENTITY this would be 2, and the test would pass alone
    # and fail in the suite — §18's order dependence, from a sequence.
    repo = AccountRepository(committed_connection)
    assert repo.create("grace@example.com") == 1


def test_committed_rows_really_are_visible_to_another_connection(cluster,
                                                                 committed_connection):
    AccountRepository(committed_connection).create("ada@example.com")

    with psycopg.connect(cluster.dsn()) as other:
        assert other.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM accounts").fetchone()[0] == 1

pytest -q tests/test_truncation.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 1.66s

RESTART IDENTITY is the option people forget, and forgetting it produces a specific, confusing bug: sequences keep counting across tests, so any test asserting on an id passes alone and fails in the suite. That is order dependence created by the teardown itself.

CASCADE truncates tables with foreign keys pointing at these. Without it, TRUNCATE on a referenced table is an error. With it, you may be truncating more than you listed — which is usually right and is worth knowing.

Truncate at setup, not only at teardown. The fixture above does both. Teardown-only cleanup leaves the database dirty if a test crashes the process, and then the next run starts polluted.

The third test shows what this strategy buys that rollback cannot: the rows are really committed, so a second connection sees them. Any test involving two connections, a background job, or a subprocess needs this.

The term above, for reference: table truncation teardown.

11.6 Seeding Data: the Front Door and the Back Door

Every integration test needs data that is not what it is testing — an account for the payment test, a catalogue for the checkout test. Section 8.14 introduced the choice; here it is in practice, and this is where it comes up constantly.

# tests/test_seeding.py
import pytest

from accounts import AccountRepository


@pytest.fixture
def seeded(connection):
    """Back door: rows straight in, no application code involved."""
    connection.execute(
        "INSERT INTO accounts (email, balance_cents) VALUES "
        "('ada@example.com', 5000), ('grace@example.com', 250), "
        "('katherine@example.com', 0)")
    return connection


def test_the_back_door_is_fast_and_precise(seeded):
    repo = AccountRepository(seeded)
    assert repo.count() == 3


def test_it_can_create_states_the_api_cannot(connection):
    # A zero balance is reachable; a row created *before* the service existed,
    # with a NULL-ish shape or a legacy value, often is not. The back door can
    # make one, which is exactly what a migration test needs.
    connection.execute(
        "INSERT INTO accounts (email, balance_cents, created_at) "
        "VALUES ('legacy@example.com', 0, timestamptz '2001-01-01')")
    row = connection.execute(
        "SELECT created_at FROM accounts WHERE email = 'legacy@example.com'"
    ).fetchone()
    assert row[0].year == 2001


def test_the_front_door_exercises_the_code_that_will_run_in_production(connection):
    repo = AccountRepository(connection)
    account_id = repo.create("ada@example.com", 5_000)

    assert repo.get(account_id)["balance_cents"] == 5_000

pytest -q tests/test_seeding.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 1.71s

The rule, restated with the reasoning now that the mechanics are visible:

Front door for the behaviour under test. If the test is about creating an account, create it through AccountRepository.create. A test that inserts a row directly and then asserts it can be read is testing your SQL literal against your other SQL literal.

Back door for the scenery. The three accounts the payment test needs are not what the payment test is about, and putting them in directly is faster, clearer, and does not fail when create breaks.

Two refinements worth adopting.

Seed the minimum. A fixture that inserts fifty rows because "that is what production looks like" makes every failure harder to read and hides which row mattered (§19's mystery guest). Three rows with meaningful names beat fifty generated ones.

Prefer a builder to a literal. make_account(balance_cents=0) with sensible defaults means a test states only the field it cares about, and adding a NOT NULL column later is one edit rather than forty (§5's object mother and test data builder).

11.7 Schema per Test, Database per Worker

Two coarser isolation strategies, for the cases the first two do not cover.

Schema per test gives each test its own namespace: CREATE SCHEMA test_x; SET search_path TO test_x and every unqualified table name resolves inside it. It handles tests that need DDL — a migration test, a test of a table-creation path — because the DDL happens in a namespace nobody else can see. Its cost is that the schema must be built each time, so the objects have to be created per test rather than once per session.

Database per worker is the answer to parallelism. Run pytest -n 4 and four processes share one server; rollback isolates them from each other only if they never commit, and truncation certainly does not. Give each worker its own database:

# tests/worker_db.py
import os


def database_name():
    """xdist sets PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER to gw0, gw1, ... — one database each."""
    worker = os.environ.get("PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER", "main")
    return f"test_{worker}"

The pattern in full: a session fixture reads the worker id, creates test_gw0 if it does not exist, applies the schema, and hands back a DSN pointing at it. Every other fixture is unchanged. Four workers, four databases, one server, and the per-test strategy inside each worker stays whatever you chose.

Creating four databases costs real time, which is why CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE is worth knowing: build the schema once into a template database, then each worker's database is a file copy rather than a migration run. On a large schema that is the difference between seconds and minutes.

11.8 Savepoints, for Code That Commits

The awkward case from §11.4: the code under test calls commit(), so the outer rollback has nothing to undo.

A savepoint is a nested marker inside a transaction that can be rolled back to without ending the transaction, and savepoint rollback is the teardown built on one. The standard recipe: the fixture opens a transaction, the test runs inside a savepoint, and the SUT's COMMIT is translated into a savepoint release rather than a real commit. Every mature ORM has a version of this — SQLAlchemy calls it joining an external transaction — and the raw mechanics are visible with psycopg:

# tests/test_savepoint.py
from accounts import AccountRepository


def commits_when_it_is_done(conn, account_id, cents):
    """Pretend this is application code you do not control. The commit is the
    problem: it ends the fixture's transaction, so there is nothing left to
    roll back and every later test starts polluted."""
    conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - %s "
                 "WHERE id = %s", (cents, account_id))
    conn.commit()


class Undo(Exception):
    """Raised to unwind a savepoint without failing the test."""


def test_a_savepoint_unwinds_only_the_inner_block(connection):
    repo = AccountRepository(connection)
    account_id = repo.create("ada@example.com", 5_000)

    try:
        # Nested inside the fixture's still-open transaction, so psycopg issues
        # a SAVEPOINT here rather than a BEGIN.
        with connection.transaction():
            repo.debit(account_id, 1_000)
            assert repo.get(account_id)["balance_cents"] == 4_000
            raise Undo
    except Undo:
        pass

    # The savepoint was rolled back. The outer transaction is still alive, and
    # the account created in it is still there.
    assert repo.get(account_id)["balance_cents"] == 5_000

pytest -q tests/test_savepoint.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 1.47s

That test does not run as written — the exception escapes — and it is here to make the mechanism visible rather than to be copied. The mechanism, and the points that matter structurally:

  • connection.transaction() nested inside another is a savepoint, in psycopg and in every driver that offers the concept. Exiting it with an exception rolls back to the savepoint and leaves the outer transaction alive.
  • The trick only works if you can intercept the commit. commits_when_it_is_done above is the case this is for, and making it work means the SUT's commit() has to become a savepoint release rather than a real commit. With an ORM that is a session bound to your connection; with raw SQL it means handing the SUT a connection object whose commit you have overridden.
  • It is a real complexity cost. Before reaching for it, ask whether the code needs to commit at all. Code that commits in the middle of a use case is often a design problem — a use case should own its transaction boundary — and fixing that makes the test simple and the production behaviour more correct.

One to keep in hand: savepoint rollback.

11.9 Migrations in Tests

The schema your tests run against must be the schema production will have. There are two ways to arrange that and only one is safe.

create from models
Ask the ORM to build the tables from the current model definitions. Fast, and it tests a schema nobody will ever run: production is built by migrations, and a migration that does not match the models is precisely the defect you needed to catch.
run the migrations
Apply the same migration chain production applies. Slower, and it is the only version that verifies the artefact that will actually be deployed.

Run the migrations, once per session, into a template database, and copy it per worker. That gets the fidelity and pays the cost once.

Three tests worth having about the migrations themselves — they are cheap and they catch things nothing else does:

A migration test proper. Insert data in the old shape (back door — this is §11.6's second test, and it is why the back door exists), run the migration, assert the data survived correctly. Nothing else checks the data-transforming half of a migration, and that is the half that loses information irreversibly.

Down, then up. If your tool supports rollback, apply and revert and apply again. A migration that cannot be reverted is a deployment that cannot be rolled back.

Models match migrations. Most tools can diff the model definitions against the migrated schema and report a difference. Run it as a test: it catches the "someone edited the model and forgot to generate the migration" defect on the commit that caused it.

11.10 Connection Pools and Resource Leaks

An integration suite is the place where §18.12's resource leaks show up first, because connections are finite and tests are numerous. A resource leak here is not an abstraction: it is a connection nobody returned, and the suite stops.

The symptoms and their causes:

hangs at test N
The pool is exhausted. A fixture takes a connection and never returns it, and the run blocks forever waiting for one.
too many clients already
Connections are created per test and never closed. PostgreSQL's default limit is 100, so it appears at test 100.
a test hangs on a write
Another connection holds a lock on the row, in an open transaction, because an earlier test never rolled back.
only under -n 4
Four workers times a pool of 20 exceeds the limit. Size the pool per worker, not per suite.

Three habits prevent nearly all of it. Every acquisition is in a with or a yield fixture, so teardown runs even when the test raises. Set max_connections deliberately on the test cluster and size pools below it, so exhaustion fails fast with a clear error rather than hanging. And assert the connection count in a session-scoped teardown — one query against pg_stat_activity at the end of the run turns "the suite is slow lately" into "test_x leaks a connection".

Testing resource pools is a separate and legitimate exercise: that it hands back a working connection after an error, that it does not exceed its maximum, that a connection closed by the server is replaced rather than handed out dead. These are integration tests of your infrastructure code, and they belong in the same suite.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: a resource leak and testing resource pools.

11.11 Making the Resource Unique

The general principle behind the free port, the private data directory and the per-worker database is one rule — make resource unique: if a test needs a named resource, generate the name. Its two siblings are inline resource, where the test creates the thing it needs rather than finding one lying about, and setup external resource, where the suite is responsible for bringing the external thing into existence at all (§11.2's private cluster is that). Port allocation is the case where all three meet: the port is created by the suite, unique per run, and released with it.

The catalogue of what should be unique per test or per worker:

  • Ports — from the OS, never a constant (§18.12).
  • Directories — tmp_path, which pytest makes unique per test and keeps for the last few runs so a failure can be inspected.
  • Database, schema and table names — derived from the worker id or a random suffix.
  • Queue and topic names, for a broker shared with anyone else.
  • Any external identifier the test creates — a customer reference, an idempotency key. A fixed one collides with the previous run's leftovers.

The counter-rule is worth stating too: a unique name is not a substitute for cleanup. Uniqueness stops tests from colliding; it does not stop the resource from accumulating. A suite that creates a uniquely-named schema per test and never drops one has a fast, green, steadily-growing database.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: make resource unique, inline resource, setup external resource and port allocation.

11.12 Testcontainers and Ephemeral Environments

The mainstream answer to §11.2 is Testcontainers: a library that starts a Docker container from your test code, waits for it to be ready, exposes the mapped port, and stops it afterwards.

import pytest
from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def database_url():
    """The shape of it. This course's own examples use a private cluster so
    that no Docker daemon is required, but this is what most teams should use."""
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:18-alpine") as postgres:
        yield postgres.get_connection_url()

What it gets right is the thing that matters: the version is pinned in the code, so every developer and every CI runner gets byte-identical infrastructure, and upgrading is a one-line change with a test run behind it. It also generalises past databases — Redis, Kafka, a mock S3, an OIDC provider, or your own service's image.

Three things to know before adopting it:

Startup cost is real. A container is a second or two, sometimes more with a readiness wait. Start it once per session, never per test.

It requires a Docker daemon, which some CI environments do not give you, and which is why the private-cluster approach in this section exists as an alternative.

Wait for readiness properly. "The container started" is not "the database accepts connections". Every Testcontainers module ships a wait strategy; a sleep(5) in its place is §18.8's antipattern wearing infrastructure clothes.

An ephemeral environment is the same idea one level up: a complete, short-lived deployment of the whole system, created per branch or per pull request and destroyed afterwards. It is where end-to-end tests (§15) should run, and its virtue is the same — nothing is shared, so nothing is polluted.

11.13 Why sqlite-for-PostgreSQL Is a Dangerous Fake

Which brings us to the tempting shortcut: run the tests against sqlite, in memory, and keep PostgreSQL for production. It is fast, it needs no server, and it is a bad idea. Here is the same SQL against both.

# dialect_drift.py
"""Run identical SQL against sqlite and against PostgreSQL, and compare."""
import sqlite3

import psycopg

from pgcluster import Cluster

DDL = "CREATE TABLE t (code varchar(3))"
OVERLONG = "INSERT INTO t VALUES ('abcdefgh')"

CASES = [
    ("adding a string to a number", "SELECT 'abc' + 1"),
    ("a value longer than the column", OVERLONG),
    ("dividing two integers", "SELECT 7 / 2"),
    ("a boolean literal", "SELECT true"),
    ("generating a series", "SELECT count(*) FROM generate_series(1, 3)"),
    ("the length of a number", "SELECT length(1234)"),
    ("a date that does not exist", "SELECT CAST('2026-02-30' AS date)"),
]


def attempt(run, sql):
    try:
        return f"-> {run(sql)}"
    except Exception as exc:
        return f"ERROR {type(exc).__name__}: {str(exc).splitlines()[0][:52]}"


def main():
    cluster = Cluster("pgdata_drift").start()
    try:
        lite = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
        lite.execute(DDL)
        with psycopg.connect(cluster.dsn(), autocommit=True) as pg:
            pg.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t")
            pg.execute(DDL)

            for label, sql in CASES:
                print(f"{label}:")
                print(f"    sqlite      {attempt(lambda s: lite.execute(s).fetchone(), sql)}")
                print(f"    postgresql  {attempt(lambda s: (pg.execute(s).fetchone() or 'ok'), sql)}")

            print()
            print("what sqlite actually stored for the over-long insert:")
            print(f"    {lite.execute('SELECT * FROM t').fetchall()}")
    finally:
        cluster.stop()


main()

python3 dialect_drift.py

adding a string to a number:
    sqlite      -> (1,)
    postgresql  ERROR InvalidTextRepresentation: invalid input syntax for type integer: "abc"
a value longer than the column:
    sqlite      -> None
    postgresql  ERROR StringDataRightTruncation: value too long for type character varying(3)
dividing two integers:
    sqlite      -> (3,)
    postgresql  -> (3,)
a boolean literal:
    sqlite      -> (1,)
    postgresql  -> (True,)
generating a series:
    sqlite      ERROR OperationalError: no such table: generate_series
    postgresql  -> (3,)
the length of a number:
    sqlite      -> (4,)
    postgresql  ERROR UndefinedFunction: function length(integer) does not exist
a date that does not exist:
    sqlite      -> (2026,)
    postgresql  ERROR DatetimeFieldOverflow: date/time field value out of range: "2026-02-30"

what sqlite actually stored for the over-long insert:
    [('abcdefgh',)]

Read the differences rather than the summary, because each one is a defect class — and the general name for the whole family is dialect drift: two SQL implementations that accept the same statements and mean different things by them.
