The failure names the field, names the interaction, and appears in the provider's build. That is the entire value proposition, and it is worth noticing how little machinery produced it: a JSON file, a subset comparison, and a state handler.

Compare the alternatives. Without contracts, this ships; the billing service starts raising KeyError in production; someone eventually correlates it with a deploy from another team. With a shared integration environment, it is caught later, slower, and by a test that says "the billing journey failed" rather than "body.total_cents is missing".

13.8 Schema as Contract, and OpenAPI

With the rename reverted — the provider puts total_cents back, because the verification told it to — there is a second, weaker form of contract worth knowing.

# provider_app.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException

app = FastAPI()
ORDERS: dict[int, dict] = {}
TOKEN = "letmein"


@app.get("/orders/{order_id}")
def get_order(order_id: int, authorization: str | None = Header(default=None)):
    if authorization != f"Bearer {TOKEN}":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="a bearer token is required")
    if order_id not in ORDERS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="no such order")
    return ORDERS[order_id]

Consumer-driven contracts need a relationship with the consumer. When you do not have one — a public API, an unknown set of clients — the provider-driven form is what is available.

Schema as contract. You publish an OpenAPI document, or a JSON Schema, or a protobuf definition, and it becomes the promise. OpenAPI as a contract is the common case, and it is weaker than a pact in one specific way (§13.3) and much cheaper to adopt. Two tests follow, and both are worth having:

provider side
Every real response validates against the published schema. Otherwise the document is documentation, and documentation drifts.
consumer side
Your doubles are built from the schema, so a stub cannot claim a shape the provider never promised.
# tests/test_openapi_as_contract.py
"""The generated OpenAPI document is the published promise; check it is true."""
import jsonschema
import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

import provider_app
import provider_states


@pytest.fixture
def client():
    return TestClient(provider_app.app)


def response_schema(spec, path, method, status):
    """Pull one response schema out of the OpenAPI document, resolving the
    $ref into the components section the way a validator would."""
    body = spec["paths"][path][method]["responses"][str(status)]
    schema = body["content"]["application/json"]["schema"]
    return {**schema, "components": spec["components"],
            "$defs": spec["components"]["schemas"]}


def test_the_document_describes_the_route_that_exists(client):
    spec = client.get("/openapi.json").json()

    assert "/orders/{order_id}" in spec["paths"]
    assert "get" in spec["paths"]["/orders/{order_id}"]


def test_a_real_response_validates_against_the_published_schema(client):
    provider_states.apply("an order 1 exists with a total of 500 cents")
    spec = client.get("/openapi.json").json()

    response = client.get("/orders/1", headers={"Authorization": "Bearer letmein"})

    assert response.status_code == 200
    # This endpoint declares no response model, so the schema is permissive —
    # which is itself the finding: an unmodelled response promises nothing.
    schema = spec["paths"]["/orders/{order_id}"]["get"]["responses"]["200"]
    assert "content" in schema


def test_the_error_response_is_documented(client):
    spec = client.get("/openapi.json").json()

    documented = spec["paths"]["/orders/{order_id}"]["get"]["responses"]
    # 422 is generated from the path parameter's type; 404 and 401 are raised
    # in code and appear nowhere. An undocumented status code is a broken
    # promise waiting to happen.
    assert "422" in documented
    assert "404" not in documented

pytest -q tests/test_openapi_as_contract.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 5.17s

The last test is deliberately asserting something uncomfortable: the 404 and 401 this endpoint really returns are not in its OpenAPI document, because they are raised in code rather than declared. That is the characteristic weakness of a generated specification — it describes the parts the framework can see, and a consumer generating a client from it will have no branch for the two error codes it will actually meet.

Writing that test is what makes the gap visible. The fix is to declare the responses; the lesson is that a generated document is a claim about the code, not about the behaviour, and it needs its own test before it can be trusted as a contract.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: openapi as a contract.

13.9 Breaking Changes and Compatibility

With a contract in place, breaking change detection stops being a judgement and becomes a computation, and backward compatibility stops being a hope. The rules are the same whether the contract is a pact or a schema.

✓
adding a response field
Safe — provided consumers ignore unknown fields, which is why the subset rule matters.
✓
adding an optional request field
Safe. Existing callers keep working.
✓
a new endpoint
Safe by construction.
✗
removing or renaming a field
Breaking if any contract names it — and now you can answer that question mechanically.
✗
narrowing a type or a range
string to enum, a wider integer to a smaller one. Breaking for a consumer sending the values you just excluded.
✗
making a request field required
Breaking for every caller that omits it, which is all of them.
?
changing a status code
Breaking if a consumer branches on it — and they almost always do. 200 to 201 is not cosmetic.
?
changing ordering or nullability
Breaking if a consumer relied on it, and contracts rarely record either. Say it explicitly in the contract if it matters.

The expand-and-contract migration is how a breaking change is made safely — contract evolution without a coordinated release — and the contracts are what make each step verifiable. Backward compatibility is preserved at every point, which is what lets the consumers migrate on their own schedule:

  1. Expand. Add the new field alongside the old one. Both are populated. No contract breaks.
  2. Migrate. Each consumer updates its contract to the new field and deploys. The provider's verification tells it when the old field is no longer named by anyone.
  3. Contract. Remove the old field. Verification is green because no contract mentions it.

Step 2 is where the value is. Without contracts, the provider has to ask every consumer whether they have migrated, and take their word for it. With them, the pact files answer the question — and answer it about the code that is deployed rather than about what someone remembers.

The terms above, gathered: breaking change detection and contract evolution.

13.10 The Broker, and can-i-deploy

The remaining problem is logistics. The consumer's pact file is generated in the consumer's pipeline; the provider needs it in theirs; and both change independently. A pact broker is the piece that sits between them: consumers publish pacts to it, providers fetch and verify, and results are recorded against versions.

That last part is what enables the question every deployment pipeline should be able to ask:

can-i-deploy billing v2.3 to production?

Yes, if for every provider billing depends on, the version currently in production has verified billing v2.3's contract. Otherwise, no, and here is which one.

what it replaces
A shared staging environment whose job was to find out whether two versions work together. That question is now answered by a query, in seconds, per deployment.
versions and tags
Pacts are published per consumer version and tagged with the environment. "Verified against the version in production" is a different question from "verified against main", and both matter.
the webhook
A new pact triggers the provider's verification build. Without it, a consumer's new requirement is discovered whenever the provider next happens to build.

Two failure modes to plan for. A contract that no provider verifies is decoration — the broker must be wired into a build that actually runs, or the whole scheme quietly stops working. And can-i-deploy must be able to block a deploy; if it is advisory, it will be overridden on the first Friday afternoon and never consulted again.

One line each, for reference: pact broker and deployment pipeline.

13.11 What Contract Tests Do Not Cover

Being precise about the limits is what keeps them from being over-sold, which is how the last generation of integration tooling died.

semantics
A contract says total_cents is an integer. It cannot say the integer is correct, or that it includes tax, or that the currency is the one you assumed.
emergent behaviour
Timeouts, retries, back-pressure, a cascade under load (§18). Every pair honours its contract and the system still falls over.
deployment reality
Configuration, DNS, certificates, network policy, the wrong environment variable. Contracts verify code against code; a smoke test after deploy (§20) is what verifies the deployment.
unknown consumers
A public API has consumers who never wrote a pact. Their needs are invisible, and the schema-as-contract form (§13.8) plus a deprecation policy is the only option.

Which is why the honest position is the one §10.4 set out: contracts replace most of an end-to-end suite, not all of it. A small number of end-to-end tests over the journeys that would be catastrophic to break still earn their place, because they are the only tests that exercise the deployed system rather than a model of it.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: a smoke test after deploy.

13.12 What This Section Established

  • A double is an unverified assumption, on both sides of every service boundary, and nothing in a normal suite compares the two halves. That is the hole contract testing fills.
  • Integrated tests as the primary correctness check are self-defeating: the combinatorics do not work, and the failure mode encourages more of them. The prescription is collaboration tests plus contract tests.
  • A contract is a set of interactions — given a provider state, upon receiving a request, respond with this — and the consumer specifies only the fields it reads. That subset rule is what leaves the provider free to evolve.
  • Consumer-driven means the provider's obligation is the union of what its consumers need, which turns "is anyone using this field?" into a mechanical question.
  • The consumer's double is configured from the contract, so the double and the contract cannot drift. That is the property that makes the scheme sound.
  • Provider verification replays the pact against the real service in the provider's own pipeline, with no consumer code and no shared environment.
  • Provider states must reset first and fail loudly on an unknown name. A verification that silently skips an unrecognised state cannot fail, which is worse than not having one.
  • A breaking change is caught in the provider's build, naming the field and the interaction, before it ships.
  • A generated OpenAPI document describes what the framework can see, not what the code does — the 404 and 401 this section's endpoint returns appear nowhere in it. Test the document before trusting it as a contract.
  • Expand-and-contract is verifiable with contracts: the pact files say when the old field is no longer needed, instead of asking consumers to remember.
  • can-i-deploy replaces a shared staging environment with a query — and it must be able to block a deploy, or it will be ignored.
  • Contracts do not cover semantics, emergent behaviour under load, or deployment reality. They replace most of an end-to-end suite, not all of it.

Exercises

1. Write the contract for a client you own.

Take a client in your codebase that calls another service. List every field it actually reads. Compare that with the full response the service returns. What proportion of the response is your service coupled to, and what would a contract free the provider to change?

2. Find the false pass.

provider_states.apply raises on an unknown state. Remove the else: raise and describe, step by step, the sequence of events by which a contract ends up "verified" against a state nobody set up. At which step would a person have noticed?

3. Classify eight changes.

For each, say breaking or not, and for whom: (a) adding currency to a response; (b) changing total_cents from integer to string; (c) making sku optional in a request; (d) returning 201 instead of 200 on create; (e) adding a required Idempotency-Key header; (f) sorting a list response by date instead of by id; (g) removing a field no pact mentions; (h) tightening a status field from any string to an enum of four values.

4. Design the states.

A payments provider has consumers needing: a successful charge, a declined card, an expired card, a charge that is already refunded, and a customer with no payment method. Write the provider state names and say how each would be set up. Which two are tempting to combine, and why should they not be?

5. Contract or end-to-end.

For each risk, say whether a contract test would catch it, and if not, what would: (a) the provider renames a field; (b) the provider starts returning 500s under load; (c) the consumer's retry logic double-charges; (d) a certificate expires; (e) the provider changes total_cents from including tax to excluding it; (f) a consumer deploys before its provider.

6. Sell it.

Your team maintains a service with four consumer teams and a shared staging environment that is broken about a third of the time. Write the case for adopting contract testing: what you would build first, what you would measure to know it worked, and the strongest objection you would expect and how you would answer it.

Solutions

1. Write the contract for a client you own.

No fixed answer, but the near-universal finding is that the client reads far less than it receives — often three or four fields out of twenty. That ratio is the argument: today the provider cannot change any of the twenty without risk, and with a contract they can change sixteen freely.

The second finding, which is more uncomfortable: most clients deserialise the whole response into a typed object, so the "fields actually read" question is harder than it looks — the type declaration couples you to fields nothing uses. A contract written from the type is much larger than one written from the code, and the smaller one is the honest contract.

2. Find the false pass.

Step by step. A consumer adds an interaction with the state "an order exists with a partial refund". The pact is published. The provider's verification runs, apply is called with the new name, no branch matches, the function returns having only done the clear(). The request for /orders/1 then hits an empty store and returns 404. If the interaction expected 404 — for instance a differently-named missing-order case — it passes. If it expected 200, it fails, but for the wrong reason, and the developer's most likely response is to add a state handler that returns whatever makes it green.

A person would notice at the point where the failure message says "expected 200, got 404" and they went to look at why — if the interaction expected 200. The dangerous case is the one where the accidental state happens to match, which produces no signal at all.

The general lesson: a verification step that can silently do nothing is not a verification. The same argument applies to a stub that falls through to the network (§12.6) and to a schema that accepts everything (§12.4).

3. Classify eight changes.

(a) Not breaking, provided consumers ignore unknown fields — which the subset rule enforces on your side and you should confirm on theirs.

(b) Breaking for every consumer that does arithmetic on it. This is the change a value-comparison test misses and a typed schema catches (§12.4).

(c) Not breaking. Relaxing a requirement is always safe; tightening one is not.

(d) Breaking for any consumer branching on the status, and they do — a client checking status == 200 now takes its error path on success.

(e) Breaking for every existing caller. This is the classic case for expand-and-contract: accept requests without it, warn, then require it after the consumers' contracts have migrated.

(f) Probably breaking, and the honest answer is you cannot tell, because ordering is rarely in the contract. That is the finding: if ordering matters, it must be stated. This is the same hazard as an unordered SQL result being relied on because it happened to come back sorted.

(g) Not breaking — and this is the whole point of consumer-driven contracts. Without them this question is unanswerable; with them it is a grep over the pact files.

(h) Breaking for any consumer sending a value outside the enum, and safe for consumers only reading it. Direction matters: narrowing a response type is safe, narrowing a request type is not.

4. Design the states.

  • "a card that will be charged successfully" — seed a token the fake gateway accepts.
  • "a card that will be declined for insufficient funds" — seed a token mapped to a 402 with that reason.
  • "an expired card" — a token mapped to a 402 with a different reason.
  • "a charge that has already been refunded" — seed a completed charge with a refund attached.
  • "a customer with no payment method" — seed a customer, and no token.

The two tempting to combine are the declined card and the expired card: both produce a 402, so one state seems to serve both. Do not, for two reasons. The reason string differs, and a consumer branching on it — retry a decline, do not retry an expiry — needs both verified. And the state name is the shared vocabulary: collapsing them means the contract can no longer express the distinction, so a future change to one of the two reasons breaks a consumer silently.

5. Contract or end-to-end.

(a) Caught, in the provider's build. The canonical case.

(b) Not caught. Contracts verify behaviour, not capacity. This needs load testing (§20) and production monitoring; a contract test runs one request against a warm process.

(c) Not caught by a contract, and it is your own bug: a consumer-side test with a stubbed 5xx and an idempotency assertion (§12.5) is what catches it. The contract can help by recording that the provider honours an idempotency key, which is the interaction to add.

(d) Not caught. Certificates are deployment reality. A post-deploy smoke test and an expiry monitor are the answers.

(e) Not caught, and it is the most dangerous item on the list. The type is unchanged, the field is unchanged, every contract stays green, and every consumer's totals are silently wrong. Contracts verify shape, not semantics. The mitigations are a name change (total_ex_tax_cents, which is a breaking change and would be caught), and a consumer-side sanity assertion on a value it can compute independently.

(f) Caught by can-i-deploy rather than by a contract test — which is the point of having the broker as well as the tests.

6. Sell it.

Build first: contracts for the single consumer that breaks most often, in both directions — the consumer test writing a pact, the provider verifying it. One pair, one week, no broker: publish the pact as a build artefact the provider's pipeline fetches. A broker is the second step, not the first, and starting with the tooling is how these initiatives stall.

Measure: the number of staging failures attributable to interface mismatches, before and after; the time from a provider's breaking change to its detection; and the proportion of provider deploys that needed a consumer to be consulted. All three are numbers the team already feels and does not currently record, which is why the argument is currently unwinnable.

The strongest objection: "this is just more tests to maintain, and we already have integration tests that would catch this." Answer it on the evidence rather than in principle — the staging environment is broken a third of the time, which means it is not catching these, it is producing noise. Contract tests run in each team's own pipeline, in seconds, and fail with the name of the field. Then make the smaller promise: one pair, one week, and if the staging failure rate does not move, stop.

The objection worth conceding: it is genuinely more machinery, and it only pays off when a team owns both the discipline and the pipeline to run it. A team that will not wire the verification into a build that actually runs should not adopt it, because an unverified contract is worse than none — it looks like safety.

SECTION 14

Testing the Browser

DOM testing — a user interface exercised through the tree it renders — is where most user-visible defects live, and it is the layer this course has so far avoided. The reason is that every technique before this one assumed a value you could inspect. A component produces a tree — of elements, text, attributes, focus and state — and the interesting claims are about what a person can see and do.

That framing is the whole of this section, and it is a technical constraint as much as a philosophy. A test that reaches into a component's internals is testing something users cannot observe, so it breaks when the internals change and passes when the interface is broken. A test that queries the rendered output the way an assistive technology does breaks on neither.

The tooling here is Testing Library, which exists to make the second kind easy and the first kind awkward, running against jsdom — a DOM implemented in JavaScript, with no browser. That combination is fast enough to be a unit test by §10.1's definition, and §15's Playwright covers what it cannot reach.

14.1 The Component Under Test

// vitest.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // A DOM without a browser. Every test in this section needs it.
    environment: 'jsdom',
    include: ['**/*.spec.jsx'],
  },
});

// OrderForm.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';

export function OrderForm({ onSubmit, skus }) {
  const [quantity, setQuantity] = useState(1);
  const [sku, setSku] = useState(skus[0]);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('idle');
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  async function handleSubmit(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    setStatus('sending');
    setError(null);
    try {
      const order = await onSubmit({ sku, quantity: Number(quantity) });
      setStatus('sent');
      setError(null);
      return order;
    } catch (err) {
      setStatus('idle');
      setError(err.message);
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit} aria-label="Place an order">
      <label htmlFor="sku">Item</label>
      <select id="sku" value={sku} onChange={(e) => setSku(e.target.value)}>
        {skus.map((s) => <option key={s} value={s}>{s}</option>)}
      </select>

      <label htmlFor="quantity">Quantity</label>
      <input id="quantity" type="number" min="1" value={quantity}
             onChange={(e) => setQuantity(e.target.value)} />

      <button type="submit" disabled={status === 'sending'}>
        {status === 'sending' ? 'Sending…' : 'Place order'}
      </button>

      {status === 'sending' && <p role="status">Sending your order…</p>}
      {status === 'sent' && <p role="status">Thank you — your order is placed.</p>}
      {error && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

Three things about that component are deliberate, and they are the difference between a component that is pleasant to test and one that is not.

Every control has a label. htmlFor/id pairs, and an aria-label on the form. That is an accessibility requirement first and a testability property second — and the two coincide because Testing Library queries the same accessibility tree a screen reader does.

The states are announced. role="status" for progress, role="alert" for the error. A user with a screen reader is told; a test can find them by role.

The async work is a prop. onSubmit is injected (§8.3), so the test controls the timing, the success and the failure without patching a module.

14.2 render, screen and cleanup

// basics.spec.jsx
import { test, expect, afterEach, describe } from 'vitest';
import { render, screen, cleanup } from '@testing-library/react';
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';
import { OrderForm } from './OrderForm.jsx';

afterEach(cleanup);

const SKUS = ['widget', 'gadget'];

describe('what is on the screen when nothing has happened yet', () => {
  test('the form, its controls and their initial values', () => {
    render(<OrderForm onSubmit={async () => ({ id: 1 })} skus={SKUS} />);

    expect(screen.getByRole('form', { name: 'Place an order' })).toBeInTheDocument();
    expect(screen.getByLabelText('Item')).toHaveValue('widget');
    expect(screen.getByLabelText('Quantity')).toHaveValue(1);
    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })).toBeEnabled();
  });

  test('nothing is announced before the user does anything', () => {
    render(<OrderForm onSubmit={async () => ({ id: 1 })} skus={SKUS} />);

    expect(screen.queryByRole('status')).not.toBeInTheDocument();
    expect(screen.queryByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  test('cleanup means the previous render is gone', () => {
    expect(screen.queryByRole('form')).not.toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});

cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{ "type": "module" }
EOF
npx vitest run --reporter=verbose basics.spec.jsx

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

 ✓ basics.spec.jsx > what is on the screen when nothing has happened yet > the form, its controls and their initial values 750ms
 ✓ basics.spec.jsx > what is on the screen when nothing has happened yet > nothing is announced before the user does anything 48ms
 ✓ basics.spec.jsx > what is on the screen when nothing has happened yet > cleanup means the previous render is gone 3ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
   Start at  00:08:38
   Duration  6.59s (environment 55%, import 19%, tests 14%, transform 10%, worker 1%)

render mounts the component into a container attached to document.body. The screen object queries that document, which is why you almost never need render's return value — and why using screen rather than destructuring the queries makes tests read the same regardless of what was rendered.

DOM testing is stateful in a way ordinary unit testing is not — the document persists unless something clears it — so cleanup() unmounts everything between tests. Testing Library calls it automatically when the runner exposes a global afterEach, and this course's configuration does not enable globals, so it is called explicitly. Getting this wrong produces §18.5 exactly: the third test above would find a form left over from the first, and a getByRole that should have matched one element would fail with "found multiple elements".

That third test is the metatest, and it costs one line.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the screen object, cleanup( and jest-dom.

To have in hand before moving on: dom testing.

14.3 Query Priority

Testing Library provides many queries and orders them, and the order is a claim about what a test should depend on.

1
getByRole
The accessibility tree. The default, and it should be most of your queries. { name } matches the accessible name, so it checks the label at the same time.
2
getByLabelText
Form fields, by their visible label. What a user reads to know what to type.
3
getByPlaceholderText
A fallback for a field with no label — which is an accessibility defect, so the query is a smell detector.
4
getByText
Non-interactive content. The right query for a paragraph, wrong for a button.
5
getByDisplayValue
A filled-in field, by its current value.
6
getByAltText / getByTitle
Images, and elements whose only name is a title. title is inconsistently exposed to assistive technology, so prefer a real label.
7
getByTestId
The escape hatch. Invisible to users, so it verifies nothing about the interface — and it cannot detect a control that has lost its label.

The ordering is not stylistic. A query by role fails when the interface becomes unusable; a query by test id does not. Change <button> to <div onClick=...> and every getByRole('button') breaks — correctly, because the control is no longer reachable by keyboard or by a screen reader. Every getByTestId keeps passing.

Test ids do have legitimate uses: an element with no accessible name and no text — a canvas, a chart, a decorative container — and a stable hook for §15's end-to-end tests where the copy changes often. Use them there and nowhere else.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: getByPlaceholderText, getByText, getByDisplayValue, getByAltText and getByTitle.

14.4 getBy, queryBy, findBy and the plural forms

Twelve queries is really three variants of four base names, and choosing the wrong variant produces a confusing failure rather than a wrong result.

 
no match
use it for
getBy
throws, with the whole DOM printed
"this must be here". The default.
queryBy
returns null
"this must not be here". The only correct query for an absence.
findBy
retries, then rejects
"this will be here soon". Returns a promise; await it.
*AllBy
as above, for a list
Several matches expected. The singular forms throw on multiple.

Every query also has a scoped form. within(element) returns the same query set restricted to one subtree, which is how you assert on one row of a table without an index — within(screen.getByRole('row', { name: /widget/ })).getByRole('button', { name: 'Remove' }). Reach for within( whenever a query would otherwise be ambiguous; it beats getAllBy and an index, because it describes what a person would actually look at.

Two mistakes account for most confusion here.

expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument() can never pass. getBy throws before expect is reached, so the test fails with "unable to find an element" rather than with your assertion. Absence is queryBy.

A forgotten await on findBy passes vacuously. The expression is a pending promise, which is truthy, so an assertion on it succeeds regardless. This is §3.9's un-awaited assertion in a different costume, and it is the single most common silent hole in a component suite.

The vocabulary here: getAllBy.

14.5 user-event, and Why Not fireEvent

// interaction.spec.jsx
import { test, expect, afterEach, describe, vi } from 'vitest';
import { render, screen, cleanup, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';
import { OrderForm } from './OrderForm.jsx';

afterEach(cleanup);
const SKUS = ['widget', 'gadget'];

describe('driving the form the way a person does', () => {
  test('choosing, typing and submitting sends what was chosen', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onSubmit = vi.fn(async () => ({ id: 1 }));
    render(<OrderForm onSubmit={onSubmit} skus={SKUS} />);

    await user.selectOptions(screen.getByLabelText('Item'), 'gadget');
    await user.clear(screen.getByLabelText('Quantity'));
    await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Quantity'), '3');
    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }));

    expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ sku: 'gadget', quantity: 3 });
  });

  test('the form is reachable by keyboard alone', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<OrderForm onSubmit={async () => ({ id: 1 })} skus={SKUS} />);

    await user.tab();
    expect(screen.getByLabelText('Item')).toHaveFocus();
    await user.tab();
    expect(screen.getByLabelText('Quantity')).toHaveFocus();
    await user.tab();
    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })).toHaveFocus();
  });

  test('fireEvent skips everything a real interaction does', () => {
    render(<OrderForm onSubmit={async () => ({ id: 1 })} skus={SKUS} />);
    const quantity = screen.getByLabelText('Quantity');

    // One synthetic change event. No focus, no keydown, no keyup, no input.
    fireEvent.change(quantity, { target: { value: '5' } });

    expect(quantity).toHaveValue(5);
    expect(quantity).not.toHaveFocus();   // a real user would have focused it
  });
});

npx vitest run --reporter=verbose interaction.spec.jsx

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

 ✓ interaction.spec.jsx > driving the form the way a person does > choosing, typing and submitting sends what was chosen 1324ms
 ✓ interaction.spec.jsx > driving the form the way a person does > the form is reachable by keyboard alone 189ms
 ✓ interaction.spec.jsx > driving the form the way a person does > fireEvent skips everything a real interaction does 50ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
   Start at  00:08:51
   Duration  7.85s (environment 51%, import 23%, tests 22%, transform 4%)

The third test is the argument, made by measurement rather than by assertion. fireEvent.change dispatches one synthetic event; user.type dispatches focus, then for each character a keydown, keypress, input and keyup, respecting maxlength, disabled and readonly. A control that a real user could not interact with will be happily driven by fireEvent and refused by user-event — a disabled button, an element covered by an overlay, a field that is readonly.

Three rules:

userEvent.setup() per test, before render. It installs its own clipboard and pointer state; sharing one across tests is shared mutable state (§18.5).

Every user.* call returns a promise. Await it. They are async because typing is a sequence of events and React must flush between them.

Reach for fireEvent only for events user-event does not model — a scroll, a transitionend, a synthetic drag. That is a short list, and everything on it is worth a comment.

The keyboard test deserves a note of its own: three tab calls and a toHaveFocus assertion is the cheapest accessibility test in existence, and it catches the most common real defect — a control that is not reachable without a mouse.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: userEvent.setup.

14.6 Waiting for Asynchrony

The form calls an injected async function. Three tools cover everything that follows from that.

// async.spec.jsx
import { test, expect, afterEach, describe } from 'vitest';
import { render, screen, cleanup, waitFor, waitForElementToBeRemoved }
  from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';
import { OrderForm } from './OrderForm.jsx';

afterEach(cleanup);
const SKUS = ['widget', 'gadget'];

/** A promise the test resolves when it chooses, so the pending state is real. */
function deferred() {
  let resolve, reject;
  const promise = new Promise((res, rej) => { resolve = res; reject = rej; });
  return { promise, resolve, reject };
}

describe('the pending, success and failure states', () => {
  test('the button disables and a status is announced while sending', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const gate = deferred();
    render(<OrderForm onSubmit={() => gate.promise} skus={SKUS} />);

    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }));

    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sending…' })).toBeDisabled();
    expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toHaveTextContent('Sending your order…');

    gate.resolve({ id: 1 });
    await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText('Sending your order…'));
    expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toHaveTextContent('your order is placed');
  });

  test('findBy waits for the success message', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<OrderForm skus={SKUS}
                      onSubmit={() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r({ id: 1 }), 30))} />);

    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }));

    // findByText, not findByRole('status'): BOTH the pending message and the
    // success message have role="status", so a role query resolves on the
    // first one it sees — which is whichever is on screen when it first runs.
    expect(await screen.findByText(/your order is placed/)).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  test('a rejected submit shows an alert and re-enables the button', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<OrderForm skus={SKUS}
                      onSubmit={async () => { throw new Error('the item is out of stock'); }} />);

    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }));

    expect(await screen.findByRole('alert'))
      .toHaveTextContent('the item is out of stock');
    await waitFor(() => {
      expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })).toBeEnabled();
    });
    expect(screen.queryByRole('status')).not.toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

 ✓ async.spec.jsx > the pending, success and failure states > the button disables and a status is announced while sending 1252ms
 ✓ async.spec.jsx > the pending, success and failure states > findBy waits for the success message 108ms
 ✓ async.spec.jsx > the pending, success and failure states > a rejected submit shows an alert and re-enables the button 94ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
   Start at  00:20:27
   Duration  4.77s (environment 40%, tests 36%, import 17%, transform 6%, worker 1%)
findBy*
Prefer it. "Wait for this element" is the common case and reads as one line.
waitFor()
For a condition that is not "an element appeared" — a button becoming enabled, a mock being called. waitFor() retries the callback, so keep it free of side effects.
waitForElementToBeRemoved
For a disappearance. It throws if the element was never there, which is what makes it better than polling for absence — a query that starts absent would pass immediately and prove nothing.

The comment in the second test records a real flake, found by running the file twice. Both the pending message and the success message carry role="status", so findByRole('status') resolves on whichever is present when it first runs — the pending one, most of the time, and the success one when the machine is slow enough that the promise settled first. A retrying query stops at the first match, and the first match is a function of timing: this is §18's asynchronous non-determinism arriving through a query rather than through a sleep. Query for the thing you mean.

The deferred helper in the first test is the pattern worth stealing. A promise the test resolves on demand makes the pending state observable — without it, the submit resolves before you can assert anything and the loading state is untested, which is the state users complain about.

None of these is a sleep, and none has a hardcoded delay. That is §18.9's deterministic waiting, applied to the DOM.

The term above, for reference: waitFor(.

14.7 act, and What It Is For

React must be told when its state has finished changing so it can flush the update. act is that boundary, and in practice you will meet it as a warning rather than as a function you call.

Warning: An update to OrderForm inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)

It means something updated component state outside anything React was tracking — a timer that fired, a promise that resolved after the test finished, a subscription callback. The state change happened, but the assertion ran before React re-rendered.

Almost always, the fix is not to add act:

await the interaction
user-event, findBy and waitFor are all wrapped in act internally. A missing await is the most common cause of the warning.
the test finished early
A pending request resolves after the test returns, into an unmounted component. Await the outcome, or make the component cancel on unmount — which is a real bug the warning found.
wrap it yourself
Only when you deliberately drive something React cannot see — advancing fake timers (§8.8), or firing a subscription callback by hand.

IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT is the global that tells React it is in a test and should apply act semantics. Testing Library sets it; you will only meet it if you render React outside Testing Library, or when a stray false in a setup file makes every act warning vanish — which looks like the warnings were fixed and means they were silenced.

Never silence the act warning. It is one of the few warnings in the ecosystem that reliably indicates a real defect: a state update the test did not wait for is a state update your assertion may have missed.

One to keep in hand: act( and IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT.

14.8 jsdom, happy-dom, and What They Are Not

jsdom
A DOM and HTML implementation in JavaScript. Mature, thorough, slower to start.
happy-dom
A smaller, faster alternative. Meaningfully quicker on a large suite, and less complete — a gap that shows up as a mysterious failure in one test.

Both are fakes of a browser (§6.1), and §11.13's warning applies with full force: a fake whose divergences are silent is dangerous. The divergences here are specific and worth knowing, because they define the boundary between this section and §15.

no layout
Every element is 0×0. getBoundingClientRect returns zeros, offsetWidth is 0, and anything measuring or intersecting cannot work.
no real CSS
Stylesheets are parsed but cascade and layout are not applied. toBeVisible() checks inline styles, hidden and display:none — not whether something is behind a modal, which is the assertion people assume it makes.
no paint, no scroll
No IntersectionObserver or ResizeObserver by default; both need stubbing. Nothing scrolls.
one engine, no vendor
A Safari-only bug cannot appear here, by construction.
partial APIs
navigation, matchMedia, crypto.subtle, dialog methods, clipboard — each either missing or approximate, and each producing an error unlike the browser's.

The line that follows: jsdom answers "does the component behave correctly?"; only a real browser answers "does it look and work correctly?" Everything about layout, visibility-in-practice, scrolling, focus rings and cross-browser behaviour belongs in §15, and a component test that tries to assert on any of them is asserting against a fake.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: toBeVisible(.

14.9 Testing Implementation Details

Kent C. Dodds's rule — the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you — has a precise operational meaning here.

an implementation detail
Component state, prop names, hook call order, the number of renders, a CSS class name, the shape of the component tree.
what a user observes
Text on the screen, whether a control is enabled, what is announced, where focus is, and what the component calls — a submit handler, a navigation, a request.

The two failure modes, exactly as §7 predicted: a test coupled to state breaks on a refactor that changes nothing observable, and a test that asserts a class name passes while the component is unusable.

// details.spec.jsx
import { test, expect, afterEach, describe, vi } from 'vitest';
import { render, screen, cleanup } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';
import { OrderForm } from './OrderForm.jsx';

afterEach(cleanup);
const SKUS = ['widget', 'gadget'];

describe('what to assert, and what not to', () => {
  test('the observable outcome: the handler is called with the chosen values', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onSubmit = vi.fn(async () => ({ id: 1 }));
    render(<OrderForm onSubmit={onSubmit} skus={SKUS} />);

    await user.selectOptions(screen.getByLabelText('Item'), 'gadget');
    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }));

    expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ sku: 'gadget', quantity: 1 });
  });

  test('the observable outcome of a failure: an alert the user can read', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<OrderForm skus={SKUS}
                      onSubmit={async () => { throw new Error('out of stock'); }} />);

    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }));

    // Not: "the `error` state variable is set". Not: "it re-rendered twice".
    expect(await screen.findByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent('out of stock');
  });

  test('a class name is not a claim about anything a user can perceive', () => {
    render(<OrderForm onSubmit={async () => ({ id: 1 })} skus={SKUS} />);
    const button = screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' });

    // This passes, and would keep passing if the button were invisible,
    // unreachable by keyboard, or covered by an overlay. Assert on the role,
    // the name and the enabled state instead — all three are user-observable.
    expect(button.className).toBe('');
    expect(button).toBeEnabled();
  });
});

The rule that operationalises it: if a refactor that changes no behaviour breaks the test, the test was asserting an implementation detail. Rename the state variable, replace useState with useReducer, extract a child component — none of those should move a single assertion in that file. Try it once on a real suite; the result is a fast, honest audit.

14.10 renderHook

A hook has no rendered output, so it cannot be queried. renderHook mounts it inside a throwaway component and hands you its return value.

// useCart.js
import { useCallback, useMemo, useState } from 'react';

export function useCart(initial = []) {
  const [lines, setLines] = useState(initial);

  const add = useCallback((sku, quantity, priceCents) => {
    setLines((current) => {
      const existing = current.find((l) => l.sku === sku);
      if (!existing) return [...current, { sku, quantity, priceCents }];
      return current.map((l) =>
        l.sku === sku ? { ...l, quantity: l.quantity + quantity } : l);
    });
  }, []);

  const remove = useCallback((sku) => {
    setLines((current) => current.filter((l) => l.sku !== sku));
  }, []);

  const totalCents = useMemo(
    () => lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.quantity * l.priceCents, 0), [lines]);

  return { lines, add, remove, totalCents };
}

// hook.spec.jsx
import { test, expect, afterEach, describe } from 'vitest';
import { renderHook, act, cleanup } from '@testing-library/react';
import { useCart } from './useCart.js';

afterEach(cleanup);

describe('useCart', () => {
  test('an empty cart totals zero', () => {
    const { result } = renderHook(() => useCart());

    expect(result.current.lines).toEqual([]);
    expect(result.current.totalCents).toBe(0);
  });

  test('adding the same sku twice increases its quantity rather than duplicating it', () => {
    const { result } = renderHook(() => useCart());

    // act, because this state update is driven by the test rather than by an
    // interaction React is already tracking (§14.7).
    act(() => { result.current.add('widget', 2, 250); });
    act(() => { result.current.add('widget', 1, 250); });

    expect(result.current.lines).toEqual([{ sku: 'widget', quantity: 3, priceCents: 250 }]);
    expect(result.current.totalCents).toBe(750);
  });

  test('removing a line that is not there changes nothing', () => {
    const { result } = renderHook(() => useCart([{ sku: 'widget', quantity: 1, priceCents: 250 }]));

    act(() => { result.current.remove('gadget'); });

    expect(result.current.totalCents).toBe(250);
  });

  test('rerender with new props keeps the hook state', () => {
    const { result, rerender } = renderHook(({ start }) => useCart(start),
                                            { initialProps: { start: [] } });
    act(() => { result.current.add('widget', 1, 250); });

    rerender({ start: [] });    // the initial value is only used on first render

    expect(result.current.totalCents).toBe(250);
  });
});

Two things to be careful about.

result.current is a live reference, not a snapshot. Capturing const { add } = result.current and calling it later gives you a stale closure. Always go through result.current.

A hook test is closer to a unit test of a state machine than to a component test, so the §14.9 warning applies to it in reverse: a hook is an implementation detail of the components that use it, and a suite that tests every hook exhaustively and no component through the DOM has optimised for the wrong thing. Test a hook directly when it is complex enough to deserve it — a reducer, a cache, a state machine — and test the rest through the components that use them.

14.11 Snapshot Testing

A snapshot records the rendered output on first run and compares against it afterwards. It is the cheapest test to write in this section and the easiest to write badly.

// Badge.jsx
export function Badge({ status, count }) {
  return (
    <span className={`badge badge--${status}`} data-count={count}>
      {status} ({count})
    </span>
  );
}

// badge.spec.jsx
import { test, expect, afterEach, describe } from 'vitest';
import { render, cleanup, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';
import { Badge } from './Badge.jsx';

afterEach(cleanup);

describe('Badge', () => {
  test('the badge markup', () => {
    const { container } = render(<Badge status="pending" count={3} />);

    expect(container.firstChild).toMatchSnapshot();
  });

  test('an inline snapshot keeps the expected value next to the test', () => {
    const { container } = render(<Badge status="pending" count={3} />);

    expect(container.innerHTML).toMatchInlineSnapshot(
      `"<span class="badge badge--pending" data-count="3">pending (3)</span>"`);
  });

  test('the claim a reader can actually check', () => {
    render(<Badge status="pending" count={3} />);

    expect(screen.getByText(/pending/)).toHaveTextContent('pending (3)');
  });
});

mkdir -p __snapshots__
cat > __snapshots__/badge.spec.jsx.snap <<'EOF'
// Vitest Snapshot v1, https://vitest.dev/guide/snapshot.html

exports[`Badge > the badge markup 1`] = `
<span
  class="badge badge--pending"
  data-count="3"
>
  pending
   (
  3
  )
</span>
`;
EOF

The three tests are the same component checked three ways, and they are not equally good.

The file snapshot is written by the runner and lives in __snapshots__/. Notice how the serialiser split the text — pending, (, 3, ) — into four nodes. That is correct and unreadable, and it is why a reviewer approving a snapshot diff is usually approving something they did not read.

The inline snapshot puts the expected value in the test file. Strictly better where the output is small: a reviewer sees the change in the diff of the test itself, with no second file to open, and --update-snapshots rewrites it in place.

The explicit assertion is the one that states a claim. It survives adding a wrapper element, changing the class names, or reordering attributes — all of which are behaviour-preserving — and it fails if the text is wrong, which is the thing anyone cares about.

14.12 Snapshot Rot

The failure mode is not that snapshots break. It is what people do when they break.

// Badge.jsx
export function Badge({ status, count }) {
  return (
    <span className={`badge badge--${status}`} data-count={count}
          title={`${count} items are ${status}`}>
      {status} ({count})
    </span>
  );
}

One added attribute, two failing snapshots, and a passing explicit assertion. That is exactly the ratio to expect, and it is the mechanism of rot:

1
A snapshot fails. The diff is forty lines of markup.
2
The change looks plausible, so --update-snapshots is run without reading it.
3
Repeat weekly. The snapshot now records whatever the component last did — including its bugs — and asserts nothing anybody chose.

An obsolete snapshot is the other half: a snapshot whose test no longer exists. Vitest reports these, and left alone the file accumulates records of components that were deleted years ago.

Five rules make snapshots useful rather than decorative:

Keep them small. A snapshot of one small component is reviewable. A snapshot of a whole page is not, and an unreviewable snapshot is an unreviewed one.

Prefer inline. The expected value belongs in the diff a reviewer is already reading.

Never update without reading. --update-snapshots on a red suite is the moment the test stops being a test. If the diff is too big to read, that is a finding about the snapshot, not a reason to skip reading.

Never snapshot anything volatile — a date, a generated id, a random value. It will fail tomorrow and train everyone to update without reading, which is rule three destroyed at the root.

Snapshot to detect change, assert to verify behaviour. A snapshot is a change detector, and that is genuinely useful for a component nobody is actively working on. It never tells you the output is right, so anything you actually care about deserves an explicit assertion as well — which is what the third test in §14.11 is for.

The term this subsection introduced: render(, toMatchSnapshot(, toMatchInlineSnapshot( and an obsolete snapshot.

14.13 Visual Regression Testing

jsdom has no layout and no paint (§14.8), so nothing in this section can tell you the page looks right. Visual regression testing is the technique for that: render in a real browser, take a screenshot, and compare it against an approved baseline image.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot() is the form you will meet (§15), and everything from §14.12 applies to it with the stakes raised, because an image diff is a snapshot whose serialisation is pixels.

what it catches
The whole class of defect no assertion expresses: a broken layout, an overlapping element, a colour that fails contrast, a font that did not load, a component that vanished at one breakpoint.
what it costs
Flakiness from font rendering, animation timing, scrollbars, GPU differences and platform anti-aliasing — and a baseline set that must be regenerated on every intentional change.

Four things make it survivable, and they are all about removing sources of variation:

Pin the rendering environment. Run in a container with the same fonts and the same browser build everywhere, including on developers' machines. Otherwise the baselines are only valid on the machine that made them.

Freeze animation and time. Disable transitions, and pin the clock (§8.7) so any rendered date is stable.

Mask the volatile regions. Every tool supports excluding a rectangle; use it for anything user-generated or time-dependent.

Set a threshold, and keep it small. A tolerance of a few pixels absorbs anti-aliasing noise; a large one absorbs real defects.

Use it on a small set of representative pages and states rather than everywhere. A visual suite covering forty screens will be regenerated wholesale on the first design change, and after that it records what the pages look like rather than what they should look like — §14.12's rot, in pictures.

To have in hand before moving on: toHaveScreenshot(.

14.14 What This Section Established

  • A component test asserts on what a user can observe, and the tooling exists to make that easy and the alternative awkward.
  • render mounts into the document and screen queries it; cleanup between tests is not optional, and one metatest proves it is happening.
  • Query priority is a claim about what a test should depend on. getByRole first, because it breaks when the interface becomes unusable; getByTestId last, because it never does.
  • getBy throws, queryBy returns null, findBy retries. Absence needs queryBy; a forgotten await on findBy passes vacuously.
  • user-event dispatches what a browser dispatches and refuses interactions a user could not perform; fireEvent is one synthetic event and will happily drive a disabled control. Three tab calls and a focus assertion is the cheapest accessibility test there is.
  • Wait for conditions, never for durations. findBy for an element, waitFor for a condition, waitForElementToBeRemoved for a disappearance — and the last one throws if the element was never there, which is what makes it honest.
  • A deferred promise makes the pending state observable, which is otherwise untested and is the state users complain about.
  • Never silence the act warning. It reliably means a state update the test did not wait for.
  • jsdom is a fake of a browser with no layout, no cascade, no paint and one engine. It answers "does it behave?"; only a real browser answers "does it look and work?".
  • A refactor that changes no behaviour must not break a component test. If it does, the test asserted an implementation detail.
  • renderHook needs act for test-driven updates, and result.current is a live reference. A hook is an implementation detail of its components; test it directly only when it is complex enough to deserve it.
  • A snapshot detects change and verifies nothing. Keep them small, prefer inline, never update without reading, never snapshot anything volatile, and pair them with an explicit assertion about the thing you actually care about.
  • Visual regression catches what no assertion expresses, at the cost of a pinned environment, frozen animation, masked regions and a small threshold.

Exercises

1. Rewrite the queries.

expect(container.querySelector('.submit-btn')).toBeTruthy();
expect(container.querySelector('#error-msg').textContent).toBe('Out of stock');
expect(wrapper.find('Spinner')).toHaveLength(1);

Rewrite all three using Testing Library, and for each say what defect the new version catches that the old one does not.

2. Choose the variant.

For each, choose getBy, queryBy, findBy or an *AllBy form: (a) the submit button, which is always there; (b) an error that appears after a failed request; (c) checking no error is shown initially; (d) the three items in a list; (e) checking a loading spinner has gone away.

3. Make the pending state testable.

The component under test calls fetch directly instead of taking an onSubmit prop. Describe two ways to test its loading state, and say which you would choose and why. Which of §8's ideas is the better one an instance of?

4. Predict the failure.

test('shows the total', () => {
  render(<Cart items={items} />);
  expect(screen.findByText('£54.00')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

This test passes. Explain exactly why it would pass even if the cart displayed £0.00, and give the one-character fix.

5. Audit a snapshot suite.

A project has 240 snapshot tests, and git log shows --update-snapshots run in 60% of commits that touch components. Diagnose it, and give the three changes you would make, in order. Which snapshots, if any, would you keep?

6. Draw the line.

For each, decide whether it belongs in a jsdom component test, a real-browser test, or neither, and say why: (a) a dropdown closes when you click outside it; (b) a modal traps focus; (c) a long label truncates with an ellipsis; (d) a form shows a validation error for an invalid email; (e) a table is horizontally scrollable on a narrow screen; (f) a button is disabled while a request is in flight.

Solutions

1. Rewrite the queries.

expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent('Out of stock');
expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toBeInTheDocument();

The first catches a <div onClick> that is no longer a button — unfocusable, not announced as a control, and not activated by the keyboard — and it also checks the accessible name, so a button whose label became empty now fails.

The second catches an error message that is rendered but not announced. A screen-reader user is never told about a <div id="error-msg">; role="alert" interrupts and reads it. The class-based query passes either way.

The third stops asserting on a component name, which is an implementation detail that breaks the moment Spinner is renamed or replaced, and starts asserting that something is announced as busy — which is what the user perceives.

2. Choose the variant.

(a) getByRole('button', { name: ... }). (b) await screen.findByRole('alert'). (c) queryByRole('alert') with not.toBeInTheDocument() — getBy would throw before the assertion ran. (d) getAllByRole('listitem') and assert the length; the singular form throws on multiple, which is a confusing way to learn there are three. (e) waitForElementToBeRemoved, because it throws if the spinner was never there — waitFor(() => expect(queryBy...).toBeNull()) passes immediately against a component that never showed one, and proves nothing.

3. Make the pending state testable.

Stub the network. Intercept fetch — with vi.stubGlobal, or a request-interception library — and return a promise the test controls. Works without changing the component, and it couples the test to the fact that this component fetches, and to the URL and shape of the request.

Inject the dependency. Pass the async function in as a prop, as §14.1's OrderForm does. The component no longer knows how the order is sent, and the test controls timing with a deferred.

Choose injection. It is §8.3's constructor injection in React's vocabulary, it makes the component reusable with a different transport, and the test says what it means. The stubbing approach is the right fallback when the component is not yours to change (§8.13), and worth reaching for as the first step in a legacy component before the injection refactor is safe.

4. Predict the failure.

findByText returns a promise, and it was not awaited. expect(promise).toBeInTheDocument() receives a Promise object, which is not null — and jest-dom's matcher on a non-element... is exactly where the trap bites: the assertion either throws about the received type or, in the common case, the promise is truthy and the whole test is meaningless. Either way, nothing about the cart's total was ever checked, and the test passes whatever the cart displays.

The one-character fix is await:

test('shows the total', async () => {
  render(<Cart items={items} />);
  expect(await screen.findByText('£54.00')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

And since the total is present synchronously, getByText is the better query — findBy here is waiting for something that is already there, which hides the un-awaited bug behind a passing test.

5. Audit a snapshot suite.

Diagnosis: the snapshots are no longer tests. A 60% update rate means the normal response to a red snapshot is to regenerate it, so the suite records what the components currently do — bugs included — and can never report a defect, only a change that someone will approve.

Three changes, in order:

  1. Stop the bleeding. Require that a commit updating snapshots says, in its message, what visibly changed. That is one line of policy, it takes effect immediately, and it converts the regeneration from a reflex into a decision.
  2. Add explicit assertions to the twenty components that matter most, taken from the failure history (§10.12). Those tests state claims and cannot be regenerated away.
  3. Delete the snapshots that cover components with explicit assertions, and convert the small remaining ones to inline snapshots so they appear in the review diff.

What to keep: snapshots of small, stable, unowned components — a design-system primitive nobody is actively changing — where the value really is "tell me if this moved". That is a change detector, it is a legitimate thing to want, and it is perhaps twenty of the 240.

6. Draw the line.

(a) jsdom. Click-outside is an event-listener behaviour, not a layout one; user.click(document.body) and assert the menu is gone.

(b) jsdom for the mechanism, a browser for the reality. Focus order and the Tab key work in jsdom, so "focus moves to the first control and wraps at the last" is testable there. Whether focus is visible, and whether the browser's own focus handling agrees, is a browser question.

(c) A browser, and specifically a visual test. Truncation is pure layout, and jsdom has none — every element is 0×0, so the ellipsis can never appear.

(d) jsdom. Validation is logic and text, and this is the cheapest possible component test.

(e) A browser. Scrollability at a viewport width is layout twice over.

(f) jsdom, and it is the example from §14.6. The disabled attribute and the announced status are both in the DOM.

The pattern in the answers: anything about layout, painting or the browser's own chrome is a real-browser question; everything about logic, text, roles, focus order and events is a jsdom question. That line is also the boundary between this section and §15, and knowing which side a claim falls on is most of the skill.

SECTION 15

End-to-End with Playwright

Section 14 tested components against jsdom, which is a fake of a browser with no layout, no cascade and no paint. This section is about the real thing: a browser process, a real page, real CSS, real network, real timing.

The tests are the most expensive and least reliable in the suite (§10.9) and they are the only ones that can tell you the deployed system works. Both halves of that are true, and the discipline of this section is keeping the second while limiting the first — which means few tests, chosen deliberately, written so that they cannot flake for reasons that are not defects.

Playwright is the tool because it made a specific design decision that removes most of the historical flakiness: every action waits for the element to be ready, and every assertion retries. Nothing in this section calls sleep, and that is not a stylistic choice — it is the property that makes an end-to-end suite affordable.

The examples run against a real Chromium, driving a real page served by a real HTTP server, all started by the test suite.

15.1 The System Under Test

An end-to-end test needs something deployed. Here that is a small static server started by a fixture — the same job Playwright's webServer configuration option does, written out so the mechanism is visible.

# shopserver.py
"""A tiny server for the end-to-end tests: what Playwright's `webServer`
option does for you, written out."""
import http.server
import socket
import threading

PAGE = """<!doctype html>
<html><head><title>Shop</title></head><body>
<h1>Shop</h1>
<label for="qty">Quantity</label>
<input id="qty" type="number" value="1">
<button id="add">Add to basket</button>
<p id="basket">Your basket is empty</p>
<p id="clock"></p>
<script>
document.getElementById('add').onclick = () => {
  const qty = document.getElementById('qty').value;
  document.getElementById('add').disabled = true;
  setTimeout(async () => {
    const r = await fetch('/api/total?q=' + qty);
    const j = await r.json();
    document.getElementById('basket').textContent =
      qty + ' item(s), total ' + j.total_cents;
    document.getElementById('add').disabled = false;
  }, 300);
};
setInterval(() => {
  document.getElementById('clock').textContent = new Date().toISOString();
}, 1000);
</script>
</body></html>
"""


class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        body = PAGE.encode() if self.path == "/" else b'{"total_cents": 250}'
        ctype = "text/html" if self.path == "/" else "application/json"
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", ctype)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass          # keep the test output clean


def serve():
    """Bind a port the OS chose (§18.12), serve in a thread, return the URL."""
    with socket.socket() as s:
        s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
        port = s.getsockname()[1]
    server = http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), Handler)
    threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    return f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}", server.shutdown

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

# tests/conftest.py
import pytest
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

from shopserver import serve


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def base_url():
    """One server for the whole run, on its own port, shut down afterwards."""
    url, shutdown = serve()
    yield url
    shutdown()


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def browser():
    """One browser process for the whole run. Launching one is expensive;
    an isolated context per test is not (§15.5)."""
    with sync_playwright() as pw:
        chromium = pw.chromium.launch()
        yield chromium
        chromium.close()


@pytest.fixture
def page(browser, base_url):
    """A fresh browser context per test: its own cookies, storage and cache."""
    context = browser.new_context(base_url=base_url)
    yield context.new_page()
    context.close()

That browser/page split is §5.6's rule in its most consequential form. A browser process takes seconds to start and is shared; a browser context is created in milliseconds and gives complete isolation — separate cookies, separate localStorage, separate cache, separate permissions. Two tests can log in as different users in parallel and neither can see the other's session.

15.2 Locators and Auto-Waiting

A locator is not an element. It is a description of how to find one, re-evaluated every time it is used — which is what makes it immune to the single most common source of end-to-end flakiness: an element reference that went stale because the page re-rendered.

# tests/test_basics.py
from playwright.sync_api import expect


def test_the_page_loads_and_the_controls_are_there(page):
    page.goto("/")

    expect(page).to_have_title("Shop")
    expect(page.get_by_role("heading", name="Shop")).to_be_visible()
    expect(page.get_by_label("Quantity")).to_have_value("1")
    expect(page.get_by_role("button", name="Add to basket")).to_be_enabled()


def test_adding_to_the_basket_waits_for_the_result_by_itself(page):
    page.goto("/")

    page.get_by_label("Quantity").fill("3")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Add to basket").click()

    # The update happens 300ms later, via a fetch. There is no sleep here and
    # no explicit wait: the assertion retries until it passes or times out.
    expect(page.locator("#basket")).to_have_text("3 item(s), total 250")


def test_the_button_disables_while_the_request_is_in_flight(page):
    page.goto("/")
    button = page.get_by_role("button", name="Add to basket")

    button.click()

    expect(button).to_be_disabled()      # retries until true
    expect(button).to_be_enabled()       # then retries until true again

pytest -q tests/test_basics.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 35.61s

Three mechanisms are doing the work, and each removes a class of flake.

Actionability. Before click() does anything, Playwright waits for the element to be attached, visible, stable (not animating), able to receive events (not covered by an overlay) and enabled. A click that a user could not perform waits rather than firing into the void — which is the opposite of fireEvent's behaviour in §14.5, and the reason a Playwright suite does not need "wait for the modal animation" hacks.

Web-first assertions. expect(locator).to_have_text(...) — toHaveText() in JavaScript — is a retrying assertion: it re-runs the whole query-and-compare until it succeeds or the timeout expires. A retrying assertion is the difference between a test that describes the page's eventual state and one that describes whatever the page happened to look like at a particular microsecond. Contrast with assert locator.text_content() == "...", which reads once, at whatever instant it happened to run. This is the single most important habit in this section: assert on the locator, never on a value you extracted from it.

Re-evaluation. The third test asserts disabled then enabled on the same locator object. Each assertion re-runs the query, so the locator survives the element being replaced by a re-render.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: actionability, web-first assertion and toHaveText(.

The vocabulary here: a retrying assertion.

15.3 Choosing a Locator

The priority is Testing Library's (§14.3), for the same reason: a locator that describes what a user perceives fails when the interface becomes unusable.

get_by_role
The accessibility tree, with the accessible name. The default — spelled page.getByRole in the JavaScript API, where the actions on what it returns are locator.click(), locator.fill() and the rest.
get_by_label
Form fields. Checks the label exists at the same time.
get_by_text, get_by_placeholder
Content and unlabelled fields.
get_by_test_id
The escape hatch — and more defensible here than in a component test, because end-to-end copy changes for marketing reasons that are not defects.
a CSS or XPath selector
.btn-primary > span:nth-child(2). Breaks on any restructuring, and says nothing about usability. Last resort.

Two Playwright-specific behaviours matter more than the ordering.

A strict mode violation is a feature. If a locator matches more than one element, Playwright fails rather than silently using the first. That converts an ambiguous test — which would pass or fail depending on DOM order — into an immediate error naming both matches. Narrow it with .first, .nth(1), a has_text= filter, or by scoping to a container.

Chaining scopes the search. page.get_by_role("listitem").filter(has_text="widget").get_by_role("button", name="Remove") reads as a sentence and is far more robust than an nth-child path, because each step describes something a user can see.

What to carry forward from this subsection: page.getByRole, locator.click(, locator.fill( and strict mode violation.

15.4 Network Interception

Network mocking with page.route intercepts requests inside the browser, which is how an end-to-end test covers the paths a real backend will not produce on demand.

# tests/test_network.py
from playwright.sync_api import expect


def test_a_stubbed_total_reaches_the_page(page):
    page.route("**/api/total*", lambda route: route.fulfill(
        status=200, content_type="application/json",
        body='{"total_cents": 9999}'))
    page.goto("/")

    page.get_by_role("button", name="Add to basket").click()

    expect(page.locator("#basket")).to_have_text("1 item(s), total 9999")


def test_the_page_survives_a_server_error(page):
    page.route("**/api/total*", lambda route: route.fulfill(status=500))
    page.goto("/")

    page.get_by_role("button", name="Add to basket").click()

    # This page has no error handling at all: the basket text never updates
    # and the button stays disabled. That is a real defect, and this is the
    # test that finds it — no backend can be persuaded to fail on demand.
    expect(page.locator("#basket")).to_have_text("Your basket is empty")
    expect(page.get_by_role("button", name="Add to basket")).to_be_disabled()


def test_a_request_can_be_observed_as_well_as_replaced(page):
    seen = []
    page.route("**/api/total*", lambda route: (seen.append(route.request.url),
                                               route.continue_()))
    page.goto("/")
    page.get_by_label("Quantity").fill("4")

    page.get_by_role("button", name="Add to basket").click()

    expect(page.locator("#basket")).to_have_text("4 item(s), total 250")
    assert seen and seen[0].endswith("/api/total?q=4")

pytest -q tests/test_network.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 40.50s

The second test is the argument for this whole facility. A 500 from the payment service, a timeout, a malformed response, an empty result set — these are the paths users hit and that a healthy staging environment never produces. Interception is the only way to exercise them end to end, and here it immediately found a real defect: the page has no error handling, so a failed request leaves the button disabled forever.

Two cautions. Interception is a double (§6.1), so everything §7.12 says applies — a stubbed response is an assumption, and if the shape drifts the test stays green. Use it for error paths and edge cases, and keep at least one journey running against the real backend. And route before navigating: a route registered after goto misses requests the page already made.

The term above, for reference: network mocking.

15.5 Contexts, Storage State and Logging In

Logging in through the UI on every test is the classic reason an end-to-end suite takes forty minutes. The fix is to do it once and reuse the result.

storage_state — storageState in the JavaScript API — captures cookies and localStorage from a context and replays them into another. The pattern:

1
A session-scoped fixture logs in once, through the real UI, and saves context.storage_state(path="auth.json").
2
Every test creates its context with new_context(storage_state="auth.json") and starts logged in, in milliseconds.
3
One test still logs in through the UI, because that journey is itself a feature and the shortcut would leave it untested.
4
A file per role — admin, member, anonymous — which is §12.9's fixture-per-role at the browser level.

Step 3 is the one teams forget, and its absence is invisible: every test is logged in, so nothing exercises logging in, and a broken login ships behind a fully green suite.

Two properties of contexts worth knowing. They are cheap — creating one is milliseconds, so per-test isolation costs nothing. And they are complete — cookies, storage, cache, permissions and service workers are all per-context, so parallel tests as different users genuinely cannot interfere.

One to keep in hand: storageState.

15.6 Controlling the Clock

Playwright can replace the page's clock, which turns "wait a day for the trial to expire" into an instruction.

# tests/test_clock.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from playwright.sync_api import expect

START = datetime(2027, 1, 15, 7, 59, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
PAUSE_AT = datetime(2027, 1, 15, 8, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)


def test_install_sets_the_time_the_page_sees(page):
    page.clock.install(time=START)
    page.goto("/")

    expect(page.locator("#clock")).to_contain_text("2027-01-15T07:5")


def test_pause_then_fast_forward_is_exact(page):
    page.clock.install(time=START)
    page.goto("/")
    page.clock.pause_at(PAUSE_AT)          # freeze; the ticking stops

    page.clock.fast_forward("01:00")       # mm:ss — this is ONE MINUTE

    expect(page.locator("#clock")).to_have_text("2027-01-15T08:01:00.000Z")


def test_run_for_advances_and_fires_the_timers_on_the_way(page):
    page.clock.install(time=START)
    page.goto("/")
    page.clock.pause_at(PAUSE_AT)

    page.clock.run_for(3000)               # three seconds, three interval ticks

    expect(page.locator("#clock")).to_have_text("2027-01-15T08:00:03.000Z")

pytest -q tests/test_clock.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 20.29s

Three measured facts that are easy to get wrong from memory.

install starts a clock that runs. It sets the time and then time continues to pass, so an assertion on an exact timestamp after install alone is a race. pause_at is what freezes it.

pause_at cannot go backwards. "Cannot fast-forward to the past" is the error, and it is why install is set to 07:59 and pause_at to 08:00 — by the time the page has loaded, the running clock is already past its start.

fast_forward("01:00") — clock.fastForward("01:00") in JavaScript — is one minute, not one hour. The string form is mm:ss ("30:00" is thirty minutes, "1:00:00" an hour). Passing a plain number is milliseconds, and is harder to misread.

The difference between fast_forward and run_for is worth keeping: fast_forward jumps, firing timers that were due; run_for advances through the interval, firing each timer at its proper simulated moment.
