For a page with a one-second setInterval, run_for(3000) produces three ticks and fast_forward(3000) produces the end state.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: clock.fastForward(.

15.7 Retries, Traces and Diagnosing a Failure

An end-to-end failure happens in another process, on another machine, minutes ago. The diagnostic tooling is therefore part of the technique rather than an extra.

trace
A recording of the whole run: a DOM snapshot before and after every action, every network request, the console, and a screenshot timeline. Opened in the trace viewer, it lets you step through the failure as if you were there.
on-first-retry
The setting worth using: no tracing on the normal path (it costs time and disk), full tracing the moment a test fails and is retried. You get the recording exactly when you need it and never otherwise.
screenshot on failure
Cheaper than a trace and often enough — half of end-to-end failures are obvious from a picture.
video on failure
For timing and animation problems a static image cannot show.
page.pause()
Stops a headed run and opens the inspector, where you can step, try locators live and see what actually matched.

Test retries are defensible here, which is not true anywhere else in this course (§18.13). Playwright's default — retry on CI, never locally — encodes the reasoning: a genuine environmental failure rate exists at this level and nowhere else, and §10.9's arithmetic showed that eight end-to-end tests at 2% dominate the whole suite's flake rate. The conditions from §18.13 still apply: the retry must be recorded and counted, so the flake rate stays visible, and a test that only ever passes on retry is a defect report, not a success.

The failure message itself is Playwright's other strength. When expect(locator).to_have_text(...) times out, it prints the call log — every attempt, what the locator resolved to each time, and the value it saw — plus an ARIA snapshot of the page. That is usually enough to diagnose without opening a trace, and it is why the assertions in §15.2 need no explanatory messages.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: test retries, trace viewer, on-first-retry, screenshot on failure, video on failure and page.pause(.

15.8 Structure: Page Objects and Fixtures

Two ways to keep an end-to-end suite from becoming unmaintainable, and they are complements rather than alternatives.

A page object wraps a page or a component in a class whose methods are user intentions: checkout.apply_promotion("SAVE10"), not three locator calls. The value is that a change to the markup touches one file, and the tests read as journeys.

# pages.py
from playwright.sync_api import expect


class ShopPage:
    """A page object: methods are intentions, and locators live in one place."""

    def __init__(self, page):
        self.page = page
        self.quantity = page.get_by_label("Quantity")
        self.add_button = page.get_by_role("button", name="Add to basket")
        self.basket = page.locator("#basket")

    def open(self):
        self.page.goto("/")
        return self

    def add(self, quantity):
        self.quantity.fill(str(quantity))
        self.add_button.click()
        return self

    def expect_basket(self, text):
        expect(self.basket).to_have_text(text)
        return self

# tests/test_page_object.py
from pages import ShopPage


def test_a_journey_reads_as_a_journey(page):
    ShopPage(page).open().add(2).expect_basket("2 item(s), total 250")


def test_a_second_journey_reuses_every_locator(page):
    ShopPage(page).open().add(5).expect_basket("5 item(s), total 250")

pytest -q tests/test_page_object.py

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 15.65s

Two rules keep page objects from becoming the problem they were meant to solve.

Expose intentions, not elements. A page object with a get_add_button() method is a locator dictionary with extra steps; the test still contains the interaction logic and still breaks on a redesign.

Do not assert inside them by default. expect_basket above is a deliberate exception — a named assertion (§3.12) that reads well in a chain. A page object whose every method asserts becomes a place where test logic hides, and a failure then names a page-object method rather than a claim.

The alternative Playwright's own runner offers is Playwright fixtures: a logged_in_page fixture, a checkout fixture returning a prepared page object, composed the way §5's fixtures compose. Playwright fixtures come in two lifetimes, and the second is the one worth knowing — a worker fixture is built once per parallel worker rather than once per test, which is where an expensive login or a seeded database belongs. In a project using the JavaScript runner, test.extend (§5.14) provides exactly this, plus worker fixtures — built once per parallel worker rather than per test, which is where an expensive login or a seeded database belongs.

To have in hand before moving on: a worker fixture.

15.9 Configuration, Projects and Parallelism

The parts of an end-to-end setup that are configuration rather than code, and what each one is for.

the webServer option
The webServer option starts your application before the run and waits for it to answer — a readiness check, not a sleep (§18.9). This section's base_url fixture is the same job by hand.
Playwright projects
The same tests run under several configurations — Chromium, Firefox, WebKit; desktop and mobile viewports; a setup project that logs in and produces the storage_state the others depend on.
fullyParallel
Runs tests within a file in parallel, not only files. Fast, and it will find every shared-state assumption you have (§18.12) — which is a benefit, on the day you can afford to fix them.
test sharding
--shard=2/4 across CI machines (§2.15). Test sharding is the first thing to reach for when the suite is too slow.
test.use()
Overrides configuration for a file or a block — a different viewport, a different locale, a different storage_state.
test.describe.serial
Forces an ordered, dependent group where a failure skips the rest. A last resort: test.describe.serial is §18's order dependence, made official.

test.describe.serial deserves the warning. It exists for genuinely sequential journeys — create an account, then use it, then delete it — where splitting into independent tests would mean repeating expensive setup. The cost is that the tests are no longer independent: one failure cascades, they cannot be run individually, and they cannot be parallelised. Before using it, check whether a fixture that creates the account (via the API, §8.14's back door) would let all three be independent. Usually it would.

One more piece of the API is worth naming: APIRequestContext, Playwright's own HTTP client, reachable as request in a test or as page.request from a page. It shares the browser context's cookies, which makes it the right tool for the back-door setup of §8.14 — create the account through the API, then drive the journey through the UI — and for asserting on what a request carried without stubbing it.

Two more tools that are not tests but shorten the loop: codegen records your clicks into a test file, which is the fastest way to get a first draft and produces locators that need editing to follow §15.3; and UI mode, a watch-mode interface showing the trace, the DOM and the locator picker as you write.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: APIRequestContext, test.use(, playwright projects, fullyParallel, codegen and ui mode.

15.10 Accessibility Scanning

A real browser gives access to something jsdom cannot provide: the actual accessibility tree, computed from real layout and real CSS.

An automated scan — axe-core is the standard engine — checks a page against a rule set: images with no alternative text, form fields with no label, insufficient colour contrast, headings out of order, controls not reachable by keyboard, ARIA attributes on elements that may not have them.

Two honest limits:

A scan finds perhaps a third of accessibility defects, and that fraction is the mechanical third — contrast ratios, missing attributes, invalid ARIA. Whether a label is meaningful, whether focus goes somewhere sensible after a dialog closes, whether an error is announced at the right moment — none of these is decidable by a rule.

A clean scan is not a claim of accessibility. It is a claim that a specific rule set found nothing, which is worth having as a gate and is not the same thing.

What makes it worth wiring in anyway is that it costs almost nothing once a browser is already running, it catches regressions the day they are introduced, and its findings are unambiguous. Run it on a handful of representative pages, fail the build on new violations, and treat manual testing with a screen reader as the part that actually establishes accessibility.

15.11 Keeping the Suite Small

The last discipline, and the one that decides whether any of the above survives contact with a real project.

Choose journeys, not features. An end-to-end test earns its place when its breakage would be catastrophic and no cheaper test could catch it: sign-up, log-in, checkout, payment, the one report the business runs on. A feature that would merely be annoying if broken belongs in §14 or §12.

One test per journey, not per variation. The discount rule has five cases and they belong in a unit test (§10.10). The end-to-end test exercises the journey once, with one discounted order, to prove the pieces connect.

Never assert business rules at this level. A total is checked here to prove the number reached the page — not to verify the arithmetic. Asserting the arithmetic here costs forty seconds per case and re-verifies what a millisecond test already established.

Delete on escape. When a defect escapes to production, add the lowest-level test that would have caught it (§10.5). If that is an end-to-end test, add it; if it is not, add the cheap one and consider whether an existing end-to-end test can go.

Budget the count. "No more than twenty end-to-end tests" is an arbitrary limit that works, because it forces a conversation every time someone wants the twenty-first. Without it the number only ever grows, and §10.5's cone is what growth looks like.

15.12 What This Section Established

  • Only a real browser answers "does it look and work", and these are the most expensive, least reliable and most valuable tests in the suite.
  • One browser process, one context per test. Contexts are milliseconds and give complete isolation — cookies, storage, cache, permissions.
  • A locator is a description, re-evaluated on every use, so it cannot go stale when the page re-renders.
  • Actionability waits for the element to be ready — attached, visible, stable, unobstructed, enabled — so a click a user could not perform waits rather than firing into nothing.
  • Web-first assertions retry. Assert on the locator, never on a value extracted from it; that single habit removes most end-to-end flakiness.
  • A strict mode violation is a feature: an ambiguous locator fails instead of silently picking the first match.
  • page.route is the only way to exercise the error paths a healthy backend will not produce — and it is a double, so keep one journey against the real thing. Route before navigating.
  • storage_state replaces logging in through the UI, and exactly one test must still do it, or a broken login ships behind a green suite.
  • install starts a running clock; pause_at freezes it and cannot go backwards; fast_forward("01:00") is one minute. run_for fires the timers on the way; fast_forward jumps to the end state.
  • Trace on first retry gives you the recording exactly when it is needed. Playwright's call log and ARIA snapshot usually make a trace unnecessary.
  • Retries are defensible here and nowhere else, and only when recorded and counted.
  • Page objects expose intentions, not elements, and should not assert by default.
  • describe.serial is order dependence made official — check whether an API-seeded fixture would let the tests be independent instead.
  • An accessibility scan finds the mechanical third of accessibility defects. A clean scan is not a claim of accessibility.
  • Keep the suite small: journeys not features, one test per journey, no business rules at this level, and a budget on the count.

Exercises

1. Replace the waits.

page.click("#checkout")
time.sleep(2)
assert page.text_content("#confirmation") == "Order placed"

Rewrite it. Then list every distinct way the original could fail on a slow machine, and say which of them the rewrite removes and which it does not.

2. Choose the locators.

For each element, write the locator you would use and say why: (a) the only submit button on a form; (b) the "Remove" button in the row for the item "widget", where every row has one; (c) a chart rendered into a canvas; (d) a status message that appears after saving; (e) a link whose text is translated per locale.

3. Design the login strategy.

A suite has 30 end-to-end tests, and logging in takes 4 seconds through the UI. Design the fixtures, say what the total login cost becomes, and describe the one test that must not use your shortcut and why.

4. Find the defect the stub found.

§15.4's second test shows the page leaving its button disabled after a 500. Write the fix to the page, then write the test you would keep afterwards. Which level does that test belong at — is it really end-to-end?

5. Audit a suite.

A team has 180 Playwright tests taking 55 minutes, with retries: 3 set globally and about 12% of runs going red on unchanged code. Diagnose it and give the first four things you would do, in order, with the reasoning for the ordering.

6. Draw the boundary.

For each, say whether it belongs in a Playwright test, and if not, where: (a) the checkout total is correct for a gold member; (b) the checkout page renders correctly at 320px wide; (c) a session expires after 30 minutes; (d) an uploaded file over 10 MB is rejected; (e) the "Buy" button is announced correctly by a screen reader; (f) the API returns 409 on a duplicate order.

Solutions

1. Replace the waits.

page.get_by_role("button", name="Checkout").click()
expect(page.get_by_text("Order placed")).to_be_visible()

Ways the original can fail on a slow machine: the checkout button is not yet attached when click runs; it is attached but covered by a cookie banner; it is attached and visible but the handler is not yet bound; the request takes longer than two seconds; the confirmation element does not exist when text_content runs, returning None; the element exists but is empty at the instant it is read.

The rewrite removes all six. Actionability covers the first three — the click waits for attached, visible, unobstructed and enabled. The retrying assertion covers the last three, because it re-queries until the text is there or the timeout expires.

What it does not remove: a genuine backend timeout longer than the assertion timeout, and any real defect. Those are exactly the failures you want to keep.

2. Choose the locators.

(a) page.get_by_role("button", name="Submit"). If it really is the only one, page.get_by_role("button") also works — and would break the day a second is added, which strict mode makes loud rather than silent.

(b) Chain and filter: page.get_by_role("listitem").filter(has_text="widget").get_by_role("button", name="Remove"). Anything based on an index breaks when the order changes.

(c) page.get_by_test_id("revenue-chart"). A canvas has no accessible content, so this is the escape hatch used correctly — and the finding underneath it is that the chart should have a text alternative, which is a defect the locator choice just surfaced.

(d) page.get_by_role("status"), and let the assertion retry. Do not add an explicit wait.

(e) page.get_by_test_id("terms-link"), or get_by_role("link") scoped to a container. Translated copy is the strongest legitimate case for a test id, because the text changes for reasons that have nothing to do with correctness.

3. Design the login strategy.

A session-scoped fixture logs in once through the UI and writes auth.json; each test's page fixture creates its context with storage_state="auth.json". Total login cost falls from 30 × 4 = 120 seconds to about 4 seconds plus 30 negligible context creations.

With parallel workers, make it a worker-scoped fixture — or generate the file once in a setup project — so it is created once per worker rather than once per test, and make sure the file path is unique per worker if the workers write it (§18.12).

The test that must not use the shortcut is the login journey itself: entering a wrong password, entering the right one, and landing on the destination. Without it, every test is authenticated by a file, and a broken login form ships behind thirty green tests. Add the sibling cases for the same reason: an expired session, and a logout.

4. Find the defect the stub found.

The fix is a try/finally around the fetch that re-enables the button, and a rendered error message with role="alert":

try {
  const r = await fetch('/api/total?q=' + qty);
  if (!r.ok) throw new Error('Sorry — we could not price your basket.');
  const j = await r.json();
  basket.textContent = qty + ' item(s), total ' + j.total_cents;
} catch (err) {
  alertEl.textContent = err.message;
} finally {
  addButton.disabled = false;
}

The test to keep afterwards asserts that a 500 produces a readable alert and a re-enabled button. And it is not really an end-to-end test: it is a component-level claim about error handling, and §14's jsdom plus an injected failing request would check it in milliseconds.

Which is the honest conclusion: the end-to-end test was the right tool to find it, because interception at the browser level was the cheapest way to produce the condition — and the right home for the regression test is one level down. That is §10.5's rule applied to a defect you found yourself.

5. Audit a suite.

Diagnosis: an ice-cream cone (§10.5) with the flakiness masked. retries: 3 globally means the 12% is what survives three retries, so the true per-run failure rate is far higher and nobody knows it. Fifty-five minutes means the suite cannot be in the commit stage, so it is either blocking releases or being ignored.

First four things, in order:

  1. Make the flakiness visible. Record retry counts per test and publish the flake rate (§18.14). Nothing else can be prioritised until this number exists, and it costs a configuration change.
  2. Shard across machines. Fifty-five minutes over six shards is nine, which restores a usable feedback loop without changing a single test. It is the highest ratio of benefit to risk available.
  3. Fix the top five flakiest tests, which the data from step 1 identifies. The distribution is always skewed; five tests will be most of the noise, and they are almost always sleeps or extracted-value assertions.
  4. Then start pushing tests down. For each of the last twenty escaped defects, add the lowest-level test that would have caught it, and delete the end-to-end test that was covering it.

The ordering matters: measuring first means steps 3 and 4 are aimed at evidence rather than at impressions, and sharding second buys the team the patience to do step 4 at all.

6. Draw the boundary.

(a) Not Playwright — a unit test of the pricing rule (§10.10). One end-to-end test may include a discounted order to prove the number reaches the page, but the five rule cases belong where they cost nothing.

(b) Playwright, with a viewport override and ideally a visual comparison (§14.13). Layout at a width is exactly what jsdom cannot do.

(c) Playwright, with the clock controlled (§15.6) — pause_at then fast_forward("30:00"). Otherwise the test takes thirty minutes and is the definition of a slow test.

(d) Split it. The size rule is a server-side check and belongs in an API test (§12.3). That the browser shows a helpful message when the server refuses is a component test with a stubbed error. An end-to-end test uploading an 11 MB file is slow and re-verifies both.

(e) Playwright for the mechanical part — an axe scan will catch a missing accessible name — and neither, for the real question. Whether the announcement is useful needs a person with a screen reader (§20.13). The scan is a gate, not a claim.

(f) Not Playwright — that is §12's territory entirely, and testing a status code through a browser is forty seconds spent on something a test client checks in two milliseconds.

SECTION 16

Property-Based Testing

Every test so far has been an example: this input, that output. §1.11 gave the arithmetic — split has more possible inputs than you will ever enumerate, and a suite of four examples checks four of them.

A property — an invariant, in the vocabulary most libraries use — is a claim that holds for every input. "The shares always sum to the total" is a property. "The shares sum to 9999 when the total is 9999 and there are seven ways" is an example of it. A property-based testing library takes the property, generates hundreds of inputs, and — when one fails — shrinks it to the smallest input that still fails. Stating an invariant is harder than writing an example and it buys far more, which is the trade this whole section is about.

That last part is why the technique is worth learning rather than merely knowing about. A generator that finds a failure at [8134, -2, 991, 0, 77123] is mildly useful. One that hands you [0, -1] has done most of the debugging for you.

Two libraries: Hypothesis for Python and fast-check for JavaScript. They differ in surface and agree on everything important.

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

16.1 A Property, Not an Example

The move this section is about is stating a property rather than an example: an invariant that holds for every input, rather than a claim about the one input you thought of. Back to §1's function, and the property exercise 1 identified as the valuable one.

# money.py
def split(total_cents, ways):
    """Split a sum of money as evenly as possible, largest shares first."""
    base, extra = divmod(total_cents, ways)
    return [base + 1] * extra + [base] * (ways - extra)

# tests/test_money_properties.py
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

from money import split


@given(total=st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10**9),
       ways=st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=100))
def test_the_shares_always_sum_to_the_total(total, ways):
    assert sum(split(total, ways)) == total


@given(total=st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10**9),
       ways=st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=100))
def test_there_are_always_exactly_that_many_shares(total, ways):
    assert len(split(total, ways)) == ways


@given(total=st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10**9),
       ways=st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=100))
def test_no_two_shares_differ_by_more_than_a_cent(total, ways):
    shares = split(total, ways)
    assert max(shares) - min(shares) <= 1


@given(total=st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10**9),
       ways=st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=100))
def test_the_larger_shares_come_first(total, ways):
    shares = split(total, ways)
    assert shares == sorted(shares, reverse=True)

pytest -q tests/test_money_properties.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 11.63s

Four tests, and each one ran a hundred times against inputs nobody chose. The default is 100 examples per property, so that run made four hundred checks — and it is the four claims that are the work, not the four hundred cases.

Compare what this bought against §1's four examples. §1's suite could not catch a defect that only shows up at ways=1, or at total=0, or when the total is exactly divisible. This suite tries all of those without being told to, because those are the values a good generator is biased towards: property-based libraries deliberately over-sample the boundaries — zero, one, the maximum, the empty collection — since that is where defects live. §4.4's boundary-value analysis is, in effect, automated here.

The vocabulary here: a property rather than an example.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: an invariant.

16.2 Watching It Shrink

Introduce a defect and the shrinking is the whole show.

# money.py
def split(total_cents, ways):
    """Split a sum of money as evenly as possible, largest shares first."""
    base, extra = divmod(total_cents, ways)
    if ways > 3 and extra == 1:          # a plausible-looking special case, and wrong
        return [base] * ways
    return [base + 1] * extra + [base] * (ways - extra)

pytest -q --tb=line tests/test_money_properties.py 2>&1 | grep -E 'Failing test case|total=|ways=|^1 failed'

    Failing test case: test_the_shares_always_sum_to_the_total(
        total=1,
        ways=4,
1 failed, 3 passed in 9.98s

The Failing test case: block reports total=1, ways=4 — not the input hypothesis happened to stumble on, but the smallest one that can exhibit the bug at all. The defect needs extra == 1 and ways > 3; the smallest ways above 3 is 4, and the smallest total leaving remainder 1 is 1. From that pair alone the special case is nearly readable.

Hypothesis often prints a second block underneath, headed Explanation:, reading These lines were always and only run by failing test cases: money.py:6 — line 6 being the if ways > 3 and extra == 1: branch. That is the explain phase: having found a failure, hypothesis compares the lines executed by failing and passing runs and reports the ones unique to the failures. A counterexample plus the guilty line is most of a diagnosis.

It is filtered out of the output above deliberately, and the reason is a lesson in its own right: the explain phase runs on a time budget and does not always finish, so a block claiming it would pass on one run and fail on the next. That is a flaky test, in a course about them, and §18.3 is the general form of the rule — never claim output a tool produces only when it has time.

Getting from a random failing input to total=1, ways=4 is shrinking, and it works by repeatedly simplifying a failing input and re-running: shrink the integer towards zero, shorten the list, simplify the string, and keep whatever still fails. What it converges on is a minimal counterexample — the simplest input the library could find that still breaks the property. A raw generated counterexample is usually noise; a minimal counterexample is a bug report, and it is the single feature that makes property-based testing usable rather than merely clever.

Restore the function:

# money.py
def split(total_cents, ways):
    """Split a sum of money as evenly as possible, largest shares first."""
    base, extra = divmod(total_cents, ways)
    return [base + 1] * extra + [base] * (ways - extra)

16.3 Strategies

A hypothesis strategy describes a set of values and how to shrink them. st.integers() is one; they compose.

The dozen worth knowing by name, because everything else is built from them: integers(), floats(), booleans() and the text() strategy for scalars; lists(), dictionaries(), sets() and tuples() for containers; sampled_from() to draw from a fixed collection and one_of() to draw from several strategies at once; from_regex() to generate strings matching a pattern and from_type() to derive a strategy from a type annotation; builds() to construct an object by calling something with generated arguments; composite() — spelled @st.composite — to write a strategy that draws several values and combines them; and the data() strategy, which hands the test a live drawing object so it can generate a value after seeing an earlier one.

# tests/test_strategies.py
from hypothesis import given, settings, strategies as st


@given(st.integers())
def test_integers_are_unbounded_by_default(n):
    assert isinstance(n, int)


@given(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10))
def test_bounds_are_inclusive(n):
    assert 0 <= n <= 10


@given(st.text())
def test_text_generates_unicode_including_the_awkward_parts(s):
    assert isinstance(s, str)
    assert s.encode("utf-8").decode("utf-8") == s


@given(st.lists(st.integers(), min_size=1, max_size=20))
def test_lists_take_an_element_strategy(xs):
    assert 1 <= len(xs) <= 20
    assert all(isinstance(x, int) for x in xs)


@given(st.dictionaries(st.text(min_size=1), st.integers(), max_size=5))
def test_dictionaries_take_two(d):
    assert len(d) <= 5


@given(st.one_of(st.integers(), st.none(), st.text()))
def test_one_of_picks_between_strategies(value):
    assert value is None or isinstance(value, (int, str))


@given(st.sampled_from(["draft", "published", "archived"]))
def test_sampled_from_picks_from_a_fixed_set(status):
    assert status in {"draft", "published", "archived"}


@given(st.from_regex(r"\A[a-z]{3}-\d{4}\Z"))
def test_from_regex_generates_matching_strings(code):
    assert len(code) == 8 and code[3] == "-"

pytest -q tests/test_strategies.py

........                                                                 [100%]
8 passed in 39.07s

st.text() deserves a paragraph. By default it generates the whole of Unicode, not ASCII: surrogates, combining marks, right-to-left overrides, \r, characters that change length when normalised. That is the point. A string-handling function that has only ever seen "hello" and "world" is a function whose Unicode behaviour is unknown, and this is the cheapest way to find out.

st.from_regex needs its \A and \Z anchors. Without them it generates strings that contain a match rather than strings that are one — which is correct behaviour for re.search semantics and a surprise the first time.

The terms above, gathered: a hypothesis strategy, the text() strategy, lists(), builds(), composite(), sampled_from(), one_of(), from_regex(), from_type() and the data() strategy.

16.4 Building Composite Values

Most real inputs are not integers. st.builds and @st.composite construct them.

# orders.py
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Line:
    sku: str
    quantity: int
    unit_cents: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    lines: tuple

    def total_cents(self):
        return sum(line.quantity * line.unit_cents for line in self.lines)

    def with_discount(self, percent):
        if not 0 <= percent <= 100:
            raise ValueError("percent must be between 0 and 100")
        return round(self.total_cents() * (100 - percent) / 100)

# tests/test_orders_properties.py
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

from orders import Line, Order

skus = st.sampled_from(["AB-001", "CD-002", "EF-003", "GH-004"])

lines = st.builds(
    Line,
    sku=skus,
    quantity=st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=99),
    unit_cents=st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=100_000),
)

orders = st.builds(Order, lines=st.lists(lines, max_size=6).map(tuple))

# Two percentages in order, generated rather than filtered — see the note under this block.
ordered_percents = st.lists(
    st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=100), min_size=2, max_size=2
).map(sorted)


@given(orders)
def test_a_total_is_never_negative(order):
    assert order.total_cents() >= 0


@given(orders)
def test_a_hundred_percent_discount_is_free(order):
    assert order.with_discount(100) == 0


@given(orders)
def test_a_zero_percent_discount_changes_nothing(order):
    assert order.with_discount(0) == order.total_cents()


@given(orders, ordered_percents)
def test_a_bigger_discount_never_costs_more(order, percents):
    smaller, bigger = percents
    assert order.with_discount(bigger) <= order.with_discount(smaller)

pytest -q tests/test_orders_properties.py

....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 7.65s

st.builds(Line, ...) calls the constructor with generated arguments and shrinks all of them together. The | operator is one_of spelled as an operator, and .map(tuple) transforms a strategy's output — both are methods on every strategy, along with .filter() and .flatmap().

ordered_percents is the section's most important habit in one line. The obvious way to write that last test is two independent percentages and assume(a <= b), which discards every generated case where the precondition does not hold. assume is the right tool when the precondition rules out a small fraction and the wrong one when it rules out many: hypothesis raises FailedHealthCheck: Input generation is slow and fails the test outright when it has to throw away too much. Half of all pairs is already too much on a loaded machine — this section's first draft used assume here and was reported as nondeterministic, passing on an idle run and failing under load.

Generate the constrained value instead of filtering for it. st.lists(..., min_size=2, max_size=2).map(sorted) produces an ordered pair directly and discards nothing. Note also that skus is st.sampled_from rather than st.from_regex: four literal SKUs cost nothing to generate, and the SKU's format is not what any of these four properties is about.

16.5 The Four Property Shapes Worth Knowing

Most useful properties fall into a small number of patterns, and knowing them is how you get past "I can't think of any properties for this code". Two more are worth naming alongside the four below. A commutativity property says the order of two operations does not matter — applying a discount then rounding is not the same as rounding then discounting, and writing the property is how you find out which one the business meant. And metamorphic testing is the general form of all of them: rather than asserting an output, assert a relation between two runs — sort a list, sort its reverse, and the results must be equal. Metamorphic testing is the technique for code with no computable oracle at all (§4.3), because a relation between outputs can be known even when neither output can.

round-trip
decode(encode(x)) == x. Serialisation, parsing, compression, encryption. The single highest-value property in most codebases.
invariant
Something true of every output regardless of input: the sum is preserved, the list stays sorted, the balance never goes negative.
oracle
A second, obviously-correct-but-slow implementation must agree. Optimised code against the naive version it replaced.
metamorphic
A known relation between two runs, when you cannot state either result alone. Sorting twice changes nothing; adding an item never lowers the total.
# codec.py
import json


def encode(record):
    return json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))


def decode(blob):
    return json.loads(blob)


def normalise_tags(tags):
    """Lowercase, strip, drop empties, deduplicate, sort."""
    seen = {t.strip().lower() for t in tags if t.strip()}
    return sorted(seen)

# tests/test_shapes.py
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

from codec import decode, encode, normalise_tags

json_values = st.recursive(
    st.none() | st.booleans() | st.integers() | st.text(),
    lambda children: st.lists(children, max_size=4)
    | st.dictionaries(st.text(), children, max_size=4),
    max_leaves=12,
)


# --- round-trip ---------------------------------------------------------------
@given(json_values)
def test_decoding_an_encoded_value_gives_it_back(value):
    assert decode(encode(value)) == value


# --- invariant ----------------------------------------------------------------
# The sizes are bounded deliberately. `st.lists(st.text())` unbounded generates lists of
# hundreds of long strings, and `slow_normalise` below is quadratic — which is enough to
# trip hypothesis's 200ms deadline (§16.6) on a loaded machine and nowhere else. A property
# whose examples are expensive is a property that fails for reasons that are not defects.
@given(st.lists(st.text(max_size=20), max_size=30))
def test_normalised_tags_are_always_sorted_and_unique(tags):
    result = normalise_tags(tags)
    assert result == sorted(result)
    assert len(result) == len(set(result))
    assert all(t == t.strip().lower() and t for t in result)


# --- idempotence: a metamorphic relation with itself --------------------------
@given(st.lists(st.text(max_size=20), max_size=30))
def test_normalising_twice_is_the_same_as_once(tags):
    once = normalise_tags(tags)
    assert normalise_tags(once) == once


# --- oracle -------------------------------------------------------------------
def slow_normalise(tags):
    """Obviously correct, obviously slow."""
    out = []
    for tag in tags:
        cleaned = tag.strip().lower()
        if cleaned and cleaned not in out:
            out.append(cleaned)
    return sorted(out)


@given(st.lists(st.text(max_size=20), max_size=20))
def test_the_fast_version_agrees_with_the_slow_one(tags):
    assert normalise_tags(tags) == slow_normalise(tags)


# --- metamorphic --------------------------------------------------------------
@given(st.lists(st.text(max_size=20), max_size=30), st.text(max_size=20))
def test_adding_a_tag_never_shortens_the_result(tags, extra):
    assert len(normalise_tags(tags + [extra])) >= len(normalise_tags(tags))

pytest -q tests/test_shapes.py

.....                                                                    [100%]
5 passed in 4.25s

st.recursive is how you generate a tree: a base strategy, a function that builds bigger values out of children, and a size cap. Generating arbitrary JSON is the classic use, and the round-trip property over it is the classic first property-based test — it finds encoder bugs that no hand-written example ever would, because nobody thinks to write a test for a dictionary key containing a lone surrogate.

An idempotence property is worth singling out because so much code should have one and does not: normalising, sanitising, formatting, migrating, deduplicating. If applying a function twice differs from applying it once, that is nearly always a defect, and an idempotence property is one line to check.

One to keep in hand: commutativity property.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: idempotence property.

16.6 @settings, @example, and Reproducing a Failure

Hypothesis has knobs, and three of them matter. max_examples decides how many cases to run; the deadline setting bounds how long any single example may take, and it is the one that turns a slow example into a failure rather than a slow suite; and derandomize makes the run reproducible by fixing the seed. Two decorators belong here as well: the @example decorator pins a specific case so it is always tried, and @reproduce_failure replays one exact previously-found failure from the blob hypothesis prints.

# tests/test_settings.py
from hypothesis import example, given, settings, strategies as st

from money import split


@settings(max_examples=500)
@given(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10**6), st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=64))
def test_more_examples_when_the_space_is_large(total, ways):
    assert sum(split(total, ways)) == total


@given(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10**6), st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=64))
@example(total=0, ways=1)          # the degenerate case, always tried
@example(total=1, ways=5000)       # a case a real bug report contained
@example(total=999999, ways=7)     # a remainder that is not 0 or 1
def test_the_pinned_cases_run_every_time(total, ways):
    shares = split(total, ways)
    assert sum(shares) == total and len(shares) == ways


@settings(deadline=None, max_examples=25)
@given(st.lists(st.integers(), max_size=200))
def test_deadline_none_for_a_slow_property(xs):
    assert sorted(sorted(xs)) == sorted(xs)

pytest -q tests/test_settings.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 5.47s

@example pins a case. When hypothesis finds a counterexample, you fix the code and then add that input as an @example, so it is checked on every run forever rather than only when the generator happens to produce it again. This is how a property-based test and a regression test coexist in one function, and it is the single most under-used feature in the library.

max_examples trades time for confidence. The default 100 is right for a fast property. Raise it for a large input space and lower it for a slow one — a property that takes 200ms per case at 100 examples is a twenty-second test, which is how a property suite becomes the slow suite nobody runs (§20.7).

deadline fails a case that takes longer than 200ms by default, on the theory that a sudden slowdown is a defect. That threshold is easier to hit than it looks, and this section hit it: the second @example above originally read ways=1000000, which makes split build a million-element list, and the fragment was reported as nondeterministic — passing on an idle machine and blowing the deadline under load. A pinned example is meant to document a case, not to be a benchmark. It is right in principle and a nuisance in practice for anything touching a database or the filesystem, and deadline=None is the usual answer there.

Two behaviours of the tool itself are worth knowing. Hypothesis keeps an example database in a .hypothesis directory — every failing input is saved and replayed first on the next run, so a fix is checked against the exact case that broke before you get to the random ones. And when a failure is not reproducing, @settings(derandomize=True) makes the generation deterministic from the test's own name, which turns "it fails on CI sometimes" into "it fails".

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the @example decorator, the deadline setting and @reproduce_failure.

16.7 Stateful Testing

Everything so far generated inputs. Stateful testing generates sequences of operations, which is what you want when the thing under test has memory.

# ledger.py
class Ledger:
    """A balance you can deposit into and withdraw from. Never goes negative."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._balance = 0
        self._history = []

    @property
    def balance(self):
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, cents):
        if cents <= 0:
            raise ValueError("deposit must be positive")
        self._balance += cents
        self._history.append(("deposit", cents))

    def withdraw(self, cents):
        if cents <= 0:
            raise ValueError("withdrawal must be positive")
        if cents > self._balance:
            return False
        self._balance -= cents
        self._history.append(("withdraw", cents))
        return True

    def replay(self):
        """Recompute the balance from history. Must always agree."""
        total = 0
        for kind, amount in self._history:
            total += amount if kind == "deposit" else -amount
        return total

# tests/test_ledger_stateful.py
from hypothesis import strategies as st
from hypothesis.stateful import RuleBasedStateMachine, invariant, rule

from ledger import Ledger

amounts = st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=1000)


class LedgerMachine(RuleBasedStateMachine):
    """Drives a Ledger through generated sequences and checks the rules after each step."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.ledger = Ledger()
        self.model_balance = 0        # an independent model of what the balance should be

    @rule(amount=amounts)
    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.ledger.deposit(amount)
        self.model_balance += amount

    @rule(amount=amounts)
    def withdraw(self, amount):
        accepted = self.ledger.withdraw(amount)
        if accepted:
            self.model_balance -= amount

    @invariant()
    def the_balance_is_never_negative(self):
        assert self.ledger.balance >= 0

    @invariant()
    def the_balance_matches_the_model(self):
        assert self.ledger.balance == self.model_balance

    @invariant()
    def the_history_replays_to_the_balance(self):
        assert self.ledger.replay() == self.ledger.balance


TestLedger = LedgerMachine.TestCase

pytest -q tests/test_ledger_stateful.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 33.77s

That single class replaces an unbounded number of hand-written sequences. Hypothesis generates deposit(5), withdraw(3), withdraw(99), deposit(1)… in every order it can think of, checks all three invariants after every step, and shrinks a failing sequence down to the shortest one that still breaks — which for a state machine means both fewer steps and simpler arguments.

The pattern in model_balance is model-based testing: keep a second, trivially-correct representation of the state alongside the real one and assert they agree. The model is allowed to be absurdly inefficient, because it only has to be right. This is the same idea as the oracle property in §16.5, extended over time, and it is the most powerful thing in this section — it is how you test a cache against a dict, a database index against a linear scan, or a CRDT against a set.

TestCase at the end is what makes pytest collect it. Without that line the class is defined and never run — a silent no-op, and one worth checking for when a stateful test seems suspiciously fast.

To have in hand before moving on: model-based testing.

16.8 fast-check: The Same Ideas in JavaScript

// src/tags.js
export function normaliseTags(tags) {
  const seen = new Set();
  for (const tag of tags) {
    const cleaned = tag.trim().toLowerCase();
    if (cleaned) seen.add(cleaned);
  }
  return [...seen].sort();
}

export function chunk(items, size) {
  if (size < 1) throw new RangeError('size must be at least 1');
  const out = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i += size) out.push(items.slice(i, i + size));
  return out;
}

// test/tags.property.test.js
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import fc from 'fast-check';
import { normaliseTags, chunk } from '../src/tags.js';

test('normalising is idempotent', () => {
  fc.assert(fc.property(fc.array(fc.string()), (tags) => {
    const once = normaliseTags(tags);
    expect(normaliseTags(once)).toEqual(once);
  }));
});

test('the result is always sorted and unique', () => {
  fc.assert(fc.property(fc.array(fc.string()), (tags) => {
    const result = normaliseTags(tags);
    expect(result).toEqual([...result].sort());
    expect(new Set(result).size).toBe(result.length);
  }));
});

test('chunking then flattening is the identity', () => {
  fc.assert(fc.property(
    fc.array(fc.integer()),
    fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 10 }),
    (items, size) => {
      expect(chunk(items, size).flat()).toEqual(items);
    },
  ));
});

test('every chunk but the last is full', () => {
  fc.assert(fc.property(
    fc.array(fc.integer(), { minLength: 1 }),
    fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 10 }),
    (items, size) => {
      const chunks = chunk(items, size);
      for (const c of chunks.slice(0, -1)) expect(c.length).toBe(size);
      expect(chunks.at(-1).length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
      expect(chunks.at(-1).length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(size);
    },
  ));
});

cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{ "type": "module" }
EOF
npx vitest run test/tags.property.test.js --reporter=dot

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

····

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
   Start at  17:31:38
   Duration  1.07s (tests 42%, transform 30%, import 24%, worker 3%)

fast-check's vocabulary maps onto Hypothesis's almost one-to-one. An arbitrary is a strategy; fc.property builds the claim; fc.assert runs it. fc.integer, fc.string, fc.array, fc.record, fc.constantFrom, fc.oneof and fc.letrec correspond to integers, text, lists, builds, sampled_from, one_of and recursive.

The differences worth knowing: fast-check runs 100 cases by default and takes { numRuns } in fc.assert's second argument rather than a decorator; a failing run prints a seed and a path which you replay with { seed, path } to reproduce exactly; and fc.pre(condition) is assume.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: fc.property.

16.9 A Real Counterexample, Shrunk

Here is a defect that examples miss and a property finds in under a second — and it is a defect of a kind that ships regularly. Note the vocabulary fast-check uses: a fast-check arbitrary is what hypothesis calls a strategy, and each generated value it produces is fed to the predicate until one falsifies it. Where a generated value is computed from another rather than drawn independently — the upper end of a range, say — it is a derived value, and deriving one is what §16.4 does instead of filtering.

// src/pagination.js
export function pageOf(items, page, perPage) {
  const start = (page - 1) * perPage;
  return items.slice(start, start + perPage);
}

export function pageCount(total, perPage) {
  return Math.round(total / perPage);       // the defect: Math.round, not Math.ceil
}

// test/pagination.property.test.js
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import fc from 'fast-check';
import { pageOf, pageCount } from '../src/pagination.js';

test('every item appears on exactly one page', () => {
  fc.assert(fc.property(
    fc.array(fc.integer(), { maxLength: 40 }),
    fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 10 }),
    (items, perPage) => {
      const pages = pageCount(items.length, perPage);
      const seen = [];
      for (let p = 1; p <= pages; p += 1) seen.push(...pageOf(items, p, perPage));
      expect(seen).toEqual(items);
    },
  ), { numRuns: 200, seed: 42 });
});

npx vitest run test/pagination.property.test.js --reporter=dot 2>&1 | sed -n '/Failed Tests/,/Shrunk/p'

⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Failed Tests 1 ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯

 FAIL  test/pagination.property.test.js > every item appears on exactly one page
Error: Property failed after 4 tests
{ seed: 42, path: "3:1:1:2:1", endOnFailure: true }
Counterexample: [[0],3]
Shrunk 4 time(s)

Read the counterexample: [[0],3] is a one-element list at three per page. Math.round(1 / 3) is 0, so the function reports zero pages, the loop never runs, and an item that exists is on no page at all. fast-check found it after 4 tests and shrunk 4 times to get there, and the { seed: 42, path: "3:1:1:2:1" } line is a complete reproduction recipe — paste it back into fc.assert's options and you replay that exact case, on any machine, with no saved state.

Math.round versus Math.ceil for a page count is a one-character defect that passes every example test anyone writes, because the examples people choose — 100 items, 10 per page; 50 items, 25 per page — are exactly the ones where the total divides evenly and the two functions agree. It only goes wrong when the remainder is less than half a page, which is the case nobody writes down.

Fix it and the property passes:

// src/pagination.js
export function pageOf(items, page, perPage) {
  const start = (page - 1) * perPage;
  return items.slice(start, start + perPage);
}

export function pageCount(total, perPage) {
  return Math.ceil(total / perPage);
}

npx vitest run test/pagination.property.test.js --reporter=dot

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

·

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
   Start at  17:31:53
   Duration  1.16s (transform 33%, tests 31%, import 29%, worker 7%)

In summary, the vocabulary here is a fast-check arbitrary and derived value.

16.10 What Property-Based Testing Costs

It is not free and the costs are specific. One of them has a name worth knowing: filtering too much. Every assume() and every .filter() discards generated cases, and when too many are discarded hypothesis raises a health check rather than quietly running a handful of examples — which is the correct behaviour and is why a generated value should be constructed to satisfy the constraint rather than filtered for it.

Finding the property is the work, and it is genuinely hard for some code. "What is always true of this function?" is a design question, and for a function that formats a receipt in a particular house style the honest answer may be "nothing beyond what the examples say". That is fine. Property-based testing is a tool for code with structure — parsers, encoders, collections, arithmetic, state machines — and forcing it onto code without any produces tautologies.

A property that restates the implementation checks nothing. assert split(t, w) == [t // w + 1] * (t % w) + [t // w] * (w - t % w) is a property, is true, and is worthless: it will pass for any implementation and fail for none, because it is the implementation. This is the property-based form of §1.7's re-implementation trap and it is easier to fall into here, because the generator's confidence makes it feel rigorous.

Failures are slower to read. A failing example test names an input; a failing property test hands you a shrunk input plus, sometimes, a shrinking process that took a while. @example and the example database exist to blunt this, and the answer to a hard-to-read failure is usually to split one broad property into two narrow ones.

Generation costs wall-clock time. A hundred cases is a hundred runs. §20.7's split between a fast suite and a slow one is where a large property suite belongs — max_examples=20 on every commit and a nightly run at 1000 is a common and sensible arrangement.

The counterweight to all four: a property is the only kind of test that gets better while you sleep. Every run tries inputs the last one did not. An example test checks the same thing forever.

What to carry forward from this subsection: assume(), the example database and filtering too much.

16.11 What This Section Established

A property is a claim about every input; an example is a claim about one. sum(split(t, w)) == t catches defects that four hand-written cases cannot, because the generator biases towards the boundaries — zero, one, the maximum, the empty collection — that §4.4 tells you to write by hand.

Shrinking is what makes it usable. A raw counterexample is noise; Falsifying example: total=4, ways=4 is a bug report. That is the feature to judge a library by.

Four shapes cover most properties. Round-trip (decode(encode(x)) == x) is the highest-value one in most codebases. An invariant holds of every output. An oracle is a slow obviously-correct implementation to agree with. A metamorphic relation compares two runs when you cannot state either alone — and idempotence is the metamorphic property that a surprising amount of code should have and does not.

assume() discards a case; generating the constrained value is better when the precondition is common, because hypothesis fails a test that filters too much.

@example pins a counterexample forever, which is how a property test and a regression test live in one function. The example database replays past failures first, and derandomize=True turns "fails sometimes" into "fails".

Stateful testing generates sequences, not inputs, and model-based testing — a second trivially-correct representation asserted to agree — is the most powerful idea here. Remember TestCase = Machine.TestCase, or the machine is never run.

fast-check is the same ideas: an arbitrary is a strategy, fc.pre is assume, and a failure prints a seed and path you replay to reproduce exactly.

A property that restates the implementation checks nothing — the same trap as §1.7, and easier to fall into here because the generated cases make it feel rigorous.

The term above, for reference: falsifying example.

Exercises

1. Four properties for a parser. Write a function that parses "key=value;key2=value2" into a dict. State and test four properties, using at least one round-trip and one invariant. Then say which of the four would still hold if the parser silently dropped duplicate keys, and what that tells you about the set you chose.

2. Find a real defect. Take pageCount from §16.9 and write the example tests you would naturally have written. Confirm they all pass against the Math.round version. Then say in two sentences why the examples you chose were the ones that could not catch it.

3. Shrink something big. Write a property over st.lists(st.integers(), min_size=50) that fails for lists containing two equal adjacent elements. Record the raw failing input hypothesis first found and the shrunk one it reported. Explain what shrinking had to discover about the failure to get from one to the other.

4. Assume, then stop assuming. Write a property about a function taking a start and end date where end must not precede start. Implement it first with assume(), then with a strategy that generates the ordered pair directly. Run both with --hypothesis-show-statistics and compare how many examples each actually ran.

5. A model-based test. Implement an LRU cache with get, put and a capacity. Write a RuleBasedStateMachine that drives it against a model built from an ordinary dict plus a list recording access order. Include an invariant that the cache never exceeds capacity. Report the shortest failing sequence you can produce by deliberately breaking the eviction rule.

6. Both libraries, one property. Implement the JSON round-trip property from §16.5 in fast-check using fc.letrec for the recursive value generator. State one thing hypothesis made easier and one thing fast-check made easier.

7. Argue against a property. Find a function in your own code where you cannot state a useful property, and write two paragraphs explaining why — being specific about whether the obstacle is the code's lack of structure, your understanding of it, or the fact that the property would restate the implementation. This is a real skill; knowing when not to reach for the technique is most of using it well.

Solution

1. Four properties for a parser.

Round-trip: parse(format(d)) == d for any dict of safe strings. Invariant: every key in the result is non-empty. Invariant: the result never has more entries than the input has ; separators plus one. Metamorphic: appending ";k=v" to the input either adds one entry or replaces one.

Under a parser that silently drops duplicate keys, the round-trip still holds (a dict has no duplicates to begin with, so formatting one never produces them), both invariants still hold, and only the metamorphic property changes shape. The lesson is that round-tripping from the dict side cannot see duplicate handling at all — the input space of the round-trip is the output space of the parser, which is smaller. A round-trip property is only as strong as the generator on the side you start from, and starting from the string side (format(parse(s)) == normalise(s)) is the version that would catch it.

2. Find a real defect.

The natural examples are 100 items at 10 per page, 50 at 25, 20 at 5 — all exact divisions, where round and ceil are identical. If you thought to add a remainder case it was probably 101 items at 10 per page, giving 10.1, which rounds up to 10... and Math.round(10.1) is 10, Math.ceil is 11 — so that one does catch it.

The reason examples miss it is that the defect lives in a band, not at a point: it appears whenever the remainder is less than half of perPage. People choosing examples pick round numbers and then, if they are careful, one "awkward" number — and an awkward number chosen by a human is usually just over a boundary, not just under it. A generator does not have that bias.

3. Shrink something big.

The raw counterexample is a fifty-element list of arbitrary integers with a duplicated adjacent pair somewhere in the middle. The shrunk one is [0, 0] — or, with min_size=50, fifty zeros, which is the smallest list of that length exhibiting the property.

To get there, shrinking had to discover that the values were irrelevant (shrink them all towards 0), that the position was irrelevant (move the pair to the front), and that the other 48 elements were irrelevant except for satisfying min_size (make them all 0 too). Each of those is a separate simplification pass, re-running the property after each attempt and keeping it only if it still fails. That is why shrinking is the expensive part of a property run and why a failing property test is slower than a passing one.

4. Assume, then stop assuming.

With two independent st.dates() and assume(start <= end), roughly half the generated cases are discarded, so hypothesis runs about twice as many to reach 100 valid ones — --hypothesis-show-statistics reports the invalid count directly.

The generated-pair version:

ordered_dates = st.tuples(st.dates(), st.dates()).map(sorted)

discards nothing. Statistics show zero invalid examples and a shorter run.

The threshold worth remembering: hypothesis raises FailedHealthCheck when it filters too much, and the message tells you exactly this. assume is for a precondition that removes a small fraction; anything more belongs in the strategy.

5. A model-based test.

The invariant that catches most eviction bugs is not "size <= capacity" — it is "every key the model says should be present is present, and no other key is". A cache that evicts the wrong entry keeps its size correct and its contents wrong, so a size-only invariant passes.

The shortest failing sequence for a wrong eviction rule (evicting the most recently used rather than the least) is typically three operations on a capacity-2 cache: put(a), put(b), get(a), put(c) — after which a correct cache holds a and c, and the broken one holds b and c. Hypothesis shrinks to that because it shrinks the number of rules applied as well as their arguments.

6. Both libraries, one property.

const jsonValue = fc.letrec((tie) => ({
  value: fc.oneof(
    { depthSize: 'small' },
    fc.constant(null), fc.boolean(), fc.integer(), fc.string(),
    fc.array(tie('value'), { maxLength: 4 }),
    fc.dictionary(fc.string(), tie('value'), { maxKeys: 4 }),
  ),
})).value;

Easier in hypothesis: st.recursive reads more directly than fc.letrec's tie-the-knot form, and @example has no fast-check equivalent — pinning a case there means writing a separate ordinary test.

Easier in fast-check: reproduction. A failure prints seed and path, and pasting them into fc.assert's options replays that exact case with no shared state, where hypothesis's replay depends on a .hypothesis directory that may not exist on another machine or in CI.

7. Argue against a property.

The strongest honest answers are the second and third. "The code has no structure" is usually a finding rather than an excuse — a function with no statable property is often a function doing several unrelated things, and the difficulty of writing a property is diagnostic. But "the property would restate the implementation" is a genuine dead end: for a function whose entire content is a house-style formatting decision, any property strong enough to be useful is the code again, and examples are the correct tool.

The one answer to be suspicious of is "the code is too complicated". That is the case where properties are most valuable and hardest to write, which is not the same as not worth writing — and §16.7's model-based approach is usually the way in, because a trivially-correct slow model is often statable when a direct property is not.

SECTION 17

Coverage and Mutation Testing

Two ways to answer "is this suite any good?", and they answer very different questions.

Test coverage measures which lines and branches the tests executed. It is cheap, universally available, and it has one property people consistently forget: executing a line is not the same as checking it. A test with no assertions at all covers everything it touches.

Mutation testing measures which defects the tests would detect. It changes the production code — a < to <=, a + to -, a True to False — and re-runs the suite. If the tests still pass, the suite would not have caught that defect. It is expensive, and it is the only automated measure of test quality that means anything.

The relationship between the two is the subject of this section, and it is best stated as a one-way implication: low coverage proves the suite is weak; high coverage proves nothing at all.

17.1 What Coverage Measures

Here is a small, complete function with a full-looking suite.

# banding.py
def band(score):
    """Bands a score. Every boundary here is a decision someone made."""
    if score < 0 or score > 100:
        raise ValueError("score must be between 0 and 100")
    if score >= 70:
        return "high"
    if score >= 40:
        return "medium"
    return "low"

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

[tool.mutmut]
source_paths = ["banding.py"]
# mutmut copies only these into its `mutants/` tree, so tell it which tests to
# run there — the other files in this section have their own demonstrations.
pytest_add_cli_args_test_selection = ["tests/test_banding.py"]

# tests/test_banding.py
import pytest

from banding import band


def test_a_high_score():
    assert band(85) == "high"


def test_a_middling_score():
    assert band(50) == "medium"


def test_a_low_score():
    assert band(10) == "low"


def test_an_impossible_score_is_refused():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        band(101)

pytest -q --cov=banding --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing tests/test_banding.py

....                                                                     [100%]
================================ tests coverage ================================
_______________ coverage: platform linux, python 3.12.7-final-0 ________________

Name         Stmts   Miss Branch BrPart  Cover   Missing
--------------------------------------------------------
banding.py       8      0      6      0   100%
--------------------------------------------------------
TOTAL            8      0      6      0   100%
4 passed in 1.04s

100% of statements and 100% of branches. Four tests, one small function, and by every number a test coverage tool can produce, this suite is complete.

It is not. §17.8 will show that it misses more than half the defects a machine can plant in those eight lines — and every one of those defects is a wrong boundary, which is exactly what §4.4 predicted.

One to keep in hand: test coverage.

17.2 The Kinds of Coverage

"Coverage" is at least six measurements, in increasing order of strictness.

function coverage
Was each function called at all? The weakest useful number, and occasionally the most revealing — a function with no function coverage is either untested or dead.
statement coverage
Was each statement executed? Statement coverage — line coverage, in most tools' wording — is the default everywhere, and the one people quote.
branch / decision
Was each if taken both ways? Meaningfully stronger, cheap to enable, and it should be on in every project.
condition coverage
Was each sub-expression of a compound condition true and false? a or b has four combinations and branch coverage checks two; condition coverage is what closes that gap.
MC/DC
Each condition shown to independently affect the outcome. Required for avionics; rarely used elsewhere.
path coverage
Every route through the function. Path coverage grows exponentially and is not achievable for anything with a loop — the same combinatorial wall as §4.1.

The gap between line and branch is the one that costs real defects:

# discount.py
def price(total_cents, is_member):
    if is_member:
        total_cents = round(total_cents * 0.9)
    return total_cents

# tests/test_discount.py
from discount import price


def test_a_member_gets_ten_percent_off():
    assert price(5_000, is_member=True) == 4_500

pytest -q --cov=discount --cov-report=term-missing tests/test_discount.py
pytest -q --cov=discount --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing tests/test_discount.py

Line coverage says 100%; branch coverage says less. Both statements ran, so no line is missing — but the if was never taken the false way, so a non-member has never been priced. That is the entire discount feature for everyone who is not a member, uncovered, behind a green 100%.

--cov-branch costs nothing and is the single highest-value coverage setting. Turn it on.

17.3 Configuration, and pragma: no cover

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

[tool.mutmut]
source_paths = ["banding.py"]
# mutmut copies only these into its `mutants/` tree, so tell it which tests to
# run there — the other files in this section have their own demonstrations.
pytest_add_cli_args_test_selection = ["tests/test_banding.py"]

[tool.coverage.run]
branch = true
source = ["."]
omit = ["tests/*", "*/conftest.py"]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
skip_covered = true
exclude_also = [
    "if TYPE_CHECKING:",
    "raise NotImplementedError",
    "if __name__ == .__main__.:",
    "@overload",
]

The tool is coverage.py, configured either in pyproject.toml as above or in a .coveragerc file; the two hold the same keys and a project should have exactly one of them. --cov-report=html writes an HTML coverage report, and that is the form worth opening — it colours each line, so "which branches are missing" becomes a glance rather than a parse of 3->5.

# pragma: no cover on a line or a block excludes it from the measurement. Three uses are legitimate and the fourth is how a coverage number becomes a lie.

defensive impossibilities
An else: raise AssertionError("unreachable") guarding an exhausted match. Covering it would mean constructing a state the type system forbids.
platform branches
The Windows arm of an if sys.platform, on a Linux runner. It is not untested; it is untestable here.
type-checking blocks
if TYPE_CHECKING: never runs. Excluding it removes noise rather than hiding anything.
anything awkward
The error handler nobody wanted to set up. This is the one that turns the number into a lie, and it is invisible in the report — excluded lines simply do not appear.

Two habits keep it honest. Every pragma carries a reason as a comment, which makes the fourth case visible in review. And the pragma count is worth watching: a codebase whose exclusions grow faster than its code has a coverage number describing something other than the code.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: coverage.py, .coveragerc and an html coverage report.

17.4 Coverage in JavaScript

Both runners measure coverage through V8's own instrumentation, so there is nothing to configure into the build.

// banding.js
export function band(score) {
  if (score < 0 || score > 100) throw new RangeError('score must be 0–100');
  if (score >= 70) return 'high';
  if (score >= 40) return 'medium';
  return 'low';
}

// test/banding.test.js
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { band } from '../banding.js';

test('a high score', () => { assert.equal(band(85), 'high'); });
test('a middling score', () => { assert.equal(band(50), 'medium'); });
test('a low score', () => { assert.equal(band(10), 'low'); });
test('an impossible score', () => {
  assert.throws(() => band(101), RangeError);
});

node's built-in report: line, branch and function percentages plus the uncovered line ranges.
NODE_V8_COVERAGE
An environment variable that writes raw V8 coverage JSON to a directory, for any Node process. The mechanism underneath everything else.
vitest --coverage
The coverage-v8 provider by default — the @vitest/coverage-v8 package — or istanbul for instrumentation-based counting. Configure thresholds and reporter: ['text', 'lcov'].
// node:coverage disable
node's pragma: no cover, with a matching enable comment. The same four uses and the same fourth trap.
lcov
The interchange format every coverage service reads. Emit it in CI even if a person never opens it.

One caveat specific to V8-based coverage: it measures the code the engine ran, which after a build step is the transpiled output. Source maps map it back, and mapping is approximate — a line that a bundler inlined or a helper the transpiler injected can show up as covered or uncovered in ways the original source does not explain. Istanbul-based instrumentation avoids that at the cost of a slower run.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: NODE_V8_COVERAGE, node:coverage disable and v8 coverage.

17.5 Thresholds

A coverage threshold fails the build below a number: --cov-fail-under=80, fail_under in the config, thresholds in Vitest. Wired into a pipeline it becomes a coverage gate (§20.8).

It is worth having and it is worth being clear about what it does. A threshold is a ratchet against decay — it stops a project drifting from 80% to 40% one hurried commit at a time. It is not a measure of quality, and a project that reaches its number and stops thinking has bought nothing.

Three refinements make thresholds useful rather than ritual:

Ratchet, do not target. Set the threshold at today's number, and raise it whenever it rises. That makes it impossible to go backwards without a deliberate decision, and it never demands a number nobody chose.

Measure the diff, not the whole. "New code must be 90% covered" is a far better rule than "the project must be 80% covered": it puts the effort where the change is, and it does not demand a retrospective campaign on a legacy module nobody is touching.

Exclude what you do not intend to test. Generated code, migrations, __main__ blocks. Otherwise the number is diluted by things nobody planned to cover, and the threshold measures the ratio of your code to your scaffolding.

To have in hand before moving on: fail_under, coverage threshold and a coverage gate.

17.6 Coverage as a Target

Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Coverage is the textbook case, and the failure modes are specific and recognisable.

an assertion-free test
Call everything, assert nothing. An assertion-free test gives 100% coverage and zero detection; §17.7 runs four of them.
testing the trivial
Getters, constructors, dataclasses — the cheapest coverage per line, and the least valuable per test (§4.11).
pragma inflation
Excluding what is awkward. Invisible in the report, because excluded lines are not shown.
deleting the hard tests
A slow integration test covering 200 lines is deleted; the percentage barely moves; the coverage those lines had was the real kind.

The honest reading of the number, in three lines:

  • Uncovered code is definitely untested. That is a fact, and it makes a coverage report an excellent gap-finding tool.
  • Covered code may or may not be tested. Execution is not verification.
  • The report is more useful than the percentage. "Which lines are uncovered?" is actionable; "we are at 83%" is not.

Which is the whole recommendation: read the report, ignore the number, and check the uncovered lines against your risk model (§4.10). An uncovered line in the payment path matters; an uncovered line in a log formatter does not, and a single percentage cannot tell them apart.

17.7 100% Coverage, Zero Assertions

The demonstration that settles the argument.

# tests/test_no_assertions.py
"""A suite with no assertions at all. Watch what coverage says about it."""
import pytest

from banding import band


def test_calls_the_high_path():
    band(85)


def test_calls_the_middle_path():
    band(50)


def test_calls_the_low_path():
    band(10)


def test_calls_the_error_path():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        band(101)

pytest -q --cov=banding --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing tests/test_no_assertions.py

....                                                                     [100%]
================================ tests coverage ================================
_______________ coverage: platform linux, python 3.12.7-final-0 ________________

Name    Stmts   Miss Branch BrPart  Cover   Missing
---------------------------------------------------
TOTAL       8      0      6      0   100%

1 file skipped due to complete coverage.
4 passed in 0.79s

100% of statements. 100% of branches. Four passing tests. And the suite would pass against a band that returned "low" for everything, or raised on every input, or returned None.

Three of the four tests assert literally nothing. The fourth asserts only that something raised ValueError — which, per §3.4, is the weakest useful exception assertion there is.

This is not a contrived example; it is what coverage-driven test writing produces when the number is the goal. It is also why §3.15's plan counts and this section's mutation testing exist: both are ways of asking whether an assertion happened, which coverage cannot answer even in principle.

17.8 Mutation Testing

Mutation testing asks the question coverage cannot: if the code were wrong, would these tests notice?

The procedure is mechanical. Take the production code, apply a mutation operator to make one small change — producing a mutant — and run the suite. If a test fails you have a killed mutant: your tests would have caught that defect. If every test passes you have a surviving mutant, and with it a defect class your suite is blind to.

The mutation operators in common use:

relational
< → <=, > → >=, == → !=. Finds every missing boundary test (§4.4).
arithmetic
+ → -, * → /
logical
and → or, and negating a condition
constant
0 → 1, 100 → 101, "x" → "XXx", True → False
statement
Delete a statement, or replace a return value with None

The mutation score is killed ÷ total. Unlike coverage it is a direct measure of detection, and it is not gameable by writing more assertion-free tests — a mutant that changes behaviour and is not detected is a real gap, and no amount of executing lines closes it.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: a killed mutant, a surviving mutant and a mutation operator.

17.9 Running mutmut for Real

Against §17.1's four tests and their 100% branch coverage.

mutmut run > /dev/null 2>&1
mutmut results

    banding.x_band__mutmut_2: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_3: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_4: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_6: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_7: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_8: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_9: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_10: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_13: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_14: survived

Ten survivors out of eighteen mutants — a mutation score of about 44%, against a coverage report of 100%.

That gap is the whole argument of this section, in one measurement, on eight lines of code.

Look at what survived:

mutmut show banding.x_band__mutmut_2
mutmut show banding.x_band__mutmut_5

# banding.x_band__mutmut_2: survived
--- banding.py
+++ banding.py
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 def band(score):
     """Bands a score. Every boundary here is a decision someone made."""
-    if score < 0 or score > 100:
+    if score <= 0 or score > 100:
         raise ValueError("score must be between 0 and 100")
     if score >= 70:
         return "high"
# banding.x_band__mutmut_5: killed
--- banding.py
+++ banding.py
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 def band(score):
     """Bands a score. Every boundary here is a decision someone made."""
-    if score < 0 or score > 100:
+    if score < 0 or score > 101:
         raise ValueError("score must be between 0 and 100")
     if score >= 70:
         return "high"

Mutant 5 changed > 100 to > 101, and it was killed — because test_an_impossible_score_is_refused happens to use 101, which is exactly the value that distinguishes the two.

Mutant 2 changed < 0 to <= 0, and it survived. Under it, a score of exactly zero raises ValueError instead of returning "low" — a real defect, on a real boundary, and no test notices because no test uses zero. The tests use 85, 50, 10 and 101, and not one of them sits on an edge except by accident.

Every survivor here is a missing boundary value, which is §4.4's argument arriving by a completely independent route. The technique that would have prevented all of them is the one that costs nothing: test each side of each edge.

17.10 Closing the Gap

Add the boundary tests the survivors named, and re-measure.

# tests/test_banding.py
import pytest

from banding import band


@pytest.mark.parametrize("score,expected", [
    (0, "low"), (39, "low"),
    (40, "medium"), (41, "medium"), (69, "medium"),
