    (70, "high"), (71, "high"), (100, "high"),
])
def test_each_side_of_each_boundary(score, expected):
    assert band(score) == expected


@pytest.mark.parametrize("score", [-1, 101])
def test_a_score_outside_the_range_is_refused(score):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="between 0 and 100"):
        band(score)

# the same run, after the boundary tests were added
mutmut run > /dev/null 2>&1
mutmut results

    banding.x_band__mutmut_2: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_3: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_4: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_6: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_7: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_8: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_9: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_10: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_13: survived
    banding.x_band__mutmut_14: survived

Ten tests instead of four, and the score moves from 44% to a number the tool prints rather than one anybody guessed. The tests that closed the gap are exactly the ones §4.4 said to write, and coverage was 100% before and after — it could not distinguish the two suites at all.

Which is the practical way to use mutation testing: not as a number to maximise, but as a list of specific, named gaps, each of which tells you which test to write.

17.11 Equivalent Mutants and the Cost

Two honest problems, and they are why mutation testing is a tool you run occasionally rather than on every commit.

An equivalent mutant changes the code without changing its behaviour, so no test can kill it and it will survive forever.

# equivalent.py
def total(items):
    running = 0
    for item in items:              # `while` with an index would be identical
        running += item["cents"]
    return running


def cache_key(user_id, page):
    # A mutant changing this to `page + 0` is behaviourally identical.
    return f"u{user_id}:p{page}"

Detecting equivalence is undecidable in general — it is the halting problem in a hat — so every mutation tool reports some survivors that cannot be killed. In practice they are a minority and they are recognisable in seconds, but they mean the mutation score has a ceiling below 100% that nobody can compute, and a target of "100% mutation score" is therefore not merely hard but incoherent.

Cost. A mutation run is roughly mutants × suite time. The measured run above was 18 mutants at about 1.2 per second — on eight lines. A real module produces hundreds, and a real suite takes seconds rather than milliseconds, so a full run is minutes to hours.

Four mitigations, all of which real tools implement:

  • Coverage-guided selection. A mutant on an uncovered line cannot possibly be killed, so it is skipped. That alone removes a large fraction.
  • Run only the tests that cover the mutated line, rather than the whole suite. This is §17.12's test impact analysis applied inside the tool.
  • Mutate only what changed. --since on a branch turns a nightly run into a per-pull-request one.
  • Stop at the first killing test. No point running the rest.

Where it earns its place: on the code where a defect would be expensive, run occasionally, and read as a list of gaps. Money, permissions, pricing, anything with boundaries. Running it across a whole codebase produces a number and a very long list, which is how most attempts at it end.

The vocabulary here: an equivalent mutant.

17.12 Stryker, and Test Impact Analysis

Stryker is the mutation tester for JavaScript, TypeScript and C#, and it works the same way with two additions worth knowing. It reports a mutant as timed out when the mutation caused an infinite loop — which counts as killed, since the tests did detect it — and it produces an HTML report showing each mutant in place in the source, which is far easier to read than a list of ids.

Test impact analysis is the related idea applied to the ordinary suite: record which tests execute which lines, and on a change, run only the tests that touch the changed lines.

what it buys
A commit touching one module runs thirty tests instead of four thousand. On a large suite this is the difference between a ten-minute build and a one-minute one (§20).
what it risks
The mapping is only as good as its notion of a dependency. Configuration, data files, dynamic imports, reflection and environment variables all create dependencies no coverage map records.

Vitest's --related is the accessible form: it uses the module graph rather than a coverage map, which is more conservative and more reliable. pytest-testmon does the coverage-map version for Python.

The rule that makes either safe: use it for the fast local loop, never as the gate. A pre-merge build runs everything; a developer's watch mode runs what changed. Trading completeness for speed is right when a full run is one command away and wrong when it is the last check before production.

17.13 What This Section Established

  • Low coverage proves the suite is weak; high coverage proves nothing. The implication runs one way only.
  • Coverage measures execution, not verification. §17.7's four tests reach 100% of statements and branches while asserting essentially nothing.
  • Branch coverage is the setting that matters. Line coverage called a discount feature fully covered while the non-member path had never run.
  • pragma: no cover has three legitimate uses and a fourth that turns the number into a lie — and excluded lines do not appear in the report, so the lie is invisible. Require a reason on every pragma.
  • V8-based coverage measures what the engine ran, so after a build step it depends on source maps; Istanbul instrumentation is more faithful and slower.
  • Ratchet the threshold rather than targeting one, and measure the diff rather than the whole.
  • Read the report, not the percentage. Uncovered lines are actionable; a number is not, and it cannot distinguish a payment path from a log formatter.
  • Mutation testing asks whether the tests would notice a defect, which coverage cannot answer in principle. It is not gameable by adding assertion-free tests.
  • Against 100% branch coverage, ten of eighteen mutants survived — and every survivor was a missing boundary value, which is §4.4's argument reached by a different road.
  • Equivalent mutants are undecidable, so the mutation score has an uncomputable ceiling and "100%" is incoherent as a target.
  • Cost is mutants × suite time, mitigated by coverage-guided selection, running only covering tests, mutating only what changed, and stopping at the first kill.
  • Use mutation testing as a list of named gaps, occasionally, on code where a defect would be expensive.
  • Test impact analysis speeds the local loop and must never be the gate, because the dependency map cannot see configuration, data or dynamic imports.

Exercises

1. Predict the survivors.

def shipping_cents(weight_g, express):
    if weight_g <= 0:
        raise ValueError("weight must be positive")
    base = 300 if weight_g <= 500 else 900
    return base + (450 if express else 0)

Given tests for (100, False), (1000, True) and (0, False), list the mutants you expect to survive, and the smallest set of extra tests that kills them all.

2. Diagnose the report.

A module shows 96% line coverage and 71% branch coverage. What kinds of code produce that gap? Which would you look at first, and what would you expect to find?

3. Justify four pragmas.

For each, say whether you would accept it in review: (a) except ImportError: # pragma: no cover around an optional dependency; (b) # pragma: no cover on a 40-line error-recovery function; (c) if TYPE_CHECKING:; (d) # pragma: no cover on a __repr__.

4. Design the gate.

A project has 62% coverage, an eight-minute suite and a team of six. Design the coverage policy: what you would measure, what would fail the build, what you would exclude, and what you would explicitly not do. Defend the threshold you choose.

5. Use the survivors.

Run mutation testing on a module you own. Take the first five survivors and, for each, write the test that kills it. Then answer: how many of the five were real gaps, how many were equivalent mutants, and how many made you change the production code instead?

6. Argue against a mandate.

Your organisation proposes mandating 90% line coverage across every repository. Write the case against, propose what you would do instead, and say what you would concede — because "no measurement at all" is not the alternative you want either.

Solutions

1. Predict the survivors.

Expected survivors, all boundaries:

  • weight_g <= 0 → weight_g < 0. Only 0 distinguishes them, and (0, False) is tested — so this one is killed. Good.
  • weight_g <= 500 → weight_g < 500. Only a weight of exactly 500 distinguishes them. Nothing tests 500 → survives.
  • The constants: 300 → 301, 900 → 901, 450 → 451. All killed, because the three tests assert exact totals — assuming they do. If they assert only that the result is positive, all three survive, which is the assertion-strength lesson from §17.7.
  • express negated, or the conditional expression swapped. Killed by the pair of tests with different express values — but note that (100, False) and (1000, True) vary both parameters at once, so a mutant swapping the two arms is killed only by luck of the arithmetic. A cleaner suite varies one thing at a time.

Smallest extra set: (500, False) and (501, False). Two tests, and they kill the band boundary and pin the discontinuity. Adding (1, False) for the lower edge is worth it too, since (0, False) only exercises the error side of that boundary.

2. Diagnose the report.

That gap means most statements run but many decisions run only one way. The producers, in order of likelihood: error handling — the try runs, the except never does; guard clauses — the happy path is tested and the early return is not; default arguments and optional parameters — the caller always passes the same shape; compound conditions, where one arm short-circuits so the second is never evaluated.

Look at error handling first, and expect to find a except SomeError: log_and_reraise(...) that has never executed — which means nobody knows whether the recovery works. That is also the code most likely to run for the first time during an incident, which makes it the worst possible place for an untested branch.

3. Justify four pragmas.

(a) Accept. The import either succeeds or fails depending on the environment, and covering both arms means two test environments. Legitimate, and worth a comment naming the optional dependency.

(b) Reject. Forty lines of error recovery is exactly the code that most needs testing and is least likely to work — and it is precisely the "anything awkward" case. If it is genuinely unreachable, delete it; if it is reachable, test it. The right response is a conversation, not a pragma.

(c) Accept, and prefer to handle it in exclude_also in the configuration so it is a project-wide policy rather than a scattering of comments.

(d) Accept reluctantly, and ask a question. A __repr__ used only in debugging is trivial (§4.11) and a pragma is cheaper than a pointless test. But a __repr__ that appears in log output is production behaviour, and one that raises on a half-constructed object will do so during an incident, at the worst moment. The question is where it is used.

4. Design the gate.

Measure: branch coverage, reported per file, plus coverage of the diff.

Fail the build on: new or changed lines below 90% covered. Not on the project total.

Exclude: migrations, generated clients, __main__ blocks, if TYPE_CHECKING:.

Explicitly not do: set a project-wide target of 80%, which would produce a multi-week campaign of low-value tests on legacy code and would move the number without moving the risk.

The threshold on the diff is 90% rather than 100% because the last few percent are almost always defensive branches and the argument about them costs more than it is worth. The project total is reported and ratcheted — it may not decrease — which stops decay without demanding a campaign. That combination puts every hour of effort on code someone is already touching, which is where it is cheapest and where the risk actually is.

5. Use the survivors.

No fixed answer, but the distribution is remarkably consistent: of five survivors, roughly three are real gaps (nearly always boundaries), one is equivalent, and one makes you change the production code.

That last category is the interesting one and it surprises people. A mutant survives, you try to write a test that kills it, and you discover that no observable behaviour depends on the mutated line — a variable computed and never used, a condition that cannot be false because a caller already guaranteed it, a defensive check duplicating one made two frames up. The mutation tester has found dead or redundant code, and deleting it is a better outcome than any test.

6. Argue against a mandate.

The case against: a uniform number ignores risk, so it demands the same effort on a log formatter as on a payment path. It is trivially satisfiable by assertion-free tests (§17.7) and by testing getters, so it will be satisfied that way under deadline pressure. It penalises the repositories that most need attention — a legacy service with 30% coverage now needs a campaign before any feature can ship. And it makes the metric a target, so it stops being a measure.

Instead: a coverage ratchet per repository (it may not go down), a diff-coverage gate on changed lines, branch coverage on everywhere, and a quarterly mutation run on the modules where a defect would be expensive. Report escaped defects and the tests that would have caught them (§10.12) — that is the outcome anyone actually cares about, and it is measurable.

What to concede: the impulse behind the mandate is right. Coverage that nobody looks at does decay, and "we test where it matters" is what every team with a bad suite says. So concede the gate — accept a hard, enforced, build-failing rule — and argue about which rule. A ratchet plus diff coverage is harder to game than a total, cheaper to adopt, and it is a gate. That is a negotiation you can win, where "no numbers" is one you cannot.

SECTION 18

Flaky Tests

A test has one job: to give the same answer every time you ask it, unless the code changed. A flaky test — Meszaros calls it an erratic test — is one that sometimes passes and sometimes fails against the same code, and it is the single most corrosive thing that can happen to a suite.

Not the most expensive. Not the most common. The most corrosive, because it attacks the property everything else depends on. Every other section of this course has assumed that a red bar means something. A suite with a few flaky tests in it has quietly withdrawn that assumption, and the damage compounds: people re-run rather than investigate, then they re-run everything rather than investigate, and eventually a real regression goes out because it looked like the usual noise.

This section is about the whole life cycle — what it costs, how to reproduce one deliberately, the five things that actually cause them, and what to do about a flake you cannot fix today. The examples are all deterministic demonstrations of non-determinism, which sounds like a contradiction and is the only honest way to teach this: every flaky behaviour below is made to happen on demand.

18.1 A Test That Is Sometimes Red

Consider a suite of 2,000 tests where each test has a 99.9% chance of behaving. That sounds excellent. The probability the suite passes on a clean commit is 0.9992000, which is about 13.5%.

# flake_math.py
suite = 2000
for per_test in (0.9999, 0.999, 0.99):
    print(f"per-test reliability {per_test:>7}: "
          f"suite passes {per_test ** suite:6.1%} of the time")

print()
print(f"Spurious failures in one {suite}-test run:")
for flake_rate in (0.001, 0.01, 0.05):
    fails = flake_rate * suite
    print(f"  flake rate {flake_rate:>5.1%}: {fails:>5.1f} failures with nothing wrong")

python3 flake_math.py

per-test reliability  0.9999: suite passes  81.9% of the time
per-test reliability   0.999: suite passes  13.5% of the time
per-test reliability    0.99: suite passes   0.0% of the time

Spurious failures in one 2000-test run:
  flake rate  0.1%:   2.0 failures with nothing wrong
  flake rate  1.0%:  20.0 failures with nothing wrong
  flake rate  5.0%: 100.0 failures with nothing wrong

This is the arithmetic that makes flakiness a systemic problem rather than a per-test annoyance. A per-test reliability that would be superb for a physical component makes a large suite useless, because failure probabilities compound across the suite while the value of the suite does not.

The costs follow from that:

the signal is gone
A red build no longer means "you broke something", so nobody reads it. This is the whole cost; the rest are consequences.
re-running becomes reflex
"Just re-run it" is a rational response to a 5% flake rate and a catastrophic habit, because it is indistinguishable from ignoring a real intermittent bug.
the pipeline slows
Every spurious failure costs a full re-run. A ten-minute build with a 30% spurious failure rate has an effective time of fourteen minutes and an unpredictable one, which is worse (§20).
the fix is blamed
A developer whose unrelated change "caused" a flake spends an afternoon on it. Repeat, and people stop touching the areas with flaky tests near them.

The most important thing to internalise is that an intermittent failure is evidence, not noise. A test that fails one run in fifty is usually telling you about a real race, a real leak or a real order dependency — and one of them is in your production code often enough that "delete the test" should never be the first move.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: flaky test.

18.2 Reproducing a Flake

Everything else in this section depends on this step, and it is the one people skip. A flake you cannot reproduce cannot be fixed, only guessed at.

Four techniques, in the order to try them:

running a test alone
If it passes alone and fails in the suite, the cause is isolation and nothing else. This single test splits the space in half and takes ten seconds.
run it many times
A loop of 200 runs turns a 1-in-50 flake into a near-certainty. If it never fails alone, the cause is external to the test.
change the order
--randomly-seed=N, or naming node ids on the command line. A seed that reproduces it is a recorded reproduction — write it in the ticket.
change the machine
Run under load, with fewer cores, with a different timezone, with a cold cache. Most timing flakes only appear on a machine slower than yours.

The useful mental model: a flaky test has a hidden input — the order, the clock, the machine's speed, another test's leftovers, a random seed. Reproducing it means finding that input and pinning it. That is the same move as §8's control points, applied to the test rather than the code.

Running a test alone is the first move because it is the cheapest and it halves the space. Bisecting a flake is the fallback when the order is the hidden input and you have 900 tests. Run the suspect test with the first half of the suite before it, then the first quarter, and so on. Ten runs identifies the polluting test out of a thousand. It is tedious, it is mechanical, and it is far faster than reading the code.

The term above, for reference: bisecting a flake.

18.3 Non-Determinism in the Report, Not Only in the Code

Before the causes, a rule that applies to every claimed output in this course and every assertion you will ever write against a tool's output: never assert on something a tool produces only when it has time.

Real tools emit opportunistic output. It is not part of the contract, it appears when a budget allows, and it disappears under load — which means an assertion on it passes on your laptop and fails on a busy CI runner, with no code change in between.

Three measured instances, all from building this course:

hypothesis
The Explanation: block after a failure comes from the explain phase, which runs on a time budget and does not always finish. A claimed output containing it goes red on its own, on a busy machine, with nothing changed. §16.2 filters it out with a grep and describes it in prose instead.
Vitest
Performance advice — transforming modules took 1.20s · 75% of tracked time — prints only when a phase crosses a share-of-time threshold. Its presence varies, so there is no value to normalise it to; it has to be dropped.
PostgreSQL
pg_stats.n_distinct is computed from a sample. Four consecutive ANALYZE runs on identical data gave 5001, 5006, 4999 and 5002. Pasting one into an expected output is writing down a coin toss.

The general rule generalises past tool output: never put a sampled statistic or an estimated value in an assertion. A query planner's row estimate, a cache hit rate, a percentile latency, a floating-point sum over an unordered collection, a "roughly N" from any monitoring system — all of these are measurements with error bars, and an equality assertion on one is a flaky test by construction.

pytest --durations makes the point visible, because it prints values that are different every single run:

# tests/test_durations.py
import time


def test_a_quick_one():
    assert True


def test_one_that_takes_a_moment():
    time.sleep(0.05)
    assert True

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

pytest -q --durations=3 --durations-min=0.02 tests/test_durations.py

..                                                                       [100%]
============================= slowest 3 durations ==============================
0.05s call     tests/test_durations.py::test_one_that_takes_a_moment

(2 durations < 0.02s hidden.)
2 passed in 2.13s

Those numbers are correct, useful and unassertable. --durations is a diagnostic, and the moment someone writes assert duration < 0.06 around it, they have written a test whose result depends on how busy the machine is. §4.7's rule about performance testing — thresholds, never exact values, and generous ones — is the same rule seen from the other side.

One line each, for reference: a sampled statistic and an estimated value in an assertion.

18.4 Fowler's Five Causes

Martin Fowler's taxonomy of non-determinism in tests has five entries, and in fifteen years nothing has been added to it. Almost every flake you meet is one of these:

1
lack of isolation
One test can see another's leftovers. The most common cause by a wide margin, and the only one whose symptom is order dependence.
2
asynchronous behaviour
The test asserts before the work finished. Almost always shows up as a sleep that is long enough on a developer machine.
3
a remote service dependency
Something outside the process is slow, rate-limited, down, or has different data today.
4
time dependence
Dates, timezones, month ends, leap days, midnight, daylight saving, and the clock on the CI runner disagreeing with the clock on the database.
5
resource leaks
File handles, connections, ports, threads. Symptom: the suite passes at 200 tests and fails at 800, or fails only on the second run.

Notice how much of this course has already been building the defences. Section 5's fresh fixtures and teardown attack cause 1. Section 8's injected clock attacks cause 4. Sections 6 and 12's doubles attack cause 3. That is not a coincidence — most good testing practice is, viewed from here, flakiness prevention.

The remaining subsections take them in turn, with a runnable demonstration of each.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: remote service dependency and time dependence.

18.5 Lack of Isolation: Shared State

The mechanism is always the same: something outlives a test. A module-level dict, a class attribute, a database row, a file, a registered signal handler, a patched global that was patched with setattr instead of monkeypatch. When the something is a fixture that keeps state between tests, the name is a leaking fixture; when two tests rely on each other's leftovers it is test interdependence, and §5.1's chained tests are that arrangement adopted on purpose.

# registry.py
"""Module state, which is to say state shared by every test in the process."""

HANDLERS = {}

# tests/test_pollution.py
import registry


def test_registering_a_handler_makes_it_findable():
    registry.HANDLERS["email"] = "the email handler"
    assert "email" in registry.HANDLERS


def test_the_registry_starts_empty():
    assert registry.HANDLERS == {}

pytest -q --tb=line tests/test_pollution.py

.F                                                                       [100%]
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
E   AssertionError: assert {'email': 'the email handler'} == {}

      Left contains 1 more item:
      {'email': 'the email handler'}
      Use -v to get more diff
/project/tests/test_pollution.py:11: AssertionError: assert {'email': 'the email handler'} == {}
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_pollution.py::test_the_registry_starts_empty - AssertionErr...
1 failed, 1 passed in 1.50s

Now run the identical file with the two tests named in the other order. Nothing changes but the sequence:

pytest -q "tests/test_pollution.py::test_the_registry_starts_empty" "tests/test_pollution.py::test_registering_a_handler_makes_it_findable"

..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 2.17s

Same code, same assertions, opposite result. Three observations that generalise:

The failing test is not the guilty one. test_the_registry_starts_empty is a perfectly good test; it is reporting a fact. The defect is in test_registering_a_handler_makes_it_findable, which mutated shared state and did not clean up. A flake's failure site and its cause are almost never the same test, which is why "just fix the flaky test" so often produces a worse suite.

The fix belongs to the polluter. Either the registry gets a fixture that resets it, or — better — the tests stop using module state at all and construct their own registry (§8.5).

Both orders are "correct". Neither test is written wrongly for the order it happens to run in. That is what makes this class of bug survive review.

The leaking fixture is the same problem with a nicer face:

# tests/test_leaking_fixture.py
import pytest


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def basket():
    """A shared fixture (§5.7). Built once, handed to every test in the module."""
    return {"items": []}


def test_adding_an_item(basket):
    basket["items"].append("widget")
    assert len(basket["items"]) == 1


def test_a_second_item(basket):
    basket["items"].append("gadget")
    assert len(basket["items"]) == 2       # only true because the first test ran


def test_the_basket_should_start_empty(basket):
    assert basket["items"] == []           # fails: it is the same dict

pytest -q --tb=line tests/test_leaking_fixture.py

..F                                                                      [100%]
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
E   AssertionError: assert ['widget', 'gadget'] == []

      Left contains 2 more items, first extra item: 'widget'
      Use -v to get more diff
/project/tests/test_leaking_fixture.py:22: AssertionError: assert ['widget', 'gadget'] == []
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_leaking_fixture.py::test_the_basket_should_start_empty - As...
1 failed, 2 passed in 4.04s

scope="module" on a mutable object is the most common way this is written. The second test is the real warning sign — it asserts == 2 and is only correct because of what the previous test did, which means it is not a test of "adding an item" at all. A fixture that returns something mutable should be function-scoped, and if it is expensive enough to want sharing, it should return something immutable or hand out a copy (§5).

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: test interdependence and a leaking fixture.

18.6 Order Dependence, and Finding It on Purpose

The defect above is invisible in a suite that always runs in the same order — and file-order execution is the default in every runner, so it can sit there for years.

pytest-randomly exists to make it visible: it shuffles tests within their module, prints the seed it used, and reuses that seed if you give it back.

pytest -p randomly --randomly-seed=1 -q --tb=no -ra tests/test_pollution.py
pytest -p randomly --randomly-seed=10 -q --tb=no -ra tests/test_pollution.py

.F                                                                       [100%]
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_pollution.py::test_the_registry_starts_empty - AssertionErr...
1 failed, 1 passed in 1.58s
..                                                                       [100%]
2 passed in 2.03s

Two runs, same command but for a number, opposite results. That is the shape of every order-dependence bug, and the seed is what turns "it fails sometimes on CI" into a reproduction you can put in a ticket.

Three practical notes.

The seed is printed on every run. Without -q the header carries Using --randomly-seed=..., which is the number to copy out of a failing CI log. Make sure your CI captures the header; a pipeline that pipes pytest through -q throws away the one piece of information that makes the failure reproducible.

Randomising ordering is a policy decision, not a default to switch on quietly. Turning it on in a suite that has never had it will produce a burst of failures, all of them real, none of them today's regression. Do it deliberately, on a branch, with time budgeted to fix what it finds.

-p no:randomly disables it and -p randomly re-enables it, in that order, on the same command line — which matters when a wrapper script has already disabled the plugin and one run needs it back. That is exactly how this course's own examples are produced: the runner pins the order for every fragment, and this subsection asks for it back.

The equivalent elsewhere: node --test --test-randomize, and Vitest's sequence.shuffle. All three exist for the same reason and all three should be turned on eventually.

To have in hand before moving on: pytest-randomly.

18.7 Hash Seeds and Iteration Order

A subtler version of the same problem has no test polluting anything: the language itself is allowed to change the order.

Python randomises the hash of str and bytes per process, as a defence against algorithmic complexity attacks. Sets and older dicts iterate in hash order, so the order of a set literal is different in every process.

# hash_order.py
import os
import subprocess
import sys

CODE = "print(hash('the-cache-key'))"


def distinct_over(runs, seed):
    env = dict(os.environ)
    env.pop("PYTHONHASHSEED", None)
    if seed is not None:
        env["PYTHONHASHSEED"] = seed
    outputs = {
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", CODE], env=env,
                       capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
        for _ in range(runs)
    }
    return len(outputs)


print("hash('the-cache-key') over 8 fresh interpreters")
print(f"  with no PYTHONHASHSEED set : {distinct_over(8, None)} distinct values")
print(f"  with PYTHONHASHSEED=0      : {distinct_over(8, '0')} distinct value")

python3 hash_order.py

hash('the-cache-key') over 8 fresh interpreters
  with no PYTHONHASHSEED set : 8 distinct values
  with PYTHONHASHSEED=0      : 1 distinct value

Eight processes, eight different hashes. Any test that asserts on the order of a set, or on anything derived from it — a joined string, a JSON dump, a hash of a serialised structure — has a one-in-N chance of passing, and N is however many orderings exist.

The fixes, in preference order:

Do not assert on unordered things. assert sorted(result) == [...], or assert set(result) == {...}. This is right regardless of hashing, because the function's contract almost certainly does not promise an order — the same argument as §4.5's median and, exactly, the SQL rule about SELECT without ORDER BY.

Sort at the boundary. If the order genuinely matters to a consumer, the code should sort, and the test should assert the sorted order. A test is not the place to discover that the contract was never stated.

Pin PYTHONHASHSEED only as a diagnostic. Setting it in CI makes the suite deterministic and hides the bug rather than fixing it — the production process still has a random seed. It is useful for reproducing a failure once, not as a permanent setting.

Note that dict is a different case: since Python 3.7 it preserves insertion order as a language guarantee, so iterating a dict is stable. It is set, frozenset, and anything built from them that moves.

18.8 Asynchronous Behaviour and the Sleep Antipattern

The second cause. The test starts something, waits "long enough", and asserts. The sleep antipattern is that phrase — long enough — written as a number.

// jobs.js
export function startJob(store, ms = 40) {
  setTimeout(() => { store.done = true; store.result = 'ok'; }, ms);
  return store;
}

export const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

// sleep.test.js
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { startJob, sleep } from './jobs.js';

test('sleeping for less than the work takes fails, always', async () => {
  const store = startJob({ done: false }, 40);

  await sleep(20);                    // "should be enough"

  expect(store.done).toBe(false);     // it is not; this is the bug, made visible
});

test('sleeping for longer works, and wastes the difference', async () => {
  const store = startJob({ done: false }, 40);

  await sleep(200);                   // five times as long, "to be safe"

  expect(store.done).toBe(true);
});

cat > package.json <<'EOF'
{ "type": "module" }
EOF
npx vitest run --reporter=verbose sleep.test.js

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

 ✓ sleep.test.js > sleeping for less than the work takes fails, always 40ms
 ✓ sleep.test.js > sleeping for longer works, and wastes the difference 202ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Start at  22:59:09
   Duration  2.47s (tests 43%, transform 30%, import 18%, worker 9%)

Both tests pass here, and that is the point: the first documents that 20 ms is not enough, the second that 200 ms is. Neither number is a fact about the system — they are facts about this machine, today. On a CI runner with four tests per core and a cold module cache, 40 ms of work can take 300 ms, and the second test starts failing while nothing has changed.

The sleep antipattern has a characteristic life cycle worth recognising:

  1. A test fails intermittently. Someone adds sleep(100).
  2. It fails again, less often. The sleep becomes sleep(500).
  3. Ten more tests copy the pattern. The suite is now four minutes slower.
  4. It still fails, once a week, and now nobody can tell whether the sleep is the problem or the fix.

Every step is locally rational and the end state is a slow suite that is still flaky. The escape is not a bigger number.

18.9 Deterministic Waiting

There are exactly two correct answers — remove the time, or wait for the condition — and which one applies depends on whether the asynchrony is real. The second is polling with a timeout: check often, give up eventually, and it is the only form of waiting that is both fast in the good case and safe in the bad one.

If the wait is artificial, remove time from the equation. A debounce, a retry backoff, a poll interval, a cache TTL — these are all just timers, and §8.8's fake timers turn them into boundary values. vi.advanceTimersByTime(299) then (1) is exact, instant and cannot flake.

If the wait is genuinely asynchronous, poll for the condition with a timeout. Do not wait for a duration; wait for the thing. Check often, give up eventually, and fail with a message that says what never became true.

// wait.test.js
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { startJob } from './jobs.js';

test('vi.waitFor retries until the callback stops throwing', async () => {
  const store = startJob({ done: false }, 40);

  await vi.waitFor(() => {
    if (!store.done) throw new Error('the job has not finished yet');
  }, { timeout: 2000, interval: 5 });

  expect(store.result).toBe('ok');
});

test('expect.poll retries the assertion itself', async () => {
  const store = startJob({ done: false }, 40);

  await expect.poll(() => store.done, { timeout: 2000, interval: 5 }).toBe(true);
});

npx vitest run --reporter=verbose wait.test.js

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

 ✓ wait.test.js > vi.waitFor retries until the callback stops throwing 69ms
 ✓ wait.test.js > expect.poll retries the assertion itself 53ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Start at  22:59:19
   Duration  2.88s (transform 52%, tests 21%, import 20%, worker 7%)

Both forms have the two properties that matter: they finish as soon as the condition holds, so the fast case costs a few milliseconds rather than the worst-case timeout, and the timeout can be generous — two seconds here — because it is only ever paid when something is genuinely broken. That combination is what a sleep can never have: a sleep pays its cost every run and gives its guarantee never.

The pattern by name, across the ecosystem:

Vitest
vi.waitFor, expect.poll, waitUntil
Testing Library
waitFor, findBy*, waitForElementToBeRemoved (§14)
Playwright
Built into every locator: auto-waiting and retrying web-first assertions, so there is nothing to opt into (§15)
Python
A five-line wait_until(predicate, timeout, interval) helper, or an event/queue the code under test can signal

Best of all, where the design allows it: make the asynchrony observable. A job runner that exposes a completion future, an event you can await, or a synchronous "run pending work now" method for tests removes the polling entirely. That is §8's argument again — the flakiness is a missing observation point.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: polling with a timeout.

18.10 Remote Services

The third cause needs the least explanation and the most discipline. A remote service dependency inherits every failure mode of that network and that service: latency, rate limits, maintenance windows, someone else's test data, an expired certificate, a DNS change.

The layered answer, from most tests to fewest:

1
Most tests never leave the process. A client double or an in-memory fake at the port (§8.12). Fast and perfectly deterministic.
2
Some tests use a local stub server or recorded traffic — responses, a cassette, a local container (§12). Real serialisation, no network.
3
A contract test checks the assumption that the doubles encode (§13). This is what keeps step 1 honest.
4
A very few tests hit the real thing — and they belong in a nightly job or a post-deploy smoke test, not in the commit stage (§20).

The rule that keeps this from eroding: the commit-stage suite must not require the network. Enforce it rather than requesting it — many teams block outbound sockets in the unit-test environment, so an accidental real call fails loudly the day it is written instead of flaking quietly six months later.

One trap specific to this cause: a test that calls a real service and retries on failure is not fixed, it is disguised. It now fails only when the service is down for longer than the retry window, which is rarer, harder to reproduce, and lands on whoever is unlucky.

18.11 Time, Timezones and Clock Skew

The fourth cause. Section 8 covered the mechanism — inject the clock — so here is the catalogue of what time dependence actually looks like, because the specific cases are more useful than the principle:

midnight
A test that computes today twice can straddle it. Rare, real, and it fails for exactly one person, once, at 00:00.
month and year ends
today + 30 days is in a different month for most of the month. A suite green all January can go red on 31 January.
leap days
date(year + 1, month, day) raises on 29 February. Once every four years, in production.
daylight saving
One day a year has 23 hours and one has 25. "Add 24 hours" and "add one day" are different operations and both are sometimes right.
timezone dependence
The developer is in UTC+1 and CI is in UTC. A date derived from a local timestamp differs by one for part of every day.
clock skew
The application's clock and the database's clock disagree by milliseconds, so a row's created_at can be after a timestamp taken later by the app.

Four rules cover all of it.

Store and compare in UTC; convert only at the edges. A timezone should appear in exactly two places: parsing input and formatting output.

Never compute an expected date with the same expression as the code. §4.3's oracle rule, and time is where it is violated most.

Pick one clock. If the database generates created_at, the application must not also generate timestamps it compares against them. Skew between two clocks is not fixable by testing; it is fixable by having one.

Test the awkward dates explicitly. 29 February, 31 December, the DST transitions for your users' zones, and the last day of a 31-day month. With an injected clock these cost one parametrized row each (§4.12) and they are the only way those branches are ever executed before a customer finds them.

The vocabulary here: timezone dependence.

18.12 Resource Leaks

The fifth cause, and the one with the most distinctive symptom: the suite passes small and fails large. Two hundred tests are fine; eight hundred fail. Or the first run passes and the second fails, because something from the first is still holding a port.

# tests/test_leaks.py
import socket
import warnings

import pytest


def test_an_unclosed_file_is_a_leak_the_interpreter_warns_about(tmp_path):
    path = tmp_path / "data.txt"
    path.write_text("hello")

    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
        warnings.simplefilter("always")
        handle = open(path)          # never closed
        assert handle.read() == "hello"
        del handle                   # dropping the last reference triggers the close

    assert any(issubclass(w.category, ResourceWarning) for w in caught)


def test_a_fixed_port_collides_with_itself(tmp_path):
    first = socket.socket()
    first.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))     # 0 means "any free port"
    port = first.getsockname()[1]

    second = socket.socket()
    with pytest.raises(OSError):
        second.bind(("127.0.0.1", port))   # the same port, still held

    first.close()
    second.close()


def test_asking_for_a_free_port_never_collides(free_tcp_port):
    # pytest 9 hands out a port nobody else is using.
    s = socket.socket()
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", free_tcp_port))
    s.close()

pytest -q -W always::ResourceWarning tests/test_leaks.py

...                                                                      [100%]
3 passed in 1.13s

The first test shows the diagnostic for a file handle leak: Python emits a ResourceWarning when a file object is finalised without being closed. It is off by default. Turn it on in your test configuration — -W error::ResourceWarning promotes it to a failure — and a whole class of leak becomes a loud, immediate, locatable error instead of a mysterious Too many open files at test 800.

The second and third show port collision and its fix. A hardcoded port in a test is a collision waiting for a parallel run (§20's parallel jobs) or for the previous run's socket to linger in TIME_WAIT. free_tcp_port is pytest 9's built-in answer; the general principle is make the resource unique, which applies equally to temporary directories (tmp_path, never /tmp/test), database names, queue names and generated ids.

The rest of the leak catalogue, with the symptom each produces:

  • Connections not returned to a pool — the suite hangs at a fixed test count, waiting for a checkout that will never come.
  • Threads or tasks not joined — output from a previous test appears during a later one, and failures move around.
  • Signal handlers, atexit hooks, patched globals — increasingly strange behaviour late in the run.
  • A uuid collision — vanishingly rare with uuid4 and certain with a test helper that does f"user-{random.randint(1, 1000)}". If ids must be unique, generate them uniquely.

The structural fix for nearly all of it is context managers and fixture teardown: acquire in a with, or in a yield fixture whose cleanup runs whatever happens (§5).

What to carry forward from this subsection: a file handle leak, port collision, uuid collision and test helper.

18.13 Retries: A Policy, Not a Fix

Every runner can re-run a failing test. Vitest takes retry per test or per config; Playwright has retries with on-first-retry tracing (§15); pytest needs a plugin. The question is not whether the feature works but what it means.

// retry.test.js
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';

let attempts = 0;

test('a test that only passes on the third attempt', { retry: 3 }, () => {
  attempts += 1;
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});

npx vitest run --reporter=verbose retry.test.js

 RUN  v5.0.0 /project

 ✓ retry.test.js > a test that only passes on the third attempt 69ms (retry x2)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
   Start at  22:59:36
   Duration  2.70s (transform 36%, import 34%, worker 16%, tests 14%, environment 1%)

The report says (retry x2), which is the only reason this feature is defensible: it is honest about what happened. A retry that reports a plain pass is a lie the pipeline tells itself.

Where retries are legitimate:

  • End-to-end tests against a real browser and a real network (§15), where a certain rate of environmental failure is genuinely outside your control. Playwright's default of retrying on CI and not locally encodes this.
  • As a temporary measure with a ticket attached, so the build stays useful while the real fix is written.

Where they are not:

  • On unit tests. A unit test has no environment to be unlucky with. A flaky unit test is a bug in the test or in the code, and a retry converts a reproducible signal into an intermittent one that is harder to find later.
  • As a default across the suite. retries: 2 in the root config makes every flake three times less visible and zero times less real. A retry masks a bug — including real intermittent production bugs, which are exactly the ones you most want to hear about.

Two conditions make a retry policy survivable: the retry must be recorded and counted, so the flake rate is a number someone looks at; and it must apply to a named list of tests rather than to the suite, so adding to that list is a decision.

The terms above, gathered: a retry masks a bug and production bugs.

18.14 Quarantine and the Flake Rate

Which leaves the practical question: it is Tuesday, a test fails one run in ten, and you cannot fix it today.

The three options are not equal.

ignore it
The default, and the one that destroys the suite. Every subsequent failure is now ambiguous.
delete it
Honest, and occasionally right — if the test earns nothing (§4.11), deleting it is better than the alternatives. Usually it is throwing away evidence of a real bug.
quarantine it
Move it out of the blocking suite into a lane that runs, reports and does not fail the build. The commit stage gets its signal back; the evidence is kept.

Quarantine works only with three rules attached, and without them it is a graveyard:

Quarantine is a queue, not a bin. Every entry has a ticket and an owner. A quarantine lane that only grows is deletion with extra steps.

The lane still runs, and someone reads it. A quarantined test that fails every time has stopped being flaky and started being a genuine regression report; you want to know.

There is a cap. "No more than five, and nothing older than two weeks" is arbitrary and works, because the alternative to an arbitrary limit is no limit.

Underneath it, the number that makes the whole thing manageable is the flake rate: what fraction of runs fail for reasons unrelated to the change under test. Recording it turns an argument about impressions into a measurement — and it is the metric that justifies spending a week on test infrastructure, because "our flake rate is 22%" is an argument a manager can act on while "the tests are annoying" is not.

Two supporting practices are worth the small effort:

  • Record every failure, not just the final result. If CI overwrites a failed run with a green re-run, the flake rate is unmeasurable by construction.
  • Track flakes per test. The distribution is always heavily skewed: a handful of tests produce most of the noise, and fixing five of them typically recovers most of the signal.

One to keep in hand: a quarantine lane.

18.15 What This Section Established

  • Flakiness compounds across a suite. At 99.9% per-test reliability, a 2,000-test suite passes 13.5% of the time. It is a systemic problem, not a per-test annoyance.
  • The cost is the loss of signal. Once red does not mean broken, nobody reads the build, and a real regression eventually ships behind the noise.
  • Reproduce before fixing: run it alone, run it many times, change the order with a recorded seed, change the machine. A flake has a hidden input; find it and pin it.
  • Never assert on output a tool emits only when it has time — hypothesis's explain phase, Vitest's performance advice — and never put a sampled or estimated value in an assertion.
  • Fowler's five causes: lack of isolation, asynchronous behaviour, remote services, time, resource leaks. Nothing has been added to the list in fifteen years.
  • The failing test is usually not the guilty one. A polluting test fails somebody else, later, and that is what makes order dependence survive review.
  • A mutable module-scoped fixture is the standard way to write this bug. The tell is a test that asserts a value only correct because a previous test ran.
  • pytest-randomly makes order dependence visible and reproducible. -p no:randomly disables it and -p randomly re-enables it, in that order.
  • set iteration order changes per process because of hash randomisation; assert on sorted or set-compared results, and use PYTHONHASHSEED only to reproduce.
  • A sleep is a fact about your machine, not about the system. Remove the time with fake timers, or poll for the condition with a generous timeout — which is fast in the good case and only slow when something is genuinely wrong.
  • Resource leaks make the suite pass small and fail large. Promote ResourceWarning to an error, and make every resource unique rather than fixed.
  • A retry is a policy, not a fix. Legitimate for end-to-end tests and as a ticketed stopgap; on a unit test it converts a reproducible signal into an intermittent one.
  • Quarantine keeps the signal and the evidence, but only with a ticket, an owner, a lane someone reads, and a hard cap. Measure the flake rate, and track it per test.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on it: set iteration order.

Exercises

1. Do the arithmetic for your own suite.

Take a suite you work on. Estimate its size and its per-run spurious failure count, and compute the implied per-test reliability. Then compute how many consecutive green runs you would need before a pass genuinely means the code is fine. What does that number tell you about how much a week spent on flakiness would be worth?

2. Find the polluter.

You have 900 tests. test_billing.py::test_invoice_numbering passes alone and fails in the full run, about half the time. Describe the exact sequence of commands you would run to identify the polluting test, and say how many runs it should take. What would you do differently if it failed only 1 run in 30?

3. Classify these.

For each, name which of Fowler's five causes it is, and give the fix:

(a) a test that checks a generated report's filename contains today's date; (b) a test that passes on a developer laptop and fails on a CI runner with 8 parallel workers; (c) a test asserting that a list of tags renders as "python, testing, ci"; (d) a test that fails only when run after the full integration suite; (e) a test that passes at 9 a.m. and fails at 11 p.m. for a developer in Australia.

4. Replace a sleep.

def test_the_worker_processes_the_queue():
    queue.put(job)
    time.sleep(2)
    assert database.count("results") == 1

Give three progressively better replacements, and say what each one costs and what it still cannot guarantee.

5. Write the quarantine policy.

Draft the four or five rules you would actually adopt for a team of eight with a 12-minute pipeline and a current flake rate of about 15%. Include what happens when the cap is reached, and who decides.

6. The uncomfortable one.

A test fails one run in twenty. You reproduce it, and the cause is a genuine race condition in production code: two requests arriving within the same millisecond can both pass a uniqueness check. Fixing it properly means a database constraint and a migration, which is two days of work. The release is Thursday.

What do you do with the test, and what do you tell the team? Set out the options and defend a choice.

Solutions

1. Do the arithmetic.

The mechanism: with n tests each independently passing with probability p, the suite passes with probability pn. Invert it — p = (suite pass rate)1/n — to get the per-test number from an observed suite rate.

A suite of 1,500 tests that passes 70% of the time on clean commits has a per-test reliability of about 0.99976, or roughly one spurious failure every 4,200 test executions. That sounds like a well-behaved suite and it produces a build people do not trust.

The second half is the argument that matters. If a green run happens 70% of the time on good code, then a red run is uninformative unless you know the base rate — and the practical consequence is that every failure costs a re-run, which is 30% of your pipeline capacity spent learning nothing. Against a 12-minute pipeline and eight developers, that is measurable in hours per week, which is the form the argument has to take to get the week funded.

2. Find the polluter.

Bisect on the set of tests that run before it:

pytest -q tests/                              # confirm it fails in the full run
pytest -q tests/billing/test_billing.py       # confirm it passes alone
pytest -q <first half of the files> tests/billing/test_billing.py

If it fails, the polluter is in that half; if it passes, it is in the other. Repeat. With 900 tests, log₂(900) ≈ 10 runs identifies a single polluting test, and in practice fewer because file boundaries usually contain it.

At 1-in-30 the strategy has to change, because a single green run no longer proves the polluter is absent. Repeat each bisection step n times — enough that a passing set is genuinely likely to be clean — which multiplies the cost by n. At that point it is usually cheaper to attack it from the other end: run the suspect test with -p randomly and many seeds, collect the seeds that fail, and look at what the failing orders have in common. It is also worth turning on -W error::ResourceWarning and any leak detection first, because a 1-in-30 rate is more typical of a resource problem than of a straightforward two-test collision.

3. Classify these.

(a) Time. Fails at midnight, and fails all day for anyone whose timezone puts them on a different date from the CI runner. Inject the clock and assert against a fixed date (§8.7).

(b) Lack of isolation, until proven otherwise — parallel workers turn a latent shared-state or shared-resource bug into a frequent one. A fixed port, a fixed temporary path or a shared database are the usual culprits (§18.12). Confirm by running with one worker.

(c) Lack of isolation in its subtlest form: if tags is a set, the rendered order changes per process because of hash randomisation (§18.7). Assert on the sorted tags, or make the code sort before rendering.

(d) Resource leaks or lack of isolation — the tell is "only after the full integration suite", which means something the integration tests leave behind: an open connection, a modified global, rows in a table, a patched module. Bisect as in exercise 2.

(e) Time, specifically timezone dependence. Australia is UTC+10 or +11, so 11 p.m. locally is the previous day in UTC. Any code deriving a date from a local timestamp and comparing against a UTC one is wrong for those hours. Store and compare in UTC.

4. Replace a sleep.

Better: poll for the condition.

wait_until(lambda: database.count("results") == 1, timeout=10, interval=0.05)
assert database.count("results") == 1

Costs milliseconds in the good case instead of a guaranteed two seconds, and the ten-second timeout is only ever paid on a genuine failure. Still cannot guarantee the right result was written — only that one row appeared.

Better still: make the worker signal completion.

future = queue.put(job)
future.result(timeout=10)
assert database.count("results") == 1

No polling at all, and the test now fails immediately with the worker's own exception if the job raised — which the polling version turns into an unhelpful timeout. Costs a change to the production API, which is §8's argument for an observation point.

Best where it applies: remove the asynchrony. Run the worker's handler directly, synchronously, in the test:

process_job(job)                 # the same function the worker calls
assert database.count("results") == 1

This is the humble-object split (§8.10): the handler holds all the logic and can be tested with no queue, no worker and no waiting. Costs the coverage of the queue wiring itself — so keep exactly one slower test that proves a job put on the queue really reaches the handler, and test the logic here.

None of the three can guarantee the system behaves under real concurrency. That needs a different kind of test entirely, and it is one of the few places where a deliberately concurrent, deliberately slow test earns its place in a nightly run.

5. Write the quarantine policy.

A defensible set:

  1. A test may be quarantined by anyone, immediately, with a ticket. No approval, because the alternative to a fast path is that people disable tests instead.
  2. The ticket names an owner and a date, and the owner is the team that owns the code, not whoever noticed.
  3. The quarantine lane runs on every build and reports, but does not block. Its results go to a channel someone reads.
  4. Cap: five tests, two weeks. Hitting either cap stops feature work on that area until it is back under. This is the rule that makes the other four real.
  5. The flake rate is on the team dashboard, reviewed weekly, with per-test counts.

When the cap is reached, the team lead decides between fixing and deleting — and deleting is an acceptable outcome, provided it is a decision rather than a drift. The one thing not on the list is a blanket retry, because at a 15% flake rate a retry policy would hide the problem well enough that nothing would ever be fixed.

6. The uncomfortable one.

The important move is to stop treating this as a test problem the moment you know what it is. You have found a production defect that can cause duplicate records under concurrent load, and the test is the only thing reporting it.

Options and their honest weights:

  • Delete or skip the test and ship. The defect ships too, silently, and the evidence is gone. The only defensible version of this is one where someone has decided, explicitly and in writing, that the duplicate-record risk is acceptable until the migration lands.
  • Quarantine with a ticket, ship Thursday, fix next week. Usually the right answer. The build gets its signal back, the evidence and the reproduction are preserved, and the risk is recorded rather than forgotten. It requires the ticket to be real.
  • Block the release. Right if the duplicate is expensive — a double charge, a duplicate shipment, a compliance record. The severity is a business question and it is not yours alone to answer.
  • Ship a partial mitigation. An application-level lock, or a uniqueness check inside a transaction, is often a few hours rather than two days. It narrows the window without the migration, and the test can be marked xfail(strict=True) (§4.13) so that when the real fix lands, the suite tells you by failing on the unexpected pass.

What you tell the team matters as much as which you choose: the test is not flaky, the system is. That sentence changes the conversation from "whose turn is it to fix the build" to "how much do we care about duplicate records", which is the conversation that should be happening. The general principle is worth keeping past this exercise: when an intermittent test turns out to be reporting a real race, it has stopped being a testing problem, and every option that treats it as one is wrong.

SECTION 19

Test Smells and Maintenance

A test suite is code, and it decays the way code decays. The difference is that nobody notices: a badly written test still passes, still contributes to the coverage number, and still looks like an asset. The cost arrives later, as a suite that takes an hour, breaks on every refactor, and that nobody trusts enough to read.

Gerard Meszaros catalogued the failure modes, and the catalogue is the useful part — not because the names are important, but because a named smell is one a reviewer can point at. "This test is confusing" starts an argument; "this is a mystery guest, and here is the fix" starts a change.

This section is that catalogue, the refactorings that address it, and the two disciplines that keep it from accumulating: reviewing tests as seriously as production code, and deleting the ones that no longer earn their keep.

19.1 Three Levels

Meszaros sorts the smells by how you notice them, which is more useful than sorting by cause.

code smells
Visible when you read a test. Obscure test, conditional logic, duplication, hard-to-test code.
behaviour smells
Visible when you run the suite. Erratic tests (§18), fragile tests, assertion roulette, slow tests, manual intervention.
project smells
Visible from outside. Production defects, high maintenance cost, developers not writing tests at all.

The direction of causation runs downwards and the direction of detection runs upwards. A project smell — "we keep shipping bugs" — is what makes someone look; a behaviour smell — "the suite is flaky and slow" — is what they find; a code smell is the cause. Fixing the project smell means fixing the code smell, and the middle layer is how you find which one.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: erratic test and developers not writing tests.

19.2 The Project Smells

Start at the outside, because these are the symptoms a team actually reports, and each one has a specific set of causes worth checking.

production defects
Escaping despite a green suite. Causes: assertion-free tests (§17.7), everything mocked so nothing is verified (§7.2), missing boundaries (§4.4), or a shape that tests the wrong level (§10).
high test maintenance cost
Every change breaks many tests. Causes: coupling to implementation (§7.7), duplication (§19.6), over-specification (§7.8). This is test cancer (§9.16) measured from outside.
developers not writing tests
Rarely a discipline problem. Usually: setup is too painful, the suite is too slow to run, the code has no seams (§8), or the last three tests they wrote broke for unrelated reasons.
buggy tests
Tests that fail when the code is right, or pass when it is wrong. The second is invisible and is what §17.8's mutation testing exists to find.

The third one deserves emphasis because it is almost always diagnosed wrongly. "The team does not value testing" is a story about people; "writing a test for this module takes forty minutes of fixture setup" is a fact about the code, and it is nearly always the real explanation. Fix the fixture, and the behaviour changes without a conversation about culture.

To have in hand before moving on: buggy tests.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: high test maintenance cost.

19.3 The Behaviour Smells

The middle layer — what the suite does when you run it.

erratic test
Sometimes red, same code. §18 in full.
fragile test
Breaks on a change that preserves behaviour. Four sub-kinds, in §19.7.
assertion roulette
A failure and no way to tell which of several claims produced it. §19.4.
frequent debugging
A failure requires a debugger to understand. The test is not localising (§1.5), and the fix is smaller tests with better names.
manual intervention
Someone must set something up, click something, or reset a database by hand. The suite is not automated, whatever it is called.
slow tests
The suite is not run during development, so it stops being a feedback loop and becomes a gate. §19.8.

Manual intervention is the one most often accepted rather than fixed. A suite needing "just reset the test database first" is one that will be run less often, by fewer people, and that a new joiner cannot run at all — and it fails on CI in a way nobody can reproduce. Everything §11.2 said about the suite owning its infrastructure is the fix.

In summary, the vocabulary here is test database and frequent debugging.

19.4 Obscure Test, and Assertion Roulette

The single most common code smell: a test you cannot understand by reading it. Meszaros gives it four causes, and here they are in one deliberately bad test.

# billing.py
def invoice_total_cents(lines, vat_rate_pct, member):
    subtotal = sum(l["price_cents"] * l["quantity"] for l in lines)
    if member:
        subtotal = round(subtotal * 0.9)
    return subtotal + round(subtotal * vat_rate_pct / 100)

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

# tests/test_obscure.py
"""Every smell in §19.4, in one test."""
import json
import pathlib

import pytest

from billing import invoice_total_cents

# A mystery guest: the test depends on a file it does not show you.
FIXTURE = pathlib.Path("fixtures/invoices.json")


@pytest.fixture(scope="module", autouse=True)
def write_the_fixture_file(tmp_path_factory):
    FIXTURE.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    FIXTURE.write_text(json.dumps({
        "customer": {"id": 7, "name": "Ada", "country": "GB", "since": "2019-04-01",
                     "tier": "gold", "credit_limit_cents": 500000},
        "lines": [{"sku": "widget", "price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2, "tax_code": "S"},
                  {"sku": "gadget", "price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1, "tax_code": "S"}],
        "vat_rate_pct": 20,
    }))


def test_invoice():
    data = json.loads(FIXTURE.read_text())

    total = invoice_total_cents(data["lines"], data["vat_rate_pct"], True)

    assert total == 702
    assert invoice_total_cents(data["lines"], 0, True) == 585
    assert invoice_total_cents(data["lines"], 20, False) == 780
    assert invoice_total_cents([], 20, True) == 0

pytest -q tests/test_obscure.py

.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 0.79s

It passes. Now count what is wrong with it.

mystery guest
The data is in a file. To know why the answer is 702 you must open fixtures/invoices.json, and to change the test you must know which of the other tests share it.
irrelevant information
The customer's country, tier, credit limit and join date are in the fixture and none of them matters. A reader cannot tell which fields the answer depends on.
hard-coded test data
702 with no working shown. Where did it come from? Nothing in the test explains it, so nobody can tell a right answer from a wrong one that was pasted in.
eager test
Four separate claims in one test: VAT, no VAT, non-member, empty. Each could break for a different reason.
assertion roulette
The consequence of the eager test: the first failure ends the run, so you learn about one of the four, and the name test_invoice tells you nothing about which.
indirect testing
The fixture describes a whole invoice when the function under test takes lines and a rate. The test reaches its subject through an object it does not need.

The same claims, rewritten:

# tests/test_clear.py
import pytest

from billing import invoice_total_cents

LINES = [{"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2},      # 500
         {"price_cents": 150, "quantity": 1}]      # 150 — subtotal 650


def test_vat_is_added_to_the_subtotal():
    # 650 subtotal, +20% VAT = 650 + 130
    assert invoice_total_cents(LINES, vat_rate_pct=20, member=False) == 780


def test_a_member_gets_ten_percent_off_before_vat():
    # 650 - 10% = 585, +20% VAT = 585 + 117
    assert invoice_total_cents(LINES, vat_rate_pct=20, member=True) == 702


def test_a_zero_rate_adds_nothing():
    assert invoice_total_cents(LINES, vat_rate_pct=0, member=True) == 585


def test_an_empty_invoice_totals_zero():
    assert invoice_total_cents([], vat_rate_pct=20, member=True) == 0

pytest -q -v tests/test_clear.py

============================= test session starts ==============================
platform linux -- Python 3.12.7, pytest-9.1.1, pluggy-1.6.0
rootdir: /project
configfile: pyproject.toml
plugins: cov-7.1.0, asyncio-1.4.0, xdist-3.8.0, anyio-4.15.0, timeout-2.4.0, hypothesis-6.167.1
asyncio: mode=Mode.STRICT, debug=False, asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope=None, asyncio_default_test_loop_scope=function
collected 4 items

tests/test_clear.py ....                                                 [100%]

============================== 4 passed in 0.78s ===============================

Every smell is gone, and note how it was done. The data is inline and minimal — two lines, only the fields the function reads. The expected values show their working in a comment, so a reader can check 650 → 585 → 702 without running anything. Each claim is a test with a name, so a failure names the rule rather than the file. And the four names, read together, are a specification of the function.

That last property is the test to apply: read the test names and see whether they describe the behaviour. For the rewritten file they do. For test_invoice they do not, and that is the smell in one line.

What to carry forward from this subsection: hard-coded test data and indirect testing.

19.5 Conditional Test Logic

A test containing an if, a loop, or a try is a test that can take more than one path — so which path it took becomes a question, and the test needs a test.

# tests/test_conditional.py
import sys

import pytest

from billing import invoice_total_cents

LINES = [{"price_cents": 250, "quantity": 2}]


def test_with_a_branch_in_it():
    """Two behaviours, one name, and one of them may never run."""
    member = sys.platform == "linux"

    if member:
        assert invoice_total_cents(LINES, 20, True) == 540
    else:
        assert invoice_total_cents(LINES, 20, False) == 600


@pytest.mark.parametrize("member,expected", [(True, 540), (False, 600)])
def test_the_same_two_claims_without_a_branch(member, expected):
    assert invoice_total_cents(LINES, 20, member) == expected

pytest -q -v tests/test_conditional.py

============================= test session starts ==============================
platform linux -- Python 3.12.7, pytest-9.1.1, pluggy-1.6.0
rootdir: /project
configfile: pyproject.toml
plugins: cov-7.1.0, asyncio-1.4.0, xdist-3.8.0, anyio-4.15.0, timeout-2.4.0, hypothesis-6.167.1
asyncio: mode=Mode.STRICT, debug=False, asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope=None, asyncio_default_test_loop_scope=function
collected 3 items

tests/test_conditional.py ...                                            [100%]

============================== 3 passed in 0.56s ===============================

The branching version reports one passing test whatever happens, and half of it never ran. The parametrized version reports two, and both ran — which is §4.12's argument, and it is why parametrization is the standard cure for conditional test logic.

The same applies to the other forms. A loop with an assertion inside makes no claim if it iterates zero times (§3.15); use parametrize, subtests, or assert on the whole collection. A try/except in a test that swallows an error turns a failure into a pass; use pytest.raises. And a sys.platform check belongs in skipif (§3.13), where it is visible in the report as a skip rather than invisible inside a passing test.

19.6 Test Code Duplication

The most common code smell after obscurity, and the one where the standard advice is most often wrong.

There are three kinds, and they need different treatment:

setup duplication
Twenty tests building the same object. Extract it — a builder (§5.12) or a fixture. This is the duplication worth removing, because a schema change otherwise touches twenty places.
assertion duplication
The same eight-line check in six tests. Extract a custom assertion (§3.12) — and remember register_assert_rewrite (§3.2), or the failures lose their values.
structural repetition
Every test being arrange–act–assert with similar shapes. Leave it. This is the repetition that makes tests readable, and removing it is how a suite becomes unreadable.

The general form is a test utility method or test helper: an ordinary function in the test tree. Three rules keep helpers from becoming the problem.

A helper must not hide the claim. assert_invoice_is_correct(invoice) moves the entire meaning of the test out of the test. assert_total_is(invoice, 702) keeps the number where the reader can see it.

A helper must fail with a useful message. It is one frame further from the test, so its failure must say what was expected and what happened — §7.6's lesson about a double that judges applies to a helper that judges.

Do not build a TestCase superclass. Inheriting shared setup from a base class is the oldest form of this, and it produces the worst version: a test whose fixture is three classes up, invisible at the point of use, and impossible to vary. Fixtures (§5) and plain functions compose; superclasses do not.

The terms above, gathered: test utility method and testcase superclass.

19.7 Fragile Test: the Four Sensitivities

A fragile test breaks when the system changes in a way that preserves behaviour. Meszaros distinguishes four causes, and naming them tells you what to do.

interface sensitivity
Breaks when a signature changes. Fix: a creation method (§5.1), so the change lands in one place.
behaviour sensitivity
Breaks when behaviour the test does not care about changes. Fix: assert less — §7.8's over-specification, and ANY.
data sensitivity
Breaks when a shared dataset changes. Fix: a minimal fixture per test (§5.5), not a standard one.
context sensitivity
Breaks when the environment changes — the clock, the timezone, the locale, another test. Fix: §8's injection and §18's isolation.

The diagnostic question when a test breaks: did the behaviour change? If yes, the test did its job. If no, you have just identified which of the four sensitivities it has, and the fix is the corresponding one — not "update the test", which leaves the fragility in place for next time.

That question is worth asking out loud in review, because the default response to a broken test is to make it pass, and that response is what converts a fragile test into a permanent tax.

One line each, for reference: interface sensitivity, behaviour sensitivity and data sensitivity.

19.8 Slow Tests

Slowness is a behaviour smell with a specific consequence: the suite stops being run during development, so it stops being a feedback loop and becomes a gate. Everything that makes tests valuable — the tight loop of §9, the confidence to refactor — depends on running them often.

The causes, in the order they are usually found:

a few very slow tests
Almost always the answer. --durations (§2.9) finds them in one command, and the distribution is always skewed.
sleeps
Every one is pure waste and also a flake (§18.8). Grep for them; the total is usually startling.
per-test setup that should be shared
A server, a browser, a compiled asset built per test instead of per session (§5.6).
the wrong level
Business rules verified through the database or the browser. §10.10's rule — verify in detail at exactly one, cheap level.
no parallelism
Usually blocked by shared state, which is a different smell wearing this one's clothes.

Fix in that order, and stop when the loop is fast enough. "Fast enough" is a threshold, not a target: under a second for the file you are editing, under ten for the module (§10.11).

19.9 Hard-to-Test Code

The smell that is not about the tests at all, and the most valuable one to recognise, because the test is reporting a fact about the design.

many doubles per test
Seven doubles means seven collaborators, which means the class has seven reasons to change. The test is reporting a responsibility problem, not a testing one (§7.13).
long setup
Forty lines to reach the state under test means the state is hard to reach in production too — which is where a defect will hide.
patching to test
Reaching for mock.patch means the design has no object seam (§8.2). The patch is compensating for a missing parameter.
testing private methods
The urge to test a private method means it is doing something worth its own name — extract it into a collaborator and test that through its own front door.
no way to observe
The effect is invisible, so the test has to reach into internals. Missing observation point (§1.8).

The reframing that makes this actionable: when a test is hard to write, the first hypothesis is that the code is wrong, not that you are bad at testing. That hypothesis is right often enough to be worth checking first, and checking it costs one question — what would have to be true for this test to be easy? The answer is nearly always a design change you wanted anyway (§9.7).

19.10 Test Refactorings

The moves that address the smells above. Each is a mechanical change with a name, which is what makes it reviewable.

minimize data
Delete every field the test does not need. The most valuable refactoring in the list, and the one that makes irrelevant information disappear.
inline the mystery guest
Move data from a file into the test. Costs duplication, buys readability — and §19.11 says take that trade.
extract a creation method
Replace repeated construction with make_order(...). Cures interface sensitivity.
extract a custom assertion
Name the repeated check. Cures assertion duplication and improves the failure message.
split an eager test
One claim per test, each named. Cures assertion roulette.
parametrize a branch
Replace conditional logic with a table (§4.12).
replace dependency with test double
Make a slow or non-deterministic collaborator injectable (§8.3) and substitute it. Cures context sensitivity and slowness at once.
delete
§19.13. The refactoring nobody performs.

One rule governs all of them: refactor tests only when they are green. A test being improved must pass before and after, and if it does not, you have changed its meaning — which may be right, but it is a different change and deserves its own commit.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: replace dependency with test double and minimize data.

19.11 DAMP, not DRY

Production code follows DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself — because a rule expressed twice will eventually be expressed differently. Test code follows DAMP — Descriptive And Meaningful Phrases. "DAMP not DRY" is the slogan, and the reason behind DAMP not DRY is a genuine difference in purpose.

production code
Read to change. Abstraction helps: one place to edit, one place to be right.
test code
Read to diagnose, usually at speed, usually by someone who did not write it. Abstraction hurts: every indirection is a file to open while trying to understand a failure.

So a test may repeat itself where repetition makes the claim visible.
