The four rewritten tests in §19.4 each restate invoice_total_cents(LINES, ...) and each carries its own arithmetic comment; a DRY version would compute the expected value in a helper and be strictly worse, because the reader would have to open the helper to know what the test claims.

The line between them is not "duplication is fine". It is:

Extract what is not the point of the test. Building the object, connecting the database, logging in — nobody reads those to understand the claim, and a change to them should land in one place.

Inline what is the point. The input values, the expected output, the specific condition. A reader must see these without leaving the test.

The review question that settles most cases: can you tell what this test claims without opening another file? If not, something was extracted that should not have been.

19.12 Organising the Suite

Four ways to group tests, and the choice affects how easily a reader finds the relevant ones.

testcase class per class
One test file per production class. The default, and it couples the test structure to the code structure — which is §9.16's mechanism in a directory layout.
testcase class per feature
Grouped by behaviour: test_discounts.py, test_refunds.py. Survives a refactor that moves code between classes, and reads as a specification.
testcase class per fixture
Grouped by the state they share: class TestAnEmptyBasket, class TestABasketWithOneItem. Setup is stated once, in the name, and every test in the group is about that state.
named test suite
A cross-cutting selection, by marker rather than by file: -m smoke, -m "not slow". Orthogonal to the other three, and how the pipeline slices the suite (§20).

The recommendation: group by feature, name by claim, and slice by marker. Testcase class per fixture is worth reaching for where several tests genuinely share an expensive state; testcase class per class is worth avoiding as a default, because it invites one test per method and therefore coupling to the class structure.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: named test suite and testcase class per feature.

19.13 Reviewing Tests, and Deleting Them

Two disciplines that determine whether the catalogue above ever gets applied.

Review tests as carefully as production code, and read them for test readability rather than only for correctness — a test nobody can read is one nobody will maintain. In practice the test half of a pull request is skimmed, because it is long, mechanical-looking and it passes. Six questions turn that skim into a review, and each maps onto a smell:

1
Can I tell what it claims from the name? (§4.17, obscure test)
2
Can I check the expected value without running anything? (hard-coded data)
3
What change would make this fail? If "any change" or "no change", it does not earn its keep (§4.11).
4
Would a behaviour-preserving refactor break it? (fragile test, §7.7)
5
Is every value in the setup load-bearing? (irrelevant information)
6
Did I see it fail? If the author cannot say what the failure looked like, nobody knows the test can fail (§9.1).

Deleting a test is the refactoring nobody performs, because a green test feels like safety and deleting it feels like removing some. Four categories are worth deleting on sight:

  • Duplicated at a cheaper level. The behaviour is verified in detail elsewhere (§10.10); this one re-verifies it slowly.
  • Testing something that no longer exists as a requirement — a rule that was withdrawn, a field that was removed.
  • Permanently skipped or quarantined past the cap (§18.14). A skipped test is a comment with a runtime cost.
  • Cannot fail. Assertion-free, or asserting something the language guarantees (§17.7).

The category not to delete is the one that tempts people most: a test that keeps breaking. That is a fragile test (§19.7) or a flaky one (§18), and both are reporting something real. Diagnose it and fix the cause; deleting it removes the report and leaves the problem.

The cultural condition that makes deletion possible is worth stating: the suite's value is not proportional to its size. A team that believes otherwise will accumulate tests forever, and the accumulation is what §9.16's test cancer feeds on.

To have in hand before moving on: test readability and deleting a test.

19.14 What This Section Established

  • Smells come in three levels — code (read), behaviour (run), project (from outside) — and detection runs upward while causation runs down.
  • "Developers do not write tests" is nearly always a fact about the code, not about the people: painful setup, a slow suite, or no seams.
  • Obscure test has four causes: a mystery guest, irrelevant information, hard-coded data with no working shown, and indirect testing. Its consequence is assertion roulette.
  • The cure is inline, minimal data with the arithmetic shown, and one named claim per test — after which the test names read as a specification.
  • Conditional test logic means the test has paths, so one of them may never run. Parametrization is the standard cure; a platform check belongs in skipif.
  • Extract setup and assertion duplication; leave structural repetition. No TestCase superclass.
  • A fragile test has one of four sensitivities — interface, behaviour, data, context — and naming which one tells you the fix. Ask "did the behaviour change?" before making it pass.
  • Slowness stops the suite being a feedback loop. Fix the few slow tests, the sleeps, the per-test setup, and the wrong level — in that order.
  • When a test is hard to write, the first hypothesis is that the code is wrong, and the check costs one question.
  • Refactor tests only when green, and treat a meaning change as a separate commit.
  • DAMP, not DRY: production code is read to change, test code is read to diagnose. Extract what is not the point; inline what is.
  • Group by feature, name by claim, slice by marker. Per-class grouping invites coupling to the class structure.
  • Six review questions, ending with "did you see it fail?".
  • Delete tests that are duplicated cheaply, obsolete, permanently skipped, or unable to fail — and never delete one that keeps breaking, because it is reporting something.

Exercises

1. Name the smells.

def test_user_stuff(self):
    u = self.load_fixture("users.yaml")["users"][3]
    if u["country"] == "GB":
        self.assertEqual(calculate_vat(u, 100), 20)
    else:
        self.assertEqual(calculate_vat(u, 100), 0)
    self.assertTrue(u["active"])
    self.assertEqual(len(get_orders(u)), 2)

List every smell, then rewrite it. How many tests does it become?

2. Decide DAMP or DRY.

For each, say whether to extract or to leave inline: (a) fifteen tests each constructing a User with eight fields; (b) three tests each asserting the same five fields of a response; (c) twenty tests each calling login() first; (d) each test's expected value; (e) the string "2026-03-01" appearing in nine tests.

3. Diagnose four broken tests.

After a refactor, four tests break. For each, name the sensitivity and the fix: (a) a renamed constructor parameter; (b) a new field added to a response; (c) a test that fails only after another test in the same file was added; (d) a test that started failing on 1 March.

4. Write the review comment.

You are reviewing this:

def test_it_works():
    result = process(load_data())
    assert result is not None

Write the review comment you would leave — specific, actionable, and not more than four sentences.

5. Decide what to delete.

A module has: 40 tests of the public API; 25 tests of private helpers; 12 tests asserting a getter returns what the constructor was given; 6 tests skipped with reason="flaky" for over a year; 3 end-to-end tests re-verifying the discount rules already covered by 8 unit tests.

Which would you delete, which would you convert, and which would you keep? Justify the ones you keep.

6. Fix the project smell.

A team says: "We don't have time to write tests." You observe that setting up a test for their main service takes about 45 minutes and requires a running database, a seeded Redis and three environment variables. Write the plan: what you change first, what you measure, and what you say to the team.

Solutions

1. Name the smells.

Mystery guest (users.yaml); irrelevant information and indirect testing — the test reaches user 3 by index, so it depends on the order of a file it does not show; conditional test logic, so half the test never runs; an eager test with three unrelated claims (VAT, activeness, order count); assertion roulette from the same; a name that says nothing; and assertTrue where assertEqual would give a useful failure message.

Rewritten, it becomes three or four tests: test_vat_is_charged_for_a_gb_customer, test_vat_is_not_charged_outside_gb (parametrized rather than branched), test_a_loaded_user_is_active — which on inspection is probably testing the fixture rather than the code and should go — and test_a_user_with_two_orders_lists_both. Each builds its own minimal user inline.

The most valuable single change is deleting the fixture file and constructing users in the tests, because that removes the mystery guest, the irrelevant information and the index-based indirection at once.

2. Decide DAMP or DRY.

(a) Extract — a builder (§5.12). Constructing a User is not the point of any of the fifteen tests, and a ninth field would otherwise be fifteen edits.

(b) Extract a custom assertion, if the five fields are one claim. If they are five separate claims that happen to be checked together, the tests should be split instead.

(c) Extract — a fixture. Logging in is scenery in nineteen of the twenty; the twentieth is the login test and must not use it (§12.9).

(d) Leave inline, always. The expected value is the claim. A helper that computes it re-implements the code (§4.3), and one that looks it up hides it.

(e) Extract a named constant — A_MONDAY = date(2026, 3, 1) — which is a middle path: the value stays visible at the point of use through its name, and the name says why that date was chosen. A bare repeated literal invites someone to change one of the nine.

3. Diagnose four broken tests.

(a) Interface sensitivity. Fix with a creation method so the parameter list appears once.

(b) Behaviour sensitivity, caused by over-specification: the test compared the whole response. Fix by asserting only the fields it cares about (§7.8), or by validating against a schema that permits extra fields (§13.5).

(c) Context sensitivity — specifically shared state, and the new test changed the order. §18.5, and the fix belongs to the polluting test, not to the failing one.

(d) Context sensitivity, of the time variety. A date-dependent assertion, and 1 March is the giveaway — either a month boundary or a "30 days from now" that crossed one. Fix by injecting the clock (§8.7).

4. Write the review comment.

This passes for any non-None result, so it would not catch process returning an empty list, the wrong shape, or a partially-processed result — which means it cannot tell us anything when it goes green. Could you assert the actual expected value for a small, inline input, and rename it to say what the claim is? Also, load_data() hides where the input comes from; putting a two-row input in the test would let a reader check the expected value without opening anything. Happy to pair on it if the data is awkward to construct — if it is, that is worth knowing about.

Four sentences, each naming a specific smell (cannot fail, obscure name, mystery guest), each with a concrete action, and the last one treating difficulty as information rather than as an excuse (§19.9).

5. Decide what to delete.

Delete the 12 getter tests. They test that the language assigns attributes (§4.11). If any getter has logic in it, that one is not a getter and keeps its test.

Delete the 6 skipped tests, or fix them this week. A year of reason="flaky" means nobody is going to; they are comments with a runtime cost and they inflate the test count (§18.14).

Convert the 25 private-helper tests. Some are testing genuine collaborators that should be extracted and tested through their own front door (§19.9); the rest are duplicating what the public-API tests already cover. Do this incrementally, deleting each only when the behaviour is verified through the public API.

Convert 2 of the 3 end-to-end tests. The discount rules are covered by the 8 unit tests; keep one end-to-end journey to prove the rule reaches the page (§10.10), and delete the two that re-verify arithmetic slowly.

Keep the 40 public-API tests, because they are the ones asserting behaviour that consumers depend on, at the level where the claims are meaningful and cheap.

6. Fix the project smell.

Change first: the setup. Write a single fixture that starts a database and a Redis in containers or as private instances (§11.2, §11.12), reads its own configuration, and needs no environment variables — then a make test that works on a clean checkout. Target: from 45 minutes to under a minute, and from "three env vars" to zero.

Measure: time from a clean checkout to a passing test run, and the number of tests written per week before and after. Both are cheap to record and both are the actual outcome, rather than a proxy.

Say to the team: not "you should write more tests". Say that you noticed writing one takes 45 minutes of setup, that this is a solvable problem, and that you would like a day to fix it. Then show the result and let the behaviour change on its own.

The reasoning matters more than the plan: "no time to write tests" is a rational response to a 45-minute cost per test, and arguing with the conclusion while leaving the cost in place cannot work. Change the cost, and the argument becomes unnecessary.

SECTION 20

Tests in the Pipeline

Everything so far has been about writing tests. This section is about what happens to them afterwards: when they run, what they block, and what to do about the defects that reach production anyway — because some always will.

The organising idea is Humble and Farley's deployment pipeline: a sequence of stages, each cheaper and faster than the next, each acting as a filter. A change enters at one end, and every stage it survives increases confidence at increasing cost. The design question is not "which tests do we have" but "at which stage does each one run, and what does it block?"

That question has a right answer, and it is decided by feedback speed. Section 10.11 set out the intervals — a second, ten seconds, ten minutes, an hour — and a pipeline is those intervals turned into infrastructure.

20.1 Continuous Integration, Actually

The practice is older than the tooling and is routinely confused with it. Continuous integration means every developer merges to the mainline at least daily, and every merge is verified by an automated build — an integration build, in the original vocabulary, because what it builds is the integration of everyone's work rather than anyone's branch. A CI server is how you run the integration build; it is not the practice.

The distinction matters because the common failure is a team with a green pipeline and week-long feature branches. That is not continuous integration; it is a build server attached to deferred integration, and it has the exact problem CI was invented to solve — the merge that is a project rather than an operation.

the mainline builds
Always. A broken mainline is everyone's problem and takes priority over new work — because every subsequent commit is now building on an unknown state.
everyone merges daily
Small changes, frequent conflicts, each one trivial. The alternative is rare, enormous conflicts.
the build is fast
Because a slow build makes daily merging expensive, and people respond by merging less.
the build is trusted
A flaky build (§18) destroys the practice more thoroughly than a slow one, because a red bar that means nothing is a filter that filters nothing.

Everything else in this section serves those four properties.

20.2 The Staged Pipeline

The stages, and what each is for.

local — seconds. The tests for what you are editing (§10.11). Not infrastructure; a habit and a watch mode.
commit stage — under ten minutes. Compile, lint, type-check, unit, integration, component. Blocks the merge. This is the stage that must never be slow and must never be flaky.
acceptance stage — tens of minutes. Contract verification (§13), end-to-end journeys (§15), a deployed environment. Blocks the release, not the merge.
a nightly suite, or another scheduled run — hours. Full property runs, mutation testing (§17), load and soak tests, cross-browser matrices, dependency audits. Blocks nothing; reports to someone.
production — continuous. Smoke tests after deploy, synthetic monitoring, real user monitoring, error budgets. The last filter, and the only one that sees real traffic.

Two principles govern the assignment.

Fail fast, and fail cheap. Order the stages so that the most likely and cheapest-to-detect failures come first. A lint error should not wait behind a nine-minute test suite; a compile failure should be the first thing anyone hears about.

Each stage runs on the artefact the previous stage produced. Build once, then promote the same binary or image through the stages. Rebuilding per stage means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped, and it is a surprisingly common source of "it worked in staging".

Named once more, since each is referred to later: synthetic monitoring, real user monitoring and error budget.

The vocabulary here: a nightly suite.

20.3 The Ten-Minute Build

The number is from Extreme Programming and it is not arbitrary. It is the interval at which a developer waits rather than context-switches — and a context switch costs far more than the minutes on the clock, because coming back to a change you have put down means rebuilding the mental state that made it easy.

# pipeline_budget.py
"""Where the ten minutes goes, and what happens when it does not fit."""

STAGES = [
    # name,             count, seconds each, can parallelise
    ("lint + types",        1,   25.0, False),
    ("unit",             4000,    0.0015, True),
    ("integration",       400,    0.18, True),
    ("component",          60,    2.2, True),
]

BUDGET_S = 600


def report(workers):
    total = 0.0
    print(f"{'stage':16} {'count':>6} {'serial':>9} {f'{workers}-way':>9}")
    for name, count, each, parallel in STAGES:
        serial = count * each
        actual = serial / workers if parallel else serial
        total += actual
        print(f"{name:16} {count:>6} {serial:>8.0f}s {actual:>8.0f}s")
    print(f"{'':16} {'':>6} {'':>9} {'—' * 8:>9}")
    print(f"{'total':16} {'':>6} {'':>9} {total:>8.0f}s "
          f"({'fits' if total <= BUDGET_S else 'OVER'} the {BUDGET_S}s budget)")
    return total


for workers in (1, 4, 8):
    report(workers)
    print()

python3 pipeline_budget.py

stage             count    serial     1-way
lint + types          1       25s       25s
unit               4000        6s        6s
integration         400       72s       72s
component            60      132s      132s
                                   ————————
total                                  235s (fits the 600s budget)

stage             count    serial     4-way
lint + types          1       25s       25s
unit               4000        6s        2s
integration         400       72s       18s
component            60      132s       33s
                                   ————————
total                                   78s (fits the 600s budget)

stage             count    serial     8-way
lint + types          1       25s       25s
unit               4000        6s        1s
integration         400       72s        9s
component            60      132s       16s
                                   ————————
total                                   51s (fits the 600s budget)

Read the first block: serially it does not fit, and the arithmetic says why. Component tests are 0.7% of the count and most of the time, which is §10.9's cost table showing up in a real budget.

The moves, in the order §2.15 gave them: parallelise, shard, then optimise. Note what the numbers say about the last one — halving the speed of every unit test saves three seconds serially, and deleting eight component tests saves eighteen. Effort spent on the numerous fast tests is almost always misplaced.

Four more levers when parallelism is not enough:

Move a stage. Component tests at two seconds each are a candidate for the acceptance stage if the commit stage is over budget. That is a real loss of feedback speed and it is better than a build nobody waits for.

Cache aggressively. Dependencies, build artefacts, Docker layers, compiled test fixtures. On many pipelines the install step is longer than the tests.

Fail fast within the stage. --maxfail=1 on a pull-request build, or lint before tests. A build that is going to fail should fail in ninety seconds.

Write the budget down. A build time budget nobody has stated is a budget nobody can defend, and the ten minutes only works as a constraint if adding a two-minute stage is visibly a decision to spend a fifth of it.

Test impact analysis for the local loop (§17.12) — never as the gate.

Worth carrying forward from this subsection: a build time budget.

20.4 The Commit Stage

What belongs in it, in the order it should run.

1
format and lint
Seconds. Catches a whole class of defect for free, and a formatting failure should never cost a ten-minute wait.
2
type check
The base of §10.6's trophy: a test that covers every line, runs in seconds, and needs no assertions.
3
unit tests
The bulk of the count, a small share of the time.
4
integration tests
Against infrastructure the pipeline starts (§11.2), never a shared instance.
5
component tests
One service in isolation. The most valuable and most often missing layer.
6
build the artefact
Once, and promote it. Every later stage tests this image.

What does not belong: anything needing a deployed environment, anything slower than a few seconds per test, anything that talks to a third party, and anything that has ever been flaky. The commit stage's whole value is that a red result means "you broke something", and every one of those admits a second meaning.

20.5 A Workflow, Concretely

A GitHub Actions workflow, since it is the one most people will meet — and every line of it has an equivalent in whichever CI system you use.

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci

on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:

concurrency:
  # A new push cancels the previous run for the same branch. Without this, a
  # busy repository spends most of its CI capacity on superseded commits.
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  commit-stage:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15          # a hung job must not block the queue forever
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false           # report every shard, not just the first failure
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:18-alpine
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres }
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip            # the install step is often longer than the tests

      - run: pip install -e ".[dev]"

      - name: Lint and type-check
        if: matrix.shard == 1   # once, not four times
        run: |
          ruff check .
          mypy src

      - name: Tests
        run: |
          pytest -m "not slow" \
                 --splits 4 --group ${{ matrix.shard }} \
                 --junitxml=reports/junit-${{ matrix.shard }}.xml \
                 --cov --cov-report=xml \
                 -ra --tb=short -p no:cacheprovider

      - name: Publish the test report
        if: always()            # especially on failure — that is when it matters
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: junit-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: reports/

Seven details in that file are load-bearing, and each has a failure mode behind it.

concurrency with cancel-in-progress. Without it, ten pushes to a branch run ten full pipelines and the queue fills with results nobody will read.

timeout-minutes. A hung test — a missing await, a deadlocked connection (§11.10) — otherwise occupies a runner until the platform's default limit, which is usually hours.

fail-fast: false on the matrix. A matrix build runs the same job under several configurations — here four shards, elsewhere three Python versions or two operating systems — and the default cancels the rest when one fails, so you learn about one shard's failures per run instead of all four.

A service container with a health check. pg_isready is a readiness check, not a sleep (§18.9), and the job does not start until the database answers.

if: matrix.shard == 1 on lint. Running the linter four times wastes three runners and produces four identical failures.

--junitxml, uploaded with if: always(). JUnit XML is what makes failures appear in the run summary rather than only in a log; uploading it only on success would be exactly backwards.

-p no:cacheprovider. The workspace is fresh every run, so the cache is useless, and on a shared or read-only workspace it can fail (§2.11).

The terms above, gathered: github actions workflow and a matrix build.

20.6 Hooks: Pre-commit and Pre-push

Local checks that run before code leaves the machine.

pre-commit
Must be fast — under a couple of seconds. Formatting, trailing whitespace, a secrets scan, a syntax check. Anything slower will be bypassed with --no-verify, and a hook people routinely bypass is worse than none.
a pre-push hook
Tens of seconds is tolerable. The fast unit tests, so an obvious breakage never reaches CI.

Two rules keep hooks useful. A hook must be reproducible in CI, because a check that only exists locally is a check that does not exist — a colleague without the hook installed simply skips it. And a hook must never be the only place a check runs: hooks are a convenience that shortens the loop, and the pipeline is the gate.

The strongest candidate for a pre-commit hook, and the one most often missing, is a secrets scan. A credential committed and then removed is still in the history, and the remediation is rotation rather than a revert — which makes this the one check whose value is entirely in catching it before the commit exists.

One line each, for reference: a pre-commit hook and a pre-push hook.

20.7 The Fast Suite and the Slow Suite

The split that makes the ten-minute build achievable, and the discipline that keeps it honest.

the fast suite
Runs on every commit and blocks the merge. Deterministic, hermetic, and every test in it earns its place by being fast.
the slow suite
Runs later — per release, nightly, or on a schedule. End-to-end journeys, large property runs (§16.10), cross-browser matrices, mutation testing.

The mechanism is markers (§2.5) and a marker expression per stage:

pytest -m "not slow and not e2e"      # commit stage
pytest -m "e2e"                       # acceptance stage
pytest -m "slow"                      # nightly

Three rules stop the split from becoming a way to hide tests.

Everything runs somewhere, on a schedule someone reads. A "slow" marker that is not in any pipeline stage is a delete with extra steps. Audit the marker expressions against the marker list occasionally; the two drift.

The slow suite's failures have an owner. A nightly build that has been red for three weeks is worse than no nightly build, because it consumes attention and provides nothing. Route the failure to a person or a channel, and treat three weeks red as a decision to delete the suite.

Moving a test to the slow suite is a decision, not a fix. A flaky end-to-end test moved to nightly is still flaky, and it is now flaky where nobody is watching (§18.14's quarantine has the rules that make this survivable).

The number to watch is what fraction of escaped defects were caught by the slow suite. If the answer is "none in a year", the slow suite is not paying for itself and the honest response is to delete most of it and put the effort into the fast one.

20.8 Gates

What a stage is allowed to block, and how.

a required status check
The commit stage must pass before a merge is allowed. The one non-negotiable gate.
merge queue
Re-runs the build against the result of merging, in order. Fixes the semantic conflict — two changes that each pass alone and break together — which a per-branch check cannot see.
coverage gate
Diff coverage, ratcheted (§17.5). Never a project-wide target.
a minimum test count
The guard against exit code 5 (§2.10) and against a selection that silently stopped matching. Parse the JUnit XML and assert a floor.
flake rate
Not a gate — a reported number (§18.14). Gating on it would make people delete flaky tests rather than fix them.

The merge queue deserves its own note, because the problem it solves is invisible until it bites. Two pull requests each pass their own build: one renames a function, the other adds a caller of the old name. Both merge, main is broken, and neither author did anything wrong. A merge queue builds the combined result before merging, which is the only place that conflict can be detected.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: a required status check and a merge queue.

20.9 The Quarantine Lane

Section 18.14 set out the policy; here is the pipeline shape that implements it.

A third lane, alongside the fast and slow suites, that runs, reports, and does not block:

pytest -m "not quarantine" --junitxml=reports/main.xml       # gates the merge
pytest -m "quarantine" --junitxml=reports/quarantine.xml || true

The || true is the whole mechanism, and it is also the danger: a lane that cannot fail is a lane nobody reads. The three rules from §18.14 — a ticket, an owner, a cap — are what make it a queue rather than a graveyard, and the pipeline should enforce the cap directly: a job that counts the quarantined tests and fails when there are more than five is a gate on the policy rather than on the tests.

JUnit XML is what makes the reporting work. Every runner emits it, every CI system renders it, and it carries per-test timings — which is what turns "the suite is slower lately" into a chart with a culprit. record_property (§5.11) attaches your own key/values to it, so a test can tell the report which ticket it belongs to.

20.10 After the Deploy

The pipeline does not end at the release. The last filters run against production, and they catch a class of defect nothing before them can: configuration, environment, infrastructure and scale.

smoke test after deploy
A handful of requests against the deployed instance: it is up, it answers, it reaches its database, its version is the one just shipped. Runs in seconds and catches the whole configuration class (§13.11).
rollback on failure
The smoke test's failure must do something. An automatic rollback makes the deploy safe to attempt, which is what makes frequent deploys possible.
synthetic monitoring
The same journeys, run continuously against production, from outside. Catches what breaks between deploys — an expired certificate, a third party going down, a DNS change.
semantic monitoring
A synthetic check that asserts a business outcome — a test order really priced, really charged against a test account, really refunded. Expensive, and the closest thing to an end-to-end test that runs forever.
real user monitoring
Measurement from actual sessions. The only source of truth about the browsers, networks and devices your users really have.

Domain-oriented observability is the practice that makes the last two useful: emit events in the domain's vocabulary — order.discount_applied, payment.declined — rather than only technical metrics. A drop in checkout.completed is a defect report; a drop in CPU is not. And those events are assertable, which is what turns monitoring into a test that runs in production forever.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: semantic monitoring, domain-oriented observability and rollback on failure.

20.11 Testing in Production

The phrase provokes — and its older, blunter spelling, QA in production, provokes more — but the practice is unavoidable: some things can only be verified where the real traffic, the real data and the real scale are. The question is whether it is done deliberately or by accident.

feature flag
Deploy the code without enabling it, then enable for one user, then a percentage. Separates deploy from release, which is the single most useful idea here.
dark launch
Run the new path on real traffic and throw the result away, comparing it against the old path. Verifies correctness and load at full scale with zero user risk.
canary release
Route a small share of traffic to the new version and compare error rates. The rollback trigger must be automatic, or the canary is decoration.
error budget
The reliability you are allowed to spend. Budget remaining → ship; budget exhausted → stop shipping features and fix reliability. It turns "how careful should we be" into a number.

Three conditions make it responsible rather than reckless, and without them the phrase is just an excuse:

Observability first. Testing in production without the ability to see what is happening is deploying and hoping. The instrumentation is a prerequisite, not a follow-up.

A fast, tested rollback. Practised, automated, and exercised often enough that nobody hesitates. An untested rollback is a plan, not a capability.

Blast radius control. Flags, canaries and percentage rollouts exist so a defect affects one user rather than all of them. Their point is to make the first observation of a failure cheap.

Feature flags have their own cost, which is worth stating: every flag doubles the number of code paths, and a flag left in for a year is a permanently untested combination. Remove them on a schedule, and treat a flag older than a release cycle as debt.

To have in hand before moving on: canary release, dark launch and qa in production.

20.12 The Slow Suite's Other Members

Three kinds of test that belong nowhere near a commit stage and are worth having.

load testing
Behaviour under expected and peak traffic. Assert on thresholds — a p99 under 400 ms, an error rate under 0.1% — never on exact numbers (§18.3).
a soak test
Moderate load for hours or days. The only way to find a slow memory leak, a connection pool that never recovers, or a log that fills a disk — §18.12's resource leaks at production scale.
chaos testing
Inject failure deliberately — kill an instance, add latency, drop a dependency — and check the system degrades as designed. Verifies the resilience you believe you have.

Chaos testing has a prerequisite people skip: you must know what should happen. "Kill a node and see" is an experiment; "kill a node and assert that requests continue to succeed with a p99 under 800 ms" is a test. Without the hypothesis, a chaos run produces an anecdote.

Named once more, since it is referred to later: a soak test.

The vocabulary here: load testing.

20.13 Exploratory Testing

Everything automated shares one blind spot: it can only check what someone already thought to check. A test suite is a set of answers to questions that have been asked. Exploratory testing is how the questions get asked.

It is not manual regression testing — clicking through a script is a worse version of what a machine does. It is simultaneous learning, test design and execution, by a person who is deliberately trying to find out something nobody knows.

an exploratory testing charter
A mission for the session: "Explore checkout with expired payment methods to discover error-handling problems." Specific enough to direct, open enough to follow a surprise.
a timebox
60 to 120 minutes, uninterrupted. Long enough to build a model, short enough to stay deliberate.
notes
What was tried, what was found, what was not covered, and the new questions. The last two are the valuable ones.
a debrief
Fifteen minutes with someone else. Findings become tickets; findings that are reproducible become automated tests (§9.9).

That structure is session-based test management, and it is what makes exploration accountable — a session produces a charter, a duration, a set of findings and a coverage statement, which is a reportable unit of work rather than "some poking about".

What it finds that automation does not: confusing flows, a good error message that appears in the wrong place, an interaction between two features nobody considered, a state reachable only by an unusual path, and everything in the category of "this is technically correct and clearly wrong". Every one of those is a question, and the automated suite can only be told answers.

The relationship between the two is the point: exploration finds the defect, automation stops it coming back. A team doing only the first re-finds the same problems forever; a team doing only the second never learns anything its tests were not already written to check.

What to carry forward from this subsection: an exploratory testing charter and session-based test management.

20.14 Definition of Done

The pipeline is the executable form of an agreement, and writing that agreement down is what stops "done" from meaning "the code is written".

A workable one:

✓
The acceptance criteria are executable tests, and they pass (§9.13).
✓
The commit stage is green, on the merge result, not just on the branch.
✓
New behaviour has tests at the lowest level that can hold them (§10.12), and someone has seen them fail (§9.1).
✓
The tests were reviewed with the same six questions as any other code (§19.13).
✓
Contracts affected by the change are updated and verified (§13).
✓
It is observable in production: the events a person would need to tell whether it is working exist and are emitted.
✓
Any flag has a removal date; any quarantined test has a ticket.

The item people leave out is the last-but-one, and it is the one that decides whether you find out about a defect from a dashboard or from a customer.

20.15 What This Section Established

  • Continuous integration is a practice, not a server: daily merges to the mainline, each verified. A green pipeline on week-long branches is not it.
  • A staged pipeline filters in increasing order of cost: local, commit, acceptance, nightly, production. Build the artefact once and promote it.
  • The ten-minute build is about attention, not throughput, and the arithmetic shows that the slowest 1% of tests dominate the budget — so effort spent speeding up the fast ones is misplaced.
  • The commit stage runs lint, types, unit, integration and component, in that order, and contains nothing slow, remote or ever-flaky.
  • Seven details in a workflow file are load-bearing: concurrency cancellation, a timeout, fail-fast: false, a service health check, running lint once, uploading JUnit on failure, and disabling the cache.
  • A pre-commit hook must be under a couple of seconds or it will be bypassed — and a check that runs only locally does not exist.
  • The fast/slow split makes the budget achievable, and it is honest only if everything runs somewhere, failures have an owner, and moving a test out is recorded as a decision.
  • A merge queue catches the semantic conflict that no per-branch check can see.
  • Gate on the commit stage, diff coverage and a minimum test count — and report the flake rate rather than gating on it.
  • The quarantine lane must not block, and its cap must: a job that fails when there are too many quarantined tests is a gate on the policy.
  • The pipeline continues after the deploy: a smoke test with an automatic rollback, synthetic and semantic monitoring, real user monitoring, and domain-oriented events that make a drop in orders visible as a defect.
  • Testing in production is responsible with observability, a practised rollback and blast-radius control — and feature flags are debt with a removal date.
  • Load, soak and chaos tests belong in the slow suite, and a chaos run without a stated hypothesis is an anecdote.
  • Exploratory testing asks the questions the suite can only answer. A charter, a timebox, notes and a debrief make it accountable; reproducible findings become automated tests.
  • Write the definition of done down, including the observability item, or "done" means "the code is written".

The term above, for reference: a staged pipeline.

Exercises

1. Assign the stages.

For each, name the stage and defend it: (a) 4,000 unit tests; (b) a contract verification for three consumers; (c) a mutation run on the pricing module; (d) a secrets scan; (e) a Playwright checkout journey; (f) a 30-minute soak test; (g) a type check.

2. Fix the build.

A commit stage takes 24 minutes: 3 minutes installing dependencies, 1 minute linting, 6 minutes of unit tests, 14 minutes of end-to-end tests. It is red about 20% of the time on unchanged code. Give the first four changes in order, with the expected effect of each.

3. Design the gates.

For a team of twelve on one repository, decide what blocks a merge and what only reports. Include coverage, flake rate, the quarantine cap, and the end-to-end suite. Defend the two most contentious choices.

4. Write the charter.

Write three exploratory testing charters for a newly-built subscription upgrade flow. For each, say what class of defect you expect it to find and why the automated suite would not.

5. Diagnose the escape.

A defect reached production: a currency conversion used a stale exchange rate whenever the cache warmed during a deploy. Walk through every stage of the pipeline and say whether it could have caught this, then say what you would add and at which stage.

6. Justify the nightly suite.

Your nightly suite takes 3 hours, has been red for six weeks, and nobody has looked. Someone proposes deleting it. Make the case for deleting it, the case for keeping it, and say what you would actually do.

Solutions

1. Assign the stages.

(a) Commit stage. Six seconds sharded, and they are the fastest feedback available.

(b) Commit stage, on the provider side. Contract verification is a fast, hermetic test against the real service with no consumer present (§13.5) — it does not need an environment and it is exactly the check that should block a merge.

(c) Nightly, on the pricing module only (§17.11). Minutes to hours, and its output is a list of gaps rather than a pass/fail.

(d) Pre-commit hook and the commit stage. The hook is where it has value — before the secret is in the history — and the pipeline is the gate, because the hook can be bypassed.

(e) Acceptance stage, after the artefact is deployed to an ephemeral environment (§11.12). Not the commit stage: it needs a deployment and it is the flakiest thing you own.

(f) Nightly, or on a schedule. Thirty minutes of moderate load blocks nothing and is the only thing that finds a leak.

(g) Commit stage, early — before the tests, because it is seconds and it covers every line (§10.6).

2. Fix the build.

  1. Move the end-to-end tests to the acceptance stage. 24 minutes → 10. Biggest single win, no test changes, and it also removes most of the flakiness because e2e is where it lives.
  2. Cache the dependency install. 10 → about 7.5 on a cache hit. Cheap and mechanical.
  3. Measure the remaining flakiness and fix the top offenders (§18.14). The 20% will have dropped a lot with the e2e tests gone; whatever is left is in the unit or integration tests and is a real bug.
  4. Shard the unit tests across four runners. 6 minutes → about 1.5, giving a commit stage around 4 minutes.

The ordering is deliberate: the first change is the largest and the least risky, and each later change is only worth doing because the earlier one revealed what remained. Do not start with "make the unit tests faster" — six minutes of unit tests is a quarter of the problem and the hardest quarter to fix.

3. Design the gates.

Blocks a merge: the commit stage (lint, types, unit, integration, component, contract verification); diff coverage on changed lines; a minimum test count parsed from JUnit; the quarantine cap.

Reports only: the flake rate; total project coverage (ratcheted, so it may not fall, but not a target); the nightly suite; the end-to-end suite in a pull request — it blocks the release, not the merge.

The two contentious ones:

End-to-end tests do not block a merge. With twelve people on one repository, a 2%-per-test flake rate on a browser suite means the merge is blocked several times a day for reasons that are not defects (§10.9), and the response will be to re-run without reading — at which point the gate is worse than no gate. Block the release instead, where a person is already in the loop.

The flake rate is reported, not gated. Gating on it creates an incentive to delete flaky tests rather than fix them, and deleting one throws away evidence of a real problem (§18.1). A visible number with an owner changes behaviour; a gate changes the number.

4. Write the charter.

Charter 1. Explore the upgrade flow with accounts in unusual billing states — mid-cycle, in a trial, with a failed payment, already upgraded — to discover incorrect proration and confusing states.

Expected defects: arithmetic and messaging for combinations nobody enumerated. The suite will not find them because the test data was written from the happy case, and the interesting states are combinations no one listed (§4.9).

Charter 2. Explore the upgrade flow by interrupting it — closing the tab mid-payment, using the back button after confirming, double-clicking submit, opening two tabs — to discover duplicate charges and inconsistent state.

Expected defects: idempotency and state-machine holes. The suite drives the flow forwards and never does anything a real, distracted person does (§12.5).

Charter 3. Explore the upgrade flow as a user who does not want to upgrade — reading the copy, looking for the cancel path, checking what is actually charged and when — to discover misleading or missing information.

Expected defects: everything in the category "technically correct and clearly wrong". No assertion can express "this pricing page is misleading", and this is the class that produces support load and refunds.

5. Diagnose the escape.

Unit tests: no — the cache-warming timing is not visible at this level, though a unit test of the cache could have covered "a stale entry is not served", which is the underlying rule.

Integration: possibly, if a test exercised the cache's expiry against a real clock (§8.7). The defect is a race between deploy and cache warm, and the rule it violates is testable even though the race is not.

Component and contract: no. Both run against a warm, steady process.

End-to-end and acceptance: no. The condition exists only during a deploy.

Smoke test after deploy: yes, if it asserted a converted amount rather than only that the service answers. This is the strongest single addition.

Synthetic and semantic monitoring: yes — a semantic check converting a known amount every minute would have caught it within a minute of the deploy, on every deploy, forever.

What I would add, in order: a unit test of the cache asserting a stale entry is never served (cheapest, and it fixes the rule); an assertion on a converted value in the post-deploy smoke test (catches this exact class at the moment it can be rolled back); and a semantic monitor on conversion (catches it whenever it happens, not only at deploy).

The general lesson: the defect was in a timing interaction with deployment, and no stage before the deploy can see one. That is precisely the category §20.10 exists for.

6. Justify the nightly suite.

For deleting: it has provided zero signal for six weeks and is providing zero now. It consumes three hours of compute a night and a slot in everyone's mental model of "we have tests for that", which is worse than nothing — it is false confidence. A red suite nobody reads is indistinguishable from a deleted one except in cost.

For keeping: the suite presumably contains something that was worth writing. Deleting it destroys that work, and the reason it is red is probably one or two broken things at the front rather than three hours of genuine failure.

What I would do: spend one day, not more, finding out. Run it, read the first failures, and classify: if the whole thing is red from an environment problem, fix that and see what remains. Then apply §20.7's test — how many escaped defects has this suite caught in the last year? If the answer is none and it is still red after a day, delete it and say so publicly, because the alternative is another six weeks of the same.

Whatever survives gets the two rules that were missing: an owner, and a failure that reaches a person. A nightly suite without both will be red again in six weeks, and deleting it a second time will be harder.

SECTION 21

Capstone: A Suite for Code You Did Not Write

Every section so far has been one idea at a time. This one is a single system, taken from no tests to a full suite, where the ideas constrain each other and the order you apply them matters.

The brief: a loyalty-points service, delivered without tests. Customers earn points on orders, points determine a tier, and points expire after a year. It is in production, it has users, and two of its behaviours are wrong — but nobody knows which two, because nothing checks.

That is the realistic starting position, and it is deliberately not "write tests for a clean design". The order of work is the lesson: characterise, then find the seams, then test properly — because writing good tests against untestable code is not possible, and refactoring untested code is not safe. The way out of that circle is the whole of this capstone.

Work each stage before reading its solution.

21.1 Stage 1 — Get It Under Test Without Changing It

Here is the code as delivered.

# loyalty.py
"""Loyalty points, as delivered. No tests, and two defects nobody has found."""
import datetime

TIERS = {"bronze": 0, "silver": 5_000, "gold": 20_000}

_BALANCES: dict[int, int] = {}       # module-level state, shared by everything


def award(customer_id, order_cents):
    """One point per whole pound spent."""
    points = order_cents // 100
    _BALANCES[customer_id] = _BALANCES.get(customer_id, 0) + points
    return points


def balance(customer_id):
    return _BALANCES.get(customer_id, 0)


def tier(customer_id):
    points = _BALANCES.get(customer_id, 0)
    if points > TIERS["gold"]:
        return "gold"
    if points > TIERS["silver"]:
        return "silver"
    return "bronze"


def expire_if_stale(customer_id, earned_on):
    """Points older than a year are lost."""
    if (datetime.date.today() - earned_on).days > 365:
        _BALANCES[customer_id] = 0

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]
# The web framework warns about its own dependencies on import; not our subject.
addopts = "-p no:warnings"

[tool.mutmut]
source_paths = ["core.py"]
pytest_add_cli_args_test_selection = ["tests/test_core.py"]

Task. Write a characterisation test — one that pins what the code does now, right or wrong — without changing a line of loyalty.py. You will hit two obstacles. Name them before you look.

Solution — Stage 1

The two obstacles are the two design defects, and meeting them is the point of the exercise.

_BALANCES is module state, so every test sees the previous test's customers (§18.5). The tests need an explicit reset, and forgetting it makes the suite order-dependent.

datetime.date.today() is called inside the function, so any test of expiry either computes its expected value with the same arithmetic the code uses — §4.3's re-implementation failure — or hardcodes a date and becomes a time bomb (§8.1).

# tests/test_characterisation.py
"""Pins current behaviour. Not a specification — a photograph."""
import datetime

import pytest

import loyalty


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def reset_the_global():
    """Obstacle one, worked around rather than fixed (§8.5)."""
    loyalty._BALANCES.clear()
    yield
    loyalty._BALANCES.clear()


def test_a_whole_pound_earns_a_point():
    assert loyalty.award(7, 1_500) == 15
    assert loyalty.balance(7) == 15


def test_part_of_a_pound_earns_nothing():
    assert loyalty.award(7, 199) == 1


def test_awards_accumulate():
    loyalty.award(7, 1_000)
    loyalty.award(7, 2_000)

    assert loyalty.balance(7) == 30


@pytest.mark.parametrize("points,current_tier", [
    (0, "bronze"),
    (4_999, "bronze"),
    (5_000, "bronze"),        # ← photograph, not specification
    (5_001, "silver"),
    (20_000, "silver"),       # ← photograph, not specification
    (20_001, "gold"),
])
def test_the_tier_as_it_currently_behaves(points, current_tier):
    loyalty._BALANCES[7] = points

    assert loyalty.tier(7) == current_tier


def test_expiry_zeroes_the_whole_balance():
    loyalty._BALANCES[7] = 12_000
    long_ago = datetime.date.today() - datetime.timedelta(days=400)

    loyalty.expire_if_stale(7, long_ago)

    assert loyalty.balance(7) == 0

pytest -q tests/test_characterisation.py

..........                                                               [100%]
10 passed in 1.93s

All green — and two of those rows are marked as photographs rather than specifications. A customer with exactly 5,000 points is bronze, and one with exactly 20,000 is silver. That is defect one, and writing the characterisation test is what surfaced it: nobody had ever written the boundary down, so nobody had noticed that > should be >=.

Note what the characterisation test is not. It is not a specification — it records behaviour including the wrong behaviour, on purpose, so that a refactor can be proved safe. The two suspicious rows carry comments, and the next stage is where they get resolved with whoever owns the rule.

The expiry test is the honest version of the second obstacle: it computes today - 400 days, so it is not a time bomb, and it cannot check the boundary at all — 365 versus 366 days is exactly where the defect would be, and this test cannot reach it. That limitation is a fact about the code, and Stage 2 removes it.

21.2 Stage 2 — Find the Seams

Task. Make the module testable without changing what it does. Specifically: make the clock controllable and the storage injectable, so a test can reach the expiry boundary and two tests cannot interfere. Do it in a way that leaves every existing caller working.

Solution — Stage 2

Split it: a functional core with no environment, and a thin shell that holds the state (§8.11).

# core.py
"""The rules. No clock, no storage, no I/O — every input is a parameter."""
from datetime import date, timedelta

BRONZE, SILVER, GOLD = "bronze", "silver", "gold"
SILVER_AT = 5_000
GOLD_AT = 20_000
EXPIRY_DAYS = 365


def points_for(order_cents):
    """One point per whole pound. Refuses what it cannot price."""
    if order_cents < 0:
        raise ValueError("order_cents must not be negative")
    return order_cents // 100


def tier_for(points):
    if points < 0:
        raise ValueError("points must not be negative")
    if points >= GOLD_AT:
        return GOLD
    if points >= SILVER_AT:
        return SILVER
    return BRONZE


def expired(earned_on, today):
    """`today` is a parameter, so the boundary is reachable (§8.6)."""
    return (today - earned_on).days > EXPIRY_DAYS


def surviving_points(entries, today):
    """entries: [(earned_on, points)]. Only the stale ones are lost."""
    return sum(points for earned_on, points in entries
               if not expired(earned_on, today))

# service.py
"""The shell. Holds the store and the clock, and decides nothing."""
from datetime import date

from core import points_for, surviving_points, tier_for


class SystemClock:
    def today(self) -> date:
        return date.today()


class InMemoryLedger:
    """A fake (§6.1): a real implementation, simplified past production."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._entries: dict[int, list] = {}

    def add(self, customer_id, earned_on, points):
        self._entries.setdefault(customer_id, []).append((earned_on, points))

    def entries(self, customer_id):
        return list(self._entries.get(customer_id, []))


class LoyaltyService:
    def __init__(self, ledger, clock=None):
        self._ledger = ledger
        self._clock = clock or SystemClock()

    def award(self, customer_id, order_cents):
        points = points_for(order_cents)
        self._ledger.add(customer_id, self._clock.today(), points)
        return points

    def balance(self, customer_id):
        return surviving_points(self._ledger.entries(customer_id),
                                self._clock.today())

    def tier(self, customer_id):
        return tier_for(self.balance(customer_id))

# loyalty.py
"""The old module-level API, kept working. Every existing caller is untouched;
new code uses LoyaltyService directly and gets the seams."""
from service import InMemoryLedger, LoyaltyService

TIERS = {"bronze": 0, "silver": 5_000, "gold": 20_000}

_default = LoyaltyService(InMemoryLedger())
_BALANCES = {}      # kept only so the old characterisation tests still import


def award(customer_id, order_cents):
    return _default.award(customer_id, order_cents)


def balance(customer_id):
    return _default.balance(customer_id)


def tier(customer_id):
    return _default.tier(customer_id)

Four things changed and none of them is a rewrite.

The rules moved into pure functions. points_for, tier_for and expired take values and return values, so they are rung 1 of §5.13's teardown ladder — nothing to set up, nothing to clean.

The clock became a parameter. expired(earned_on, today) makes the 365/366 boundary directly reachable, which Stage 1's test could not do at all.

Storage became a collaborator, so two tests cannot interfere and a real database can be substituted later (Stage 5) with no change to the rules.

Expiry became per-entry. The old expire_if_stale zeroed the whole balance; surviving_points drops only the stale entries. That is defect two, and it was invisible until the rule was written as a function that had to say what it meant.

The old module still works, so no caller had to be found and edited — §8.6's rule about adding a control point without breaking the interface.

21.3 Stage 3 — The Boundaries

Task. Write the unit tests for core.py. Use §4.4's technique deliberately: list every boundary before writing a line, then test each side of each one. Include the two defects Stages 1 and 2 found.

Solution — Stage 3

The boundaries, listed first: order_cents at −1/0 and at 99/100/199/200; points at −1/0, 4,999/5,000, 19,999/20,000; days at 365/366.

# tests/test_core.py
import datetime

import pytest

from core import EXPIRY_DAYS, expired, points_for, surviving_points, tier_for

TODAY = datetime.date(2026, 9, 4)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("cents,points", [
    (0, 0), (99, 0), (100, 1), (199, 1), (200, 2), (1_500, 15),
])
def test_each_side_of_the_pound_boundary(cents, points):
    assert points_for(cents) == points


def test_a_negative_order_is_refused():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="must not be negative"):
        points_for(-1)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("points,expected", [
    (0, "bronze"),
    (4_999, "bronze"),
    (5_000, "silver"),        # the fixed defect: exactly the threshold qualifies
    (5_001, "silver"),
    (19_999, "silver"),
    (20_000, "gold"),         # and here too
    (20_001, "gold"),
])
def test_each_side_of_each_tier_boundary(points, expected):
    assert tier_for(points) == expected


def test_a_negative_balance_is_refused():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="must not be negative"):
        tier_for(-1)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("age_days,is_expired", [
    (0, False), (364, False), (365, False), (366, True), (400, True),
])
def test_each_side_of_the_expiry_boundary(age_days, is_expired):
    earned_on = TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=age_days)

    assert expired(earned_on, TODAY) is is_expired


def test_only_the_stale_entries_are_lost():
    entries = [
        (TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=400), 5_000),   # gone
        (TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=366), 1_000),   # gone
        (TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=365), 2_000),   # kept: exactly a year
        (TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=10), 3_000),    # kept
    ]

    assert surviving_points(entries, TODAY) == 5_000


def test_an_empty_ledger_survives_to_nothing():
    assert surviving_points([], TODAY) == 0


def test_the_expiry_window_is_stated_rather_than_assumed():
    # A guard on the constant itself: if someone changes the policy, the tests
    # that depend on it fail with a name that says which policy changed.
    assert EXPIRY_DAYS == 365

pytest -q tests/test_core.py

.......................                                                  [100%]
23 passed in 2.00s

Twenty-three tests from eight functions, every one of them milliseconds, none of them needing a fixture. That is what pushing the rules into a functional core buys — and note that the two defects are now fixed and pinned: rows (5_000, "silver") and (20_000, "gold") are the specification the characterisation test could not state, and test_only_the_stale_entries_are_lost is the rule the old expire_if_stale got wrong.

The last test looks odd and earns its place. EXPIRY_DAYS == 365 asserts a policy, not an implementation: if someone changes it to 180, twelve tests break and one of them says exactly what changed. Without it, twelve tests break and none of them says why.

21.4 Stage 4 — The Properties

Task. Three claims about core.py hold for every input, not just the ones above. Find them and write them with hypothesis. Then say what each one catches that the parametrized tests do not.

Solution — Stage 4 
# tests/test_properties.py
import datetime

from hypothesis import given, settings
from hypothesis import strategies as st

from core import expired, points_for, surviving_points, tier_for

TODAY = datetime.date(2026, 9, 4)
ORDERS = st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10_000_000)


@given(ORDERS)
def test_points_never_exceed_the_pounds_spent(cents):
    assert 0 <= points_for(cents) <= cents / 100


@given(smaller=ORDERS, extra=ORDERS)
def test_spending_more_never_earns_fewer_points(smaller, extra):
    assert points_for(smaller + extra) >= points_for(smaller)


@given(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=1_000_000),
       st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=1_000_000))
def test_more_points_never_means_a_lower_tier(points, extra):
    order = {"bronze": 0, "silver": 1, "gold": 2}

    assert order[tier_for(points + extra)] >= order[tier_for(points)]


@given(st.lists(st.tuples(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=800),
                          st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=50_000)),
                max_size=20))
@settings(max_examples=200)
def test_survivors_are_a_subset_of_everything_earned(raw):
    entries = [(TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=age), pts) for age, pts in raw]

    total = sum(pts for _, pts in entries)
    survivors = surviving_points(entries, TODAY)

    assert 0 <= survivors <= total


@given(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=2_000))
def test_expiry_is_monotonic_in_age(age):
    earned_on = TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=age)
    older = TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=age + 1)

    if expired(earned_on, TODAY):
        assert expired(older, TODAY)

pytest -q tests/test_properties.py

.....                                                                    [100%]
5 passed in 11.81s

What each catches that a table cannot.

Monotonicity — spending more never earns fewer points, and more points never means a lower tier. A table checks the ordering at seven chosen values; the property checks it at every pair. A tier ladder with a transposed threshold passes a badly-chosen table and fails this immediately.

The subset property — survivors are between zero and everything earned. This is the invariant the old expire_if_stale violated in the other direction: it returned zero when some entries were fresh. Any future change that double-counts, or that loses a fresh entry, breaks it.

Monotonic expiry — if something is expired, something older is too. It sounds trivial and it is the exact claim a > written as < violates, at every input rather than at one.

The general shape, from §16.5: these are all claims about a relationship between two calls, which is where properties are strongest and example-based tests are weakest, because a table can only ever check the pairs someone wrote down.

21.5 Stage 5 — The Real Store

Task. The ledger will be a PostgreSQL table. Write the repository and prove it behaves like the in-memory fake — using one suite, run against both (§11.14).

Solution — Stage 5 
# pgledger.py
"""The real ledger. One query per method, no rules of its own (§11.1)."""
SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ledger (
    id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id integer NOT NULL,
    earned_on   date    NOT NULL,
    points      integer NOT NULL CHECK (points >= 0)
);
"""


class PostgresLedger:
    def __init__(self, connection):
        self._conn = connection

    def add(self, customer_id, earned_on, points):
        self._conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO ledger (customer_id, earned_on, points) "
            "VALUES (%s, %s, %s)", (customer_id, earned_on, points))

    def entries(self, customer_id):
        rows = self._conn.execute(
            "SELECT earned_on, points FROM ledger WHERE customer_id = %s "
            "ORDER BY id", (customer_id,)).fetchall()
        return [(row[0], row[1]) for row in rows]

# pgcluster.py
"""A private PostgreSQL for the suite (§11.2)."""
import os
import pathlib
import shutil
import socket
import subprocess

def find_pgbin():
    """Where initdb and pg_ctl live: $PGBIN if set, then PATH, then Debian's layout."""
    if os.environ.get("PGBIN"):
        return pathlib.Path(os.environ["PGBIN"])
    if shutil.which("pg_ctl"):
        return pathlib.Path(shutil.which("pg_ctl")).parent
    return next(p for p in sorted(pathlib.Path("/usr/lib/postgresql").glob("*/bin"))
                if (p / "initdb").exists())


PGBIN = find_pgbin()


class Cluster:
    def __init__(self, datadir):
        self.datadir = pathlib.Path(datadir).resolve()
        with socket.socket() as s:
            s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
            self.port = s.getsockname()[1]

    def start(self):
        if not (self.datadir / "PG_VERSION").exists():
            # -E UTF8 --locale=C: a test cluster must not inherit the machine's locale.
            # Without them initdb follows the environment, and under LC_ALL=C that means an
            # SQL_ASCII database — where psycopg hands back `bytes` for every text column and
            # `version.startswith("PostgreSQL")` raises TypeError.
            subprocess.run([str(PGBIN / "initdb"), "-D", str(self.datadir),
                            "-U", "postgres", "-A", "trust", "--no-sync",
                            "-E", "UTF8", "--locale=C"],
                           check=True, capture_output=True)
        opts = (f"-p {self.port} -c listen_addresses=127.0.0.1 "
                f"-c unix_socket_directories= -c fsync=off")
        subprocess.run([str(PGBIN / "pg_ctl"), "-D", str(self.datadir), "-o", opts,
                        "-l", str(self.datadir / "log"), "-w", "start"],
                       check=True, capture_output=True)
        return self

    def stop(self):
        subprocess.run([str(PGBIN / "pg_ctl"), "-D", str(self.datadir),
                        "-m", "immediate", "-w", "stop"], capture_output=True)

    def dsn(self):
        return f"host=127.0.0.1 port={self.port} user=postgres dbname=postgres"

# tests/conftest.py
import pytest

# The imports are inside the fixtures on purpose. `conftest.py` is imported for
# every run, including the mutation run of §21.7 — which copies only `core.py`
# into its working tree, so a top-level `import pgcluster` there would fail
# before a single mutant was tested.


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def cluster():
    import psycopg

    from pgcluster import Cluster
    from pgledger import SCHEMA

    server = Cluster("pgdata").start()
    with psycopg.connect(server.dsn(), autocommit=True) as setup:
        setup.execute(SCHEMA)
    yield server
    server.stop()


@pytest.fixture
def connection(cluster):
    """Rollback teardown (§11.4): nothing is ever committed."""
    import psycopg

    conn = psycopg.connect(cluster.dsn(), autocommit=False)
    try:
        yield conn
    finally:
        conn.rollback()
        conn.close()

# tests/test_ledger_contract.py
"""One suite, two implementations. Any divergence is a named failure."""
import datetime

import pytest

from pgledger import PostgresLedger
from service import InMemoryLedger

TODAY = datetime.date(2026, 9, 4)


@pytest.fixture(params=["in-memory", "postgresql"])
def ledger(request, connection):
    if request.param == "in-memory":
        return InMemoryLedger()
    return PostgresLedger(connection)


def test_a_new_customer_has_no_entries(ledger):
    assert ledger.entries(7) == []


def test_an_added_entry_comes_back(ledger):
    ledger.add(7, TODAY, 150)

    assert ledger.entries(7) == [(TODAY, 150)]


def test_entries_come_back_in_the_order_they_were_added(ledger):
    ledger.add(7, TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=2), 100)
    ledger.add(7, TODAY, 200)

    assert ledger.entries(7) == [(TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=2), 100),
                                 (TODAY, 200)]


def test_one_customers_entries_are_not_another_s(ledger):
    ledger.add(7, TODAY, 100)
    ledger.add(8, TODAY, 999)

    assert ledger.entries(7) == [(TODAY, 100)]


def test_a_zero_point_entry_is_allowed(ledger):
    ledger.add(7, TODAY, 0)

    assert ledger.entries(7) == [(TODAY, 0)]

pytest -q --collect-only tests/test_ledger_contract.py
pytest -q tests/test_ledger_contract.py
