10 tests collected in 2.04s
..........                                                               [100%]
10 passed in 12.77s

Ten tests from five, and every one is a claim about the port rather than about either implementation. The fake is now verified rather than assumed, which closes the hole §7.12 opened.

Two things this exercise reliably surfaces, both of which appeared here.

Ordering is a contract that nobody wrote down. test_entries_come_back_in_the_order_they_were_added passes against the fake because a list preserves insertion order, and passes against PostgreSQL only because the query says ORDER BY id. Remove that clause and the test still passes — most of the time — which is the SQL hazard §11.13's cousin: an unordered SELECT returns rows in physical order and looks deterministic. The test is what forces the ORDER BY to be written down.

The CHECK (points >= 0) exists in one implementation only. The fake accepts a negative entry and the database refuses it, so a test asserting the refusal belongs in the PostgreSQL-only file (§11.14). Knowing which tests cannot be shared is exactly the map of where the fake stops being trustworthy.

21.6 Stage 6 — The HTTP Boundary

Task. Expose POST /customers/{id}/awards and GET /customers/{id}. Write the API tests: status codes, validation, the schema, and the error paths. Then say which claims belong here and which do not.

Solution — Stage 6 
# api.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from service import InMemoryLedger, LoyaltyService

app = FastAPI()
SERVICE = LoyaltyService(InMemoryLedger())


class AwardIn(BaseModel):
    order_cents: int = Field(ge=0)


@app.post("/customers/{customer_id}/awards", status_code=201)
def create_award(customer_id: int, body: AwardIn):
    if customer_id <= 0:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="no such customer")
    points = SERVICE.award(customer_id, body.order_cents)
    return {"customer_id": customer_id, "points_awarded": points,
            "balance": SERVICE.balance(customer_id)}


@app.get("/customers/{customer_id}")
def read_customer(customer_id: int):
    if customer_id <= 0:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="no such customer")
    return {"customer_id": customer_id, "balance": SERVICE.balance(customer_id),
            "tier": SERVICE.tier(customer_id)}

# tests/test_api.py
import jsonschema
import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

import api
from service import InMemoryLedger, LoyaltyService

CUSTOMER = {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["customer_id", "balance", "tier"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
    "properties": {
        "customer_id": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1},
        "balance": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
        "tier": {"enum": ["bronze", "silver", "gold"]},
    },
}


@pytest.fixture
def client():
    """Fresh state per test: the service is module-level (§12.2)."""
    api.SERVICE = LoyaltyService(InMemoryLedger())
    return TestClient(api.app)


def test_awarding_returns_201_and_the_new_balance(client):
    response = client.post("/customers/7/awards", json={"order_cents": 1_500})

    assert response.status_code == 201
    assert response.json() == {"customer_id": 7, "points_awarded": 15,
                               "balance": 15}


def test_reading_a_customer_matches_the_schema(client):
    client.post("/customers/7/awards", json={"order_cents": 2_000_000})

    response = client.get("/customers/7")

    assert response.status_code == 200
    jsonschema.validate(response.json(), CUSTOMER)
    assert response.json()["tier"] == "gold"


def test_the_schema_would_reject_something():
    with pytest.raises(jsonschema.ValidationError):
        jsonschema.validate({"customer_id": 1, "balance": -1, "tier": "gold"},
                            CUSTOMER)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("payload", [
    {"order_cents": -1}, {"order_cents": "lots"}, {},
])
def test_invalid_input_is_422_and_names_the_field(client, payload):
    response = client.post("/customers/7/awards", json=payload)

    assert response.status_code == 422
    assert all("loc" in p for p in response.json()["detail"])


def test_an_unknown_customer_is_404(client):
    assert client.get("/customers/0").status_code == 404


def test_a_state_reset_really_happened(client):
    assert client.get("/customers/7").json()["balance"] == 0

pytest -q tests/test_api.py

........                                                                 [100%]
8 passed in 4.28s

What belongs here: status codes, validation, serialisation, the schema, and the wiring — that the endpoint reaches the service and returns its answer.

What does not: the tier ladder and the pound arithmetic. test_reading_a_customer_matches_the_schema uses one gold customer to prove the tier reaches the response; the seven boundary rows stay in test_core.py, where they cost microseconds. Adding them here would triple the cost and detect nothing new (§10.10).

The -1 case is worth noticing. order_cents: int = Field(ge=0) means Pydantic refuses it with a 422 before points_for is reached — so the API's validation and the core's ValueError are two guards on the same rule. That is not duplication to remove: the core must refuse a negative because it is called from elsewhere, and the API must refuse it early because a 422 is a better answer than a 500.

21.7 Stage 7 — What the Suite Still Misses

Task. The core has boundary tests, property tests and 100% coverage. Run mutation testing against it and act on what survives.

Solution — Stage 7 
pytest -q --cov=core --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing tests/test_core.py
mutmut run > /dev/null 2>&1
mutmut results

.......................                                                  [100%]
================================ tests coverage ================================
_______________ coverage: platform linux, python 3.12.7-final-0 ________________

Name      Stmts   Miss Branch BrPart  Cover   Missing
-----------------------------------------------------
core.py      21      0      8      0   100%
-----------------------------------------------------
TOTAL        21      0      8      0   100%
23 passed in 1.03s
    core.x_points_for__mutmut_4: survived
    core.x_tier_for__mutmut_4: survived

Read the two together. Coverage says the core is fully exercised; the mutation run says what a machine can break without the suite noticing — and here it is two mutants, both of them the same thing, which is a far better result than §17.9's ten and is still worth reading.

Both survivors replace an error message with a wrapped version of itself:

-        raise ValueError("points must not be negative")
+        raise ValueError("XXpoints must not be negativeXX")

And they survive even though the tests do check the message — because pytest.raises(match=...) is re.search (§3.4), so the pattern "must not be negative" is still found inside the mutated string. The mutation genuinely changed behaviour, and the assertion genuinely cannot see it.

That is the classification exercise in miniature, and the three categories to sort survivors into are:

A real gap. A mutated constant or comparison that changes an answer nobody asserted. Each names the exact test to write, and each is a boundary — which was §17.9's entire finding on different code.

Near-equivalent (§17.11). These two: the behaviour changed, but nothing any consumer depends on did. The honest response is a decision rather than a test — is the exact message text a contract? Here it is not, so the survivor stands and is understood, which is a different thing from being ignored.

A finding about the production code. A survivor whose mutated line nothing observable depends on has found dead or redundant code, and deleting it beats any test.

The discipline that makes this useful is §17.9's: treat the output as a list of named gaps, not as a score to maximise. The number has an uncomputable ceiling; the list is actionable.

21.8 Stage 8 — The Pipeline

Task. Assign every test written so far to a pipeline stage, choose the markers, and write the definition of done for a change to the tier ladder.

Solution — Stage 8

The assignment, by §20.2:

commit stage
test_core.py (23), test_properties.py at max_examples=100, test_api.py (8), test_ledger_contract.py (10, with the private cluster). Under a minute in total.
acceptance stage
A deployed smoke test: award, read back, check the tier. One journey, not the ladder.
nightly
Properties at max_examples=2000 (§16.10), and mutmut on core.py.
production
A loyalty.tier_changed event, so a ladder change is visible as a distribution shift rather than as a support ticket (§20.10).

The markers, in pyproject.toml, with --strict-markers so a typo is a collection error (§2.5):

markers = [
    "db: needs the private PostgreSQL cluster",
    "slow: long property runs and mutation testing",
]

pytest -m "not slow"            # commit stage
pytest -m "slow"                # nightly

The definition of done for a change to the tier ladder — say the silver threshold moves from 5,000 to 4,000:

  1. The boundary rows in test_core.py are updated to 3,999/4,000, and someone watched them fail before the constant changed (§9.1).
  2. test_the_expiry_window_is_stated_rather_than_assumed's sibling for the tier constants fails, and is updated deliberately — that is the guard doing its job.
  3. The property tests are unchanged, because monotonicity does not depend on where the threshold is. If a property test breaks, the change was bigger than advertised.
  4. test_api.py is unchanged: it asserts the tier reaches the response, not which tier.
  5. The schema's enum is unchanged. Adding a fourth tier would change it, and that would be a breaking change for consumers (§13.9).
  6. The contract with any consuming service is re-verified (§13.5).
  7. A loyalty.tier_changed event exists, so the shift is observable within a day.
  8. The migration for existing customers — who moves tier, and are they told? — is a product decision the tests forced someone to make.

Item 3 is the one worth keeping. A well-layered suite tells you the size of a change: a threshold move touches seven rows in one file, and if it touches more than that, the change is not what it was described as.

21.9 What the Capstone Established

  • The order of work is forced. You cannot write good tests against untestable code, and you cannot safely refactor untested code. Characterise, then add seams, then test properly.
  • A characterisation test is a photograph, not a specification — and writing one is what surfaced the tier defect, because nobody had ever written the boundary down.
  • The two obstacles were the two design defects: module-level state and a clock read inside a function. Both were found by trying to write a test, which is §19.9's argument in practice.
  • Splitting into a functional core made the rules testable at rung 1 of the teardown ladder — no fixtures, no cleanup, microseconds — and it exposed the second defect, because a rule written as a function has to say what it means.
  • The old interface kept working, so no caller had to be edited: a control point added without breaking anything (§8.6).
  • Boundaries first, properties second. The table pins the specific thresholds; the properties pin the relationships between calls, which no table can express.
  • One suite against the fake and the real store verified the fake and surfaced two things nobody had written down: that ordering is a contract, and that the CHECK constraint exists in only one implementation.
  • The API layer asserts wiring, not rules. Seven boundary rows stay where they cost microseconds; one gold customer proves the tier reaches the response.
  • Coverage said complete and mutation testing disagreed, exactly as in §17 — and the survivors sort into real gaps, equivalent mutants, and findings about the production code.
  • A well-layered suite tells you the size of a change. A threshold move touches seven rows in one file; if it touches more, the change was not what it was described as.

Exercises

1. Do stage 1 on your own code.

Take a module you work on that has no tests. Write a characterisation test for it without changing a line. Record the obstacles you hit, and classify each using §19.9's list.

2. Add the fourth tier.

The business adds a platinum tier at 50,000 points. Work out every file that changes and every test that breaks, before writing anything. Then do it, and compare. What did you miss, and what does that tell you about the layering?

3. Find the third defect.

There is a behaviour in the delivered loyalty.py that neither Stage 1 nor Stage 2 addressed, and that would matter in production. Find it. (Hint: consider what happens to award under two concurrent requests for the same customer, and what §11.4's rollback fixture would and would not detect.)

4. Move the expiry.

Points currently expire 365 days after they were earned. Change the rule to "365 days after the customer's last order". Which tests break? Which should break and do not? Write the missing test first.

5. Price the layers.

Time each test file. Then compute what the suite would cost if every claim in test_core.py were also asserted through the API, and again through a browser. Use §10.9's cost table for the levels you cannot measure, and say what the numbers imply for a team adding one rule a week.

6. The uncomfortable stage.

Stage 1's characterisation test pinned two behaviours that were wrong. Suppose you cannot reach the product owner for a week, and a release is due. What do you do with those two rows, what do you ship, and what do you write down?

Solutions

1. Do stage 1 on your own code.

No fixed answer, but the obstacles cluster tightly: a module-level singleton or cache, something read from the environment at import time, a clock or a uuid4, and a constructor that opens a connection. Every one of those is on §19.9's list, and every one is a missing parameter (§8.3).

The useful part is the count. If a characterisation test needs four workarounds, the module has four undeclared dependencies — which is a number you can put in a ticket, and a much better argument than "this code is hard to test".

2. Add the fourth tier.

Changes: core.py gains PLATINUM_AT and a branch; test_core.py gains two rows (49,999 and 50,000) and its existing gold rows still pass; the API's schema enum gains "platinum".

Breaks: the schema metatest if it asserted the exact enum; any consumer contract naming the tier set (§13.9 — this is a breaking change for a consumer that switches on the value, and safe for one that only displays it).

Does not break, and should not: the property tests, because monotonicity does not care how many tiers there are. That is the signal that the change is well-contained.

What people miss: the consumer side. A tier value the consumer has never seen may fall through a match with no default, and nothing in your repository will tell you. That is exactly the gap contract testing exists to close, and the fact that adding a tier is invisible from inside your own suite is the argument for §13 in one sentence.

3. Find the third defect.

award does a read-modify-write in the old version, and in the new one it appends to a ledger — which is why the refactor accidentally fixed it. The delivered loyalty.award reads _BALANCES.get(...), adds, and writes back; two concurrent requests for the same customer both read the old value and one write is lost. The ledger version has no such race, because it only ever inserts.

What §11.4's rollback fixture would detect: nothing. It uses one connection and one transaction, so there is no concurrency to observe — the technique that makes integration tests fast is the one that makes this class of defect invisible. Detecting it needs two connections and committed data (§11.5), or a database-level guarantee that makes the race impossible in the first place.

The general lesson is worth more than the specific bug: an append-only ledger removed a concurrency defect without anybody testing for concurrency. Choosing a data model that cannot express the wrong state beats testing that the wrong state does not occur.

4. Move the expiry.

expired(earned_on, today) no longer has enough information — it needs the customer's last order date — so its signature changes, and every test using it breaks. That is interface sensitivity (§19.7), and here it is correct: the rule genuinely changed.

surviving_points(entries, today) breaks in the same way and must take the last order date.

Should break and does not: nothing in the current suite asserts that a fresh order rescues old points. Under the new rule, a customer with a 400-day-old entry who ordered yesterday keeps everything — and the old suite would pass a broken implementation that dropped those points anyway, because no test describes that case.

So write it first, watch it fail, then change the rule:

def test_a_recent_order_rescues_old_points():
    entries = [(TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=400), 5_000)]
    last_order = TODAY - datetime.timedelta(days=1)

    assert surviving_points(entries, TODAY, last_order) == 5_000

That is §9.9's sequence applied to a requirement change rather than to a bug, and it is the same discipline.

5. Price the layers.

Using §10.9's figures — 0.002 s per unit test, 0.25 s per integration test, 30 s per end-to-end test — the 21 core tests cost about 0.04 s. Through the API with a test client they would cost roughly the integration figure: about 5 seconds. Through a browser: about 10 minutes.

At one new rule a week with, say, four boundary cases each, the unit suite grows by 0.008 s a week and the browser suite by two minutes a week. After a year the first is imperceptible and the second is an hour and a half — for exactly the same claims.

That is the whole argument for §10.10's rule stated as a rate rather than a ratio, and the rate is what makes it urgent: the cost of testing at the wrong level does not merely start high, it accumulates every time anyone adds a rule.

6. The uncomfortable stage.

The two rows are pinning behaviour that is wrong: a customer with exactly 5,000 points is bronze when they should be silver.

What to do with the rows: leave them, and mark them. Change each to pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True, reason="ticket LOY-114: is exactly 5000 silver?") — no. That would be wrong, because the test currently passes; xfail(strict=True) would fail the build. Keep the assertion as it is, and add a comment naming the ticket, so the test says "this is the current behaviour and it is disputed".

What to ship: the refactor, not the fix. Stage 2's seams change no behaviour and are provably safe against the characterisation test — that is what a characterisation test is for. The threshold change is a product decision affecting real customers' entitlements, and shipping it without the owner is making that decision on their behalf.

What to write down: a ticket with the two specific inputs, the current outputs, what you believe the intended outputs are, and how many customers are currently on each side of the two boundaries. That last number is what turns the question from a preference into a decision, and it takes one query.

The general principle: a characterisation test lets you separate "is this what it does" from "is this what it should do", and ship the first while waiting on the second. Without one, you have to answer both questions before changing anything, which is why untested code is slow to change even when the change is small.

You started this course able to write a test. You now know what a test is worth — which is the difference between a suite that makes change safe and one that makes change expensive, and the two look identical from the outside.

What you can now do

  1. State a claim precisely. A test asserts one thing, in a name a colleague can read at 2 a.m., with an expected value a human computed rather than the code produced. If the expected value could have come from running the code, it is not an oracle.
  2. Choose the inputs. Exhaustive testing is unavailable, so testing is sampling: partition into equivalence classes, take each side of every boundary, run the standing checklist (empty, single, duplicate, ordered, aliased), and stop. Off-by-one errors live exactly at class boundaries and nowhere else — which is why mutation testing kept reporting the same finding by a completely different route.
  3. Decide what a double is for. Five kinds, and the two distinctions that matter: stub versus spy is the direction of the data; mock versus spy is where the assertion lives. unittest.mock refuses a mistyped assertion name — but mailer.verify(999) passes while checking nothing.
  4. Verify state where you can see it, behaviour where you cannot. Command-query separation sorts the collaborators for you. In the running example that was one collaborator out of three, and that ratio is typical.
  5. Recognise a design problem wearing a testing problem's clothes. Seven doubles per test, forty lines of setup, a mock.patch because there is no seam — each is the code reporting on itself, and the fix is nearly always a change you wanted anyway.
  6. Control time. A clock wrapper makes a fourteen-day trial testable in microseconds. Freezing time is not the same as controlling it, and fake timers turn a duration into a boundary value — 299 ms then 1 ms.
  7. Pick the level. Verify each behaviour in detail at exactly one, cheap level and connect it at the levels above. A threshold move should touch seven rows in one file; if it touches more, the change was not what it was described as.
  8. Run the real thing where the real thing is the point. A private PostgreSQL, started by the suite, on its own port. Constraints are behaviour, and a fake does not have them.
  9. Close the double-shaped hole. A contract test verifies, in the provider's own pipeline, that the thing your double pretends to be really behaves that way — and the failure names the field.
  10. Test a browser at the right layer. jsdom answers "does it behave"; only a real browser answers "does it look and work". A retrying assertion on a locator removes most end-to-end flakiness on its own.
  11. Diagnose flakiness rather than retrying it. Five causes, and the first one — lack of isolation — is most of them. The failing test is usually not the guilty one.
  12. Read a coverage report and ignore the number. Uncovered code is definitely untested; covered code may be tested by nothing at all.
  13. Keep the suite honest over years. Name the smell, apply the refactoring, review tests with the six questions, and delete the ones that cannot fail.

What was measured rather than repeated

Every number and every output in this course came from running something. Several contradict what is widely repeated.

pytest does not put the working directory on sys.path; python -m pytest does. One line — pythonpath = ["."] — and the same project stops working for one colleague and failing for another.

pytest 9 has a seventh exit code. MAX_WARNINGS_ERROR = 6, from --max-warnings: everything passed, and the warning budget was exceeded. And exit code 5 means nothing ran, which a pipeline checking for "not 1" reports as success.

pytest.approx's tolerance is max(rel * expected, abs), with abs=1e-12. Against zero the relative half contributes nothing, so 1e-9 is not approximately zero. The draft of that section said the opposite and the runner corrected it.

Assertion rewriting applies only to modules pytest collected. A custom assertion in a helper module reports a bare AssertionError with no values, until register_assert_rewrite is called in conftest.py.

t.plan(n) in node:test does not wait for a later callback. It reports plan expected 2 assertions but received 0. await, { wait: ms } or the { plan: n } option are the three forms that work.

test.each spreads an array case into separate arguments and test.for does not — [[1, 3]] gives (a, b) to one and [1, 3] to the other.

pytest.HIDDEN_PARAM removes the bracketed id entirely, so the test collects under its bare name.

-p no:randomly disables pytest-randomly and -p randomly re-enables it, in that order on one command line. Seed 1 and seed 10 gave opposite results on the same two tests.

Python randomises string hashes per process: eight fresh interpreters produced eight different values for hash('the-cache-key'), and one with PYTHONHASHSEED=0.

Playwright's clock.install starts a clock that runs. pause_at freezes it and cannot move backwards — "Cannot fast-forward to the past". And fast_forward("01:00") is one minute; the string form is mm:ss.

sqlite is not a fake of PostgreSQL. Measured side by side: 'abc' + 1 is 1; a varchar(3) column stores an eight-character value in full; length(1234) works in one and does not exist in the other; and CAST('2026-02-30' AS date) becomes the number 2026. Silent, total corruption behind a green test.

Against 100% statement and branch coverage, ten of eighteen mutants survived — and every survivor was a missing boundary value.

A suite of 2,000 tests at 99.9% per-test reliability passes 13.5% of the time. And in the pyramid's own cost model, eight end-to-end tests at a 2% flake rate dominate the whole suite's red-for-nothing rate.

A retrying query stops at the first match. Two elements shared role="status", so findByRole('status') resolved on the pending message or the success message depending on machine speed — asynchronous non-determinism arriving through a query rather than through a sleep.

And one measured while writing this course's own tooling, which is the same lesson from the other side: three of the twelve clean cases in the runner's calibration suite were written from memory, and all three were wrong — a coverage percentage, a failing line number, and the output of a | tail -2.

The habits that outlast the tools

Watch every test fail. It is the only evidence you will ever have that it can fail. A test written after the code and never seen red may be asserting nothing at all — §17.7's four tests reach 100% coverage while checking essentially nothing.

Ask what change would make this test fail. If the honest answer is "any change" or "no change", the test is not earning its keep. That single question, applied in review, does more for a suite than any coverage target.

Ask whether a behaviour-preserving refactor would break it. If yes, the test is pinned to the implementation, and the suite is on its way to preventing the change it was bought to make safe.

Measure rather than remember. Every claimed output in this course was produced by running the tool, twice, and compared. Six of them contradicted the sentence that had been written first. A README, a runbook and a test all make claims about what a tool prints, and all three rot the same way.

When a test is hard to write, suspect the code first. That hypothesis is right often enough to be worth checking, it costs one question — what would have to be true for this to be easy? — and the answer is usually a design change with its own justification.

Where to go next

The parts of testing this course did not cover are mostly specialisations rather than gaps: fuzzing beyond property-based testing, formal methods and model checking, performance engineering past a threshold assertion, and security testing, which is its own discipline with its own threat model.

The books worth reading in full. Meszaros's xUnit Test Patterns is the catalogue this course draws its vocabulary from — long, dry, and the reference you will return to. Feathers's Working Effectively with Legacy Code is the definitive treatment of §8.13. Humble and Farley's Continuous Delivery is where §20's pipeline comes from.

The living sources. martinfowler.com/testing is a curated index rather than a blog, and its articles are revised as practice changes. Each runner's changelog matters more than its tutorial: pytest 9's built-in subtests, free_tcp_port and --max-warnings are all recent, and every one of them replaces something people still write by hand.

The next system you work on. Take the last twenty defects that reached production, and for each write down the cheapest test that would have caught it. That tally is your suite's shape (§10.12), derived from evidence rather than from a diagram — and it is a better first week than any amount of reading.

One thing to keep

If everything else fades, keep this: a test is a claim, and its value is what it would catch.

Not coverage, not the count, not whether it was written first. A test that cannot fail is not a test. A test that fails when nothing broke is worse than no test, because it teaches everyone to stop reading the build. And a suite of four thousand tests that would not have caught the last three incidents is expensive and weak, and it got that way one unexamined test at a time.

Every technique in this course — boundaries, doubles, seams, contracts, properties, mutation testing — is a way of asking the same question about a test before you keep it: what would this catch?
